#1. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#2. The Best Musky Reels of 2026, Tested on the Water

Updated Oct 20, 2026 9:12 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Musky. The name alone elicits a variety of reactions from anglers, some good, and some painful. However you feel about musky, there’s no denying their appeal as a top-tier freshwater sportfish that puts tackle, especially musky reels, to the test. The work to land these freshwater beasts often has anglers screaming in agony more than joy, and even with the proper gear, fishing for musky is a challenging enough pursuit on its own. The last thing you need is to hook into the fish of your dreams and find your reel isn’t up to the task. To help you avoid that fate, I’ve used my musky fishing experience as well as input from trusted guides to compile a list of the best musky reels.

To make your musky reel decision ask yourself two questions:

There’s no denying musky gear can get expensive quickly, so there’s no need to spend a ton of money if you’re only going to fish for them a few times a year. You’ll probably be fine with one of the less durable but still extremely capable reel options. But, if musky are your new favorite species then it’s worthwhile to invest in the best musky reel you can afford.

If you’re throwing larger lures and casting all day, something lighter and smoother is probably the best choice. If you are trolling and not casting as much, weight and castability are less of a factor.

If you’re a serious musky angler who throws a variety of lures and spends a lot of time and effort chasing these fish, this is the reel for you. While pricey, it’s a step above all others in quality and functionality and well worth it for the dedicated musky angler.

The Shimano TranX line has been around for over a decade, and when it first appeared, it immediately made a statement about the ability of low-profile baitcasters. While they had previously been in the realm of bass fishing, the TranX helped pioneer the new generation of purpose-built low-profile reels capable of handling big gamefish.

The 300 and 400 models are ideal for throwing smaller finesse glide baits and spinners, as well as capable of handling some of the best musky lures like larger swimbaits and plugs that are notorious for making musky fishing so painful. The 500 is a reel designed to handle big saltwater gamefish. Still, its indestructible design and robust frame make it ideal for heaving the heaviest musky baits on the market while still allowing for a smooth retrieve and delicate touch during the fight.

The only downside to the TranX series is the drag for the 300 and 400 sizes. While the reels are significantly lighter and easier to use than the 500 (around 12 ounces), they range from 18 to 22 pounds of drag, which is less than some competing reels in the category. The 500 tops out at 25 pounds of drag, which is solid but still not enough to target anything that swims. The TranX is also a great reel for throwing the best swimbaits for bass.

Honestly, it was a toss-up between the Daiwa Lexa HD and the Shimano Tranx for best overall. Many anglers and guides are split on which they prefer, with the slight edge going to the Shimano. With a proven design and high-end capability, the Daiwa Lexa HD is no slouch.

Being built for both fresh and saltwater use, the Lexa HD can withstand a lot of abuse and keep on cranking. The light aluminum frame and side plate are complemented by stainless steel gearing, which helps maintain strength and enhance durability. It comes stock with a counterbalanced power handle and EVA foam grip, which both enhance comfort and help with cranking ability.

Most impressive, the 400 size alone comes in five different models and gear ratios, allowing the Lexa HD to be tailored to any task the angler needs.

Guide Austin Conrad of Virginia Trophy Guides prefers the 400 size Lexa HD in the 7.1:1 and 8.1:1 ratios. “I’ll throw anything from jerks to glides to heavy rubber on them,” he says. Conrad is also a fan of the Lexa HD’s durability. “The hardware is more bombproof than other models because its designed for use in salt,” he says. Conrad has a full lineup of Lexa HD reels that have held up great through the years.

Regardless of where and how you’ll be musky fishing, the Daiwa Lexa HD likely comes in a model that will be an exceptional option.

While musky fishing is typically a game of “bigger is better,” that’s not always the case. Sometimes the fish are keyed in on smaller presentations or exceptionally spooky. The Shimano Curado DC 200 is the perfect reel for this scenario, built specifically for heavy duty use while maintaining its lightweight, functional design.

The spool of the Curado DC holds 120 yards of 50-pound braid, which is impressive for a 200-size reel. Additionally, the Digital Control allows anglers to throw a larger variety of presentations and sizes with less fear of backlash. Guide Sam Scott of Blue Ridge Musky uses the Curado DC specifically for smaller lures with his clients. Smaller, lighter lures are notorious for causing backlash, and the Digital Control helps eliminate that worry for clients who may not be as familiar with baitcasters.

While it certainly isn’t as durable as other reels on this list, the Curado DC 200 is more than capable of handling the rigors of fishing for and fighting musky. Its lightweight size and versatility should be appealing to any musky angler looking to expand their arsenal with something different.

The Lew’s SuperDuty 300 is a functional reel in an affordable package. It offers many of the same great features as higher-end models and would serve as a solid option for most casual musky anglers. It’s ideal for throwing smaller to mid-size musky lures but may not be suited for throwing larger lures on a consistent basis.

Any reel that falls squarely into the musky category is usually going to be on the more expensive side. That said, the Lew’s SuperDuty 300 is about as close as you can get to a reasonably priced option that still has all the function and backbone required to tackle those long, arduous days of musky fishing. Like the Lexa, the SuperDuty 300 has a solid variety of styles and options to choose from (though not as many). These include the counterbalanced Power Knob handle for better cranking power and torque, which is a real benefit when throwing big lures for big fish. Also, like the Lexa, the SuperDuty series includes custom Winn grips on the handles, which drastically improve comfort during use. Perhaps most impressively, the reel tops out at under 10 ounces, making it much lighter than any baitcaster on the best musky reel list.

There’s no denying that weight matters when it comes to casting heavy gear all day long, and even a few ounces trimmed off can help alleviate some of the soreness inherent to the pursuit. Unfortunately, it’s hard not to notice that some of that weight may be due to a lack of structure-enhancing components. While the reel I tested has held up and done its job for a year of consistent use, some issues with the gearing and frame have led to slippage and warping. Particularly when using heavier lures or fighting bigger fish, the cranking ability seems to waver as the reel is under stress. This causes the reel to lose a lot of its smoothness and can lead to a jerkier fight that is less than ideal for musky.

Of all the spinning reels I’ve tested under $100, the Exceler LT by Daiwa was far and away the nicest to fish. It’s the only reel in this price range that legitimately feels like it should be far more expensive than it is. This reel was perfect for everything from river smallmouth bass fishing with jerkbaits to deep-water reservoir fishing with jigs.

With a super light carbon fiber frame and Daiwas AirDrive rotor and bail, the Exceler has many of the features of Daiwas higher-end reels at a fraction of the cost. It has an impressive 22-pounds, the silky-smooth drag held up incredibly well to fish that were far outside the scope of its intended use. It landed multiple musky and striped bass during testing, handling them all with relative ease. In addition, its lightweight carbon frame and machined aluminum handle were as comfortable to fish as any reel out there, regardless of price.

It casts like a dream, with feathery line release from the spool and a nice even line-lay on the retrieve. Overall, despite being at the top edge of the price range, the Daiwa Exceler LT is an exceptional reel and well worth the cost.

Look, let’s get it out of the way right now; spinning reels generally don’t belong in the musky fishing category. This has always bothered me as a saltwater angler who targets fish considerably larger and stronger than musky with spinning gear. However, the reason for the lack of musky-oriented spinning gear is simple: it’s the size of the lures, not the size of the fish. When most people think of musky, they generally think of lures that are 1 to 2 ounces at the lightest and up to 12 ounces at the heaviest.

The complexity of a spinning reel and the physics of how it works are generally not designed to handle casting lures of this size. The bail and inner mechanics of spinning gear are designed for finesse, putting all the dirty work and heavy lifting on the rod. On the other hand, a baitcaster is essentially a glorified winch with mechanics that allow for a significantly higher workload. That said, modern spinning reels have come a long way, and many of the issues seen as inherent deal breakers for musky fishing have been alleviated or outright eliminated. Additionally, there are many anglers who are more comfortable fishing spinning gear or want something that’s more well rounded than the typical heavy-duty musky baitcaster. For those reasons, I think it’s important to include a spinning option on this list.

All that being said, the Shimano Stradic FL, specifically in the 5000 size, is a great option for those looking to add a spinning reel to the arsenal. I’ve used the Stadic FL for tackling both fresh and saltwater giants and found it to be durable, well-sealed, and smooth. I’ve fought tarpon on mine so it’s more than capable of handling a musky on the line. With an impressive drag max of 24 pounds and 40 inches per retrieve, this reel is a formidable machine when paired with the right rod. While no spinning reel will be ideal for working the ultra-heavy swimbaits and plugs often used for musky, they can be a great choice for many of the lighter finesse musky lures, such as glide baits and smaller jerkbaits.

While spinning gear may be out of place in the musky world, fly fishing gear certainly is not. In recent years it’s become so popular that many musky guides always have at least one fly setup rigged and ready on the boat. The Redington Behemoth is the perfect fly reel for those looking to target musky. As the name suggests, it’s a reel designed for tackling large fish in fresh or saltwater. The 7/8 or 9/10 sizes are what most anglers prefer for musky, and the large arbor allows you to use a size heavier rod and line than the reel size. So, the 7/8 will work well on 9 weight and the 9/10 will work on an 11 or 12 weight.

The large arbor design allows for fast line retrieve, and the impressive carbon drag system boasts a 30 pound max, giving you serious stopping power with a fish on the line. The price is also remarkably affordable compared to many other reels in the category. Lastly, the unique V-shaped spool design holds an incredible amount of backing, making for an impressive line capacity.

Musky fishing can be highly specialized, so having a reel dedicated specifically to the task can be a smart move for anglers willing to expand their arsenal. The Daiwa Prorex TWS was designed with this dedication in mind, as it’s the only reel on this list designed and sold solely to target musky. Even more to the point, this reel is built to be the ideal tool for casting large lures all day long with minimal hassle and maximum effectiveness.

The Prorex has several features that make it well suited for targeting these giant, toothy fish. First, it’s exceptionally light for its size, coming in at only 12.2 ounces despite being a 400-class reel. Being built of an aluminum frame with an aluminum side plate helps keep the weight down while keeping the strength intact. This is a beneficial trait, especially when you consider the size and weight of many musky lures. Anything to help ease the strain on an angler’s arms and shoulders after a day of casting is a win.

This reel also comes equipped with an adjustable length power handle out of the box. The adjustability is what separates the Prorex from other reels with power handles, as the length adjustability is both simple and incredibly helpful for adapting to different lures and anglers on the fly.

While it may be the simplest feature, Daiwa’s T-Wing line guide system is perhaps the most beneficial. The line guide has a unique “T” shape (hence the name) that allows for heavy line to be cast more cleanly and helps prevent friction and backlash.

It may be a drawback to some anglers who value versatility, but the single-purpose design of the Daiwa Prorex TWS makes it an exceptional tool for the dedicated musky angler.

The Abu Garcia Revo Toro Beast is an exceptional reel with an obvious purpose: to tackle big fish. This will be a good choice if you’re looking for one reel to target musky specifically. But if you’re trying to outfit an entire lineup, the lack of versatility may not work for you. The name may be a mouthful, but it’s certainly an accurate reel description. As it implies, this reel is more than capable of wrangling beasts, particularly musky.

The Abu Garcia Revo Toro Beast is another reel that pushes the boundaries of what a low-profile baitcaster is capable of, and it packs a ton of punch into a compact design. Weighing only 13.8 ounces, the reel boasts an impressive max drag of 25 pounds with a carbon fiber drag system. The exceptional drag and gearing system combined with a lots of line capacity gives this reel a ton of torque and versatility in a surprisingly sleek package.

One of the few downsides to the Revo Toro Beast is the limited range of sizes. While it does come in a regular and high-speed model (gear ratios 4.9:1 and 6.2:1, respectively), it does not have a range of sizes for handling a wider array of fishing styles. When musky is the target, it’s generally better to be overpowered than under, and the Toro Beast more than fits the bill.

Not at all. While the old adage “you get what you pay for” is true in many ways, there are plenty of quality options on the market for someone looking to target musky on a budget.

While baitcasters are ideal and preferred, there’s nothing wrong with branching out into spinning or fly gear in the right situations.

While having a powerful drag is certainly helpful for stopping big fish, the more important factor is the quality of the drag. A good drag system allows for a smoother fight and increases your likelihood of landing the fish.

Musky fishing is one of the most daunting freshwater fishing pursuits in North America. There are many ways to target these fish, and most of them require serious dedication. The proper gear is critical to help ensure you make the most of every opportunity on the water, as musky don’t offer many. It’s important to have the best musky reel for the task to ensure you avoid heartbreak and hoist a trophy after a long day of musky fishing.

#4. Review: Skygoat Half Zip AIR 70 Pullover Hoody

The SkyGOAT Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover Hoody is an ultralight microgrid fleece that fills the gap between a standard sun hoodie and a heavy mid-layer.  It’s perfect for cool mornings when you want a little more insulation before the sun comes up, or as an ultralight mid-layer under a windbreaker or softshell jacket when you know you’ll generate a lot of body heat while hiking or climbing a mountain. It’s equally at home in town and sporty enough for a date night when you don’t want to be weighed down by a heavier sweater.

The SkyGOAT Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover Hoody features a custom 70 gsm ultralight grid fleece with a highly porous knit that provides excellent breathability. While slightly less breathable than Polartec Alpha Direct, it is more structured, wind-resistant, durable, low-shedding, and low-maintenance. I simply throw mine in the wash with the rest of my hiking clothes and wash on cold/tumble dry on high without a care.

The Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover Hoody has features that make it good for hiking, backpacking, and trail running across a wide temperature range, with or without an external shell.

Combination Hood and Collar: While Skygoat calls this garment the “Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover,” it also includes an under-helmet-sized hood. The combination is a real plus and not something you find on other hoodies, providing extra warmth around the neck when the hood and the center zipper are up and cover the front of the neck, preventing warmth from escaping. This subtle adjustment is the hallmark of good layering and thermoregulation for hiking and backpacking.

Half-length Zipper: Lets you dump extra warmth to prevent overheating and perspiration

Thumbloops: Thumbloops keep your wrists warmer and make it easier to pull on a windbreaker or shell layer.

No Kangaroom Pocket: Reduces weight and makes it easier to layer under a climbing harness.

The Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover Hoody works well on its own or layered with other garments in a wide range of conditions. It’s a great mid-layer under a windbreaker or softshell, retaining extra warmth while you warm up at the start of a hike and retaining it after you delayer. It’s also thin and breathable enough that you can push up the sleeves or unzip the front zipper to vent excess heat, so you don’t have to take it off when you start to perspire. This makes it an exceptional choice, especially in colder weather, when stopping to remove a layer can chill you, and it’s best to keep moving to stay warm.

The SkyGOAT Half-Zip Air 70 Pullover Hoody is a versatile ultralight layer for hikers, backpackers, climbers, and trail runners who need more warmth than a sun hoodie provides without the bulk of a traditional fleece. Its breathable 70 gsm grid fleece, deep half-zip, combined hood and collar, and thumb loops make it easy to regulate temperature while you stay on the move. At just 5.4 ounces, it adds useful insulation without weighing down a pack, and its durable, low-maintenance fabric makes it practical for regular use.

Although it lacks a pocket and breathes slightly less than Polartec Alpha Direct, the added structure, wind resistance, and durability are worth the trade-off. Whether worn by itself on a cool morning or under a windbreaker in colder conditions, the Half-Zip Air 70 is a comfortable, efficient mid-layer that earns a place in a lightweight layering system.

Disclosure:  SkyGoat donated a garment for review.

#6. The Best Inshore Spinning Reels of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Updated Oct 20, 2026 9:03 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Whether I’m catching backcountry tarpon, bull reds in the Chesapeake Bay, or jigging flounder, a good inshore spinning reel is a must. That’s why I spent months testing eight reels in Florida’s Nature Coast and coastal Virginia. After all, quality is hard to judge without hands-on experience over a long period of time.

What I found is that proven favorites continued to earn their keep, but there were a few surprises — especially in the budget category. So whether you’re looking for a dependable, high-quality reel or something to get started in saltwater fishing, there’s a reel for you on my final list of the best inshore spinning reels.

When I set out to test inshore spinning gear my goal was simple: test as many spinning reels as possible in as many situations as possible. Florida’s Nature Coast provided the perfect initial testing ground because it’s home to every inshore gamefish in Florida, and it has diverse habitats to target them.

I learned a lot about the reels in that week of catching fish using a variety of techniques. But I wanted to see how these inshore reels held up over a longer period of use. So I spent the last few months using and abusing the reels in my home inshore waters.

I divided reels into two categories: light and heavy duty. The light-duty reels were in the 3000 size class and were paired with 7-foot, medium rods and spooled with 10-pound PowerPro. The heavy-duty reels were 4000 to 6000 sizes and were paired with 7- to 8-foot, medium-heavy or heavy rods and spooled with 30-, 40-, or 65-pound PowerPro.

The light-duty reels were used for finesse fishing with soft plastics on 1/8 to ¼-ounce jig heads, as well as throwing plugs of different sizes and weights. I used the heavy-duty reels for heavier jigging with ½ to 2 ounce jigs and bucktails, as well as throwing larger swimbaits and plugs.

I targeted snook, redfish, speckled trout, sheepshead, black drum, and Spanish mackerel in Florida. In Virginia, the reels were used for targeting striped bass, redfish (including giant bulls), speckled trout, and cobia. The size and fight of these fish varied greatly, allowing me to see which reels handled which fish the best.

The Shimano Stradic series has been my favorite inshore reel for years, a status that hasn’t changed with the FM iteration, despite some very stiff competition on the market. While the FM doesn’t do much to differentiate itself from the previous model, the FL, it doesn’t need to. The FL was one of the biggest jumps forward in quality and performance for the series, and the FM simply carries that on.

This reel performed incredibly well during all phases of testing. It’s light and easy to cast all day long, but more than capable of handling larger fish and longer fights. Most notably, it barely flinched when landing several large blue catfish I caught while striper fishing. The Hagane gears and frame lived up to legend status, and I didn’t feel any flex or experience any degradation of smoothness through months of use. The Stradic’s performance made it my favorite reel for my favorite activity: tackling medium to large redfish on the flats. Overall, the Stradic FM is the perfect inshore spinning reel at a price that’s hard to beat.

I’ll be honest, when I saw the moniker “BG” on this reel I assumed what it would fish like. As a longtime user of the classic Daiwa BG lineup, I was expecting a reel that carried most of the same qualities that the BG is known for: dependability, simplicity, and being heavier than a brick. I could not have been more wrong.

When I first picked this reel up, I thought it was way too light and good looking to be a Daiwa BG. I know that may sound like I’m throwing shade at the older BG models, but I assure you, I’m not. I was actually a fan of their heavy, durable feel and they always performed well enough for me. In reality, I’m simply amazed at just how much of an improvement the new BG MQ is over the older models.

The new all-aluminum body and enhanced gearing, combined with a style makeover, helped make this reel virtually unrecognizable as a BG. An upgrade hasn’t been this drastic and complete since Steve Rogers went into the machine and came out as Captain America. The best part? After months of thorough testing, I can comfortably say the BG MQ hasn’t lost any of the hallmark durability and strength.

In fact, with drastically upgraded water resistance and the new one-piece Monocoque body (hence the MQ abbreviation) the BG MQ is substantially more rigid and durable than its predecessors. It also has Daiwa’s new Digigear technology, which uses larger gear teeth and more refined machining to help increase durability and smoothness.

This reel has been a pleasure to fish, and I’ve particularly enjoyed throwing topwater plugs and larger swimbaits, utilizing this reel’s extra line capacity and retrieve rate. It landed bull-class redfish and over-slot snook with ease. Overall, the Daiwa BG MQ is neck and neck with the Stradic for taking the crown of best all-around inshore reel, with only a few ounces separating the two.

The Shimano Vanford is essentially a Stradic crafted with Ci4+ carbon material to reduce overall weight and size drastically. I’ve always been a huge fan of the Stradic Ci4+ series, as their lightweight and compact design made for an incredibly comfortable and enjoyable reel, particularly for light tackle. The Vanford continues this trend, while making some significant upgrades to enhance durability.

While the basic design of the Vanford is essentially the same as the Stradic, the Ci4+ material allows for a more compact frame while significantly reducing weight. It still includes high-end Shimano features like X-Protect and Hagane gearing. It also includes the Cross Carbon drag system, which has proven to be a much smoother and more durable upgrade over previous felt drags.

The one-piece bail design is also a significant improvement, preventing the corrosion and bail loosening of older models. The reduced weight and compact design make this reel more versatile than similar reels in its class. A larger size is still capable of fishing lighter tackle, while smaller sizes still have the backbone to catch big fish.

Of all the reels tested, the Vanford is the one I’ve used the most, simply due to its comfort and versatility. It has the same level of performance and ability as the Stradic, while being just light enough to really tell a difference when fishing. Frankly, the biggest downside to the Vanford is its price, which makes it a hard sell over the $40 cheaper Stradic.

The Penn Spinfisher lineup may be the most storied saltwater spinning reel name on this list. While previous iterations had notable issues, it seems the new Spinfisher VII is doing its best to reclaim that former glory. Growing up Penn reels were synonymous with quality and dependability to me, so it was a hard pill to swallow when I had to acknowledge they had fallen off significantly. Given their history, it was a true pleasure fishing the new Spinfisher VII and feeling that same assurance and sturdiness of older Penn reels.

The first thing that struck me about the Spinfisher VII is how solid it feels. The full metal body has the right combination of heft and rigidity I expect of a saltwater workhorse, and it’s surprisingly smooth on the retrieve. The Spinfisher VII is also well sealed from top to bottom, with an IPX5 waterproof rating for the drag and internals.

The strength and durability of the Spinfisher does add weight, making this reel a hefty 12.3 ounces. While that’s not terrible, it’s almost twice the weight of some other inshore-specific reels. This weight can make it tiring to cast all day but is less of a hindrance when fishing live bait or jigging.

While the Spinfisher VII is a bit bulky to be considered a light tackle inshore reel, it does have a great combination of features that make it a great crossover option for anglers looking to target both inshore and larger nearshore species by boat. The high line capacity, full seal, and durable metal frame make this reel ideal for live-lining bait or jigging up bottom fish.

Finding any reel capable of withstanding saltwater under $100 is a challenge, let alone one specifically designed for it. The Penn Pursuit IV is one of the rare spinning reels that’s built to handle the rigors of saltwater while not breaking the bank.

One of the first things you notice right out of the box is the amount of plastic used in the construction of this reel. While that’s obviously a drawback for long-term durability and overall strength, it’s worth remembering that plastic doesn’t corrode. Though not as fancy as its higher-end Penn counterparts, the Pursuit IV still carries many of the trademark features that have made Penn so popular in the salt game. With a durable, corrosion resistant graphite body and sealed stainless-steel bearings, the Pursuit IV is well suited for targeting inshore gamefish. Its drag system is smooth and easy to manage during fights, although somewhat weak at only 12 pounds.

This reel has a slightly bulky overall feel, with a heavier bail and frame than most of the other reels on this list. The reel itself is comfortable to fish, but its heavy weight and bulky build do make it less suited for continuous casting. Additionally, it’s not nearly as smooth in comparison to the rest of the reels tested, but at this price point that’s to be expected.

Ultimately, the Penn Pursuit IV is a budget reel designed for saltwater use, and its weaknesses reflect that. While it may not be ideal for finesse fishing or casting plugs all day, it’s an excellent option for the casual angler looking to soak bait or throw a popping cork. When it comes to a budget-friendly saltwater reel, there aren’t many better choices on the market.

The Shimano Sustain FJ occupies a tough space in the inshore spinning reel market. Historically, the Sustain series was seen as the bridge between the Stradic and the ultra-high-end Shimano models like the Stella and Twin Power. However, with the ever-improving quality of reels like the Stradic and Vanford, it’s hard to say where the Sustain fits in these days. That’s no fault of the Sustain, as this reel is still top-notch in just about every way.

From a features standpoint, the Sustain FJ still has the edge in a few categories. In addition to Shimano staples like X-Protect and Micromodule II gearing, this reel takes the best elements of the Stradic and Vanford and combines them, while adding a few upgrades. Featuring the same Hagane aluminum frame as the Stradic, the Sustain also utilizes Ci4+ material to reduce weight and increase rigidity. Perhaps the biggest upgrade over the Stradic and Vanford is the Rigid Support Drag system. The Rigid Support system utilizes the Cross Carbon drag of other models to keep the reel from flexing and the drag smooth under heavy load. This feature is particularly noticeable when fighting stronger, faster fish, and makes this reel more capable for offshore and big game use.

At $329, it’s admittedly tough to justify purchasing the Sustain over the much cheaper Stradic or Vanford. However, for anglers looking for the ultimate light tackle setup, this reel does provide enough of a performance boost to be worthwhile. Also, it’s just plain sexy. The drag sounds meaner than other reels as line rips off the spool, and the rigid matte-black frame looks slick. The Sustain FJ is the definition of luxury over necessity, but if it’s within your budget then it’s hard to argue against having one.

The words “budget” and “heavy-duty saltwater reel” rarely go together in a meaningful sense. The rigors required for fighting big fish in harsh environments typically dictates cost. That said, the KastKing Kapstan SE does a remarkable job of making the case that low cost doesn’t mean low quality.

Let’s start with the nuts and bolts, since the Kapstan SE boasts some impressive features for a reel at this price point. It has an IPX6 waterproof rating thanks to 15 EverSeal rubber gaskets. With a primarily aluminum body and graphite rotor, this reel is extremely corrosion resistant. The Kapstan SE also features a five-disc carbon fiber drag system, which is both corrosion resistant and has an impressive 30 pounds of drag. Lastly, the hardened manganese gearing combines with a stainless-steel main shaft, which creates a sturdy reel capable of handling intense fights.

All of these features combine to create a reel that feels impressively smooth while giving the impression that it could winch a car out of a ditch. Yes, it’s very heavy, which makes it less than ideal for lighter applications. I found its design and overall size a bit unwieldy, with the handle and body having some strange metal protrusions that can take some getting used to. All that said, the KastKing Kapstan SE packs a punch for a remarkably low price, and is a fantastic option for the inshore angler looking to tackle big game on a budget.

This reel is a joy to fish, full stop. Of course, that should be expected at nearly $600, but it’s still impressive just how nice the Twin Power SW feels in your palm. It would be tempting to lump this reel into the same category as the Sustain, more luxury than necessity, but that would be a disservice to this reel and what it’s capable of.

I fished the Twin Power SW in direct competition with the Shimano Saragosa SW, primarily targeting bull redfish and cobia. I’ve used the Saragosa line for years, and I’ve always considered them to be an excellent big game reel. While both reels performed exceptionally, there was no denying the superior nature of the Twin Power. Where the Saragosa has flex, the Twin Power remains rigid. Where the Saragosa lacked stopping power, the Twin Power slammed on the brakes. The Saragosa is an excellent reel, to be sure, but it’s hard to win in a competition with the Twin Power SW.

This reel is significantly lighter than most other reels in the category yet feels substantially more rigid and durable. Fully sealed and loaded with all of Shimano’s top-tier features, including a beastly Ci4+ carbon handle fighting knob, the Twin Power SW is an absolute weapon for tackling big game. This reel put the hammer down on multiple 40- and 50-pound class redfish, allowing me to land them in far shorter time than other anglers on the same school.

While the Twin Power is expensive, most anglers dedicated and willing to chase big game understand that cost comes with the territory. The reality is that once you get into the world of big game fishing, nothing comes without a price, and with the Twin Power SW you know exactly where that cost goes.

As with most fishing gear, understanding when and where you’ll be using the reel is the first step in deciding which one is best for you. Know what species you’ll be targeting and how you’ll primarily be fishing before deciding what reel style best suits you.

Inshore fishing can include a wide range of different styles and techniques, and knowing how you’ll be fishing is key to knowing which reel to buy. If you prefer light tackle and like throwing small jigs and twitch baits, a lighter reel that’s sensitive and can be cast comfortably all day is important. Likewise, if you prefer heavy jigging or throwing large plugs, you’ll want a reel that’s built to handle that kind of strain.

Spinning reels generally come in sizes ranging from 1000 all the way up to 20,000, with 1000 being the smallest and getting increasingly larger as the number goes up. Reels in the 2500 to 4000 sizes are generally preferred for most inshore applications. If you’re targeting larger game or need something capable of holding more line, you may want to upsize to a 5000 or 6000 size reel.

Not all inshore spinning reels are created equal. If you plan on primarily fishing saltwater, verify that the internal components of a reel are designed and capable of that. Corrosion-resistant materials like aluminum and stainless steel are critical, as well as ensuring the reel has a good seal.

The outer materials are also important. While the same corrosion-resistant materials are critical, you must also consider what kind of stress the materials are capable of handling. While having a superlight carbon fiber or graphite frame can be great for keeping weight down, it may reduce durability and rigidity when casting heavy lures or fighting larger fish. This could be worthwhile if you’re fishing light tackle for fish that don’t put too much strain on a setup, such as speckled trout. However, if you’re targeting larger game that can put a lot of stress on your gear, you’ll probably want to make sure the reel is made of a rigid material like aluminum.

Another important element to consider is the type of drag material that the reel uses. While not necessarily related to corrosion, different drag materials hold up differently to intense usage and long fights. Felt drag washers are common, and while they’re very smooth, they don’t have nearly the same durability as carbon or composite drag materials.

Read Next: How to Catch Inshore Redfish, Trout, and Flounder from a Kayak

All these reels performed well enough right out of the box, but some have held up better than others over time. While the quality certainly varies, each of them have proven their worth in the world of inshore spinning reels. They all have things that make them better suited for specific situations; it’s up to you to decide which reel best fits your application. Having a good grasp on when and where you’ll be using the reel is critical to understanding which purchase makes the most sense.

I’ve put all these reels through the paces, and each of them has landed their fair share of quality inshore and nearshore gamefish. Whether you’re considering buying one right now or just need some basic information for a future investment, I hope this list helps you better understand what to look for in an inshore spinning reel. Ultimately, while my testing and reviews can provide a basis for you to approach buying a reel, every angler is different. What feels sturdy to me may feel stiff to you, so get out there and try some reels yourself. Every angler loves the sound of drag screaming, and it’s better when it’s coming from the reel in your own hands.

#9. She’s Building the Women’s Ski She Couldn’t Find

You wouldn’t think being the director of operations at Quinn, an audio erotica company for women, would lead naturally into launching a women-owned ski brand to make women-specific skis. Then again, both involve listening to what women want.

Enter Anna Dailey, whose new ski brand, Rumor, launches today (Oct. 20) with a single ski, aptly named the Debut 102. Rumor is, as far as we could fact-check, the only brand of its kind anywhere, since Coalition Snow folded earlier this year.

And as for what women want, both in erotica and in skis? Authenticity, Dailey says. “The through-line is that women found what was offered in the typical space totally fake. Women see right through that. That’s true of women as consumers in any kind of industry—they want to know that people are making products for them with them in mind.”

Dailey grew up skiing on the Palisades Tahoe ski team and later coached it. She also spent time as chief of staff for Coco Robotics, which makes autonomous delivery vehicles. “I picked up a love of hardgoods there and got to learn the nitty-gritty of supply chain,” Dailey says.

She decided to start Rumor at a pivotal time in the industry, when many brands have eschewed women-specific skis altogether and are now making unisex skis in shorter lengths.

Dailey, however, has other plans. The Debut 102 is a burly, 102-mm-waisted ski with a full sheet of Titanal added to its poplar and ash core. She also designed it in longer lengths—169, 176, and 183cm—than are typical for women’s skis, noting that most shops put women on skis that are far too short for them, adding to the instability problem that many women describe.

Also Read: Do Women Actually Want Women’s-Specific Skis?

The Debut’s preferred habitat is soft snow, and it’s undeniably aimed at strong intermediates all the way up through IFSA competitors, several of whom tested it recently in Chile to positive feedback. But for Dailey, the Debut 102 is about more than building a beefier women’s ski. It’s about rethinking the assumptions behind women’s ski design in the first place.

Since Jeannie Thoren, a U.S. Ski and Snowboard Hall of Fame inductee, pioneered women’s ski gear in the 1980s, the industry has gone back and forth on what, if anything, women’s bodies need from a ski. The first wave of women’s skis was criticized as being shorter and less powerful versions of the men’s skis. And, according to Dailey, those complaints continue because the people actually making and testing the skis are still, by and large, men. (Some brands do still run dedicated and reputable women’s programs with extensive testing by women, but they are the exception.)

The unisex trend, she believes, is a direct result of women’s skis not meeting the needs of actual women skiers. Hence her brand’s name: “I heard a rumor that women’s skis weren’t designed for women or by women,” Dailey explains. “Brands haven’t been able to figure out what women want, so they’re giving up. They’re trying to improve margins, and they’re, like, ‘we haven’t nailed these products, so let’s just call them unisex and call it a day.’”

As far as building true women-specific skis, Dailey’s brand has one core tenet: “I’m going to continue to take feedback from women skiers.” She is careful to acknowledge that there are a million different body types, and that no one ski will be right for all women. However, she did take into consideration some key insights when it came to building her skis.

First, Dailey addressed the complaint that women’s skis were too flimsy, and that most women she talked to felt more supported and stable on a men’s ski. She also heard repeatedly that the sidecut radius on women’s skis was too short, which made them hooky.

“I couldn’t find much info as to why men’s ski companies think women are going to want assistance in making their turn,” she says. “I looked into the biomechanics, and because women have a larger Q angle”—the angle from hip to knee—“they actually have an easier time angulating and initiating a turn than a man with a smaller Q angle. So the assumption that we would need the shorter sidecut was ass-backward.”

She also came to the same conclusion that Thoren did in the ’80s when it comes to mounting point: Because of women’s musculoskeletal structure and lower center of gravity, a more forward mounting point “allows us to get over the front of our skis a little easier,” says Dailey.

To create a new ski completely from scratch, she worked with an engineering team out of a ski factory in Europe. “This is not like me buying someone else’s mold and slapping my logo on it,” Dailey says. “It’s a design that I worked on from the ground up, with custom molds and custom tooling.” She also funded the entire project herself so she could control every part of the process.

Related: The Best Women’s All-Mountain Wide Skis of 2027, Tested and Reviewed

For the ski itself, the poplar and ash core keeps its swingweight low, and the Titanal provides stability and vibration damping. A second layer of Titanal underfoot offers added edge grip and a sidecut with a 20-meter radius delivers stability and power.

“It has a fluid turn shape rather than a hooky, tight one that feels unpredictable before you’re ready to make a turn,” says Dailey. “It’s stable and sturdy, without losing the playful pop that I love in a ski.”

On the Debut 102, consumers can choose one of three topsheet options in three lengths, but Dailey has a 163 and 190cm in the works. If she adds more widths, each will come in multiple graphics. “Pretty much every ski width on the market has one graphic option, and I felt like that was really limiting,” she says. “Generally, women value aesthetics, and we want something we love and that goes with different outfits and vibes.”

As for authenticity, Dailey plans to deliver. “I want to pull back the curtain, showing the process as much as I can,” she says. “Women want to know and be able to trust you, and I want to give them as much confidence as possible in me.”

You can purchase the Debut 102 directly through her website for $959 (shipping is free in the U.S.).

#10. How to Deal with a Damp Tent Without Sitting in Camp Waiting for it to Dry

A tent in the mist (Photo: MR.WUTTISAK PROMCHOO / Moment via Getty)

I like to leave camp fast in the morning. I have a hard time lingering with the day’s miles hanging over my head, so I usually pack up and zip out bright and early. I can always sit around later in the day, after all, and if I have a lot of miles to put away, I don’t have time for a leisurely breakfast anyway. On many of those mornings, my tent is soggy from condensation or overnight rain. If I’m feeling lazy, the whole sodden mess goes into my pack as I pledge to myself that I’ll deal with it later.

While it’s not the end of the world to unpack a still-damp tent at camp, there are ways to mitigate the mess. Not only is this more comfortable, but it’s also better for your tent’s longevity and can prevent mildew and odor buildup. Here’s how I’ve learned to keep my tent as dry as possible while maximizing efficiency during longer trail days.

It’s kind of cheating to make this the first tip, but it’s pertinent, especially if you’re camping somewhere without precipitation but with potential condensation buildup. If you can, avoid camping in enclosed spaces surrounded by tall grass, in low points of gullies or valleys, or near water. All of these tent-pitching locations increase condensation buildup thanks to the higher humidity and increased ground condensation. Airflow is also important: If your tent has vents and weather allows, prop them open overnight or keep your fly partially open. This will help prevent condensation buildup inside your tent.

You can exponentially speed up the drying rate by absorbing water droplets before you fold it up. Grab a buddy, hang onto all four corners, and snap the tent as hard as you can like you’re a fourth grader playing with the giant parachute in gym class. The more water you shake off before strapping it to your pack or stuffing it inside, the less you’ll have to deal with later. Plus, it’s kind of fun to see the water drops fly off.

Once you snap the tent out, you can take care of water in the corners or particularly soggy spots by wiping them down with a camp towel. (I try to hit any muddy spots here, which can help prevent material degradation from dirt and abrasion. It also makes it less gross to climb into that night.) If I don’t have a microfiber cloth, I wipe my tent out with an old sock (sorry), which is better than nothing.

It’s not often I choose to sit in the wind on purpose, but if I stuffed a soggy tent into my pack in the morning, I’m going to seek out an open, breezy spot to shake it out. My main stop during the day is lunch, so if my tent was wet in the morning, I try to time my lunch break for peak warmth and sun height. As soon as I stop, I take the tent out of my pack and lay it flat out while I eat. Anchor the corners so it doesn’t blow away; I also recommend adjusting it for best sun exposure and airflow as each section dries. This works best if you drape the material over brush, branches, or across taller rocks to maximize airflow, and don’t forget to shake it every now and again to clear actual water drops as they condense, which speeds up the process.

This isn’t as efficient as spreading the whole thing out during a lunch break on a breezy hillside, but on days where I don’t plan to stop as much—or the sun is particularly hot—I fold the fly into a large square to maximize surface area, then attach it under the Y-straps on the top of my pack, draping it down the back to catch as much moving air as possible. Every time I stop for water, I flip the tent fabric over to expose more of it to the sun and air.

Since I don’t sit around camp in the morning, I often finish my miles earlier and sit around camp in the evening. This is entirely personal preference, but it also gives me time to get the tent dry while the air is still warm and the sun is still up. Instead of flopping down immediately and elevating my feet, I set up my tent and shift it around for the best sun exposure as soon as I get to camp. On days when elevating my feet simply cannot wait, I drape the tent body and fly across branches or sturdy bushes and let the dry air do its thing.

#11. Adam Ondra Just Downgraded the World’s First Proposed V18. We Should Have Seen This Coming.

(Photo: Courtesy of Petr Chodura via Adam Ondra)

About our reporting: Associate editor Sam MacIlwaine pulls from a prior interview with Elias Iagnemma, a Testpiece Climbing podcast episode, Adam Ondra’s public posts, several YouTube videos, and records from Climbing’s digital archives to explain the history of Ondra’s downgrades and why the world’s first V18 was no exception.

On Sunday, October 18, Czech climber Adam Ondra announced that he made the second ascent of Exodia, the world’s first proposed V18, in Piemonte, Italy. The 33-year-old Olympian, who is arguably the most accomplished rock climber of all time, downgraded the boulder from V18 to V17. His downgrade ended nearly a year of speculation over whether the first-ever proposed V18 would hold up in future repeats.

“It’s very much my style,” Ondra wrote in an Instagram post caption, adding that the climbing was “extremely cool and very fun to project.” He took four days in total to send it, noting that he was in “possibly my best ever” shape for climbing it.

Exodia marks Ondra’s second V17, after Soudain Seul in Fontainebleau, France. However, he remarked that it “felt harder than Soudain Seul,” making Exodia his most difficult bouldering send to date. Read on for a history of Ondra’s biggest downgrades.

Last November, Italian climber Elias Iagnemma shocked the climbing world when he finally sent his 211-session, four-year project, Exodia. He then proposed it as the world’s first V18. Prior to Exodia, Iagnemma had sent Burden of Dreams, the world’s first V17 and a benchmark for the grade, in 25 sessions. He also put up his own first ascent, The Big Slamm, in 35 sessions, proposing V17; however, it has not been repeated. Exodia took him six times as long as either boulder. After his send, he told Climbing that it was “the hardest thing I’ve ever done in my life.”

In broad terms, Iagnemma described Exodia in two parts, a V14 and a V16, with an inverted kneebar rest between them. It contains approximately 25 hand moves across a blocky overhang traverse. Iagnemma compares the boulder visually to “the face” of the Exodia Yu-Gi-Oh card, which inspired the problem’s name.

Since November, several elite boulderers, including Soudain Seul third ascensionist Camille Coudert, have traveled to Piemonte to try Exodia, according to a Testpiece Climbing podcast episode interviewing Iagnemma. But it wasn’t until Ondra showed up, fresh from a spree of V14 and V15 first ascents in Italy, France, and the Czech Republic, that Exodia saw a second ascent.

When Ondra visited the boulder in September, Iagnemma showed up and offered all his beta. “Adam thinks the first part is 8B+/V14 hard,” the Italian said on the September 28 podcast episode. “For me it’s just 8B+. But for the second part, Adam doesn’t think it’s 8C+/V16.”

In Iagnemma’s send video, he jumps to a pinch and cuts feet shortly after exiting the kneebar. But for this move, he claimed, Ondra did not need to cut feet. “When I jump to the pinch, Adam’s still with the toe hook to the pinch, and maybe this way, it’s a bit easier than 8C+,” Iagnemma said. “I’m a little bit smaller and I lose my feet.”

Ondra confirmed this advantage in his send announcement. “The second part is even more my style,” he wrote. “I can reach one hold from one toe hook without cut[ting] loose.”

Iagnemma responded to the announcement with congratulations. “You’re not only the strongest climber in the world, but an amazing person as well,” he wrote publicly in Ondra’s comments. “I hope we get to climb together someday.”

With Exodia, Iagnemma joins a long list of elite climbers to have experienced an Ondra downgrade of their first ascent, including Stefano Ghisolfi, Jonathan Siegrist, Magnus Midtbø, Will Bosi, Dave Graham, and Aidan Roberts.

In 2003, Spanish climber Barnabé Fernández claimed the first ascent of the 270-foot Chilam Balam in Málaga, Spain, calling it the world’s first 5.15c. However, he did not provide proof of his ascent, and the 5.15c grade was called into question by Alexander Huber and many others. Eight years later, Ondra swept in, made the first confirmed ascent, and downgraded it to 5.15b, a grade that had been already established by then.

One of Ondra’s most memorable downgrading sprees occurred back in 2012, during his first visit to the U.S., when he quickly disposed of three of the hardest routes in the Red River Gorge. He onsighted both Jonathan Siegrist’s Pure Imagination and Adam Taylor’s The Golden Ticket on the same day, then downgraded both from 5.14d to 5.14c. A few days later, he flashed Taylor’s harder route, Southern Smoke Direct, and downgraded it from 5.15a to 5.14d. “Adam Ondra pretty much wrecked the Red,” wrote routesetter Aubrey Wingo in a blog post about the sending spree.

One of the reasons that Ondra is known for downgrades is his geo-agnostic philosophy on grading, which adheres to a universal scale instead of bending to the subjectivity of local standards. “What is a grading system worth if we are not even trying to make it objective?” he told this magazine after his Red River Gorge massacre. “We’re just lying to ourselves to get the highest number possible. I am always trying to compare my ascents with other benchmarks of that grade, so climbing said grade feels the same in the Red, the Alps, Norway, or Spain. It seems to me that grades were really stiff in the 1980s and `90s, but then, strangely enough, inflation occurred.” He also noted, “I wouldn’t call it downgrading—I would call it a personal suggestion or opinion.”

But while Ondra considers his downgrades “opinions,” nearly all of his suggestions tend to stick. Others have acknowledged that Ondra’s ascent of their route is what defines the grade. In 2025, Magnus Midtbø jokingly pointed out that Ondra’s 2012 downgrade of his boulder Blood Redemption from V15 to V14 came one day after day after Midtbø beat Ondra in a competition in Norway. “I almost had a V15 under my belt until Adam Ondra ruined it,” Midtbø mock-complains in a YouTube video. However, later in the video, he admits that V14 is “probably a more accurate grade.”

Ondra has acknowledged his power over the community, too. In recent years, he’s become more careful to stress that his downgrades are not personally motivated. In 2021, he downgraded Stefano Ghisolfi’s Erebor, then considered the hardest route in Italy, from 5.15b/c to 5.15b, right after Laura Rogora redpointed it and became the first woman to climb 5.15b/c. “The fact that Laura did Erebor is one of the most impressive achievements in climbing ever,” Ondra wrote in an Instagram post caption, “but my suggestion is just my honest opinion and not a way to put down her achievement.”

At this point, when Ondra comes to town, it’s normal for any first ascensionist to prepare for the re-evaluation of their life’s biggest accomplishment. In 2017, when Ondra tried Steve McClure’s Rainman (5.15b), the hardest sport climb in the U.K., McClure himself showed up to watch. A video published by the British Mountaineering Council shows him visibly nervous.  Rainman was McClure’s seven-year obsession; it took him 127 sessions to finally get it done. But Ondra didn’t send that day. “You can be relaxed,” Ondra told McClure, laughing, after he fell from high up on McClure’s route. The 47-year-old grinned in obvious relief. Today, Rainman remains 5.15b.

Given Ondra’s unique reputation as possibly the best climber in the world, British climbers Tom Randall and Pete Whittaker have jokingly invented a new grading scale based on Ondra’s ability level. “The O-grading system starts at 0, so if Adam flashes anything, it’s just O-zero,” said Randall in a 2023 YouTube video of Ondra visiting his famous Cellar in Sheffield. “O1 will be, it will take him one session. That could be the second go, or it could be the 25th go of the session. It’s always O1. O2 is two sessions; O3 is three sessions, and so on.”

Ondra joined in the joke in 2024. On April Fool’s Day, he posted the O-grades for a few of his biggest accomplishments, adding the plus and minus effects to note effort and to narrow the scale. Silence (5.15d) and La Dura Dura (5.15c), two of his most groundbreaking redpoints, were labeled O60 and O42+ respectively.

But at this point, the O-grade system is probably worth taking seriously, if only to get inside Ondra’s head and anticipate a future downgrade. Like any other climber, Ondra relies on his past experiences on various routes and boulders to determine the grade for his current one. Yet unlike most other climbers, his opinion carries significant implications for us all. One may wonder whether Rainman survived a downgrade simply because in 2017, Ondra hadn’t yet flashed 5.15a, the benchmark for O-zero; therefore it had to be at least O1, which was (and is still) 5.15b.

By contrast, Exodia took Ondra four sessions, which means it’s O4—slightly lower on the O-grade scale than Ondra’s only other V17, Soudain Seul (O5). In that line of logic, the downgrade suddenly makes perfect sense.

#12. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.
