#33. Whatever You Think of Him, Mark Dowdle Is Built for the Backyard Ultra

At lap 87 of the Last Soul Backyard Ultra in Bornheim, Germany, this August, Mark Dowdle transformed (or regressed, he’s not entirely sure) into the football and lacrosse player he was in college.

To be fair, Ayyoub “Ello” El Osrouti pretty much started it. A backyard ultra, as you probably know by now, is a last-person-standing race not much different from “The Long Walk”—the movie about 100 boys who walk until there’s one left—except the runners in backyard races aren’t shot after they drop.

Now at 4 a.m. on August 18—three days and 15 hours into the race—it was just down to El Osrouti and Dowdle, who were engaged in a Hamilton-like duel to determine the winner. Ello busted out of the gate. The German had been trying to run faster laps to break Dowdle, but this was, by comparison, a sprint. Dowdle, deviating from his tactic of running his own race, decided to stay right with him.

Dowdle completed the lap in 38 minutes—his fastest of the race by over 5 minutes. El Osrouti got up and finished four minutes later, also his fastest lap.

But about half way through the lap, El Osrouti stopped and sat down. Dowdle stopped, too, and just stared at him in silence. It was both competitive and a little chilling, like Dowdle thought the Last Soul race was a literal invitation to collect his competitors’ souls along the way.

Dowdle’s behavior left many of his hundreds of thousands of followers on Instagram, Youtube, and TikTok a little stunned. The 29-year-old Minnesotan has become a wildly popular Internet figure through dishing out zen advice and positivity. Rich Roll, the addict turned endurance athlete who serves up mindfulness every week on his podcast, called Dowdle a “changemaker” when he had Dowdle on the show. There was a good reason for it: Basically every time Dowdle took a breath, he said something enlightening or inspiring about hard work, endurance, or self-improvement.

With two backyard ultra wins in 2026 alone, there’s little doubt that Dowdle is one of this year’s ultrarunning breakout stars, partly because of his success in the backyard format and partly because of his social media savvy. But he didn’t get that way by reading scripted platitudes on TikTok; Dowdle isn’t faking that zen.

When I told him about the Taco Bell 50K and how it attracted those who wouldn’t normally even consider running an ultra, he said, “people want to be challenged. Sometimes they just don’t know it yet.” Even when he was a football and lacrosse player at the University of St. Thomas in Saint Paul, Minnesota, drinking way too much and trying to please others at the expense of himself, he would think about the meaning of life and why people do the things they do. He attributes his personal growth to running, but also to journaling.

“These are the kinds of things I think about all the time,” Dowdle said. “I was constantly thinking about this connection between words and action and who I wanted to be.”

Dowdle works as a motivational speaker now. But deep down, he’s got an edge.

It’s that edge that makes him stand out (and ruffle feathers) in a sport known for its kumbaya positivity, especially the camaraderie-focused backyard ultra community. Dowdle likes being a little weird and competitive and even scary: He once made a YouTube video called “Ultrarunning Has A Mark Dowdle Problem.” He compares himself to Dennis Rodman, the wildly divisive and brilliant NBA player.

“I’m sure that some of these other guys who are competitive will want to put that competition right back on me,” Dowdle said. “I welcome that.”

His friend and rival Harvey Lewis seems like a golden retriever to Dowdle’s heeler. Dowdle sort of agrees with that comparison and sort of doesn’t. He points out that he and Lewis aren’t that different. (Lewis agrees with him, for what it’s worth.)

“I think Harvey Lewis is competitive in a way that’s much tricker to identify,” Dowdle said. “But I don’t hide it. There are times I don’t care. I’ll show everything on my sleeve.”

Lewis believes that Dowdle’s zen, more than his competitiveness, is what’s carried him to so much recent success. But for now, they’re teammates: Lewis, 50, leads a U.S. team of 15 against the world’s best at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship starting on Saturday, October 17. Team USA will compete on the Big’s Backyard Ultra course in Beltbuckle, Tennessee, the original backyard ultra devised by Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell.

The Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is held every two years, alternating with the individual world championship. At 6 a.m. Mountain Time on Saturday, October 17, 69 national teams will compete simultaneously around the world.

Each team of 15 runners will run a 4.167-mile loop every hour, on the hour. The country with cumulatively the most loops completed across all 15 runners wins the team title. Team USA will race on the original backyard ultra course in Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Belgium has won the event two out of three times since its inauguration in 2020 and looks to have the deepest team. The U.S. isn’t far behind: The team features two Big’s Backyard champions in Harvey Lewis and Scott Snell, as well as Jon Noll, who reached 111 laps (462 miles) at Big’s last year, and Mark Dowdle, who won Last Soul with nearly 400 miles. Seven runners return from the third-place U.S. team in 2024, and five return from the winning team in 2022.

Lewis said Dowdle’s “why” is perhaps the strongest he’s ever seen. It “cements his discipline and his unwavering desire to not give up.”

“Mark has a great energy force,” Lewis said. “He has a level of enthusiasm that’s immeasurable.”

But what, exactly, is an energy force? Is it zen or competitiveness? Dowdle likes to ask it another way: Why can’t it be both?

Take a wild guess who inspired Dowdle as a collegiate football and lacrosse player to turn his life around and start running. It wasn’t Joe Rogan, but if that was your first guess, you’re on the right track.

Feeling sorry for himself on the bus ride home after losing two of three lacrosse games his senior year, he listened to David Goggins on Joe Rogan’s podcast. Goggins talked about how running carved him into the person he was today. The way he bragged about pissing blood, shitting himself, and eating only saltine crackers during his long runs spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle already knew he needed to change.

He went for a run when they got back to campus—even though it was 2 a.m.

If Goggins lit the fire, James Lawrence, the Iron Cowboy, stoked it. Lawrence had completed the 50/50/50 challenge, or 50 Ironman-length triathlons in 50 days across 50 states. The way he leaned on his family during that journey spoke to Dowdle. Dowdle, to this day, gives all the credit to his wife, Lucy, for centering him and scolding him whenever he acts, for lack of a better description, too much like a bro.

Dowdle tried for many years to make it as a running guru—some might say influencer—and ultrarunner. He found some limited success. Runner’s World interviewed him in 2023 for his calendar challenge, when he ran the number of miles corresponding to the day of the month, for a full month. (For example, 26 miles on the 26th.) By the beginning of 2026, he had 40,000 Instagram followers and a modest apparel sponsorship that netted him $200 a month. And then he entered the BPN Go One More backyard ultra this April.

Dowdle had already won the Arrowhead 135-miler in January, finishing in 35:48:00—a four-hour improvement over his 2025 fourth-place finish. But he chalked that up to his ability to withstand the Minnesota winter conditions that dropped to minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

The BPN Go One More was another story; he hadn’t even made it to 100 miles in a backyard ultra before. He could sense other peoples’ doubts—they didn’t drive him, but they did irritate him a little. He mumbled at one point that they “had no fucking idea.”

Dowdle ended up running 306 miles in 73 hours of rainy and muddy conditions, and the way he did it captivated people: He looked fresh and happy most of the time, like he was playing tag on the playground. In a few days, his Instagram following jumped to 108,000, and brand deals were knocking at his door. He also began booking keynote speaking events, sometimes for conferences that he helped set up the year before for one of his odd jobs to get by while he pursued running.

He proved that BPN was no fluke two months later, finishing second to Lewis at the Mid-State Mile, a last-person standing event in Franklin, Tennessee.

But Last Soul sent him into a new stratosphere. After their fateful showdown on lap 87, Dowdle and El Osrouti dueled for another six hours. And despite the German banking a cumulative five hours of extra rest over the course of the race, after that 93rd lap he gave out. Dowdle ran the final lap solo to win the race with 94 loops, or 391.7 miles. The race attracted 10 million viewers to the livestream and more than 100,000 at any one time, attention that Lewis called “freakishly different” than any other ultra in history, even Western States or Rachel Entrekin’s historic overall win at the Cocodona 250.

After Last Soul, Dowdle’s Instagram following jumped from 108,000 to over 400,000.

“It’s been everything I’ve been trying to build for several years now,” Dowdle said. “But nothing really has changed. It’s sort of weird because I’ve been saying the same thing now that I have over the past seven years. But people are willing to listen more when I go 94 hours in a backyard.”

Dowdle, a Christian who has described his goal in races to experience suffering in a way that brings him closer to Jesus Christ and to others, says he’s handled his newfound success because of his wife. Everyone, he said, should get a Lucy. On the way home from the BPN race, Lucy saw his phone blowing up and reminded him that many of those people were loving him because of what he just did, but that she and his friends loved him for who he was.

Dowdle’s breakthrough would not be possible without the backyard ultra format, and not just because he’s one of the best in the world at it. The race, as Lewis alluded to, is insanely popular: What started as another one of Laz’s harebrained ideas with the Big’s Backyard Ultra in 2011 has ballooned to over 1,000 independent backyard ultras across the globe.

Lewis was perhaps the event’s first breakout star. He was known, he said, after winning Badwater in 2014, but the attention was far different after he won Big’s Backyard in 2023, his second victory, and set a backyard world record by running more than 450 miles. The format changed the high school teacher’s life.

“I was doing other cool stuff but never got noticed,” Lewis said. “But after the backyard, I was invited to all these running events, at no cost, places I’d never get to go to as a teacher. Australia, Botswana, all over the place. In Botswana, people knew who I was, and I was like, ‘really’? It just created so many more doors opening.”

Backyard ultras favor a unique skillset. Neither Lewis or Dowdle have the legspeed to compete for a top spot at a “fast” ultra like Western States. But, Lewis counters, a top contender at Western States may struggle at a backyard ultra.

“I’ve seen collegiate-type runners, and they get totally destroyed,” Lewis said. “It’s a different type of grit that’s required for running five straight days.”

Lewis and Dowdle possess that special mindset that doesn’t have much to do with a training plan. Lewis is writing a book on mindset, in fact, that will be released next fall. For Dowdle, the ultimate challenge (and intrigue) comes in the unknown.

“You have no opportunity to say ‘in 10 miles this race will be over,’” Dowdle said. “You just have to wrestle with the discomfort.”

Dowdle does that, he said, by using skills he learned from his parents. His relentless, even disturbing, will comes from his mother, and he got an addict’s penchant from his father. His dad, he said, has been sober for nearly 30 years by using his addictive personality for good, investing his energy in Alcoholics Anonymous and helping others overcome their itches.

But Dowdle also excels by finding out who he was as a person: “Running helped me figure out the person I was running away from and also running toward the person I wanted to be.”

There is a dual narrative in his head, one that every ultrarunner facing the highs and lows of a long race knows. The first tells him he’s not worthy. The other feels only elation. Neither, he said, is true.

“I know that the narrative playing in my head at that moment is not the full truth,” Dowdle said. “And the narrative that tells me I’m not good enough. As long as my feet are still moving forward, I can combat that thinking and know that’s not the full truth.”

Proving that imposter syndrome wrong is his part of his “why,” the magic power that he and Lewis seem to possess that helps them run much farther than just about anyone else. But that’s not his only motivation.

Dowdle was, at one point, a football coach. But when he examined his life, he didn’t think football was the right avenue for what he truly wanted to do. He wanted to connect with young men and try to help them crawl out of the same situation he was in years ago, before he began running and journaling. So he traveled across the country and hosted beer miles. He still does this, though he drinks non-alcoholic varieties now, or he simply challenges athletes to beat his beer mile time. (It’s 5:51.57.)

When the race is over, he sits down with athletes and talks with them about their lives. He tells them he was like them once, a little lost and full of doubt and pain, with only alcohol seeming to help. There are other ways, he tells them. Running could be one. A personal journey, like that of the Iron Cowboy, could be another.

“I watched the Iron Cowboy documentary, and it made me realize that I do have control, and that I can do hard things and I’m capable of more,” Dowdle said. “That’s the gift he gave me in that moment. Now I’ve been on a mission to try to give that gift to other people.”

#37. Fractals in the Dirt

A dusty exploration of the least-appreciated geology on the Colorado Plateau.

Not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun. That isn’t a buddy’s quirky nickname, as in: Yo, my man Mancos, my Shaley bro, hand me the Doritos and Sour Patch Kids, would ya please? It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. To an unsuspecting bystander, a turkey vulture or big-rig trucker, I must have seemed to be a lone soul on a desert road trip, only the radio’s pop divas, evangelical preachers, and static for company. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

#38. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 20

As we pointed out last week, most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents that have come to light recently.

Chamois in France. Photo: Ludovic Laude/L’Est Republicain

A normally timid mountain ungulate has been attacking runners on the outskirts of Besançon in eastern France.

One victim, a 30-year-old woman jogger, was knocked unconscious and suffered a punctured shoulder and serious scalp wounds requiring stitches and staples. The incident occurred just a few hundred meters from the outskirts of the city.

“I didn’t hear it coming,” the woman, known only as Milena, told Le Monde. “I only had time to see its head 10 centimeters from me, and then, nothing, total blackout…”

The woman was unconscious for about five minutes.

Another runner had been attacked days earlier. The incidents occurred near La Chapelle des Buis. Wildlife authorities described the behavior as highly unusual and authorized the animal’s removal. The cause of its aggression remains unclear.

A 71-year-old Winter Garden, Florida fisherman, Steven Hamilton, was posing for a photograph with a fish when a large alligator lunged from the water, seized his leg, and pulled him into a pond.

Emergency crews responded, but the alligator refused to let go of his body, according to Fox News. By the time they released him and killed the alligator, Hamilton was dead. The medical examiner identified drowning and blunt-force injury to his left leg as causes of death, with alligator tooth marks on both sides of the leg.

Alligator attacks are rare but occur occasionally. According to the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, there have been a total of 500 alligator bites against humans since 1948, including 32 fatal encounters.

Vladimir Odulo, a fisherman from Primorye in Russia’s Far East, survived an attack by an Asiatic black bear, also known as a Himalayan bear.

The bear attacked while Odulo was fishing. He tried to defend himself with his fishing rod, but the animal knocked him into the water. Odulo continued fighting as it “beat his face like a boxer,” Russian media reported the fisherman saying. Suddenly, the bear stopped the attack and fled into the forest.

Odulo suffered several wounds and a serious eye injury, but survived. Doctors in Vladivostok were able to save his eyesight.

A venomous Caspian cobra, which now occurs high in Himachal Pradesh. Photo: Shutterstock

Two deaths in the Indian Himalaya have been attributed to Caspian cobras. Native to Central Asia, this venomous species has expanded its range eastward into the higher reaches of Himachal Pradesh. It now also occurs in Pakistan and Kashmir.

The first death occurred when a 40-year-old man accidentally stepped on a Caspian cobra while spraying an apple orchard. Wearing open-toed footwear, he sustained two bites on his leg. He was taken to a local faith healer before being shifted to the hospital, where he was declared dead, according to the Tribune of India.

In the second case, a 62-year-old man stepped on a snake while on his way to work and was bitten on the leg. He collapsed within half an hour and was taken to a health facility, where he died.

These fatalities occurred some time ago, but the report on them was published just this week in the journal Epidemiology International. The Caspian cobra generally inhabits higher, open, rocky terrain at elevations of 2,000m or higher, where both incidents occurred. Researchers suggest its range may now include lower elevations.

Two men died in separate elephant attacks in northern Kenya.

On October 11, Eisimgai Gorow Ltarakwa, 41, was herding goats near Nguposorogin village when a lone elephant attacked him. He suffered severe injuries and died at the scene.

Two days later, Mukhtar Abdoy Hussein, 64, was grazing livestock near Benane village when a herd of elephants trampled him to death.

The incident highlights the risks faced by herders in areas where livestock grazing activities bring communities into close proximity with wildlife. Under a conservation initiative, the families are entitled to receive compensation, according to Kenyan media.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#39. Why Red Bull Got Into the Ski Business—And Teamed Up with an Austrian Racing Legend to Do It

VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports skis. (Photo: Kleinmond-Georg Lindacher)

Plenty of skiers are gear-obsessed, but Marcel Hirscher is in a league of his own. Over the course of his 15-year racing career, the legendary Austrian skier and founder of VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports would drive his coaches and teammates crazy with constant chatter about tech specs and modifications. Maybe not the guy you want to challenge in gear trivia, but definitely the guy you want designing your skis.

Which is why he’s the first person to convince Red Bull to co-own a ski brand.

Born in Salzburg and raised in the Austrian Alps, Hischer made his World Cup debut in March 2007 and found himself catapulted into the limelight. In 2008, he bagged his first World Cup podium, and in 2009, his first win. Over the next 10 years, he became the winningest Austrian ski racer of all time, turning heads with masterful racing strategy and unparalleled technique. Credit those skills to his uncompromising perfectionism, a characteristic that drove him to 67 World Cup wins, two Olympic gold medals, and eight consecutive overall World Cup titles. And when he retired from ski racing in 2019, it’s what drove him to start manufacturing his own skis.

Hirscher has always been a tinkerer by nature—maddeningly meticulous and chronically detail-oriented. Red Bull already knew that after a decade of working with him as a sponsor and supporter. So, when Hirscher said he was launching his own company in 2021, their ears perked up.

Hischer called his brand VAN DEER, a name that plays up his half-Dutch heritage and winks at the fact that hirsch is German for “deer.” The goal was to give the brand some racing pedigree without directly naming it after a pro. After all, Hirscher never set out to make skis just for the elite.

Hirscher’s overarching philosophy is that all skiers are equal. It doesn’t matter if you’re a bunny-hill newbie, a weekend warrior, or a champion racer. Everyone can benefit from a ski that fits, and everyone can access the sublime sense of flow and rhythm that only skiing can offer.

“Nothing feels quite like a perfectly carved turn,” Hirscher says. “When a ski truly fits its skier, you feel it through a certain naturalness of movement.” He’s honed his sensitivity to that feeling through decades of racing. Now, he’s applying that fine-tuned sensibility to ski design.

“For a ski racer, skiing is a constant search for hundredths of a second, where even a tiny change in edge angle or flex can make a huge difference,” says Hirscher. “The real challenge is transferring that knowledge from the racecourse to everyday skiers in a way that makes them better.” That process requires converting raw data and physics into the unquantifiable feeling of human movement. That’s the alchemy Hirscher lives for.

He spent the first months of his new project immersed in the all-consuming process of design. Then Red Bull stopped by. After such a longstanding partnership, maybe it’s no wonder that Hirscher and Red Bull had developed a strikingly similar vision for the future of alpine skiing. Regardless, a collab was an easy yes. Red Bull got a peek at what Hirscher was doing, liked what they saw, and came on as a partner in 2022. The result: VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports.

Since then, the Alps-based brand has become a beacon of Austrian heritage. The skis are sleek, classic, and no-nonsense. Their craftsmanship is decidedly traditional, but the high-tech materials and rigorous testing are as modern as it gets. The skis get put through their paces on mountains all over the world—including on World Cup courses where they’ve already earned gold medals and dozens of podium finishes. Hirscher even wore them himself when he returned to racing for the 2024/25 season.

Better yet, the athletes who ride those skis deliver their feedback to VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, a tight-knit partnership that continues to drive the pace of innovation. Two of those skis—the FREERIDE SERIES, which is exactly what it sounds like, and the H-POWER SERIES, which is designed for all-day skiing in any terrain—bring Hirscher’s profound knowledge and racing heritage to skiers across a wide range of skill levels. The new launches are also designed to complement the brand’s four existing lines: the PRO SERIES, RACE SERIES, JUNIOR PRO SERIES, and TOURING SERIES.

“My mission is to make the feeling I have while skiing accessible to others,” Hirscher says. “With us, there is no racing privilege when it comes to material quality—we build skis with World Cup quality, adapted for free skiing.”

Because while World Cup racing will always have a special place in Hirscher’s heart, his primary mission is to help up-and-coming skiers accelerate their mastery of the sport he loves. The goal isn’t only to help that new generation win more medals. It’s to help them fall in love with skiing—with each drop, each pole-plant, each turn—exactly in the same way he did.

At VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, founded in the Austrian Alps by ski legend Marcel Hirscher, we do things differently. We believe in the power of “new” and a no-compromise approach to skiing and equipment. Together with  Red Bull, we combine racing  expertise with innovation to create world-class skis for a new generation.

#40. The Best Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Published Oct 19, 2026 5:19 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A lot of hunting gear has reached a performance plateau, but that hasn’t happened yet for the best trail cameras. The new models released this year are more advanced and easier to use than the previous generation. So, if you’re in the market for a new trail cam you’ll be treated to more features, better photos, and more performance for your money than ever before.

For the most part, cellular trail cameras have taken over the market. These cameras pair with apps and send images and videos directly to your phone. There are now several excellent cell cam options in the $100 to $150 range. This is on par with what a decent standard camera costs (but of course, you also have to pay for the data plan with cell cams). That’s why we focused most of our review on cell cams.

But not all hunting areas get cell reception and not all states allow the use of cellular trail cameras for hunting. With this in mind, we’ve included two great standard trail camera options.

We’ve also noticed that there’s a growing category of security cam and trail cam hybrids. These cameras promise a live video feed from the woods. In our field testing, however, most of these cameras didn’t perform up to our standards, and only one of them made the cut for this review.

Our trail camera testing really never ends. We’ll continue running these cameras and new additions throughout the fall. In this review, we’ve included both brand-new cameras and the top-performing cameras from previous seasons.

Each camera in this review was tested while selecting the best cellular trail cameras and the best budget trail cameras, and represents the top performers from those tests. We put each camera through a consistent test protocol to evaluate trigger speed, detection range, image quality, and reliability. Here’s how we did it.

Each cellular trail camera was set to its fastest shooting mode and highest sensitivity. Markers were placed at 10 feet, 60 feet, and 110 feet. The tester walked past the camera (from left to right, then right to left) at a medium pace at each distance. The walk-through test was then repeated at night. The test is meant to measure the camera’s detection range, trigger speed, shutter speed, and flash range. We looked for blank photos, failures to trigger, blurry images, and overall photo quality.

From there, we set each camera in the field to see how it performed in real-world conditions. In the field, we evaluated the camera’s photo quality, reliability, and ease of setup. This included the ability to use each camera’s app to review and sort photos. Some of these cameras were field tested for an entire hunting season. Others are so new that they’ve only been in the field for a few weeks. We’re constantly testing the latest cameras and will update this review later this fall.

Read our full cellular trail camera guide for more options.

In the walk-through test the Pro 4.0 triggered with 100 percent reliability at 10 and 60 feet, catching me as I entered the frame from both directions during the day and at night. It did not trigger at 110 feet, day or night, which isn’t uncommon. With the camera set to Low Glow, it puts out a nice, even IR flash that illuminates a wide area out to about 100 feet. What I appreciate most is that it doesn’t blow out detail up close and still has plenty of brightness to clearly see animals at 60 feet. Like the 3.0, you can adjust between No Glow and Low Glow settings right in the app.

The new Reveal 4.0 cameras come in three models, the 4.0, Pro 4.0, and Pro 4.0 Solar. I’ve tested all three and they all perform great, but I’d recommend the Solar for most people because it’s such a great value. If you were to buy a 4.0 Pro and an R5 battery pack separately, your cart total would be $220. But the Pro 4.0 Solar costs $200 and includes a solar panel — so it’s the better buy for anyone who’s already thinking about getting an R5 for their trail camera. If you want to get the larger R10 battery and don’t need the solar panel then the 4.0 or Pro 4.0 would be the better option — the main difference between the two is the Pro’s built-in monitor.

In the field, the 4.0 Pro and 4.0 Pro Solar are capturing valuable deer intel for me. I have one set up on a travel corridor and it’s grabbing photos of deer at 20 to 25 yards. One of my favorite Tactacam features is that you can have the camera set to take a photo and a video on the same trigger. This is huge in the timber when the deer’s head is behind a tree in the photo or you want to see how deer are entering or exiting a spot.

The battery life on the Reveal cameras is good. The R5 battery is lasting me a little over a month with instant send and several hundred photos per week. If you really want to put a camera out for the entire season, the R10 battery will double the R5’s battery life and you can extend it further with a solar panel.

If you’re really into adjusting your camera settings to maximize battery life, there’s a Battery Center feature in the Reveal app. It shows a summary of battery usage, how well the solar panel or external battery pack is performing, and suggested settings for maximizing battery life. You can click the Battery Saver setting and hit Apply to get the most battery life possible — or just keep the settings on Instant if you’re like me.

If you buy the Stealth Cam Fusion Max 3 in a two-pack, it costs $75 per camera. It’s packed with features, has a very fast trigger speed and has been reliable in the field with great battery life.

In the daylight walk-through test at 10 feet, it caught me twice while I walked from right to left. When I walked from left to right, I got two blank photos. At 60 feet, it took four photos of me walking right to left and two walking left to right. It didn’t trigger at 110 feet.

The night performance was similar, with multiple captures at 10 and 60 feet and no trigger at 110 feet.

In the field, I aimed the Fusion Max 3 at a cluster of oaks dropping acorns. I don’t have a lot of oaks where I hunt, so several in one spot are a major draw. In a month, the Fusion Max 3 racked up 1,600 photos of deer, squirrels, raccoons and turkeys. The battery is still full with the send setting on instant, though I’m using the optional lithium cartridge upgrade. The photo quality is good overall. The night photos are especially good, with a nice, even flash that doesn’t blow out any details — even when deer are very close to the camera.

The app lets you filter by species, and it even separates whitetail does from whitetail bucks. You can locate the camera by GPS right in the app. The app also has a huge amount of data on how many photos were taken during different moon phases, wind directions and temperatures.

The Fusion Max 3 has good performance, excellent battery life and a powerful app at a very reasonable price. That makes it my pick for the best-value trail camera of 2026.

There’s a reason why most professional wildlife researchers who use trail cameras rely on Reconyx: Their cameras are known for reliably delivering high quality images. Hardcore hunters who want that same type of performance lean toward Reconyx, too. This camera performed well in the walk-through test, triggering out to 60 feet day and night and also catching me at close range. It’s the only camera we tested that’s made in America.

Importantly, it was the only camera that truly stopped motion at close range at night (you can see that image below). The other cameras produced slightly blurry images of me walking close-range at night.

At close range, I could hear other cameras firing, and at night I could see their bright red flashes at 60 feet (the Stealth Cam is the exception here). This was not the case with the Reconyx. There was no visible flash and there was no trigger noise whatsoever.

Surprisingly, I had issues with the camera in the field. First, the app crashed several times when I started using it. I had to delete the app and reload it three different times. In the app store, I saw several reviews with users complaining about the same issue. Happily, all my photos were saved in my profile and Reconyx seems have to solved the issue. Second, the camera fogged up for a few days during the summer. I received several foggy pictures, and when my buddy went to check on the camera, there was a condensation spot inside the housing. We pulled the camera, I opened it up to dry it out, and set it again. The Reconyx went back to capturing clear images. But then a big snow storm hit our area and the camera went down again, with more condensation inside the body.

The camera has a five-year warranty, so this would be a fixable issue. I know several hardcore deer hunters who run Reconyx cameras and never have problems. But still, in our testing and review, we had to ding this very expensive camera for its failures in the field. —A.R.

Most cell cams require users to buy individual plans for each camera. But Spartan allows users to share data plans across multiple devices. So if you have one camera over a food source that gets 20 photos a night and another camera on a trail that gets 5 photos a night, you don’t have to get unique plans for each scenario.

This is a great system for serious trail cam users who run their cameras through the majority of the year (not just deer season).

But beyond the plan structure, the camera showed solid performance in the walk-through test, capturing all distances during the day and out to 60 feet at night. However, it should deliver excellent field performance. I was a little disappointed with the nighttime image quality. But we’ll be interested to see how it performs over the course of several months in the field.

Lone Wolf came up with a solution to shimming sticks between your camera and a tree to get the angle just right: their ball-joint mount. The Undercover is also one of the few budget trail cameras that can transfer photos to your phone over Wi-Fi with an app. The app can also organize and store photos based on several filters.

The Undercover’s camera performance was a little disappointing. At 12 megapixels, it’s not going to capture print-quality images for the trophy wall. The battery life on it was iffy past 6,500 images, which is below average compared to many of our other cameras.

The daylight performance of the camera is definitely as advertised with satisfying trigger speeds. It captured me in the center of the frame at the 10-foot distance. The colors were also rich and the image sharp. At night, the camera triggered at 10 feet, but the photo quality was not great. The camera did not trigger at 60 or 110 feet. –D.P.

I tested four of Amazons top-selling security trail cameras, and only one of them worked. Two of the cameras I couldn’t get up and running out of the box, the live functionality didn’t work on the third, and the fourth worked as advertised.

I found that the apps didn’t have the functionality I was used to with name brand trail cameras. It’s pretty obvious that these cameras are being made by people who don’t hunt and don’t understand the features hunters need. The apps are a little sketchy too, and I’m skeptical about who gets access to the data they collect.

For the most part, these cameras aren’t ready for prime time. But, with a little product development they could be the next big trend in trail cameras. —S.E.

This camera has unique features you won’t find in other cell cams. You can view a live stream through the app and move the camera left, right, up, and down. Unlike the other security cameras I tested, this one had just a one- to two-second delay on the live video and adjustment.

In the walk-through test the S40 triggered at 10 feet from both directions day and night, but didn’t trigger at the farther distances. I tried a few impromptu tests to see how far beyond 10 feet it would trigger and 30 to 45 feet seemed to be its max for consistent captures.

I placed the S40 on a travel corridor, and it captured a ton of deer activity. The deer mostly moved perpendicular to the camera on trails 15 to 30 feet away. The video quality wasn’t great overall, and it was especially poor at night. What makes it worse is that the IR light over exposes the image and then adjusts down to a good setting. That blooming effect cost me a clear look at what I think is a stunner buck. One more knock on the night performance is the IR doesn’t illuminate brightly beyond 10 feet. A unique feature is that you can run a white light in video mode for color video. You can also remotely turn on the white light while viewing the live stream.

I think this trail and security camera hybrid has limited use cases for hunting, but in the right scenario it could be an asset. Probably the best use for it is to position it over a feeder. Before you walk into the stand over the bait site, you can turn on the live feed and use the camera panning feature to scan the area. If you’re in a state with hogs, you could use the camera’s white light as a feeder light. —S.E.

Cellular trail cameras offer the most convenience because you can hang them and leave them in the woods until the batteries die — all while getting near real-time scouting information sent to your phone. That saves time and gas. More importantly you’re not bumping deer and leaving scent by going into the woods to check camera cards. The main downsides are that you need cell service in the location you’re placing the camera, and cell cams come with additional monthly costs. Cell camera plans typically range from $4 to $15 per month, with additional charges for downloading full-length HD videos or hi-res photos. Cellular trail cameras are more tightly regulated with some states allowing standard trail cams but banning the use of cell cams.

Standard cameras don’t have monthly fees and have longer battery life. They also rival cell cams in photo quality. Of course, the main downside is that you have to physically check the cameras, and the data you’re getting is old.

Just like cameras used for photography a more expensive camera usually produces a better image and has more features. We’ve provided sample photos for each camera to help you see the difference between a $40 Tasco, a $150 Tactacam, and a $600 Reconyx.

Most hunters will either buy the cheapest trail cam and replace it every few years, or buy one in the $100 to $150 range. We’ve found that above $200 you start to lose value for your dollar, and running multiple cameras becomes very expensive. There are now several great cameras in the $100 to $150 range.

There are pros and cons for each type of camera flash. Here’s a quick and dirty break down.

We’ve looked into if trail camera flash spooks deer and after talking to biologists and hunters, several of them prefer white flash and feel it spooks deer less often. They especially like the color images provided by a flash. However, most of the best trail cameras are not offered with white flash.

Low-glow IR cameras produce a visible red glow from the infrared emitters when they take a picture or video at night. The red glow is typically faint, but can be seen when looking directly at the camera. These cameras typically take superior night images compared to the no-glow cams. Many hunters and experts believe the flash can be detected by deer.

No-glow cameras like the Tactacam and Stealth Cam have black filters over the infrared emitters to hide the red flash. These cameras are sometimes described as black flash cams. No-glow cams are much less likely to be detected by deer or humans at night, but they typically produce lower-quality nighttime images. However, Stealth, Tactacam, and Reconyx have proven to be exceptions to this rule.

There is some controversy in the hunting community about using cellular trail cameras to hunt big game (make sure to check your local regulations before buying and using a cellular trail camera). In 2022 the Boone and Crockett club revised its policy in regard to cell cams, stating: “The use of any technology that delivers real-time location data (including photos) to target or guide a hunter to any animal in a manner that elicits an immediate (real-time) response by the hunter is not permitted. ‘Real time’ is the key concept. Seeing a photo and harvesting an animal a few hours later, or even the same day, uses this technology to assure a kill. It also takes advantage of the animal, which cannot detect impending danger from a camera. Waiting several days, or even until the following season, to pursue an animal captured on camera is different, and would not be deemed an unethical use of a trail camera.”

Right now, I don’t see many hunters using cell cams to capture images of a buck on a food plot or corn pile and then running out there to kill him that moment. As live-feed video in cellular trail cam technology becomes more advanced and wide spread, however, it could be come a problem for fair-chase standards. More states will likely look to restrict the use of this technology for hunting. It’s up to hunters to use the tech responsibly. At their best, trail cams can provide consistent data on deer movement and hunters can interpret that data when making decisions on where to hunt. Most of us have limited days to hunt, so picking a prime spot is critical. But we must still use our woodsmanship, hunting knowledge, and fair chase principles. I think the trail cameras can only help with that. —A.R.

With modern trail camera technology, we don’t have to guess if deer are in the area or what time they’re moving. When used consistently, trail cams can paint a vivid picture of deer activity patterns in your area. But trail cameras are also notorious for malfunctioning, bugging, and dying in the field. So if you want to get serious about patterning the deer you hunt, do yourself a favor and get one of the best trail cameras available. Actually, get a few of them.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#43. The Future Wild

In Spain’s emptying countryside, nature is moving back in.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

I was on the trail of abandonment, particularly what follows when humans leave the countryside, which is happening not just in Spain, but across Europe, and

#44. Hike These 6 Endangered Trails Before It’s Too Late

A hiker gazes at the massive stone bridges in Coyote Gulch (Photo: kojihirano via Getty)

From the border wall complicating access to long trails’ southern termini to the potential repeal of the Roadless Rule, nature, wildlife, and public lands are currently facing unprecedented threats. The White House has already stripped national monuments’ protections. Wildernesses that have been safe from roadway construction could soon be torn up for vehicle access. And ecosystems around the country are threatened by potential new mining operations sprouting up in remote, pristine areas.

Without significant changes, many trails across the country stand to be changed forever—whether by construction, resource extraction, or other types of development. Here’s a small sample of endangered trails worth seeing—and fighting for—now.

Location: Northern Minnesota Distance: 39 miles, point-to-point Elevation gain: 3,681 feet

Why it’s threatened: In April, the Trump administration rolled back a 20-year federal mining ban in the Boundary Waters. The move could open large parts of this region to sulfide-ore and copper-nickel mining.

This rugged, challenging trek crosses an impressive stretch of wilderness. It requires some logistics and planning, but the views and solitude are mythic. Hikers pass more than a dozen lakes, meaning water sources are abundant, and designated campsites are rarely far from the main trail.

Start at the Snowbank Trailhead outside Ely, MN, and finish your trek at the Kekekabic Trailhead East on Gunflint Trail. You’ll have to arrange a shuttle or pickup to get back to your car or into town.

Location: Southern Utah Distance: 20 miles, point-to-point Elevation gain: 1,293 feet

Why it’s threatened: The protective boundaries of Bears Ears National Monument were reduced in July by 90 percent, potentially opening it to extractive industries like mining or drilling.

Grand Gulch is a mesmerizing red-rock canyon wilderness in southern Utah. Hidden among the sprawling canyons is a vast record of human history in the form of Ancestral Puebloan dwelling sites and rock art. These cultural treasures lie far from paved roads, deep in what was once part of the National Monument, making this trail a mesmerizing one for backpackers willing to go far.

Kane Gulch to Government Trailhead is one optional route that winds along the bottom of Grand Gulch, then exits Bullet Canyon to Government Trailhead. You’ll need to self-shuttle back up the road to the starting point, so be sure to plan your ride.

Location: Southern Utah Distance: 6.5 miles, loop Elevation gain: 659 feet

Why it’s threatened: At the same time the Trump administration shrank Bears Ears, it also shrank Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument, potentially opening it up to mining and drilling as well.

For unparalleled desert adventure in classic southern Utah slot canyons, head to Peekaboo and Spooky Slot Canyons in what was once GSENM. What this day hike lacks in elevation change, it makes up for with picturesque canyon walls, technical stretches of trail, and more than a few potholes where you’re likely to get your feet wet.

Sections are exceedingly narrow—even backpacks can make for a tight squeeze—and the road in can be rough. However, the rock formations and magical light deep in the canyons are worth the trouble. Start at Lower Dry Fork Trailhead and loop Spooky Slot Canyon and Dry Fork Trails.

Location: Arizona (Mexico to Utah) Distance: 800 miles, point-to-point Elevation gain: 102,772 feet

Why it’s threatened: Border wall construction along the Arizona-Mexico Border this April closed the trail’s final mile.

This long trail traverses Arizona’s entire length from its southern border with Mexico to its northern border with Utah. It crosses deserts, multiple mountain ranges, canyons, forests, the North and South Rims of the Grand Canyon, and many unique communities along its 800 miles. It’s a stunning route that requires relatively advanced desert backpacking and logistics planning skills.

However, there is currently no southern terminus. The final mile between Montezuma Pass in Coronado National Memorial and the border is indefinitely closed for border wall construction, preventing hikers from celebrating their accomplishment at the iconic terminus monument. The Continental Divide Trail suffers from the same problem, leaving hikers and trail associations scrambling to identify alternative endpoints.

Location: Georgia to Maine Distance: 2,200 miles, point-to-point Elevation gain: 464,500 feet

Why it’s threatened: The Roadless Rule is a 2001 federal conservation policy that protects millions of acres of undeveloped National Forest System lands from road construction and timber harvesting. The federal government is currently trying to repeal it. That would open huge swaths of remote wilderness to construction, new traffic, and logging activity.

The Appalachian Trail is one of the world’s most famous long trails. It passes through 14 states from Georgia to Maine and offers a wide range of landscapes, wildlife, environments, and cultures. From rolling green hills to rocky climbs to snow-dusted mountains, the AT takes the average thru-hiker six months to complete. It’s a route that’s inspired many adventurers and more stories for Backpacker over the years than we can count.

But if the Trump administration continues its push to rescind the Roadless Rule, some 45 million acres of national forests would be open to roadbuilding and logging. Numerous portions of the Appalachian Trail pass through roadless areas that are now threatened, including segments through Bald Mountain National Roadless Area, Lance Creek and Beaver Dam Creek Roadless Areas, Mount Rogers and Whitetop Mountain Fringe, and more.

Location: Tumalo Roadless Area Distance: 7.2 miles, out-and-back Elevation gain: 1,128 feet

Why it’s threatened: Repeal of the Roadless Rule

The Tumalo Roadless Area is sometimes called the “heart of Bend, Oregon’s drinking watershed.” It abounds with waterfalls, and this trail in particular takes hikers past dozens of them. It winds deep through old-growth forests populated with pine, hemlock, spruce, and fir trees. Following the creeks, hikers will find one successive cascade after another.

The Tumalo Falls Day Use Area is just 11 miles east of Bend. It’s a popular spot, especially on summer and fall weekends. But once you get a few miles in, crowds thin, and you have the trail, the creeks, and waterfalls mostly to yourself. This 14,829-acre Roadless Area protects drinking water for more than 100,000 people, according to Oregon Wild. It’s also a pristine place for hiking, backpacking, and outdoor recreation.

#45. 20 Years Ago, Reel Rock Set Out to Make Climbing Films More Interesting Than “Watching a Car Rust”

Josh Lowell shows Chris Sharma some freshly shot footage in Céüse, France, circa 2006. (Photo: Courtesy Nick Rosen / Sender Films)

When this year’s Reel Rock premieres at the Boulder Theater on Thursday, October 22, it will officially mark the twentieth lap across the screens of mountain town theaters and climbing gym walls.

The three founders—Peter Mortimer, Nick Rosen, and Josh Lowell—met at Colorado College in Colorado Springs in the early aughts. Originally, they wanted to create an annual film tour for climbers like Warren Miller or the annual Teton Gravity Research set does for skiers.

Their first official film, First Ascent: The Movie, explored various pioneering exploits on rock. They followed Didier Berthod on Cobra Crack (5.14) and Dean Potter on Epitaph (5.13b). Their cameras rolled as David Lama put up deep water solo FAs in Thailand and locals sent untouched lines in the Black Canyon. And they captured Timmy O’Neill “doing Urban Ape-style climbs,” as Rosen puts it, referencing O’Neill’s moniker in Reel Rock films.

Two decades later, Rosen sees the Reel Rock filmmaking ethos as one that defies an old analogy that watching climbing is about as entertaining as observing a car rust. “What Pete and Josh started, and what we developed from there, was the idea of character- and story-driven films about climbers,” Rosen told Climbing. “Climbing really benefited from that because watching raw climbing can be slow. Josh brought cutting, shooting, and editing climbs to a new level to make them as exciting as possible.”

Alongside Reel Rock, Sender Films, the production company behind the tour, has also put out a number of award-winning documentaries, from The Alpinist to Valley Uprising. Most recently, the team brought The Dark Wizard to life on HBO this year. The four-part docuseries about the complicated and troubled life of free soloist and BASE jumper Dean Potter stirred controversy and won acclaim. Rosen says more unflinching documentaries like Potter’s are in the works.

Two decades in, we caught up with two of the three Reel Rock guys. We asked Rosen and Mortimer about their favorite films, how their approach to filmmaking has evolved over time, and what the future of Reel Rock looks like.

Peter Mortimer: We’ve made maybe 100 short films for Reel Rock over the years. The biggest challenge is keeping the films fresh, finding unexpected stories, unlikely characters, unreal climbs, surprising relationships. We’re always looking for that special something. Over the years, we’ve worked with more filmmakers and cinematographers to document the climbing journey, but in the end the spirit of the films is the same: Go deep, capture the magic, and bring the story to life.

Nick Rosen: In recent years, our films have gone beyond climbing into broader social ideas. For instance, in 2019, we started filming a group of African American climbers from Memphis Rocks expanding beyond the gym into ice climbing. That film came out during the Black Lives Matter movement and felt very resonant. The following year, we told a story about climbers in the West Bank of Palestine, which made a huge impact on our audience. We also filmed Ukrainian climbers holding a competition in Kyiv during bombings.

Rosen: Resistance Climbing is high on the list. Another standout is Point of No Return. Over 20 years, we’ve faced real tragedies during production. In 2008 in China, an avalanche killed our close friends: Jonny Copp, Micah Dash, and our 21-year-old crew member Wade Johnson.

It was devastating. Three years into filmmaking, I considered quitting entirely. But making Point of No Return helped us and the community process grief, offering context and closure through art.

Mortimer: I’m gonna go with an obscure one: United States of Joe’s, which tells the story of bouldering’s development in Joe’s Valley, Utah and how climbing came head-to-head with the local Mormon mining community. It’s a feel-good film about people from different walks of life building bridges to make the place better for everyone.

Rosen: That happened often because we committed to uncertain stories dependent on weather and injuries. A million things that can go wrong.

Mortimer: Oh man, there are so many. We’ve supported various expeditions over the years, where climbers were shut down by weather, conditions, or other outside factors. It’s tricky supporting expeditions because they’re so high-consequence, the motivation has to be pure, and you don’t want the climbers weighing the importance of a film crew waiting on them when making decisions.

Mortimer: Josh and Nick and the crew are basically my closest friends and we’ve worked together for 20-plus years now. We’re all opinionated and disagree on things, but we also respect each other creatively and appreciate what the others bring to the table whenever we don’t see eye to eye. I, in particular, tend to have a pretty overbearing intense personality (I’ve been told) and these guys are good at rolling their eyes when I drink too much coffee.

Rosen: It’s like a marriage, so we’ve had heated creative arguments over the years. As we get older, our egos get less in the way.

Mortimer: Definitely not with us running it. It’s so hard to make these films good every year, we put so much of ourselves into it and we’re totally gutted for weeks or months afterwards. We fantasize about young filmmakers taking over and carrying the torch, taking it in new directions, keeping it relevant for future generations, but so far that’s not happening. We all have kids—maybe some of them will catch the bug.

Rosen: I’ll be like 78 years old. We’d love for Reel Rock to continue, but someone has to make the films. Every year, we ask if there’s more to say, but new generations push limits and diversify the sport. The evolving culture keeps compelling us to document it. Twenty years later, we are still drawn to telling these stories.

The global Reel Rock tour kicks off in October and runs through the fall. You can watch the trailer above and check out some stories behind the films of Reel Rock 20 this year below.

In June, the Slovenian legend became the second woman to climb the penultimate grade on the scale: 5.15c/9b+. After sending Bibliographie in Céüse, France, Janja Garnbret struck filmmaker Jon Glassberg—who directed the film—as still having “way more in the tank.”

“I was genuinely scared of getting stuck there,” Colin Haley told Climbing last September. He was referring to a vertical crevasse of sorts that he had to squeeze through to reach the summit. He said it was the “craziest tunneling experience” he’d ever had. See the mind-boggling photos and get the soloist’s story.

Born with spina bifida, Ben Mayforth spent 42 days working Slim Shady (5.13)—and finally got it. While we didn’t cover the ascent that’s the subject of this Reel Rock film, you can read a story we wrote about him a few years ago before you watch the film.

While the subject of the Reel Rock 20 film is Michaela Kiersch’s “global sending spree,” we will point you toward a particularly notable moment in the pro climber’s stacked 2025 resume: making the hardest first ascent by a woman in North America since Beth Rodden’s Meltdown. Kiersch FA’d Mad Lib (5.14d) on a trip to Vermont last September.

#46. Seven Alpine-Style Climbs Happening Now in Nepal

Several small teams are attempting difficult climbs on Nepal’s 6,000 and 7,000m peaks. Unfortunately, they rarely report on their plans or progress until they return, and often only if they succeed.

This is what we know about the ongoing expeditions:

Three young French climbers, members of the Military High Mountain Group from Chamonix, celebrated their organization’s 50th anniversary with a new route on Peak 41. This 6,654m mountain is located in the Khumbu region and is often called the “true Mera Peak.”

Konrad Piontek, Amaury Fouillade, and Clovis Paulin took advantage of a good weather window and achieved the first ascent of the peak’s northeast face. They climbed in an alpine-style single push over four days. The result is a beautiful 1,400m line with difficulties up to ED+ 5+ M6 A1 90°. They descended via the southeast face. The team named their line Bon Matin (good morning).

Nivel Meroi and Romano Benet are acclimatized and ready to attempt a new route on Jugal II, but the Italian couple will be on their own. Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, has left due to illness.

Meanwhile, in the Kangchenjunga region, a large Russian team has also finished acclimatizing. The team trekked in the area and crossed a number of high-altitude passes, the latest of them at the top of an icefall at 5,750m. They reported lots of snow above 5,000m but are ready to attempt a new route on the formidable Jannu (7,710m) from its southeast side.

The team comprises Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin.

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan traveled to Nepal in September, aiming to achieve the first ascent of Gangapurna West (7,455m), also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal. They have provided no news since, but they probably had to retreat when an intense snowstorm hit the Annapurna region three weeks ago.

Location of Gangapurna West on a Google Earth screenshot. Notes by Lindsay Griffin for the American Alpine Journal.

Meanwhile, a second team has reached the base of the peak with the same objective. Valery Shamalo, Natalia Zanina, Maksim Trufanov, and Ruslan Kirichenko arrived at the beginning of October and saw no one else there. They reported that recent precipitation had left the trail in a poor state; the climbers had to cross landslides and swollen rivers to reach base camp.

The team has completed two acclimatization climbs, looking for a passage through the icefall at the base of the mountain and then a series of couloirs. They reached 5,900m and, on a second trip, 6,600m. Deep snow covered the peak, which slowed progress. Finally, they launched a summit bid last week.

From 6,600m, they spent a day on technical ice sections of 70–80º. In poor visibility, they endured spindrift and were showered by small ice chunks.

“In the afternoon, the weather deteriorated sharply,” Natalia Zanina said. “Heavy snowfall began, and we started being struck by large, continuous avalanches. At 6,800m (340m from the summit), we decided to turn back.”

A note on names: according to 8000ers.com, Asapurna should be the correct name for this peak because — although it is closer to Gangapurna — Asapurna’s summit ridge connects directly to Annapurna III.

The list of climbing permits granted by Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism points to some other interesting expeditions, some of them in remote western Nepal. There is a permit for Nyalu Kang (6,265m), only opened to foreign climbers in 2024 and reportedly unclimbed, and Ardang, summited once by Canadians Bryce Kendall and Sunny Twelker in 2019. Victor Saunders and Mick Fowler of the UK attempted Ardang last year.

#47. Why 5 Days of Heat Training May Be Enough

In a perfect world, we’d spend the month (or more) leading up to toasty races like the Javelina Jundred training to handle the heat. Actually, in a perfect world, we would heat train all year round to reap the potential physiological rewards, such as increased plasma volume, and maybe even improved Vo2 max and lactate threshold.

But we’re not all pros with flexible schedules and not everyone lives in the Arizona desert, where the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit.

The last thing any of us want is to succumb to hot conditions, much less end up in the med tent, because we were too busy for heat training. But many heat training protocols call for weeks and even months of heat sessions to induce positive physiological adaptations; time we don’t often have to spare while juggling work, sleep, family obligations, and the ever-important logging of miles.

So when I found out that endurance gravel cyclist Metheven Bond claimed he managed to acclimate to the heat in only 5 days, I was curious: Can runners implement a similar protocol?

Off his 5-day protocol, Bond rode for 43 hours and 6 minutes with no sleep through the sweltering desert of Eastern Andalusia to finish sixth overall in The Badlands. If you’re unfamiliar with the gravel cycling race, Badlands runs some 507 miles across the Gorafe and Tabernas deserts in Spain,where temperatures regularly exceed 104 F.

To find out exactly what he did and how it may apply to runners, I spoke with Bond himself, as well as Aline Barre, a competitive ultra-cyclist and triathlete with a master’s degree in Sports Performance Analysis, and Daniel Snape, Ph.D., a performance physiologist, accredited sport and exercise scientist, and researcher in endurance and environmental physiology.

Earlier this year, Bond, who races for Ribble Outliers gravel cycling team, competed in some hot races in Spain and Switzerland. Temperatures reached nearly 97 degrees.

“I fell apart even though I thought I did everything right,” he told Trail Runner. “I froze all of my bottles and was drinking over a liter an hour for hydration, but my power still dropped off a cliff, my heart rate was through the roof, and I couldn’t think properly. I knew it was from the heat.”

Racing in hot conditions can compromise endurance capacity, and, as Bond discovered the hard way, it’s not always enough to rely on mid-race cooling. “I needed to find ways to adapt so the heat bothers me less, so I looked into heat acclimation.”

The goal of heat acclimation is to cause adaptations that allow the body to more effectively function in high temps. That process involves exposing the body to hot conditions that cause core body temperature to rise. Done long and consistently enough adaptations can include a lowered heart rate and body temperature, a higher sweat rate, improved performance, and better heat resilience.

“Before Badlands, I looked at the weather forecast and knew the heat was going to be bad. I’m in the North of England where it’s colder and somehow needed to get ready to be thrown into the heat,” Bond said. He visited the lab of Precision Fuel and Hydration, a sponsor of Ribble Outliers, for a focused heat training block. There, the Precision team implemented a protocol before Badlands consisting of five one-hour heat training sessions of cycling in a heat chamber set to 102 degrees over five consecutive days.

The team monitored Bond’s performance markers—such as heat transfer and skin temperature—throughout the block via sensors like the Core 2 Thermal Sensor, which mounts to any heart rate strap and transmits data in real-time to an app or wearable.

As the sessions progressed, Bond was able to push harder without a corresponding increase in cardiovascular effort. The result: Higher power output, lower average heart rate, and improved resistance to the fatigue of heat stress.

Aline Barre is a cyclist, triathlete, and endurance performance lead at Core. Like Bond, Barre had an equally unpleasant experience racing in the heat.

“My first endurance race was Ironman Frankfurt. For training, I didn’t do any running in the heat,” Barre said. “Race day was super hot and I was cooked. I was drinking a lot, but I felt horrible during the run. I was so afraid of the heat that I went to Finland for my second Ironman.”

Barre concluded the heat was holding her back—until she focused on acclimation. “Heat training is even more important for ultrarunners than endurance cyclists. In most cases, it’s easier to cycle in the heat than to run in the heat,” she said. “That’s because you move forward at a faster pace when riding a bike than running, creating substantially more airflow to help cool your skin through sweat evaporation.”

Combine this with the fact that running creates higher metabolic heat than cycling and it’s no wonder that medical teams see more cases of heat stroke at endurance running events than at cycling races. Additionally, some studies suggest that female athletes may require a slightly longer heat exposure period (10-14 days) or stronger heat stimulus relative to male athletes (seven days) to fully develop certain adaptations, particularly those related to sweating

“Most athletes see the majority of gains after 4-5 heat sessions and the full adaptation after doing 10 to 12 sessions within two to six weeks,” Barre said.

But for Bond, five days was enough. Performance physiologist and researcher Daniel Snape explains why.

“When you heat train, the main response you get is an increase in your blood plasma volume. For Bond to increase his plasma volume across those five days is a very normal and achievable response,” Snape said. Snape is part of a team of experts at the Health and Performance Hub at Leeds Beckett University. He works with professional ultrarunners like 2025 UTMB winners Tom Evans and Ruth Croft to develop specific heat acclimation strategies.

“Also you’re becoming more familiar with the heat, so your body doesn’t have that: ‘Oh no, I’ve got to increase my heart rate to cope with this stressor’ fight or flight response. That’s why five days straight was enough time for Bond to adapt and be able to hold a higher power output at a lower heart rate.”

While five days may be enough for a professional male endurance athlete who has a stellar baseline and access to a heat chamber, core body temperature sensor, and a team of experts, it might not be for many ultrarunners.

“Even I had to continue with three sessions per week of heat acclimation at home to maintain the adaptation, riding wrapped up in layers. I kept this up until a week before Badlands, when it was time to taper,” Bond said. He also points out that while significant adaptations can occur in five days, a few weeks is preferable for the mental preparation.

“The more times you train in the heat, the more confidence you have when you face it on race day,” he said. “You think: ‘Okay, it’s uncomfortable, but not as uncomfortable because I’ve been exposed to it. I’m used to this’.”

If you’re short on time and you want to have some semblance of conditioning going into Javelina or another toasty ultra, Core has a simple but mighty indoor heat training plan to build heat into your workouts with five sessions over 2 weeks. (See below.) It includes a long run where you start cool, then dress in warm layers for the last 75 minutes, as well as an easy 50-minute run where you run cool, but add a 30-minute passive heat session after.

The long run  is best done inside on a treadmill, but a smart trainer, stationary bike, or even a rowing machine will work as well. For your layers, you’ll need clothing that is non-permeable and traps heat against your body,  such as a heat suit, thermal top, down jacket, rain jacket, fleecy sweat suit, and/or wool hat. As a last resort, Bond recommends using a trash bag with holes cut out for your head and arms.

The passive heat session consists of time in a sauna, steam room, hot tub, or even the bathtub. If you’re preparing for a hot desert race, a sauna is the way to go if you can access one. Research shows that repeated post-exercise sauna sessions can enhance key components of heat adaptation, such as blood plasma volume and thermoregulatory efficiency. To prepare for a trail run in the tropics, a steam room or steamy bath are the best options.

Alternatively, you can do a micro heat training block that includes five days of only passive heat sessions immediately after your normal training runs, when your heart rate and core temperature are still elevated. According to Dr. Snape, even this can be effective at improving performance come race day.

The benefits of heat training extend beyond simply ramping up for a 100-miler under the desert sun, however.

“With the sauna for example, we know that if you do a hill workout, then go into the sauna, it has some muscle hypertrophy benefits, helping with recovery,” Snape said. “We also know that saunas improve your immune function. And if you do a sauna session late at night, it can actually improve sleep quality.”

Before starting a heat training plan, you should already be used to training for a minimum of four days per week and at least four hours of total weekly volume. You should also be able to complete a 60-to 75-minute run workout.

“You can do heat training right up until taper week. But don’t start heat training too close to your race. If you start two weeks before your race, the chance is quite high that you’ll expose your body to unnecessary fatigue because it’s not used to the heat,” Barre said. “We recommend starting four to five weeks out. During heat sessions, monitor your skin temperature, sweat rate, and heart rate so you don’t overdo it or get a heat illness, which can be life-threatening if you’re not careful. And hydrate before, during, and after heat sessions.”

It’s important to note that even if you use a Core sensor as part of your heat acclimation protocol, you can’t wear it into saunas or your bathtub at home, so there’s no way of knowing your internal body temperature during those passive sessions. As such, active and passive heat training should only be done when someone else is with you or in a nearby room.

“Any heat acclimation protocol will induce a training stress. Respect it as an additional thing to recover from,” Snape said. “That means you will have to take some training off the table elsewhere when undergoing a heat training block. That could mean cutting nine hours of running down to eight hours.”

Heat acclimation doesn’t have to be a part-time job. If you have time for 7-14 heat sessions during or after the run workouts on your training plan, you should experience full adaptations. But if you only have time for a 5-day heat adaptation block, it’s still more beneficial than not training for the heat at all, helping you develop a base adaptation that can make it mentally and physically easier to stay on pace when the heat is on.
