#49. The Biggest Myths About Deer Rifles, Cartridges, and Shooting

Published Oct 19, 2026 5:16 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Outdoor Life’s shooting editor John B. Snow cut his teeth hunting Michigan’s Northwoods in his youth. Now, all these years later, he lives in Bozeman, Montana—the beating heart of big-game hunting in the West. He shoots in precision rifle competitions and, quite frankly, is a total long-range shooting nerd.

So, I’m counting on Snow to unite the two divided camps of deer hunters: those who hunt in the big woods with grandaddy’s old rifle vs. those who hunt in open country with the latest and greatest rig. We recently sat down to discuss and dispel some of the biggest myths around deer rifles, cartridges, and shooting. As editors and deer hunters, we hear the following misconceptions all the time. Here’s why they are total B.S.

The 6.5 Creed isn’t really overrated or underrated, it’s just misunderstood. It is not an ultra-fast, flat-shooting, physics-defying, super cartridge that some of its proponents make it out to be. Likewise, it’s not some pipsqueak of a cartridge that’s incapable of cleanly killing big game and is only popular because hipsters and metrosexuals think it’s cool.

In reality, the 6.5 Creed delivers projectiles with high ballistic coefficients from a smartly designed case that embodies all the elements of modern cartridge design. While classic 6.5 cartridges can be modified to incorporate most of what the 6.5 Creedmoor brings to the table, they aren’t able to deliver the whole package. The fact is we know more about how to design a better cartridge than ballisticians did in decades past. And the 6.5 Creedmoor’s track record in competition and in the field bears that out. Over years of rigorous testing, it’s proven to be an incredibly accurate cartridge in general.

“The 6.5 Creedmoor is an extraordinarily capable big game round and is more than sufficient for any whitetail that trots across the face of North America,” says Snow, who has hunted with the 6.5 Creedmoor all over the world and killed giant eland (which can weight 2,000 pounds) with it. “It’s a wonderfully balanced and inherently accurate round. It’s easy to shoot, has relatively mild recoil, and it’s also the type of cartridge that promotes and encourages people to practice and become better marksmen.”

In other words, it’s an ideal cartridge for medium-sized game like whitetail deer.

“Most people think about performance purely in terms of muzzle velocity,” Snow says. “They’ll say ‘well, this cartridge spits out this bullet faster, therefore it is a better performer.’ But that’s not a very sophisticated way of looking at performance. There’s more that goes into it than just muzzle velocity.”

Read Next: Why Small Cartridges Are So Effective for Big Game

“I’ve been guilty of using the term ‘knockdown power’ in the past, but that’s really a misunderstanding of terminal ballistics,” says Snow. “There’s no such thing as knockdown power with a cartridge.”

That’s because bullets kill in only two ways: they take out the central nervous system (a shot to the spine or brain), or through blood loss through tissue damage (known as exsanguination).

“How the bullet behaves within the target and also where that bullet is placed in the target define how effectively a bullet kills. The bullet doesn’t knock the animal down,” Snow says. “So if you start to think of the terminal effectiveness of a cartridge in those terms, it kind of shifts it a little bit too. Bullets that are a little smaller, driven at moderate velocities can do as much damage, in some cases even more, than a big boomer.”

But what about that time you watched granddaddy drop that big 10 pointer in its tracks with one shot from his old .30-06? Isn’t that knockdown power?

Actually, no. Animals will drop for a variety of reasons, but they’re not being knocked off their feet. Plus, every shooting scenario is unique. Sometimes a well-hit animal will run 100 yards before dropping (even if it was hit by granddaddy’s old .30-06). These personal experiences in the field all serve as impactful anecdotes, which work to form strong opinions among hunters, but they are not useful data.

Read Next: Debunking the Infamous Rifle Knockdown Power Myth

OL staff writer Tyler Freel did an in-depth test on the “brush busting bullets,” which you can read about here: The Best Brush Busting Bullets Put to the Test. His takeaways were pretty straight forward: the .45-70 Govt. is by far the best busting round; and mono-metal, copper bullets (like Black Hills’ HoneyBadger) deflected the least when shot through brush.

With that said, all bullets did deflect to some degree. And since most deer hunters aren’t shooting .45-70 these days, none of us should shoot through brush if we can avoid it.

“Except for very rare circumstances [like for a follow-up shot] we should not be shooting through brush at all,” Snow says. “It will deflect and possibly damage the bullet and introduce all sorts of vectors of chaos into the shot. Even with the .45-70 I wouldn’t take that initial shot through the brush.”

They just don’t make rifles like they used to—they make them much better.

“Look at the introduction of precision CNC machining, which is now commonplace in the gun industry,” Snow says. “It’s allowed companies, large and small, to manufacture barrels and actions to such a degree of perfection that you can literally buy the components yourself, screw them together and have a really high performing rifle. Whereas if you look at a classic Remington 700 from back in the day, their ability to control even the head spacing on the barrel was so poor that they would have a series of bolts to try to mix and match to get it to close correctly on the gauges they used to deem the rifle in our out of spec.”

But there is one thing that those old wood-stocked deer rifles did have going for them: craftsmanship and hand checkering.

“One of the things that’s been sad to see is that we have lost some of the craftsmanship, specifically in terms of checkering and nice wood stocks,” Snow says. “There’s still high-end gunmakers doing really nice checkering, but it is a bit of a dying art. We don’t have the benefit of that with our modern guns as everything has gone toward synthetics or in some cases laminates. The checkering such as you do see if often executed by machine and it looks ok—but you can tell that it’s been done by machine.”

Choosing the best deer cartridge used to be an important task. But today, bullet selection is really more important than cartridge selection.

“People do talk about cartridge selection a lot and certainly back in the day—rewind the clock 30 or 40 years—and we had a good variety of cartridges and a really minimal selection of bullets,” Snow says. “And those bullets weren’t very good, for the most part. Now we have these amazing bullets to choose from, which have cropped up in the last 20 years. So when looking at a hunting scenario, the bullet selection question really trumps the cartridge question. There are certain types of scenarios when one cartridge will outperform another, but take out the extremes and it comes down to bullet selection. And, we’re lucky for that to be the case.”

Many rifle companies promise “sub-MOA accuracy” out of the box and some will even send you a shot target with group that measures under an inch. But as Snow wrote about last month, those sub-MOA guarantees don’t really mean much.

“I think the whole obsession with the targets and the sub-MOA stuff has really clouded the reality of what even competition shooters need, let alone deer hunters,” Snow says. “We shoot thousands of rounds through dozens of guns every year [for review of the best rifles]. We have our 5-shot-group protocol, so we have a huge data set to look at. And really, with most hunting rifles and common factory ammo, if it shoots 1.25-inch, 5-shot groups, it’s a damn good rifle.”Plus, a rifle is only as accurate as the hunter who’s shooting it. So spend less time worrying about your deer rifle’s theoretical accuracy, and more time practicing for better accuracy in the field.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

#53. Australian Grandfather Attempts 1,650Km River Swim

Australian grain farm manager Scott Gladman, 63, is attempting to swim the length of the Darling River, Australia’s third-longest river. It begins in New South Wales and finishes at its confluence with the Murray River at Wentworth. Gladman believes he will be the first person to swim the entire 1,650km route.

Gladman started on September 1 from near Brewarrina in far north New South Wales. At the outset, he budgeted 103 days to complete the swim, averaging around 16km per day. So far, he is largely on track. After 49 days, he has covered 660km, leaving just under 1,000km to go.

Interestingly, the expedition is not born from a love of endurance swimming. Gladman was inspired to find a fundraising challenge to support friends impacted by Motor Neuron Disease and Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, a rare form of Parkinson’s. Initially, he considered the Murray. “I just thought I could swim the Murray River, but people have done that,” he told ABC News. “No one has had a crack at the Darling.”

The location of the Darling River in Australia. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Gladman gave himself 18 months to train. In the summer, he swam in the Murray River at Boundary Bend, Victoria, and during winter he completed laps in indoor pools. Now out on the Darling, a support boat of family and friends keeps him company, alongside a canoeist.

“There’s no real form of communication, and I wear earplugs…he’ll [the canoeist] either have to hit me on the back of the head with a paddle to get my attention, or he’ll just start steering toward me, and that will push me one way or the other,” Gladman said.

Despite its length, the Darling River is sometimes so shallow that Gladman needs to float through sections on his back, or walk. The support boat also sometimes requires saving, with Gladman having to help clear a path through river debris:

#54. 3 Dead After Avalanche Sweeps Backcountry Mountaineers Into Lagoon in Chile

Laguna del Inca, Ski Portillo, Chile (Photo: Getty Images)

Three people were killed and four more injured on Saturday, Oct. 17 when an avalanche swept a group of seven into Laguna del Inca near Ski Portillo, Chile.

The group was mountaineering toward the summit of Cerro Los Tres Hermanos when they triggered a slab avalanche, according to information released by Ski Portillo management. The resort’s rescue team and Chilean Carabineros police responded within 10 minutes, rescuing four survivors and transporting them by helicopter to Los Andes Hospital.

The tragedy occurred amid unusual spring snowfall in the central Andes, where rising temperatures have increased avalanche danger as the snowpack becomes less stable. In a statement, Ski Portillo General Manager Miguel Purcell expressed condolences to the victims and their families. He also said the group had entered an unpermitted area outside the ski resort that was heavily signed as an avalanche danger zone. Ski Portillo had closed for the season on Oct. 11, nearly a week before the accident, and resort personnel had warned the group earlier that morning against traveling into the backcountry, according to Portillo management.

The avalanche came at the end of an exceptionally snowy season in Chile’s central Andes. After a slow start, a series of powerful winter storms delivered record-breaking accumulations at several resorts. Portillo reported nearly 40 feet of snowfall for the season—well above its historical average of about 17 feet—while heavy late-season snow prompted nearby Valle Nevado to extend operations into November, an unprecedented move in the resort’s 38-year history.

#55. I’ve Hunted All Around the World, But This Was the Single Most Difficult Hunt of My Life

Published Oct 19, 2026 5:01 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The hands pouring a hot cup of coffee shook. The fingers, more crooked than I recalled. The aging man looked at me, smiled, and kept pouring. Slowly my cup filled.

I’d just got in from a 25 mile boat ride down Alaska’s Egegik River. I was cold.

“As you can see, I’m not doing that great,” said Bruce Hallingstad as he returned to his seat at the rickety, wooden table, across from me. “Don’t think I’m going to be able to make it up river to camp this year.”

My heart sank. After all, I’d come to Alaska to hunt with Bruce. It was going to be our last moose hunt, together.

Bruce is the longtime owner of Becharof Outfitters (becharof.com). We met 19 years prior, when he invited me to film a couple episodes for an outdoor TV show I hosted. Back then, coho and ptarmigan were our targets. A few years later I hunted fall brown bear in the same area with him. Four years after that we took the biggest brown bear of my life, a 10’ 9” behemoth.

In 2017 a buddy and I joined Hallingstad for a moose hunt up the King Salmon River, northeast of the village of Egegik. We shot two exceptional bulls. At that time my back problems had intensified. I struggled to even walk, let alone pack meat. I figured it would be the last moose hunt of my life. But two back surgeries later, I felt like a new man.

“I’m thinking of selling the operation in a year or two, so why don’t you come up for one last moose hunt this fall, just you and me,” Bruce offered last spring. He had battled some health issues, himself and now he wasn’t faring as well as we’d hoped when we’d set our plans in the spring.

“Don’t worry, I’ll have you head up to Carl’s camp for your moose,” Bruce continued as we sipped coffee, gazing out the big window overlooking Alaska’s Egegik Bay. From the old house I could see where many fond memories were made.

“There are two clients in that camp, so you can help them out, pack meat, and when they’re done you’ll hunt,” Bruce said. “It’s our farthest camp upriver, lots of moose move through later in the season, as the rut approaches. Fifteen days will be plenty.”

The day before the moose opener, Carl Adams, Tom Roll—another stud of a guide—myself and two clients, Peter and Stan, arrived in moose camp. The 23 mile boat ride quickly passed. “Okay guys, we’re camping in thick alders and moose can be around us at any given time,” Adams said before we hopped out of the boat. “We need to whisper all the time and be sure to have your rifle because brown bears are thick in here.”

Both clients were well into their 70s. It was their first time to Alaska. Peter was nearly deaf. Stan, not much better. Every word they spoke was just below a shout. “Guys, inside voices, remember,” Carl encouraged more than a half dozen times in the first hour.

I glassed nonstop for 13 hours each of the first three days. In that time, Peter spent less than an hour looking for moose. He stayed in the cook tent, drinking coffee and talking to anyone who walked by.

On the evening of day two, Adams spotted a big bull across the river. “Peter, you’ll want to come take a look at this bull,” he said. It was 8:00 p.m. Peter had been in bed for an hour. An hour of daylight still remained. “Is it big?” Peter asked. “He’s pushing 60 inches,” Adams replied. “Is that good?” Peter wondered.

Adams went to Peter’s tent and whispered, “Get your waders on, we can cross the river and sneak to within 300 yards of the bull, maybe even shoot it on the river bank.”

“I’ll just shoot it tomorrow,” Peter replied.

Adams tried to urge Peter to change his mind as he knew the opportunity at stake, with three tags to fill. “Stan, do you want to shoot it?” Adams asked. “Oh no, I’ll keep going on boat rides up river with Tom; any bull around camp, Peter can shoot.”

My spotting scope was set up so I captured several photos of the big bull, along with some videos. “Here, go show this to Peter, that’ll make him get up,” I whispered to Carl as I handed him my phone.

But the hunter’s response was, “I’ll just look at it tomorrow,” not even unzipping the tent fly.

The bull got to 517 yards. I had my rifle set solid in the tripod shooting sticks and the scope on 18x. “Peter, all you have to do is come out of the tent, walk 15 steps, shoot Scott’s gun, and you’ll have your dream Alaska moose,” Adams tried convincing him, one last time. “That’s too far,” Peter answered. Adams sensed my frustration.

“That’s part of being a guide,” Carl shrugged. “It’s the client’s hunt, not mine. Sometimes these hunts aren’t about filling a tag.”

The next morning Peter drank coffee and talked loud as ever for three hours. I sat on a knob glassing for moose nearly 200 yards away and could hear every word he uttered. Tom took Stan to another spot by boat that morning. Not until almost 10:30 a.m. did Peter ask about the bull from the previous night. When I finally showed him the video, Peter said, “Wow that’s big but I don’t really care if I kill a moose, I’m just here to have fun and hang out with you guys.”

“I’m not shooting a moose until you two tag out, and that bull cost us valuable time,” I responded. “There’ll be more,” Stan hollered, stumbling back to the cook tent, tipping the bottom of his coffee cup skyward.

That afternoon, Stan told me he didn’t care if he killed a bull, either. Here were two clients paying $30,000 each to hunt moose and they didn’t care if they shot a bull. As a full time outdoor writer of nearly 30 years whose career has been built on consistently killing game, it put me in a bad place.

All of Hallingstad’s moose camps are equipped with Starlink. Having lived for several years in remote Alaska, and traveled much of the state for the past 36 years, I think it’s safe to say that this technological advancement is a game changer. It greatly alleviates the stress of being out of touch with family and it increases people’s safety in many ways.

On day five, I was glassing for moose from camp when I got a call from Bruce. “Elise just got her hunter a bull, so I’m going to have you move down with her,” he shared. I was elated.

Elise Adams is Carl’s daughter. She’s 23 years old and had just finished nursing school, where she graduated at the top of her class. I’ve known Elise since she was four years old and I watched her grow up on the Egegik River. She runs her own commercial fishing boat, has guided salmon anglers for nearly a decade, and successfully guided hunters to six brown bears in recent years, including two over 10 feet. This was her first solo guided moose hunt, and she was the first in five camps to tag out.

Before I could hang up the phone with Hallingstad, I got a call from Tiffany, my wife, who was back home in Oregon. I ignored it. She immediately called again. I was still getting details from Hallingstad. Then Tiffany texted me. “Call me NOW!”

She was bawling and could hardly speak. I feared something had happened to one of our two sons, or our aging parents. “It’s Kona, he has stomach twist and they have to put him down.”

Kona, our prized Pudelpointer, was in his prime, only 10 years old. I’d hunted with his dad, Lon, the most decorated Pudelpointer ever to set foot on American soil. Until Kona, Lon was the best dog I’d hunted with. Kona ran circles around anything Lon ever did. He was that once-in-a-lifetime dog for me, and I’ve owned a number of them. Most were good. Kona was exceptional.

Kona survived stomach twist when he was four. We were minutes away from losing him, then. This time it struck in the intestines. Though Tiff got Kona to the vet with plenty of time, no tests, or even x-rays, pointed toward torsion. By the time it was figured out, it was too late.

I spent the next two days in my tent, alone. I didn’t want to see or talk to anyone. I tried getting home but couldn’t because the river was too rough to navigate in the extreme winds. I cried more than I can ever recall. I couldn’t eat for two days. An 80-inch moose could have stood outside my tent and I couldn’t have cared less.

I don’t know what was worse, knowing Tiffany was dealing with Kona, alone, or being helplessly stranded in isolated Alaska. I’ve survived sinking boats, a downed bush plane, a submerged Argo, getting lost in storms and being stuck for days in 45º below zero temperatures in total darkness. But this was the most desolate Alaska had ever felt. I’d never felt so helpless and trapped by the wilderness.

Carl consoled me. He was right, being a guide is about more than just filling a tag.

Finally, two days later, conditions calmed and Elise made it upriver to get me. By now, the last place I wanted to be was home. I wanted to hold my wife, but I couldn’t yet face being home without Kona. He was always at my side, his spirits high. He knew what I was going to do before I did it. We spent every day together. He hunted for upland birds, waterfowl, sheds, squirrels and was great at it all. It is not an exaggeration to say that he was my best hunting partner.

“I’m so sorry about your dog,” Peter told me in a firm voice as I left camp, putting his hand on my shoulder. “People don’t realize how hard it is losing a truly special dog,” he continued. “My wife recently passed away, then, right after that, my dog of 14 years did too. It was the best hunting dog a man can ask for,” he told me. “It’s hard but you’ll make it through this.”

That’s when I realized that amid my selfishness of trying to get a moose, I’d failed to hear Peter’s full story.

“Now, go get a big bull,” Peter said. “I don’t care if I shoot one.”

That afternoon, Elise was preparing dinner when my wife texted me with more news. “She’s okay, but your mom is in the hospital with heart issues. She’s getting ready for a long surgery. Send prayers.”

By now our oldest son had flown home to be with Tiffany. Between them and my dad, Tiff’ assured me they had things under control and that there was nothing I could do, even if I was there. “Just do what you need to do to get through this,” she followed up. Tiffany is the strongest, most caring woman I’ve ever met. We’ve endured a lot, together.

After dinner, Elise and I hiked to a high point to glass until dark. Exactly 2.18 miles away, we saw a bull moose with the naked eye. It was standing across an expansive, marshy flat and its white antlers looked like two sheets of plywood. “That’s the biggest bull I’ve ever seen,” Elise said. I agreed.

“If you’re up for it, we’ll be here at daylight, try to find that bull, then make a move on it,” Elise suggested.

The next morning we found the bull, half the distance away as the evening prior. It was in a swamp surrounded by 30-foot-tall alders. “It’s impossible to get close to that thing in this wind,” Elise said. “Let’s watch and try to see where it goes.”

After 15 minutes, the bull lay down. We watched the spot for 12 hours but never saw it move.

The following day, the bull was closer to where we’d first seen it. “Let’s get Greg and go after that thing,” Elise decided. I again agreed with my young guide.

Greg Zackar is a native kid from the village of Igiugig, Alaska, near Lake Iliamna. Elise comes from a native lineage, too.

This was a dream I so wanted to relive. I needed it.

In 1989, I went to dinner with Tiffany. We grew up together, had known each other since first grade. Our parents and grandparents went to school together. We were fresh out of college, each with teaching degrees. “What are you going to do now,” Tiffany asked. “I’m moving to Arctic Alaska to teach and learn to hunt and fish with the Eskimos,” I told her. (That was a politically correct term back then, in fact, they were proud to be recognized as such). “Well, you better do it now while you’re single because no woman will ever follow you up there,” she replied.

Four months later, we were engaged. Four months after that, we were married and living in Point Lay, Alaska, a village of fewer than 100 Inupiat people at the time. That was 36 years ago.

For the next seven years, I hunted, fished, and trapped with the indigenous people of the high Arctic. Those were some of the most memorable times of my life. The outdoors connected our two worlds. We shared a common passion in a harsh, yet glorious part of the world that few people will ever truly understand. Out there, the genuine nature of the native peoples shone. They’re among the most caring, giving, hard-working cultures I’ve met. Elise and Greg carried the same values.

Moose or no moose, just being with those two kids helped heal me. Many hours were spent glassing, exchanging only smiles. That’s what I needed. No words. No condolences. Just an occasional, heartfelt smile I knew meant something.

Following a five-mile boat ride and a four-mile hike, Elise, Greg, and I were glassing for the bull from an elevated knoll. We eventually spotted it in the bottom of the swamp, 1.4 miles away. We hiked over 12 miles that day in some of the most demanding terrain imaginable. I’ve been fortunate to make a living hunting big game around the world. Of all the habitats I’ve been in, the tundra ranks as the most challenging to navigate. More times than not, it’s simply impassable. This was one of those times.

On the last of our seven days together, the wind was finally right to make a move on the big bull. We towed a raft downriver, paddled 1.25 miles up a slough, hiked another mile through a bog and dense alders, and got to where we’d last seen the bull. Fresh rakes on tattered alders were prevalent, and the stench of bull urine in multiple dry wallows permeated the air. Then the winds picked up.

In a matter of minutes, swirling gusts up to 40 mph left us helpless. We tried calling, but the wind was too powerful. We hiked in circles amid thick alders, trying to locate the bull. With visibility through the dense cover being less than 15 yards most of the time, our efforts were futile.

Read Next: My Greatest Day in 30 Years of Guiding Backcountry Hunts

We’d put all our efforts into one bull and came up empty. I could have shot two lesser bulls, but didn’t. One hunter in camp shot the first bull, a 60-incher that appeared tiny compared to the monster we were after. Carl informed us Peter had shot a bull on day 10, and Stan filled his tag on day 12. I was happy for them.

Returning home to Oregon was hard, much harder than anticipated. Thankfully, my mom was recovering from heart surgery, slowly. But the house was so empty, so calm. With upland season in full swing and waterfowl season about to kick off, I felt lost. I still have Echo, Kona’s half-sister, to share hunts with. But the clock is chasing her, too. She’ll be 13 years old soon. Together, we’ll hunt when we can this season. It won’t be easy, but we’ll make the most of it. I owe that to her.

Kona took a piece of me with him. There’s a void in my heart I fear will forever remain. But he left me with so much more than what I had before he came into my life. Looking at pictures of Kona and all the adventures that we had together is painful. But those memories are what help heal me. For all who knew him, Kona made the world a better place. He made me a better man, and that’s the ultimate reward of getting to share time, be it brief, with a hunting dog you know can never be replaced.

Note: For signed copies of Scott Haugen’s best-selling book, Hunting the Alaskan High Arctic, visit scotthaugen.com.

Scott Haugen grew up in western Oregon, lived a semi-subsistence lifestyle in Alaska’s Arctic, and has traveled to more than 40 countries. Scott’s wife, Tiffany Haugen, is a nationally-known wild game and fish cookbook author.

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

#59. The Volpi FastPack 30 Might Just Convince Me to Ditch My Hipbelt

Hipbeltless packs are normally not part of how I hike. As a Backpacker editor, I’m blessed with a pretty deep gear closet, and I use most of the packs in there regularly: Burly conventional packs for gear-intensive winter and family trips, frameless ones for personal outings where I can pack as light as I want, and lightweight backpacks with a frame for anything in between. But like leaving my shelter at home or using my spork to dig a cathole, ditching the hipbelt always seemed like one of those cuts that took things a step too far.

After taking Volpi’s FastPack 30 on the trail, though, I’m reconsidering my stance. This lightweight pack—a pound flat for the Ultra version—sat comfortably on my shoulders thanks to its vest-style carry and had enough organization that I was always able to find what I needed without fumbling. Hipbeltless packs still have their downsides, and we’re looking forward to testing the FastPack 30 more. In the meantime, here are my thoughts after my first trip with it; stay tuned for our full review.

I like to go light, but I’m not the kind of person who will cut weight at any cost. There are certain things I’m not usually willing to give up when I go backpacking, and one of them is a hipbelt. I’ve used frameless packs in the past and liked them, but I haven’t used many packs without a hipbelt that I’ve really been willing to take out on my own time.

But right now, I’m on the Ice Age Trail in Wisconsin, and I am trying out a pack that I think, for one of the first times, I would use on a personal trip, and that is the Volpi FastPack. Volpi is a company from Mexico. It was made by a couple of thru-hikers who wanted to make the kind of gear that they’d like to use. And the FastPack is a really good example of that. It’s a fairly compact, frameless pack. It’s got a vest-style carry, but no hipbelt. And I found it really comfortable to use so far, surprisingly comfortable for a pack with no hipbelt.

Because it has a vest-style carry, it has pretty good storage on the shoulder straps. I’ve got a water bottle, a soft flask, in each pocket. It has a generous stuff pocket in the back where I’ve put some of the stuff I expect to need today, I’ve stuck my extra layers. And it has some side pockets good for carrying whatever. It sits fairly high on your back because it is on your shoulders rather than sitting on your hips.

There are obviously a couple of tradeoffs. With no hipbelt, it gets a little harder to carry weight, since it’s all on your shoulders. These wide straps distribute it well, but there’s a limit to how much they can do. There’s the capacity issue—this would not be a great pack for long carries. We’re out for three days, so I haven’t had to bring too much. And we also, critically, have pretty abundant water. I probably wouldn’t bring this pack to the desert or anywhere where I expected to have to carry a lot. I’ve carried two gallons of water at a time in a frameless pack, and that’s pretty rough even with a hipbelt. I wouldn’t necessarily want to do it with this one. But for trips where you’re prioritizing moving fast and don’t have to carry a lot, this is a pretty comfortable option.

One downside of using this pack is it does have a roll-top closure. It can be really inconvenient to get stuff in and out, so it’s best if your strategy is generally to pack your pack in the morning and not really open it the rest of the day. I’m hiking with a hip pack, where I’ve got my lunch and most of the stuff I expect to need. The stuff pocket in the back is where I’ve kept my rain jacket, my grid fleece, stuff I may need, but I’m probably not going to need constantly or quickly.

Obviously, as a frameless pack, you’re going to want to be really careful in how you pack this. I took the time to arrange my stuff pretty carefully to avoid barreling, and used my sleep system to eat up the extra space, so it’s sitting pretty comfortably on me right now.

There are some good attachment points on the pack for keeping some gear that you may not want to put inside the pack. You can see I’ve got my sleeping pad sitting on the top. There’s a really easy buckle and strap closure to put it there. And I’m not using it right now, but there are also nice attachment points for trekking poles, if you don’t want to use your trekking poles for a while.

All in all, this is a really nice pack with good organization, and it sits more comfortably than you would think.

#60. Alaska to Patagonia, One Summit at a Time

Since 1972, Alaska to Patagonia has been a classic cycling route of 30,000km or more. At any given time, several ambitious cyclists are attempting it. But no one is doing it quite like Tobias Renggli of Lucerne, Switzerland.

The 23-year-old endurance athlete is not only pedaling the distance but also climbing the highest peak in each of the 35 countries he passes through. And although it’s part of the marketing rather than the adventure, the imagery so far — shot both by Renggli and by a film production group he belongs to called the Black Forest Collective — is stunning for such a difficult journey.

Despite his age, this is not Renggli’s first adventure. In 2022, at the age of 18, he cycled all 44 European countries within seven months, climbing the highest peak of each and camping every night. In 2024, he climbed the highest mountains of all 26 Swiss cantons in about three weeks.

Renggli began in April from Deadhorse, Alaska, on the shores of the Beaufort Sea — still deep winter at that latitude, though the long Arctic days had returned. Pedaling 1,200km in temperatures as low as -30˚C, he made his way to Talkeetna, then skied in for eight days while pulling a sled.

He then summited 6,190m McKinley with his occasional partner, Heli Hofmann — the first party atop the peak this year, which meant they had to break trail through the deep snow. It took them 36 days.

Next, it was onto 5,959m Mount Logan, Canada’s highest peak. Again with Heli Hofmann but no guide, they summited in late June. This time, they were the last party of the year to summit Logan.

Renggli then cycled with another friend to Vancouver, took a two-week break after covering 3,000km and summiting two of the hardest peaks he would encounter, then continued alone through the U.S. Typically, he cycles 100 to 160km per day, with some shorter days.

Unlike most Trans-America cyclists, he chose to take Baja California rather than mainland Mexico. Crossing Baja was more difficult than expected. He described temperatures exceeding 40°C and a 120km stretch toward Loreto that he began with only two liters of water.

Later, near Ciudad Insurgentes, thunderstorms flooded the roads. At night, he carried his bicycle through a fast-moving, thigh-deep flood while vehicles turned back.

Renggli had intended to take no motorized transportation, only sailboats when confronted with water — he also wants to climb 12 high points in the Caribbean. However, this is such a massive undertaking that he’s not being too strict on himself. Although he skied into Denali, for example, he flew back out to Talkeetna. And from La Paz in Baja, he caught the ferry to Mazatlan on the mainland and continued from there.

Details have been sparse since Baja, but Renggli recently crossed into Guatemala. Presumably, he climbed 5,636m Pico de Orizaba before leaving Mexico and is now headed to 4,220m Volcán Tajumulco, Guatemala’s highest peak. He has been on the road for 202 days.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#61. In Historic First, Connor Baty and Max Krieger Link 6 Zion Big Walls in Just 19 Hours

(Photo: Courtesy Connor Baty and Max Krieger)

On October 12, 2026, Connor Baty (23) of Colorado and Max Krieger (27) of Utah became the first team to link six Zion big walls in under 24 hours. They completed the enchainment in just 18 hours and 52 minutes—well under target, on their first attempt, and on the only day they had set aside to do it this season.

The linkup included Monkeyfinger (5.11 A0; 9 pitches), Lunar Ecstacy (5.10 C2+; 9 pitches), Sheer Lunacy (5.10 C2-; 8 pitches), Moonlight Buttress (5.8 C1; 10 pitches), Touchstone Wall (5.10- C2; 9 pitches), and Prodigal Sun (5.8 C2; 9 pitches). That’s 54 pitches, 5,920 feet of climbing, and 6,520 total feet of rappelling.

Prior to their attempt, the record was four walls, first completed in 1992 by Conrad Anker and Doug Heinrich, who used speed and aid tactics to link Touchstone, Moonlight Buttress, Monkey Finger, and Spaceshot (5.7 C2; 8 pitches). The last recorded attempt of five walls in a single day was in 2003, by longtime Zion climbers Ammon McNeely and Ryan McCray. Ten years later, Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell set a new speed record on the four-in-a-day, freeing Sheer Lunacy, Moonlight Buttress, Touchstone, and Spaceshot in just 16 hours. But no one, to Krieger and Baty’s knowledge, had ever attempted six.

Connor Baty first got the idea after linking Touchstone, Moonlight, and Prodigal Sun solo in October 2024. The enchainment took him 12 hours.

“Right after that, someone made a joke—‘Hey, if you can do three in 12, that means you can do six in 24,’” Baty recalls. But though he’d mentioned the idea to Krieger, one of his main wall partners at the time, the two didn’t start to make plans in earnest until late September, 2026. That’s when Baty announced he’d be in town for a two-week stopover in the midst of his year-long quest to paddle from Colorado to Mexico along the Colorado River. (He’s already back on the water; he took the call for this interview from the middle of Lake Mead.)

“Do you want to do the six?” Baty texted Krieger. Krieger’s answer was an enthusiastic yes. The only problems were that the two had just a few weeks to prepare, and their only good weather window would be on October 12—the very last day Baty would be in town before he’d need to hop back on the river.

Krieger, who works full-time as a hot air balloon pilot in St. George, asked for two days off work to practice. During that time, he and Baty did dress-rehearsal laps on Monkey Finger, Sheer Lunacy, Prodigal Sun, and about three-quarters of Touchstone. They skipped Moonlight, which Baty had already climbed 13 times. Baty then did an additional solo burn on Lunar Ecstasy to ensure that he had the gear memorized. He says he can still name just about every piece and move on the six-wall linkup in order.

Practice went well, but rain threatened their single weather window. Krieger asked for the day off anyway. Their plan was to climb as much as they could before the first drops fell.

“The logistics were pretty simple,” Krieger says. “Monkey Finger is at the end of the canyon, so we did that first and got it out of the way.” Then, they moved downcanyon, employing speed-climbing tactics for each wall, and re-upping on food and water at every base. Friend Gus Barnett crewed them through the whole attempt, providing rides and switching out racks. A fixed line on Moonlight streamlined the rappels for Sheer Lunacy, Lunar Ecstacy, and Moonlight Buttress. They saved Prodigal Sun for last.

The two split up the load by skillset: Baty, the faster aid climber, took Lunar Ecstacy, Moonlight Buttress, and Prodigal Sun, while Krieger, the stronger free climber, took Monkeyfinger, Sheer Lunacy, and Touchstone. Krieger started strong, giving the team an hour lead on their goal time for Monkeyfinger. The momentum carried, each wall going hours faster than expected.

Unfortunately, that meant they got to Sheer Lunacy well ahead of schedule, right when the wall was in full sun. Krieger, who had been dealing with dehydration cramps on and off all day, took the lead in 90-degree temperatures. By the top, he was dizzy and nauseated.

“I thought I was going to throw up—maybe a bit of heat stroke,” he says.

“He had to trooper it out,” says Baty. “He had a hard time in the heat.” Some water and a short rest got Krieger feeling well enough to follow Baty up the next wall, Moonlight. The next low didn’t come until a few walls later.

“The worst part for me was Touchstone at Sunset,” Baty says. “Max and I both hit a low when we got to the top and realized we had two more pitches left. We did not want to be up there.”

Things turned around when they found Barnett waiting at the base with slices of pepperoni pizza from Domino’s—and a handful of other friends who’d arrived to cheer them on.

“The moral support was huge,” Krieger says. “If it was just me and Connor out there, it would have been a whole lot trickier for us. Having some people to egg you on and keep you talking about things other than the climbing—that was pretty key.”

The last challenge struck about halfway up the sixth and final wall. Spiders crawled in and out of all of the placements. That was eerie enough, Baty said. Then he scared something much larger out of the crack.

“It looked like a giant chicken. It came at me, and I ended up having to fistfight this bird right around midnight on Prodigal Sun,” he says. “It kept dive-bombing me, and I [was massively runout] at that point so I was not happy.” (If you see a large splatter on his helmet in the photos, that’s why.)

The team topped out Prodigal Sun and stopped the clock at 11:52 p.m., having set a new standalone FKT for Lunar Ecstasy at 2 hours 10 minutes, as well as FKTs for the five- and six-wall enchainments. Right as Baty’s feet touched the ground after the final rappel, it started to rain.

Their time on each route, including its respective descent, is as follows:

“The reason we picked the six we picked is that those are the classics of Zion. People come to Zion, and those are the walls they go and climb. It’s like doing a season in a day,” says Krieger. In the future, he’d like to tack on the other two classics—Space Shot and Desert Shield (5.11- C3; 9 pitches)—for an eight-wall single-day linkup. “That’s something for down the road,” he says. If he hopes to do it with Baty, though, it’ll have to wait; the very next day, Baty left town for the river. He’ll be paddling for the next 30 days.

In the meantime, Krieger and Baty say they’re just proud to have added another chapter to Zion speed-climbing history.

“We wanted to set the five- and six-wall benchmark so people can see what’s possible and to bring a little more credit to Zion,” Krieger says. “It’s a pretty cool feeling to be a part of it, and it would be cool if we saw more people coming out here and trying new linkups—a new era of speed-climbing for Zion.”

#63. How to Blood Trail a Deer Properly: The Ultimate Guide to Recovering Your Buck

Published Oct 19, 2026 1:36 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Sometimes a deer will simply drop in its tracks, ending your hunt the moment you squeeze the trigger. Just as often, a deer will run out of sight and start the next chapter of your hunt. Once you touch off that shot, you’re obligated to do everything you can to recover any deer you may have hit. That’s why learning how to blood trail a deer effectively is a critical skill every deer hunter must develop. Obvious blood trails are fun to follow while unraveling more challenging tracks can prove painstaking, puzzling, disheartening, and — in the best cases — incredibly rewarding. The toughest trails will test all your woodsmanship skills. That’s why we pulled together general blood-tracking wisdom, plus handy tips to help rookies and experienced trackers alike.

Usually, you don’t need any special gear to follow a strong blood trail. Simply grab your flashlight if it’s getting dark and follow splotches of blood to a dead deer. Eventually, however, you’ll face a trickier trail. That’s when you’ll be glad you packed at least one or all of the following:

It’s also wise to save contact information for your local blood-dog tracker or a drone-recovery team (where legal) to your phone ahead of time. You might not have enough service where you’re hunting to Google tracking-dog handlers in your area, but a phone call or a text might get through with a marginal connection.

Read Next: What Data on 2,000 Blood Trails Tell Us About Broadheads, Shot Placement, and Deer Tracking

Tracking a deer starts as soon as you take your shot and doesn’t finish until you either find your deer or throw in the towel. While there are nuances to tracking a deer for bowhunters and gun hunters, these general guidelines are universal unless otherwise mentioned.

Note first how you felt during the execution of the shot, and how the deer reacted to it. Did you feel confident or did it seem like you could’ve pulled the shot? Did the deer duck the string or tear out of there? While terminal ballistics are ultimately unpredictable and so are deer, there are still some classic guidelines for assessing your hit:

Before you climb down to look for the hit site, do a little prep work to ensure you can actually find it first. Remember that if you’re hunting from an elevated blind or tree stand, everything will look different once you’re on the ground. Here are two simple ways to orient yourself first:

Once you find the hit site, analyze all the sign you find. Combine physical sign with your assessment of the shot you made.

Bubbly, frothy blood is usually the oxygenated blood of a lung hit. The more bubbles, the better. Just a few bubbles here and there can indicate a marginal lung hit, which deer can recover from if you struck a small piece of one lung.

Bright red blood can also indicate lung blood, but it also could just as easily come from a superficial muscle wound. “Bright red blood doesn’t always mean a lung shot,” says Shane Simpson, an experienced blood-dog tracker. “Bright red blood could be muscle. Blood coming from the lungs is highly oxygenated, it’s bright red and when it goes out to the different muscles in the body, it’s still bright red … You could hit a deer in the leg and the blood will be bright red.”

Dark red, maroon, or purplish blood usually indicates a liver hit. It can sometimes appear thicker than other blood.

Clear, yellow, or green slime that smells like guts means your bullet or arrow passed through the digestive track. You may even find a green slurry or undigested bits of vegetation. Sometimes you’ll find evidence of a gut shot paired with good blood in the event of a hard quartering shot.

Hair can indicate a lot of different types of hits, and is more common to find when bowhunting or if you made a near-miss with a firearm — just shaving hair but not hitting home. Identifying the type of hair can help you determine where you hit. Here’s bowhunter-ed.com’s guide to deer hair identification:

No blood doesn’t necessarily mean you missed the deer or even that you made a bad shot. Both are possibilities, but so is a perfectly lethal shot. This is when it’s especially important to consider how confident you felt at the time of the shot and the deer’s reaction. Go to the last place you saw the deer — often a field edge or trail — and begin searching for blood there. I have shot plenty of deer that didn’t produce visible blood trails at the hit site, but that begin bleeding once they ran a little ways, or barely bled at all.

Conventional wisdom dictates big-game hunters should wait a minimum of a half hour to pursue their quarry after any shot that requires trailing. The idea is that an animal doesn’t always die right away, and by giving it time and space to expire, you’re not spiking its system with adrenaline that might cause it to run farther. Waiting lets an animal bed down and bleed out, aiding your eventual recovery.

But on a safari for Namibian plains game a few years ago, my professional hunter didn’t wait even 30 seconds after my shot. He would chase game that fled at the hit, leaving me to scramble for my safety and run after them both. I was intrigued by this rule of the bush — unless you see your quarry drop, grab your shooting sticks and start sprinting — and wondered how it might apply at home. The short answer is that you can immediately start tracking a wounded deer, sometimes to greater effect than if you had waited the requisite 30 minutes. It all depends on what kind of hit you made. To help you make the call, consult this flowchart.

Depending on the amount and type of blood, a blood trail can indicate a fatal hit or a hit that might cause a deer to bleed out if pushed. Never push a gut- or liver-shot deer.

Deer die immediately or within a few minutes of a good shot to the heart, lungs, spine, or brain, or in the event a major artery was severed. If you’re 100 percent confident you made one of these shots, it’s okay to pursue your deer sooner than 30 minutes (particularly if it’s hot out).

This is a lethal hit, but it typically takes longer (think hours) for a liver-hit deer to expire. Avoid pushing your deer and instead return in at least six hours, potentially longer, to track your deer.

This is a fatal shot, but it can take a long time for a deer to die from a wound to the digestive track. Don’t pursue a deer if you only find evidence of a gut shot. Instead, back out, give the deer plenty of space to bed nearby, and return at least 8 to 12 hours later with backup, including (ideally) a tracking dog.

Many hunters who hit deer “just a little back” assume they hit both the lungs and the liver, meaning a quick kill. In reality, these are often the gut/liver shots, and those hunters usually take up the blood trail too soon. They bump the deer out of its first bed, which greatly decreases the chances of recovering the deer.

“A lot of people think that liver hits kill pretty quickly, and it does in some cases,” Simpson says. “But I’ve tracked deer that were alive after 16 hours after they were hit, and it was a liver shot.”

Hunter-Ed.com: An excerpt from the curriculum approved in 45 states: “You should wait for at least a half hour to an hour before trailing a deer, unless the downed deer is in sight.”

National Bowhunter Education Foundation: The NBEF states that “a wise bowhunter gives the animal time to expire,” and that the normal waiting period after arrowing a big-game animal ranges from 30 to 60 minutes. A caveat to this is quick pursuit in the event of a poor hit outside the chest or body cavity (neck, leg, rump, or back). In such instances, the deer might run away quickly but then calm down, stop bleeding, and possibly survive. “If you can follow the animal rapidly and aggressively, it will continue to bleed, even from a relatively minor wound…It may lose enough blood to get careless and give you another shot. It may even die from a wound that would not normally be considered fatal.”

John Jeanneney: Tracker, tracking-dog breeder, and author John Jeanneney advocates taking advantage of the onset of shock in an animal immediately following a shot. He recommends carefully approaching wounded game for a finishing shot. Allowing an animal shot in the heart, lungs, shoulder, or leg time to collect its wits could result in a wounding loss.

Bowhunters can read more here about how long to wait to start tracking, and how to blood trail a deer.

Everyone tracks a little differently, but these are a few universal guidelines for how to blood trail a deer.

If your deer crossed a property line, check your state regulations about recovering hit game, and ask for permission from the landowner to keep tracking if necessary. Even if it’s legal to check private property for hit game, it’s usually a good idea to ask for landowner permission to maintain friendly neighbor relations and so they can keep an eye out for your deer if necessary.

The hardest blood trails are often those that have little to no blood at the hit site, or that appear to have no blood at the hit site. Every hunt is different and even mortally wounded deer do unpredictable things. Here’s how to pick up the trail when you can’t find any blood, or when the blood trail runs out.

If none of these tips work, consider backing out now and contacting a tracking dog handler. (Check out United Blood Trackers.) The more you disturb an area before calling in a blood dog, the harder it will be for the dog to single out the scent of a wounded deer. Remember, blood-tracking dogs don’t actually track the scent of blood — they’re trained to follow the scent left by a wounded deer’s interdigital gland, or the scent gland between its hooves. That’s why they can keep tracking a deer that’s no longer leaving blood.

If you’re still looking for your deer well after the window of safe meat recovery, try these last resorts.

If you’re concerned about tracking conditions where you hunt (maybe you hunt in thick timber, wet weather, swamps, etc.) consider choosing an arrow set up or cartridge that you expect to completely pass through your deer and leave a large exit wound.

“If you like two leaky holes, and there’s a lot to be said for that, you’re going to want to shoot something like a Nosler AccuBond, a Barnes Monolithic, or a Hornaday GMX,” shooting editor John B. Snow once advised while explaining why some hunters have reported bad blood trails with the 6.5 Creedmoor. “If you want lots of internal damage but not necessarily a pass-through, look at the Hornaday ELD-X or a Nosler Ballistic Tip — any of those lighter, polymer-tip bullets should fit the bill. Just know that there’s still a chance that it’ll blow through the deer.”

Shot placement is always key, and that remains true for blood trailing. It’s particularly critical for bowhunters. Shooting from an elevated position and aiming for a pass through can produce low exit wounds that bleed heavily and create stronger blood trails.

One of the hardest blood trails I’ve ever had to follow was a doe that I shot with my compound just before last light. I knew I’d hit the deer but I didn’t find my arrow or any blood at the hit site. Eventually, I found a single drop of blood more than 60 yards from the hit site. I inched along the scant blood until it ran out and, eventually, spotted the doe lying another 50 yards away. My broadhead had lodged inside the deer’s far shoulder, resulting in a high entry wound and no exit. If I had selected my shot a bit better, I’d have had a good trail to follow and saved myself the stress.

While it’s gotten trendy to film your own hunts in recent years, it’s actually a smart idea to record your shot when possible. Reviewing the tape can help determine where your bullet or arrow struck, or to identify precisely which way your deer ran. This is particularly true if you’re hunting solo and don’t have the benefit of a spotter, if you’re a new hunter and need advice from buddies, or you tend to experience high adrenaline during your hunts (which can make it difficult to remember exactly what happened in those hectic moments after the shot). Blood-trailing dog handlers also like to have video to review before pursuing a deer.

You can easily record videos with just your cell phone and a simple tripod that wraps around your treestand rail, limb, or blind strut.

Blood-tracking dogs are legal to use in almost every state, although each state has typically has regulations about how to proceed (for instance, some dogs must be leashed or you must track in the presence of a game warden). According to Blood Trackers United, blood dogs are illegal statewide only in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Oregon, Nevada, and Arizona. To review regulations in your state, click here.

At the time of publication, drones are legal for deer recovery in at least 14 states, according to the National Deer Association: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Ohio, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Wisconsin. (Missouri is the most recent state to legalize drone recovery for deer.) It’s also legal in the Canadian province of Manitoba.

Some states allow drones with thermal imaging for deer recovery (see above). Many states prohibit handheld thermal devices for deer recovery, some allow them, and others still don’t address them at all. Your best bet is to check your state’s regulations or contact a game warden.

Sometimes blood trailing a deer can be obvious, with huge splashes of bright red blood leading you directly to your deer. Other times it requires careful, methodical work to unravel. Do your best to make an honest assessment of the hit and decide how to pursue. When in doubt about your shot, back out and call for reinforcements. And never give up while there’s sign to follow. Sometimes visible blood trails can taper or disappear, but your deer might be lying ahead, just out of sight.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#65. I Was Leading the Moab 240 When Extreme Weather Hit. Here’s What It Was Like.

Aaron Kubala runs through mud and rain at the Moab 240 (Photo: Courtesy Aaron Kubala)

Ultramarathon runner Aaron Kubala was leading the Moab 240 trail race in Utah on October 11 when severe weather caused flash flooding and deadly winds. Race organizer Destination Trail eventually called off the event, prompting a flurry of reactions from runners and crew on social media. After that setback, Kubala, 31, was hospitalized with Rhabdomyolysis. He told Outside what it was like to endure the ordeal.

It was day two, and I had been running in pouring rain for 12 hours, from Road 46 through Pole Canyon and to the long climb up Geyser Pass. Once I got above 10,500 feet elevation, the rain stopped and it got extremely cold. I was soaked to the bone. I couldn’t stop shivering.

Then the wind started gusting at 50 miles per hour.

This was mile 180, and I entered a section that goes over ridges and canyons filled with dead trees, thousands of them. The wind would blow and I’d hear hundreds of trees crack and fall over. The whole forest echoed with the sound of cracking trees. And then the trees started getting blown over very close to me. One fell ten feet behind me, and then another landed five feet in front. It was nighttime and it was a pretty scary experience. You’d hear a tree crack nearby and have no idea where it would land. At times it felt like I was in the middle of a death trap.

My pace slowed. In the past, for this section, I might have been running a 12-minute mile. Now it took me 40 minutes to cover a mile because I’d have to go over or under downed trees. At some point, my mind switched from race mode to sheer survival mode.

My motivation couldn’t have been higher coming into the Moab 240. I was chasing the 200-miler Triple Crown record (combined time for the Tahoe 200, Bigfoot 200, and Moab 240). I knew I was faster at Moab 240 than the time I’d needed to beat it. I wanted to get the Triple Crown record and also the course record for Moab 240 (55 hours, 49 minutes, 48 seconds).

I lost my mother several weeks before the Tahoe 200 in June, and I’ve turned my racing campaign into a fundraising effort for Breast Cancer research. Having this extra mission alongside my own personal goals has given me a ton of motivation during the season.

I led the Moab 240 from the start, and I had my pacing plan extremely dialed. I was ahead of the course record. The first two days were phenomenal, and I shared the trail with my pacers. We ran through the beautiful Moab terrain. It’s one of my favorite places in the USA to run because of the scenic views you get of the desert.

Honestly, it was almost a perfect race until the end of day two, which is when we start climbing into the La Sal Mountains east of Moab around mile 180.

The bad weather wasn’t a total surprise. I could hear my race crews’ phones beeping with weather alerts, even though they didn’t want to tell me about it. Also, you can see the La Sal Mountains from 50 miles away, and as I approached them, could see that they were covered in thunderstorms.

Because I was ahead of the other racers, I didn’t get caught in any of the flash flooding or river crossings that were documented on social media. I got caught in pouring rain and had to deal with the trail being washed out, but I never had to cross a river with water up to my chest.

I trusted the race organizers that if the situation became too dangerous, they would do something about it. I actually got in touch with them at the Pole Canyon aid station and told them the trail was completely impassable with downed trees and mud, and that the runners behind me would have a really hard time with the terrain.

I was about six miles from the Geyser Pass aid station in a section with a lot of downed trees when my pacer got word that they were canceling the race. I wasn’t surprised—I was almost surprised they hadn’t called it sooner. It made sense, and I didn’t question the decision. But then I thought about what it meant for my record-breaking season, and I was pretty devastated. To have this historic season of mine end in such an anticlimactic way felt empty.

I still think the race organizers made the right decision. I didn’t want any other runner to experience that section of falling trees like I did.

When the race was called off, I did have a brief thought: I should just finish the route. We were less than 30 miles from the finish line, and it was mostly downhill. We just had to enter a wide dirt road section of bike trail and dirt roads, and it would be smooth sailing.

But I knew that the race organization needed to account for everyone, and they wanted me safe at an aid station. It felt better to be compliant.

Afterward, I saw some participants saying they wished the race would allow them to finish on their own, despite the danger. I just think some racers didn’t really understand the gravity of the situation. Most people never made it to the La Sal Mountains where they could have seen just how dangerous it was. It wasn’t safe for anyone to be out there. They would have been jeopardizing search and rescue resources if someone had been hit by a downed tree.

When I was running on day two I was having back spasms, and at some point I had a lot of trouble picking up my legs to climb over the blown down trees. I’d never had that before. I still felt strong enough to have finished the race, but looking back on it, something was wrong.

After the race, I was having hematuria, or blood in my urine. And the next day I was still peeing blood, so my partner and I checked into the emergency room in Moab. Eventually, I was airlifted to the University of Utah Hospital in Salt Lake City.

I was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. I’ve never had it before, so I didn’t know the symptoms. The doctors don’t have a sense of what caused it. They think the hypothermic shivering for 12 hours may have contributed negatively to it.

It’s been a week since the race endee, and I’m still in the hospital. I wish the race would have awarded positioning finishes to the athletes, because it was pretty clear where we were on the course, and I’d love for it to count for something. I don’t know if that will happen. But having something to acknowledge our accomplishments, despite the conditions, would be great.

As told to Frederick Dreier. Edited for length and clarity.

#66. Courtney Dauwalter Has Me Rethinking Failure

This is a special edition of Managing Editor Abby Levene’s newsletter from October 9, 2026. Every week, she shares her most unfiltered thoughts on the sport and beyond. But it doesn’t usually make it onto the website. It’s a newsletter, after all. To have it delivered straight to your inbox, sign up for her newsletter here.

Aloha from the Ironman World Championship in Kona! This morning I was running on Ali’i, the main drag along the water here on Hawai’i’s Big Island, with … Courtney Dauwalter. (Yes, the Baggy Shorts Boss is in Kona, more on that in a second.) We’re both training for the California International Marathon in December so we were doing a little interval workout.

This is my fourth time covering this race in Kona with our sister publication, Triathlete, so I’ve spent a lot of time running back and forth on this infernal road waving to the throngs of racers running and biking along it. By this point in the week three days out from the race, everyone is pretty locked in. Those spandex-clad triathletes on Ali’i are nervous; they’re looking inward, not smiling or waving back much.

Courtney and I were in the middle of our workout when I saw my colleague Chris running towards us. I smiled and waved, trying to get his attention with my eyes. (We were working hard, after all.) He stared blankly at me. Then he saw Courtney behind me, and it clicked.

“I didn’t recognize you; you looked so serious!” he said to me afterward. “But Courtney had a huge smile on her face and gave me a big wave.”

WTF man, I was smiling and waving too! Well, Chris told me, Courtney has an aura.

And he’s right. Throughout the run, legions of triathletes smiled and waved to us (well, to Courtney). I felt transported into a different, brighter, bubblier world. A positive feedback loop of joy. But it wasn’t just Courtney’s dazzling smile that was rubbing off on me and everyone else on Ali’i this morning. That infectious enthusiasm stems from a place much deeper inside her, I think, as evidenced by a conversation we had about failure earlier in the week.

Courtney is here because in a shocking plot twist, Salomon—the beloved mountain brand best known for its snow and trail running equipment—is taking over the Ironman World Championship title sponsor. More on that and what it means for the future of endurance sport next week.

In an exclusive interview, I had the privilege of being the first journalist to ask Courtney about UTMB. (The three-time champ DNFed at mile 40.) What she had to say illuminated a lot about how she thinks about athletics, and it’s a perspective I’ll be trying to adopt forever:

Courtney’s main focus this year was the Cocodona 250 in May followed by the Hardrock 100 in July, she said. (Narrator: In case you forgot, those both went quite well, including a course record at Hardrock.) UTMB was the cherry on top.

“After Hardrock the body was all in one piece,” she said. “The brain was feeling decent. I took some recovery, tried to recharge the batteries, and then decided let’s just push the marble forward and see if we could make UTMB happen, because in our minds we were like, why not try? Why not pin on the bib and just see?”

She wasn’t sure if her body and mind were in fact recharged. And well—

“When the race started, it was pretty clear that the answer to those questions was a definitive ‘no, there’s nothing there for you,’” she said. “Everything felt pretty horrible from the start.”

She kept going, thinking maybe things would turn around, but they didn’t. But that’s not actually why I’m telling you this; it’s because of what she said next:

“It’s a bummer that trying can’t just be the cool part by itself. I would like if trying hard things could just be the win alone. I understand, of course, it’s a race, and with races are results. But I think athletes would maybe be more inclined to jump into more random ideas or challenges if a DNF wasn’t such a dark cloud that some people associate it with.”

I think it’s easy to discredit how brave Courtney is because she’s so freaking good at running. She tries new things, and she most often wins. But as evidenced by her willingness to try events ranging from the Western States 100 to Big’s Backyard Ultra to road marathons, she seems genuinely driven by curiosity. (“Joy is in the driver’s seat,” she told me in another interview this spring.) That curiosity is a positive force that overshadows fear of failure—a remarkable feat for someone so in the public eye that everyone recognizes her at a race in a totally different sport.

Speaking of that totally different sport, after that discussion I had to ask the obvious question: Does being here make any part of her maybe want to race an Ironman?

“I didn’t know that I was Ironman-curious or triathlon-curious, but I also am definitely crazy-idea-curious, always,” she said. “And so I would say there’s probably a 100% chance I’ll try.”

Hearing the excitement in her voice filled me with newfound courage. I’ve been super nervous to try a road marathon after so many years of focusing on the trails, worried it might not go as well as I want. Reframing that fear of failure to curiosity to try is immensely empowering to me. That’s not to say the result doesn’t matter to Courtney, or that our own results shouldn’t matter to us. It’s that even for someone like Courtney, who has won basically everything, the trying part is where the magic happens. And trying is something we can all do, too.

Before she races an Ironman, Courtney needs help with the swim, she said. She’s never biked over 100 miles. But really, there’s just one real problem she needs to solve:

“Do you think that you can wear baggy shorts?” she asked. “I’m concerned about my outfit.”

How a former gang member found a different kind of vigilance in the Montana wild.

One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

#68. First Look: the Austrian-Made, Athlete-Approved, Ready-for-Anything FREERIDE 98

Marcel Hirscher is the Austrian racing legend behind VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports. (Photo: (c) Kleinmond - Georg Lindacher)

When Austrian racing legend Marcel Hirscher started making skis, he began with what knows best:  fast, powerful, race-ready planks. But that was never the whole goal. Even before partnering with Red Bull in 2022, Hirscher’s dream has been to deliver pro-level gear to skiers at every level. After all, you don’t need to be racing royalty to benefit from a stable, versatile, finely tuned ski.

With the FREERIDE SERIES, Hirscher and the rest of his team at VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports are zeroing in on that mission. The series features two skis: the FREERIDE 98 and the FREERIDE 108. Both models keep recreational skiers in mind, designed to boost confidence and control across a vast range of terrain—from mellow groomers to icy bumps to tight trees.

While the 108-mm offers a touch more float in powder, the surfy tip rocker and a 98-mm waist on the flagship model, the FREERIDE 98, hits the sweet spot between versatility and performance. The narrower waist boosts agility on treed steeps, and the finely tuned edges make carving effortless.

Not only that, but VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports has gone the extra mile to ensure you can retain that performance across the entire lifetime of the ski: every model comes with its own hyper-specific tuning recommendations to keep the ski in out-of-the-box condition year after year. You don’t have to take your kit back to Austria to get it done, either; VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports currently works with factory tuning partners all across the U.S. Just bring in your sticks to any of these locations to get them back in shape.

Like other skis from  VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, the series features race-quality materials, like a beech-poplar wood core reinforced with double titanal and carbon layers. The result is just the right amount of flex: The FREERIDE 98 is snappy and playful but not chattery, and it boasts serious stability at high speeds. Full ABS sidewalls permit individual edge tuning, the secret to maximum grip and control—and therefore confidence—even in sub-par conditions.

These promises aren’t just theoretical, either.  Hirscher’s team painstakingly designs and tests every ski right at home in the Austrian Alps.  That’s where he cut his teeth as a young ski racer, and it’s where  VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports is still headquartered today: in the mountain village of Scheffau am Tennengebirge just south of Salzburg.

It’s a small-batch operation through and through:  Instead of mass-producing piles of product, VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports builds one small, dedicated series at a time. Because of the slower pace of production, the skis benefit from more time in the design and testing phase. They also stay in the press longer than usual, which ensures a stronger bond between materials and, ultimately, better performance. Because in Hirscher’s mind, a high-performance ski is one that’s more fun to ride. And at the end of the day, that’s what it’s all about.

At VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, founded in the Austrian Alps by ski legend Marcel Hirscher, we do things differently. We believe in the power of new  and a no-compromise approach to skiing and equipment. Together with  Red Bull, we combine racing  expertise with innovation to create world-class skis for a new generation.

#69. Everest Climbers Return to West Ridge With One Member Less

On their second venture up Everest, the Russian team is aiming to progress further along the West Ridge. This time, they will be a team of just three: Natalya Belyankina was airlifted out yesterday due to health problems.

Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will climb one of the longest routes of Everest, with no supplemental oxygen, no support team, and no clear idea about the exact line they will follow.

Kondrashkin recently posted details about their previous ascent to the Lho La and the beginning of the ridge last week. As he noted, their route skirts below gigantic hanging seracs. They felt safe traversing the area on the way up because they saw no avalanche debris. However, after they reached the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide col, the boom of a falling serac below them reminded them of the risks.

On the following morning, the climbers approached the first part of the West Ridge.

“[It was] a sharp ascent to the ridge: first, on a 50˚ snow slope and, higher up, more than 100m of 60˚ glacial ice,” Kondrashkin recalled. “Then, climbing over a slight snow cornice, we emerged onto the ridge.”

Shipilov and Vasiliev climbed further up a rocky outcrop, looking for both the most suitable line and a potential campsite on the ridge. They also photographed the sections ahead. As Kondrashkin and Belyankina watched from below, “It felt like we were looking at it from the very foot of the mountain, just how enormous it is,” Kondrashkin wrote about Everest’s upper half:

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Serguey Kondrashkin

The team returned to Base Camp the following day, finding a better route that involves less time under the hanging seracs.

Since then, they have been resting and preparing for the next foray up. However, the rest was not enough for Natalya Belyankina, who was already suffering from a bad case of Khumbu cough.

Natalya Belyankina in the helicopter back to Kathmandu today. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

“It’s a real pity,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote today. “Natasha did so much to make this expedition happen, but it’s impossible to continue in this condition.”

Vasiliev then confirmed that Kondrashkin, Shipilov, and he are heading up again today for about a week.

The Russians are the only climbers currently on an 8,000m peak, and their goal is among the most ambitious on Everest in years. They intend to climb the mountain entirely on their own, without supplemental oxygen, in a light style, via the West Ridge.

On Pete Poston’s graph of Everest routes, the Yugoslavian route is #5 in pink, and the 1963 U.S. route is #2 in green.

The West Ridge of Everest has been climbed just three times, each via different variations, all of them epic and sometimes tragic expeditions. Climbing the West Ridge involves two possible routes. First, an endless climb along the ridge from Nepal like the 1979 Yugoslavian team did (Andrej Stremfelj, Nejc Zaplotnik, Stipe Bozic, Stane Belak-Srauf, and Ang Phu Sherpa).

Second, they could cross into Tibet at some point and continue up the North Face via the Hornbein Couloir. This route retraces the steps of Americans Tom Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, who started up the normal route to Camp 2, then joined the West Ridge and crossed to what became known as the Hornbein Couloir to the summit in 1963.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.
