#72. This Is the Secret to Calling in a Fall Gobbler, According to a Turkey Hunting Legend

Published Oct 19, 2026 11:30 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

One of the biggest myths in all of turkey hunting is that male turkeys respond to calling only in the spring. The fact is, toms gobble all fall, too, and are sometimes more vocal in autumn than in spring. And they can be very responsive to a call.

Just as in the spring, a hunter’s job is to get gobblers excited, because that’s when they make mistakes. And to do that, you have to sound like a gobbler when you call, imitating a newcomer that’s challenging the old boys’ club. It’s a pecking order thing. They come to the calling because they want to see who you are, and because they want to kick your behind.

Unlike in spring, turkeys are driven by food in the fall rather than the need to reproduce. Therefore, scouting food sources is one of the best ways to find fall toms. In early autumn, look for soft-mast foods such as hawthorn, dogwood berries, wild grapes, persimmons and crab apples.

Rounding out the fall smorgasbord are a variety of insects, assorted seeds, grasses, cherries and agricultural crops of clover, beans, small grains and waste grain that’s left on the ground in freshly harvested fields.

Later in the autumn, turkeys feed primarily on hard mast dropped by a variety of oaks and maples, as well as other trees that produce nutlike seeds. However, trees don’t produce these every year, so the trick is to know the foods turkeys prefer and to find which foods are available in your hunting area.

As long as the habitat and food sources don’t change, neither will fall roost locations, and these bedrooms are the best places to begin your fall hunt.

Always set up tight on a roost way before first light and on the same side or in the same direction as the previous evening’s fly-up. Listen for the first turkey to call, and then duplicate whatever the turkeys do, but with more enthusiasm. If turkeys yelp, you yelp; if they cluck, you cluck, but with more feeling. Work them into a frenzy.

When it comes to cutting, putting, purring and other sounds, there is no reliable difference between a hen and a tom; they all do it. When a gobbler gets excited, it will sometimes yelp 30 times in a row and do a lot of high-pitched putting.

One way to tell the difference between hen and gobbler yelps is the rhythm. A hen’s note is relatively faster and shorter in length. When a gobbler is yelping, each note is more drawn out, with a slightly slower rhythm. It can also sound coarser, or “throatier,” than a hen’s.

A quality slate or glass call is one of the best devices to use on fall turkeys. The slate will produce great soft tree talk, purrs and hen yelps, as well as realistic gobbler yelps. My favorite is the mouth call. I can imitate almost any turkey sound with the diaphragm call, including jake kee-kees, gobbler yelps and cutting.

Read Next: The Best Turkey Calls, Tested and Reviewed

Calling, pecking order and gobbler social status mean everything when it comes to your success during this time of year. You must call to individual birds in order to strike a chord with the turkeys and bring them in.

Yelping: Aim to match the volume and pitch, then add emotion and listen for the response.

Purring: Just as in the spring, this is a great way to put nervous birds at ease.

Putting/Cutting: Cutting at a fall gobbler with a bit of an attitude gets it excited and challenges its social status.

#73. A Saguaro Fell on a Hiker’s Head and Sent Her to the Hospital. Here’s How Bad Cactus Injuries Can Get

Sonoran Desert National Monument (Photo: Bob Wick / BLM)

I was lost in the endless starry skies of southern Colorado when I walked directly into a cactus.

I was 24 and on a camping and climbing trip to Shelf Road, near Cañon City, and as some readers may have already guessed, I was not exactly sober. After killing the better part of two bottles of Trader Joe’s Blended Scotch with my buddies around a campfire, I got up to relieve myself. It was a cold, clear night, and the edge-on disk of the Milky Way cut a slash across the sky. I was so enraptured by it that I didn’t see the large cholla cactus right in front of me.

The feedback to some mistakes is immediate and visceral. I yelped, then yelped again when I instinctively reached out a hand and stabbed that, too. I pulled a handful of the prickers out before deciding I needed help. Back at the campfire, my friend Kelly, who wasn’t quite as deep in the bottle as me, managed to extract about a dozen of the barbed needles from my shoulder and side. The next morning, after I had slept off the booze, I woke up with an aching hip and discovered more spines there.

My mishap at Shelf Road isn’t the only cactus injury I’ve suffered over my years in the desert, but it’s my worst to date. This weekend, however, a hiker in Arizona discovered just how bad a run-in with a cactus can get after a rescue that ended with her in the hospital.

The hiker was on the Bell Pass Trail, a roughly 6.6-mile out-and-back near Scottsdale, when a saguaro fell over in strong winds and hit her in the head on October 17. The Scottsdale Fire Department said its technical rescue team climbed the trail and discovered the stricken hiker about two miles in.

Amy Johnson, a hiker who was on-scene for the accident, told The Arizona Republic that the cactus knocked the victim out for between five and ten minutes and left her with injuries from both the weight of the plant and its spines. A companion managed to use a strap to lift the several-hundred-pound fragment of cactus off her, but the injured woman appeared to have suffered head trauma, and Johnson said she was unable to remember the year or who the president was.

Rescuers evacuated her on a litter and via UTV before transporting her to a local trauma center for follow-up care.

The McDowell Sonoran Preserve, where the Bell Pass Trail is located, is home to many saguaro cacti. The saguaro is the largest cactus in the United States, with some specimens on record reaching heights of more than 78 feet and weights of more than 10 tons. It’s also the only species of cactus in America on record to kill someone: In 1982, 27-year-old Arizonan David M. Grundman was shooting at a 23-foot-tall specimen with a shotgun when one of its arms collapsed and crushed him underneath its bulk. (Unlike Grundman or me, there’s no evidence that the hiker hurt in this week’s incident bears any of the blame for her injuries.)

While serious cactus injuries are extremely rare on desert trails, lesser incidents are not. Chollas, a bushy-looking variety common throughout the southwestern U.S., are particularly pernicious: A study published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B in 2018 found their hooked spines lodged securely enough in flesh that just one of them could lift a half-pound of pork shoulder. (I can attest that they hurt as much going out as they do going in.)

Fortunately, most cactus injuries are minor, and hikers can manage them with a basic first aid kit. In a guide for Backpacker, Buck Tilton, author and cofounder of the Wilderness Medicine Institute, had the following suggestions:

#76. The IAT is a Kinder, Gentler National Scenic Trail

The Ice Age Trail would make an ideal first-time thru-hike. It’s in excellent condition, which means you can leave your route-finding and blowdown-hurdling skills at home. The IAT Alliance‘s budget for blazes appears to be infinite, so you won’t get lost. You won’t be short of breath either, because Wisconsin isn’t known for its mountains. No permits are required, wildfires are a non-issue, and your chance of a true-thru is as good as it gets. Also, if you prefer a toilet to a cat-hole, you’ll appreciate the trail’s central and eastern sections.

There are plenty of towns and gas stations near the trail, so you can keep your resupplies small and your pack light. I didn’t mail myself any resupply boxes, I only hitched once, and even that one time wasn’t strictly necessary. It was, however, cheaper than the $50 taxi fare back to the trail. In the two small towns where I tried using Uber, it was useless.

Much of the trail has cellphone coverage, even though the signal is sometimes too weak for data. Once, I was able to call and book a state park campsite, even though I couldn’t access their website. I frequently charged my phone at picnic pavilions in county and city parks, and didn’t use my power bank at all during the trail’s central and eastern sections.

My 15℉ bag was complete overkill. Low elevations and a late-July start meant round-the-clock, warm, humid conditions. Until mid-September, I mostly relied on a sleeping bag liner. A stove was also unnecessary – a hot evening meal just made me sweatier.

Ticks are still a problem in late July, mosquitoes and deer flies are a nuisance until at least mid-August.

In a handful of places, signs warned of an invasive weed called Wild Parsnip. I’d never heard of it, but it produces chemicals that cause severe burns when they’re on the skin and exposed to sunlight.

Finally, a possible downside to the IAT is that you’re never far from civilization. If you’re looking for a social experience rather than an escape, this isn’t an issue. I didn’t mind the fact that at many of my campsites, I could hear traffic in the distance. Of course, where there are people, there are people-related problems. I did mind having to vacate a campsite in late afternoon because a bear wanted my food, and wouldn’t leave. I’ll get to that story in a couple of weeks.

The Ice Age Trail in Wisconsin, alongside some mileage stats.

The IAT’s water sources weren’t great. It shouldn’t really have come as a surprise given the potential distance that water had travelled. The trail averages about 1100 feet above sea level, and its minimum elevation is about half that value. It’s low enough to give rainfall time to accumulate all sorts of undesirable qualities on its way to the ocean, especially with so much farmland nearby. Here are some comments about Mauthe Lake Recreation Area from the FarOut navigation app.

“Water near ranger station, but tastes like sulfur” Navigator2023, 9/5/2026

“Water taste funny” The_Boy_MacGyver, 6/17/2025

“Water is *spicy*” chinaaddison, 10/29/2022

Having drunk from that same source, I can confirm that these comments are 100% accurate. They’re actually referring to the water fountain at an entrance station, so you can imagine what people had to say when they sampled the IAT’s ponds and marshes. Filtering water from the outlet of Straight Lake on day two was when I realized I’d be taking part in a flavor crapshoot.

“Warm and earthy, with a hint of iron. Tastes like Guinness.” LowRange, 7/24/2026

Six weeks after that, I drank the crappiest water yet. It came, in part, from the Oconomowoc River, was clear and brown after filtering, and tasted a bit woody. On its own, not too bad. About half a liter remained when I reached Pike Lake picnic area the next day. There, I passed an out-of-the-way spigot, brushed away its cobwebs, and filled my bottle. The water was opaque and tasted strongly of iron. The reason it was cloudy, I assumed, was because it was no longer under pressure, and tiny air bubbles had formed. I took another liter, then topped up the half-full container I’d been drinking from that morning.

A couple of hours later, I finished my water bottle, and unscrewed the top. The dead spider inside made me think that flushing the pipeline would have been wise. After disposing of the body, I refilled my bottle from the container containing the 50:50 mixture, and didn’t give much thought to the milky tea inside. Wild swings in water quality were nothing new. The now skunky flavor was unexpected, and half a bottle later, I’d had enough.

My guess is that something in the treated water reacted with something in the river water. That would explain why the mixture tasted so much worse than either of its component parts. I dumped the brown liquid, and filtered the precipitate from the white liquid. It quickly clogged my filter, but the water was clear afterwards, even though it still tasted of iron. I didn’t get sick, and decided not to add a FarOut comment. Unfounded rumors about water quality are hard to dispel.

I went EABO because I wanted to end my hike on the shores of Lake Michigan. In hindsight, there are three better reasons to go EABO.

Starting at the eastern terminus, you’ll be able to keep your resupplies small initially. Unfortunately, your first week will include a 20 mile and a 28 mile road-walk, both of which have no camping or hotel options. During the next few trail segments, camping is still highly restricted.

The eastern section contains Kettle Moraine State Forest, which covers about 130 trail miles. There are three dispersed camping areas intended for IAT hikers, and the sites are first-come, first-served. There are nine shelters which can be booked in advance, but they’re popular, and you’re unlikely to get one last-minute. If you can’t commit to being in specific locations on specific dates, there are also nine campgrounds which will probably still have space by the time you show up. One of those is Horseriders Campground, but alas, it can only be reserved by people who bring a horse. When I arrived, on my imaginary horse, Friday afternoon of Labor Day weekend, only a handful of sites were occupied.

To summarize, starting at the eastern terminus requires bigger-mileage days early in the hike, and solid planning to keep those bigger days under control. If you start at the western terminus, you’ll have your trail legs by the time they’re a necessity.

The signature blaze of the IAT is a yellow rectangle, and as I mentioned earlier, trail segments are well marked. On the other hand, road-walks (aka Connecting Routes) are generally unmarked. FarOut displays a blue line where there are blazes, and a green line otherwise. The rule is: blazed=blue≈trail, unblazed=green≈road.

When you reach the bifurcation in the IAT’s central section, if you head west, you’ll walk the longest unbroken green line on the FarOut map: 75 miles. Going east, the longest road-walks are 11, 12, 21, and 22 miles. I went east.

In my experience, a National Scenic Trail is just a collection of shorter trails that are sometimes linked by roads. You’ll be aware, by now, that the IAT has a significant number of these connecting roads. You might think that no self-respecting thru-hiker would replace any part of the trail with road. You’d be wrong. You might think that it isn’t a proper thru-hike unless you’ve touched every inch of official trail. I disagree. The CDT, for example, is highly customizable, and the IAT is similar in this regard. It’s different in that its alternates are snack-sized rather than four-course meals.

After each of my thru-hikes, for about a week, I had the same dream every night. In the dream, I’m relaxing in my tent in the evening, when I suddenly realize I haven’t completed my miles for the day. In a panic, as darkness falls, I start to break camp. That’s when I wake up and realize I’m at home.

I’ve been known to take a few shortcuts when under pressure to make miles. Some of my IAT alternates were planned, some were spur-of-the-moment. Some cut a few tenths, others cut a mile or two. Sometimes I was motivated by the thought of donuts at a Kwik Trip, and once or twice, my incentive was a Culver’s burger. Often, I just wanted a break from the infernal mosquitoes. In the end, my detours probably shortened the hike by about 50 miles.

“Thanks for the rest and the water. Beautiful shaded spot on a hot day. The bifurcation and all the road walks had gotten me down, but I’ve met so many wonderful people on the sections afterwards that my spirit and love for the trail have grown immensely.” FireFly Bzzz, 7/26/26, log book entry at mile 711

“Hey FireFly Bzzz – why’d you graffiti the post at the D.C.A. on the blue segment?! NOT COOL!” Unsigned log book entry

“FireFly Bzzz has been tagging the entire trail. Picnic table at North Lake, hiker shelter at Lincoln County, etc.” Unsigned log book entry

Mr. Bzzz, may I call you FireFly? Great! I, too, noticed your “artwork” in several places, and I’m not a fan. For a start, you misspelled IAT on the D.C.A. signpost, and firefly when you scrawled all over that big sign on Levee Road. The reviews are in, and the majority of hikers don’t like what you’ve done. To spare your feelings, I’ll explain as kindly and gently as I can why you shouldn’t write on things that aren’t yours.

Imagine, for a moment, that you work for the IATA. You’ve set aside a small area for camping near Rice Lake, but subsequent FarOut comments mention the lack of access to clean water. You extend the spur trail to the creek, go to the trouble of building a jetty, and put up a signpost. You’d probably feel unappreciated if a thru-hiker came along and defaced your hard work. Their behavior might get you down.

If I understand correctly, you’re in your late 30’s or early 40’s, and you’re from Tennessee. Your most recent long trail before the IAT was the Arizona Trail, which means the AZT probably has your graffiti all over it too. The hiking community is more tight-knit than you realize, and sooner or later, someone will connect your trail name with your real name.

At many of the trailheads, I saw signs reminding me that the IAT is maintained entirely by volunteers. I passed a handful of trail crews, some of which were doing routine stuff like clearing blowdown, but one crew was replacing a bridge, and another was installing a boardwalk. I also met plenty of segment hikers in the process of piecing together the entire trail, many of whom had volunteered on maintenance projects. Everyone I met was proud of the IAT, and I have the lasting impression that it’s the most enthusiastic, supportive trail community I’ve encountered thus far.

I also need to mention the FarOut users. Their comments were funny, helpful, and sometimes crucial, for example, if I needed a flat spot in order to rest for a few hours.

I only met one thru-hiker, but I’m sure there are others out there. They might find this list of resupply options useful. The table contains an example from every town within a reasonable distance of the trail. And here’s a link to the Garmin data I used.

#78. Lara Neumeier Makes First Female Ascent of ‘Rhapsody’ (E11)

Lara Neumeier climbs one of the hardest sections near the top-out on the route Rhapsody (E11) at Dumbarton Rock, Scotland, on October 7, 2026. (Photo: Chris Prescott via Red Bull Content Pool)

On October 7, Lara Neumeier topped out one of the hardest trad lines in the world amid approaching rain, standing high above the nearby castle walls as a blue-and-white Scottish flag flew in the bracing wind. The 28-year-old German climber just made the first female ascent of Rhapsody (E11 7a/5.14c) at Dumbarton Rock near Glasgow, Scotland, 20 years after it was established by Dave MacLeod as the world’s first E11. With her send, Neumeier became the fifth woman to climb a 5.14c trad route, joining Beth Rodden, Barbara Zangerl, Hazel Findlay, and Emma Twyford. Neumeier is the first woman to succeed on the British E11 grade.

Over two visits to Scotland this spring and fall, Neumeier worked the route alongside Austrian climber Nemuel “Nemo” Feurle, who sent shortly after her on the same day. The pair made the tenth and eleventh ascensionists respectively. British climber Buster Martin also sent the line the previous week.

Rhapsody’s 35-meter (115-foot) line involves an easy slab up to a 7c+/5.13a hand crack ahead of a poor rest and a final cluster of small gear: two brass nuts and a micronut. After that, it continues to a V11/8A crux headwall sequence on crimps, with a 10-meter (32-foot) runout. The climbing difficulty is estimated to be around 8c+/5.14c, similar to Meltdown in Yosemite.

On the first ascent in 2006, MacLeod’s belayer was secured to the rock to minimize fall distance. Since then, the preferred method has shifted to dynamic belaying for a longer fall but a softer catch above the belay ledge. Today, the route still carries the potential for huge, 60 to 70-foot whippers.

Dumbarton Rock is a 240-foot volcanic basalt plug with a 1,500-year-old castle on top. The riverside cliff is the epicentre of hard Scottish trad climbing, sport climbing, and bouldering, made famous by Dave MacLeod. When MacLeod established Rhapsody after two years of effort and proposed a world-first grade of E11 7a, he described projecting the route as “an exceptionally arduous experience in every way.” His violent falls resulted in several lower leg injuries.

“It was lovely to hear Rhapsody got a first female ascent from Lara and that people have been keen for that route in general,” MacLeod told Climbing after Neumeier’s ascent. “I always found that wall an inspiring sheet of rock, but wasn’t sure if that was just because it was my home crag as a kid. So I’m really pleased to see that Rhapsody has encouraged lots of folk from around the world to come over, and they seem to have enjoyed the route.”

Neumeier was born to climbing parents in Füssen in Germany’s Allgäu Alps and started climbing at the age of two. She adds Rhapsody to a list of achievements in trad and big wall climbing, including two notable free climbs on Yosemite’s El Capitan: a first female ascent of El Corazón via the Muir Blast (5.13b; 3,000ft) with Zangerl in 2023 and a free ascent of El Niño via the Pineapple Express variation (5.13c; 2,500ft) with Feurle in 2024. This summer, Neumeier became the second woman to complete the original Alpine Trilogy, which consists of three 8b+/5.14a multi-pitch sport routes across the Alps: Silbergeier, Des Kaisers neue Kleider and End of Silence. She was also the first woman to complete it within a year.

I met Neumeier the day after her climb to learn about why she chose to project Rhapsody, how it compared to other 5.14c trad climbs that she has tried, what her training involved, and how the big whipper felt.

Lara Neumeier: I was extremely happy and also really proud of myself. I have never put more energy and hard work into a route, so it felt really special.

Neumeier: I first thought of trying Rhapsody at the beginning of 2025, when I did Psychogramm (5.14a R/8b+) at Bürser Platte in Austria, because I really like trying hard trad routes. I enjoy the process: You work the line on top rope first, and only go on lead when you really feel ready.

I first heard about Rhapsody when Jacopo [Larcher] did it. I researched it and thought it would be cool to try.

We came this spring for 10 days to see if I could do all the moves, because I knew it was around 8c+/5.14c. We climbed for five days on top rope, then we had two days of lead attempts.

What makes Rhapsody really special is that it’s a super long trad climb with super compact rock. The rock type is volcanic basalt, and it feels a bit like sandstone. The moves are super nice and technical.

Neumeier: It’s hard for me because I’m really bad at grading. The first 15 meters is easy, maybe 6a/5.10a. Then you have a big ledge where you can get a no-hands rest, and I put on my crack gloves there. Then you have the hand crack, which is graded around 7c+/5.13a on trad gear.

The upper part starts from the last placement. It’s 25 moves to the top with no gear. I’d break it down into three sections: the first crux, the traverse and the second crux. People have said the upper boulder problem is the hardest part, and the top crux is an 8A/V11 boulder problem.

Neumeier: After the summer Alpine Trilogy, my training wasn’t super specific. In August, I climbed cracks in Lofoten, [Norway,] which probably helped with the Rhapsody crack. Back home, I focused on spray wall sessions and improving my finger strength. I tried to practice long, reachy moves and also did a lot of core training.

The Alpine Trilogy also showed me that I’m really strong mentally. When you take on a big project, you don’t know beforehand whether you can do it. I realised that you just have to commit and invest a lot of time, and then it becomes possible. You just have to dream big!

Neumeier: In spring, I took the fall three or four times. This trip, I took the fall maybe 20 or 30 times.

I was really scared before I went on lead. On my first lead attempt, I passed the first crux and then fell. I felt completely fine afterwards. It wasn’t a problem or dangerous.

But I always fell either on the traverse or two or three moves above it, so I wasn’t very high above the last placement. If you fall at the very top, on the top move or the two moves below, it’s definitely scary.

Neumeier: I think 8c+/5.14c works quite well. It’s always hard to say, because it can feel different for different people, but for me, it didn’t feel like 8c/5.14b. I don’t think it’s 9a/5.14d either, so I think 8c+/5.14c works well. Compared with other hard trad climbs I did or tried in Yosemite, it felt like a good grade.

Neumeier: It’s hard to say because I tried Magic Line and Meltdown but haven’t done them, so it’s always difficult to comment on the grade if you haven’t climbed a route.

I think Meltdown felt harder than Magic Line. Rhapsody might be similar to Meltdown, but it’s hard to compare because the styles are completely different. On Meltdown, the crux is in the lower third of the climb, whereas on Rhapsody the crux is at the very top. Rhapsody is also much longer. They’re just different.

Neumeier: For me, it was definitely physically very hard. In sport climbing, 8c+/5.14c is my personal best. I’ve never invested a lot of time in sport climbing, but this felt quite hard.

In the top section, I used super small footholds, and it felt really insecure. Every time I got up there, I could do the traverse, but I would fall on the upper part because the footholds felt so bad. It always felt like I was going to slip, and sometimes I did.

It’s also mentally challenging when the crux is right at the top and you have to climb the whole 30 meters to get there, try the moves, fall, and then do everything again.

Neumeier: It was really cool to do it with Nemo because on a route which is close to your limit, it’s really hard. You have bad weather, and you really have to keep your motivation up.

If you’re with someone who’s also trying the same route, it’s just easier. Buster was trying it, too, so we had a really good crew. We got really psyched when someone did well on a lead attempt, and then the next person was psyched and tried to get a new high point.

We had 15 climbing days in total across both trips, and eight days of lead attempts overall.

Neumeier: We had a proper Scottish celebration! First, we got pizza just around the corner. After that, we went to a pub, drank some whisky and played darts.

Neumeier: It’s really cool to be the first woman to climb this route because it has such a big history and is such an iconic line. It’s crazy that, in 20 years, no other women have done it.

I think Meltdown would be E11 if it had an E grade, and it has been climbed by other women, Beth [Rodden, 2008 FA] and Babsi [Zangerl, 2023]. But there’s only a small circle of women who have climbed at that grade, and being able to add my name to that list makes me really proud.

Neumeier: It’s maybe because of its reputation. It’s known to be really scary, but I think the core climbing community knows it’s safe. There are lots of videos online where you see those big whippers, with Dave crashing into the wall and getting injured. But I think you can make it safe nowadays. Maybe people still have it in their heads that it’s scary and a little bit dangerous.

It’s also known for having really reachy moves. Babsi Zangerl, who tried it before, said she struggled with some of the moves. Maybe now that I’ve done it, some other women will get psyched to try it. There’s beta for shorter people, too.

Neumeier: It’s a very special place because you have world-class hard bouldering, sport climbing, and trad climbing, but there’s graffiti on all the boulders and on some days local kids come along to drink or just enjoy life. It’s interesting how lots of different people come together here.

We were quite lucky on this trip because we had really good weather, and there were always lots of people at the crag. We just had really good vibes, and everyone was so supportive.

(Editor’s note: ‘Headpointing’ refers to the practice of rehearsing a route on top rope before leading it.)

Neumeier: Yeah, definitely. I really enjoy working a route and trying hard. For me, it’s a mix of doing multi-pitch routes and really hard, single-pitch routes. I’m really psyched to find another hard trad line for next year.

#79. Forgotten 7,000'ers: Changtse

Changtse is a rarely climbed peak in Tibet in the Everest massif, flanked by the Main Rongbuk and East Rongbuk Glaciers, and linked to the world’s highest mountain by the North Col. With a prominence of only 497m, Changtse is subordinate to its parent peak.

Modern Chinese mapping lists Changtse at 7,543m, though older sources cite figures up to 7,583m. The Changtse Glacier flows north into the East Rongbuk system, and some geographic surveys note a glacial lake on the glacier near 6,216m, ranking it among the world’s highest.

Because of Changtse’s connection to the classic northern approach to Everest, early mountaineering parties repeatedly crossed its flanks long before treating it as an independent objective.

In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine became the first climbers to set foot on Changtse. They climbed the East Ridge while scouting camp locations during the British Everest expedition.

During the 1935 British Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition led by Eric Shipton, the team divided to scout possible climbs before targeting Changtse. Bill Tilman and Edmund Wigram considered the peak’s Northwest Ridge but deemed it impracticable and crossed north of Changtse to Camp 2.

Meanwhile, Michael Spender and Charles Warren established high-altitude survey stations, and Shipton and Dan Bryant explored the West Rongbuk Glacier. Shipton’s primary goals were to photograph Everest’s upper sections and gather data on monsoon snow behavior. Despite deteriorating weather and waist-deep snow, they established three high camps.

On August 21, 1935, Shipton, Tilman, Wigram, Bryant, and Warren launched an attempt on Changtse. They climbed to within 460m of the summit before dangerously deep, soft monsoon snow forced them back. They spent a freezing night at high camp. Then, confronted by unstable slopes and buried tents, they abandoned their summit attempt.

Moving down the East Rongbuk Glacier on August 23, the climbers reunited with Spender, who had completed his difficult survey work, and headed toward the Kharta Changri Pass.

Base Camp of the 1924 Everest expedition. Photo: Royal Geographic Society

In 1952, during the British Cho Oyu Expedition, Edmund Hillary, George Lowe, and three Sherpas illegally crossed the Nup La Pass into Chinese-controlled Tibet after abandoning their Cho Oyu climb.

The group traveled to the North Side of Everest, exploring the East Rongbuk Glacier and visiting pre-war British base camp sites. Subsequently, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier for a direct attempt on Changtse’s summit. They reached 6,600m before a lack of food and supplies forced them to turn back. They returned over the pass to meet up with Shipton.

On October 3, 1982, Dutch climber Johan Taks, a member of the Dutch Everest expedition, climbed Changtse without a permit and against the wishes of his expedition leader. Contemporary Dutch accounts described him setting out alone after being ordered not to, returning later that day to announce success.

Changtse from the upper slopes of Lhakpa Ri. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

Eleven days after Taks’ unauthorized solo push, on October 14, 1982, the first official ascent of Changtse was achieved by members of a German party.

The German Alpine Club team, co-led by Eduard Geyer and Hansjuergen Tauscher, approached the mountain via the East Rongbuk route. The expedition included climbers Paul Braun, Thomas Dunsser, Martin Engler, Walter Ernst, Rudolf Frick, Andreas Heckmair Jr., Ludwig Hoesle, Peter Lechart, Udo Zehetleitner, and Wilfried Zink.

The team drove from Lhasa and established their Base Camp near the final moraine of the Rongbuk Glacier at 5,105m. From there, they pushed up Everest and Changtse without the help of high-altitude porters. The climbers relied on their own strength and a team of six yaks to establish Camp 1 at 5,601m on October 2, followed two days later by Camp 2 at 6,096m, at the foot of Changtse’s long northeast ridge.

To get higher, the climbers first had to climb a difficult 610m snow-and-ice slope mixed with exposed rock. They established Camp 3 at 6,400m, sheltered behind a protective rock spur. Above this point, they fixed ropes along a steep slope on a wide ridge that curved first north and then sloped east. On October 13, they successfully placed Camp 4 high on the ridge at 6,903m.

On October 14, Zehetleitner completed the first official ascent, climbing via the four-kilometer northeast ridge, starting from the junction of the East Rongbuk and Changtse Glaciers. Two days later, on October 16, Braun, Frick, Hoesle, and Engler also topped out. They listed Changtse’s height as 7,550m.

Everest and Changtse. Photo: Himalayanwonders.com

In May 1983, the first Chilean expedition to Everest was already stretched thin by high altitude and extreme logistics when internal friction pushed the team over the edge. Among the climbers was 25-year-old glaciologist Gino Casassa, who had been temporarily sidelined by altitude sickness and was sent down to Base Camp to recover.

As his health improved, Casassa grew restless under the strict commands of his expedition leader, Gaston Oyarzun. Forbidden from taking unnecessary risks, Casassa instead fixed his sights on Changtse. At 3:30 am on May 14, Casassa secretly slipped out of camp alone, starting an unauthorized solo attempt up the mountain’s long northeast ridge — the same route used by the Germans.

Moving rapidly in the subzero darkness without a permit, radio communication, or backup, he gambled everything on a lightweight style. By 3:30 pm, he was just 10m below the summit. However, the upper sections of the ridge deteriorated into unstable snow cornices and deep powder. Casassa narrowly escaped disaster when the snowpack fractured and slumped 4.5m beneath his boots, threatening to trigger a massive avalanche down the face.

Refusing to retreat, Casassa bypassed the unstable ridge by traversing directly onto the steep, exposed north face. He finally reached the summit at 5:00 pm. After a difficult descent in the dark, he reached Camp 2 at 11:00 pm, exhausted and dehydrated.

Back at camp, his unexpected return sparked outrage rather than celebration. While Casassa was on the peak, his teammates were managing a high-altitude medical emergency, and his unauthorized disappearance had caused immense panic.

Because the climb lacked official Chinese permits, it also carried diplomatic risks for future Chilean expeditions. The Chilean Mountaineering Federation officially expelled Casassa, concluding one of the era’s most astonishing solo feats with immediate controversy.

In May 1986, a massive Chinese–Japanese expedition (17 Japanese and 19 Chinese climbers) targeted the mountain. After establishing an Advance Base at the confluence of the Changtse and East Rongbuk Glaciers, they pushed up the Changtse Glacier and the northeast ridge.

On May 10, 16 climbers reached the summit. Among them was Tibetan climber Gunsang (also spelled Guisang), who became the first woman to summit Changtse. A second wave of eight Chinese climbers topped out the following day, while the remaining Japanese climbers withdrew to assist a teammate suffering from high-altitude sickness. According to the Himalayan Database, Gunsang remains the only woman to summit.

Ed Webster’s photo on August 26, 1986, during his first attempt on Changtse’s Northeast Ridge. Two days later, he established a new route, solo via the Southeast Face. Photo: Ed Webster

Later that same summer, American mountaineer Ed Webster arrived to attempt a bold, lightweight climb.

On August 26, 1986, he initially turned back from 7,163m on the right side of the face because of dangerously thin snow over brittle shale. After just a single rest day, he launched another attempt on August 28 and established a landmark new route up the southeast face.

Starting from an Advance Base at 6,126m near the foot of the North Col, Webster climbed the lower, highly avalanche-prone sections in total darkness to capitalize on the stable nighttime freeze. He navigated a prominent snow gully between two massive rock buttresses, traversed the upper face, and connected with the German northeast ridge route to reach the summit alone in a 15-hour round trip.

In September 1987, an Australian expedition led by Robert Turner arrived at the East Rongbuk side of the mountain. On September 29, despite punishing high-altitude winds and deteriorating conditions, Turner and Glen Nash reached the summit. They climbed via a central couloir to the left of the north face icefall. This completed a line that was closely related to a route scouted by a Japanese team the previous year.

Changtse attracted global attention in late summer 2016 because of two remarkable solo ascents. Jordi Tosas of Spain reached the summit via the east ridge on August 27, and Kilian Jornet followed on September 11, via a variant line up the northeast face.

The total number of Changtse summits remains low, at around 60. The standard line remains the northeast ridge.

Illustrated photo of the 2016 expedition for the American Alpine Journal. From the approach to the north: (A) Point 6,822m; (B) Everest; and (C) Changtse. (1) Approach to the east ridge of Changtse (first ascent 1982). (2) Jornet variant on the north face (2016). (3) Japanese variant on the north face (1986). Photo: Jordi Tosas

KrisAnnapurna is a writer with ExplorersWeb.

Kris has been writing about history and tales in alpinism, news, mountaineering, and news updates in the Himalaya, Karakoram, etc., for with ExplorersWeb since 2021. Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#80. The Best Fleece Jackets for Men and Women (2027)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

October 2026: The best fleece pullover for men and women overall is the Mountain Hardwear Airmesh Long Sleeve Hoody for its incredible moisture management and “warmer-than-it-looks” hollow-fiber construction. For those seeking the most wind- and weather-resistant option, the Blackstrap Tribrid Grid Fleece Jacket is our top pick. For both sustainability and dollar value, the Black Diamond Rift Full-Zip Fleece Jacket is a standout.

Four-plus decades after it was invented, fleece is still the undisputed king of breathable midlayers, from fall and winter hiking and mountain biking to skiing and snowshoeing. The fluffy, airy synthetic structure delivers both warmth and ventilation and moves perspiration and excess heat away from your body. But with more materials and construction styles than ever before, finding the right layer takes some work. We put more than 40 to the test last winter to narrow it down to just seven of the best fleece jackets for men and women.

Sizes: XS-XL (women’s), S-XXL (men’s) Weight: 6 oz (women’s and men’s)

Pros and Cons + Very warm + Great moisture management + Low bulk – No recycled content

This hooded pullover handily outperformed most fleeces we tested in terms of its ability to wick sweat effectively. Credit goes to the fabric’s 100-percent polyester “octa” fibers, which are hollow in the center and feature eight fins that mop moisture as fast as wearers produce it. Hurrying up a skin track trying to keep pace with faster skiers, one tester got warm but not steamy. Despite the fabric’s relative thinness, its insulation value is impressive (the fibers’ hollow cores trap warmth more effectively than solid yarn).

Because it’s fuzzy on the inside and smooth knit-mesh on the outside, this piece also appeals to folks who don’t love fleece’s fluffy aesthetic. Yet the piece is reversible, and wearing it mesh-side-in purportedly improves breathability by 28 percent. Multiple testers confirmed the boost in ventilation; however, warmth takes a dip, and the small, zippered hip pocket isn’t accessible when worn inside-out. The hood includes a high collar that stands in for a neck gaiter in blustery conditions, and thumb holes extend the sleeves over the backs of the hands for extra warmth. Bonus: It’s less stinky than most fleeces, thanks to an anti-odor finish that kept this hoody fresh-smelling for hours (even multiple days) of wear. Downside: Sustainability suffers with all-virgin materials.

Sizes: S-XXXL, Tall L-XXL Weight: 9.4 oz (medium)

Pros and Cons + Wind-buffering + Very breathable + Three tall sizes – Primaloft clumps over time

Outdoor Vitals is far from the only brand to mix super-breathable active insulation like Polartec Alpha or Octa with more durable face fabrics, but the Pursuit Hybrid Fleece might be our testers’ favorite chimera. As a stand-alone layer, it blocked wind, insulated, and breathed well enough for a speedy, sweat-free traverse of Stowe’s Pinnacle Trail in Vermont.

This hoody is body-mapped with 75-gram Primaloft Evolve synthetic insulation and 30-denier stretch nylon over most of the garment, with stretchier grid fleece under the arms and lower body. The grid fleece areas offer maximum breathability, but also better flexibility and structure in places that are notorious for getting stretched out. The stretch-nylon face fabric is robust enough to protect the very warm, breathable Primaloft from getting snagged, with a light DWR to fend off drizzle.

At 9.4 ounces in medium, the Pursuit Hybrid Fleece is lighter than most of the faced ultralight fleeces we’ve tested, like Dynafit’s Tigard Alpha Direct Jacket. It kept our Vermont-based tester comfortable down into the 40s during late fall backpacking trips and makes for a killer baselayer on frigid days that inch down into the single and negative digits.

Pros and Cons + Excellent breathability + Packable – No pockets

This zippered pullover isn’t terrifically warm—and that’s the point. Made for hikers, climbers, and skiers who are constantly on the move, this fleece provides scant (but effective) insulation and outstanding breathability. “It’s perfect for hurried lunchtime workouts and hot laps on powder fields,” says our Colorado tester, who reached for it more often than she expected because the ultralight fabric provides just-right warmth for conditions above 18 degrees. Similar to Mountain Hardwear’s Airmesh, but with a low-pile gridded pattern that provides less insulation, the Futurefleece uses octa fibers that are hollow and polygonal for maximum moisture transport (and minimal weight). It virtually eliminated clamminess, even during high-output effort.

Features are minimal, consisting of elastic thumb loops at the cuffs and a deep half-zip for ventilation. There are no pockets or bulky shell fabrics to add weight, making this topper very packable (softball size) but also wind-permeable. “As soon as I stopped, I felt chilled unless I topped this with a shell or puffy,” said our tester. The body-hugging fit doesn’t layer neatly over thicker base layers, but mobility is excellent thanks to stretchy underarm gussets that give arms full freedom to move.

Sizes: XS-XL (women’s), S-XL (men’s) Weight: 8 oz (women’s), 10 oz (men’s)

Pros and Cons + Sustainable materials + Approachable price – Below average breathability – Not particularly durable

Proof that inexpensive gear doesn’t always signal sub-par performance, this lightweight fleece impressed testers with its field cred and its environmental scorecard. The 100-percent recycled polyester addresses fleeces’ dirty little secret: Most shed tiny fragments of plastic that persist in waterways. But this fabric actually biodegrades—fibers are embedded with a patented ingredient that lets microorganisms decompose the material. And the thinner fabric proved ideal for year-round wear while skiing, camping, and hiking in cool conditions: Our Maine tester wore it beneath a shell while skiing Sugarloaf in 38-degree weather, and over a tee while packing up the tent on 60-degree mornings.

A zippered chest pocket holds a phone, and two hand pockets secure keys or a snack. The hoodless design layers tidily beneath a shell, and the fit is efficiently trim but unconfining. But breathability is a shortfall: Compared to other fleeces we tested, this one feels clammier, making it best for moderate- to low-exertion activities. And the soft fibers pilled from skirmishes with backpack straps. But when paired with a shell or during light activity, this affordable fleece earned testers’ enthusiastic endorsement.

Sizes: XXS-XL (women’s), XS-XXL (men’s) Weight: 8 oz (women’s), 10 oz (men’s)

Pros and Cons + Warm + Fairly breathable + Affordable – OK packability

A true generalist, this midweight fleece ticks boxes for warmth, breathability, durability, and even value (it’s a killer deal at $109). The hollow fiber, 100-percent recycled polyester is sewn in a zig-zag pattern with ventilating channels. Although it doesn’t prevent stickiness as effectively as the Mountain Hardwear Airmesh, it comes close: Wearing this midlayer skiing T-to-B at Sugarloaf, Maine, our tester felt no sweat buildup and only noticed dampness during a 10-minute bootpack.

The crew’s fit is looser than the body-hugging R1 Air full zip (which best suits slim builds) and comfortably tops the full range of base layers. One zippered chest pocket holds snacks or a smartphone. And the seam-free shoulders feel smooth beneath a backpack, even with direct contact (the fibers also proved rugged enough to resist pilling from abrasive straps). As you’d expect from a midweight fleece, packability is not stellar: It’s volleyball-sized when toted (similar in packed size to the Black Diamond Rift, but warmer.)

Sizes: XS-XL (women’s), S-XXL (men’s) Weight: 19 oz

Pros and Cons + Blocks wind + Breathable + Stretchy – Expensive

A fleece that feels comfortable in virtually all conditions? We didn’t think it existed, until we threw on the Tribid. This magical layer kept testers dry while they climbed (even during snowfall), protected from chilling gusts, and warm (but not smothered) throughout moderate-to-strenuous activity. Its formula pairs gridded polyester fleece (60-percent recycled) with a soft and stretchy windblock woven nylon (with 20-percent Spandex) shell that’s dense enough to buffer 20-mile-per-hour gusts, but breathable enough to foil clamminess on sustained uphills in 20-degree temps. “I could wear it until I was really warm without sweating it up, which isn’t true for most fleeces,” one tester reported. Under the arms, shell-free fleece panels facilitate moisture transport.

Adjustable with an elastic cinch cord around the face, the hood earned raves for its comfortable fit and effective protection. “I barely felt like I had a hoodie on—it was tight enough to stay put but moved with me and didn’t feel cumbersome,” said another tester. Three zippered pockets—two hand, one chest—hold keys or dog treats. Femmes, take note: The square cut doesn’t accommodate a bosom: with no chest darts shaping the fit, one average-sized tester reported a tight fit across the breasts.

Sizes: XS-XL (women’s), S-XXL (men’s) Weight: 13 oz (women’s), 15 oz (men’s)

Pros and Cons + Very warm + Packable + Breathable – Relatively heavy

This Merino-based midlayer matched competing synthetics for technical performance and bested most for temperature regulation. “It’s crazy how warm it is, because the fabric isn’t at all bulky,” reported one wearer after ski-touring in 15-degree temperatures. When packed, the Cloudripper is roughly cantaloupe-sized. The gridded fleece combines 69-percent Merino wool with 15-percent recycled polyester and 3-percent Spandex. Under the arms and across the lower back, Ridge Merino uses a thinner, less-insulating version with more polyester and lycra to trim bulk and improve layering (testers in bib pants loved this hybrid feature).

As you’d expect from a gridded fleece, the fuzz-free channels facilitate ventilation, so that testers only experienced clamminess in temperatures above freezing. “I love that I can keep it on while I’m moving, when I’m stopped, and across a whole spectrum of effort levels so that I don’t have to bother with a lot of layer changes,” one reported. The Merino’s natural water repellency handles light flurries. The hood is thin enough to fit under a helmet, and elastic trim snugs it in place during windy conditions (gusts above 20 mph had one tester reaching for a shell, however). And stink prevention is tops, with one tester boasting, “I never washed mine all season, but could still wear it to work because it developed no offending smell.” Downside? It weighs more than comparable synthetics.

Fleece jackets range widely in warmth, breathability, and weather protection. Materials also vary. Synthetic fleece is quick-drying, making it a smart choice for damp conditions, and abrasion-resistant. Unlike wool or even cotton, synthetic fibers can hold their own against friction from backpack straps. But fleece made from merino wool is particularly warm and temperature-regulating (wearers avoid clamminess through a broad spectrum of temperatures). Hybrid constructions—a trend that continues to gain momentum in this category—combine various fabrics in multi-paneled jackets that pair breathable fleece in the hot zones such as underarms with wind-resistant fleece in exposed areas like the shoulders.

Here’s how to judge what will serve your needs.

As a rule, a fleece isn’t as compressible as, for example, a down jacket. So it takes up considerable space in luggage or backpacks. If you need heavyweight insulation but know it will remain packed most of the time, you might consider other, more space-saving insulated jackets.

Some fleeces use a dense construction that traps body heat but limits breathability. If you’re cross-country skiing, running, or logging other high-output outdoor workouts, look for lightweight fleeces or hybrid constructions that use body mapped insulation and place breathable panels under the arms and in other hot spots.

Most fleeces offer some water-resistance, but that varies—and no fleece can be counted on to deliver waterproof protection against serious rain or sustained snowfall. Most fleeces are also porous enough to let breezes in, which is great for sweat mitigation but bad for comfort amid 30-mph winds. Consider whether you’ll wear a shell sometimes, always, or never: Ski-tourers might choose a fleece with some weather-resistant panels so they can skip a shell in milder conditions, while resort skiers are often better off with breathable fleece worn as a midlayer under a full shell jacket.

If you’ll wear the fleece in 0- to 10-degree F temperatures, or if you’re always chilly no matter the conditions, choose a high-pile fleece with cozy insulation.

Yes, many fleeces offer a combination of breathability, warmth and durability that makes them ideal for snowshoeing, skiing, and other cold-weather sports.

Not always. Petroleum-based fibers and the shedding of micro-plastics lower fleece’s sustainability score. But some fleece fabrics stand out, thanks to technology that minimizes micro-plastics (see the Black Diamond Rift) and/or prioritizes recycled content (such as The North Face Futurefleece, Patagonia R1 Air, and Blackstrap Tribrid). Some (such as the Merino-based Cloudripper) limit the use of synthetic fibers in favor of natural material.

Yes, all fleece offers some insulation to hold in body heat, but warmth depends on fabric pile and other factors: Generally, high-pile materials feel warmer than short-pile fleeces.

Our testers don’t just spend a lot of time outdoors. Yes, they are gifted skiers, mountaineers, ultrarunners, climbers, hikers, and view-admirers. But they also possess the gift of gab. Our testers must be able to say much more about a piece of gear than “It’s awesome” or “It sucks.” Instead, we choose industry professionals, lifelong athletes, and fellow gear reviewers who can both identify a product’s strengths and weaknesses and talk at length about the nitty-gritty details that make a jacket shine in some areas—and fall short in others. Over the course of each testing season, each tester keeps notes on their samples’ fit, how much wind protection each delivers, its ability to retain warmth, and whether it plays nice with a backpack. They geek out on the gear and its performance, and then deliver those notes to us for final analysis.

For this test, we evaluated 42 of the most promising fleeces on the market, including full-zip and pullover styles. We pored over our testers’ notes to nail down each jacket’s best application: Is the fleece best for dog-walking? Nordic skiing? Après at the resort? All of the above? Only the items that earned raves on both performance and livability earned coverage among these reviews.

Kelly Bastone ski-bummed in the Colorado Rockies from 2002 and has pursued outdoor sports ever since. A freelancer who writes about gear and other outdoor topics for publications such as Backpacker, AFAR, and The Red Bulletin, Bastone has contributed many gear reviews to Outside over the years. An avid skier (resort, Nordic and backcountry), fly-fisher, mountain biker and mushroom forager, she gets the news she needs from the weather report.

Bastone’s backing band of gear testers includes ski bums across resorts in Maine, New Hampshire, and Colorado: These diehards click into touring, downhill, or cross-country boards each and every day of the season. A wildlife researcher and ultrarunner punished jackets in Minnesota; another ultrarunner and backcountry rescuer tested insulation on all-weather runs and missions in northwest Colorado; a rancher wore test puffies while exercising horses in Montana.

#81. What Trail Runners Need to Know Before They Go (Number 2)

Sometimes you can’t stop nature from calling, but don’t let the infamous Hyrox incident stop you from getting to the start line. The perfect poop starts with a plan, and believe it or not, it’s far easier on trails than in a convention center. Sarah Wassner Flynn fleshes, or should we say flushes, out the rules for a courteous crap below.

Last month, Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk was competing at Hyrox Beijing, an indoor fitness competition, when she suffered a sudden bout of fecal incontinence roughly halfway through her race. Rather than step off the shared course, she kept going, through burpees on a carpeted floor, a stint on the seated rowing machine, and running segments, ultimately winning the race in just over an hour.

The story, to no one’s surprise, went mega-viral. Sure, there was the shock value of an athlete losing control of her bodily functions on camera. But that’s an unfortunate side effect many endurance athletes have experienced or witnessed on a race course at some point. Marathoner Paula Radcliffe popped a squat on the side of the road in front of live TV cameras while leading the 2005 London Marathon. 2026 Ironman World Champion and four-time Ironman 70.3 World champion Taylor Knibb famously quipped to a broadcast cameraman, “I just s*&% myself, so can you not get my ass?” en route to winning the T100 final in 2024. What made Wietrzyk’s case different from those other bowel movements etched in sports history was the indoor setting on shared equipment, with other athletes racing around (or behind) her the entire time.

The backlash that followed was less about the accident itself and more about how Wietrzyk was allowed to continue racing while putting other competitors at risk. Hyrox responded to the incident within days, updating its rulebook to allow race officials to pull an athlete whose “blood, vomit, urine, or feces” pose a health or contamination risk to themselves or others—an addition that, notably, hadn’t existed until now.

Of course, trail running doesn’t have Hyrox’s shared-equipment problem—there’s no carpet to contaminate and everything takes place outside. But in a sport where pooping mid-race is more or less a given over the course of enough miles, the underlying questions are the same. Are race organizers doing enough to provide proper bathroom access on remote courses? And what obligations, written or unwritten, do runners have to protect the trails and each other?

Ask any longtime ultrarunner and they’ll tell you: bathroom stops are a long-standing, half-joking, half-serious topic of conversation in the sport. Hours of running and bouncing shake up your gastrointestinal system. Throw in early-morning coffee, gels, and nerves, and it’s inevitable you’ll need to go at some point. Many races provide porta-potties at aid stations, but in longer races, when there’s no bathroom for miles, stepping off-course to relieve yourself is a near-given.

“Whenever you have a race of more than eight hours, if you don’t have some kind of bathroom urge, you’re likely severely underfueling,” says Kristen Kelman, an ultrarunner in Deerfield, Illinois and the 2021 Road Runners Club of America 50-Mile National Champion. “It’s often not logistically possible to have any sort of bathroom nearby. It’s a reality of the sport.”

For ultrarunners, that reality comes with a responsibility to take care of the land they’re using, which means being just as deliberate about how they go as where they go.

“It’s an issue of trail stewardship,” Kelman says. “We have a responsibility to take care of the trails and the land we are using so that we can continue to explore and challenge ourselves in these wild and beautiful places. That includes being responsible about your poop.”

While expectations and guidelines vary from race to race, most events follow the seven principles of Leave No Trace, which aim to protect natural spaces and ensure a sustainable future for the planet. The principles apply to everything from disposing of waste to where to wander in the woods, with poop being a paramount point of concern.

“Human waste is often cited as one of the most concerning impacts from recreation that land managers are facing,” Erin Collier, director of education for the Leave No Trace organization in Boulder, Colorado, says. “Given the popularity of [trail running], the scale of the events, and the often-remote nature of the courses, it’s safe to assume the potential for human waste impact is high. When human waste isn’t disposed of properly, the potential for environmental and public health impacts is significant.”

Collier adds that more than 100 protozoans, bacteria, and viruses have been identified in human waste, including Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium parvum, various coliform bacteria, and viruses such as Hepatitis A.

“These can contaminate water sources and spread disease,” she says. “This is why proper burial techniques or packing it out is so important. A common misconception is that if a bear can poop in the woods, so can you. ”

In other words, simply ducking a few feet off-trail to go behind a tree isn’t enough. Standard Leave No Trace guidance is straightforward: If you need to go, get at least 200 feet from the trail and water sources, dig a 6-to-8-inch cathole, and bury your waste thoroughly. Runners should carry their own supplies—like toilet paper, wipes, and a trowel—and pack out their used materials.

In some environments, however, experts recommend taking things a step further and suggest pooping in a plastic bag filled with waste-alleviating gel, also known as a WAG bag.

“WAG bags are recommended or required when you are unable to dig an adequate cathole, get the appropriate distance from water, or are in specialized or high-use environments like the desert terrain of the [American] Southwest, deep snow, or high alpine where soil is too rocky to dig,” Collier says. “It’s important to understand the waste disposal requirements for the area you’re running in.”

Who’s responsible for what when a runner has to go mid-race?

“Both runners and race organizers have important roles to play, and one shouldn’t replace the other,” Collier says.  While the onus should fall largely on runners to prepare for their own needs and pack out what they bring in, race organizers set the tone for what’s expected, though in many cases official race policy on the subject is quite thin.

The race regulations for the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), one of the most prestigious trail running festivals on the planet which hosts some 10,000 runners each August across its various events, don’t specifically address bathroom protocol on the trails. Participants receive plastic bags at packet pickup along with their race bibs to be used for “soiled paper used during any urgent need along the route” and runners are reminded to “keep their rubbish and wrappers with them until they can throw them in the bins at an aid station.” A separate section of the UTMB website dedicated to “good practices on the trails,” is more direct: “If you’re caught short in the wild, move away from trails and water points, don’t stop behind a shelter, hut or refuge, and take your paper with you.”

The race guide for Cocodona 250, a point-to-point ultramarathon in Arizona, is more prescriptive than UTMB, though different from Leave No Trace’s standard policy of going 200 feet off-trail. Under “Restroom use on Course,” the rules say: “It happens. Step 30 feet off the trail and dig a 6 inch (or deeper) hole. Used wet wipes / TP must be packed out in a zip-lock. DO NOT LEAVE TP ON THE TRAILS!”

And the rules for the Leadville 100, the 100-mile endurance race held in the Rocky Mountains near Leadville, Colorado, include a line prohibiting “public urination,” but don’t specifically address pooping (that likely falls under the race’s Leave No Trace policy: “No garbage, clothing, or race-related items may be left on course”).

Some race directors don’t feel the need to go out of their way to spell out bathroom expectations. Andy Bacon, owner of Ex2 Adventures, an events management company that hosts dozens of trail-running and adventure races throughout the Washington, D.C. metro area each year, says while pointing out porta-potties is standard, telling people where to poop elsewhere is never on his to-do list.

“People are always asking about the bathroom situation, and I make sure they know about the porta-potties we provide at the start and sometimes along the course, but I’m not providing information about where to go when you can’t make it to a porta-potty,” he says. “My role as a race director is to inform people of what their options are, but I don’t think I have to tell people, ‘hey, you should carry toilet paper in case you need to go to the bathroom in the woods.’”

In the culture of ultra-distance and trail running, Bacon says the hows and wheres of relieving yourself are “sort of just an unspoken rule.” “Most people know that if you’re going to be spending most of your day out in the woods, you’re going to have a pack with a plastic bag with toilet paper in it,” he says. “And if you have to go, you’re prepared for it, you do what you have to do, and you move on. It’s not a big deal.”

Many ultrarunners we spoke to were equally nonchalant. Asked about his own methods, uber-ultrarunner Michael Wardian, who had just finished running all 2,650 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail, said simply, “I try to get well off trail and then bury anything.”

Awkward encounters happen, especially in the late stages of an ultra, when sleep deprivation and fatigue can lead to poor decision-making.

“I’ve definitely seen a lot more than I signed up for,” Kelman says. “For me, seeing another runner go is one thing. But if it’s a family hiking with small kids out there and they [witness] someone pooping, that’s definitely over the line.”

While individual runners may be reluctant to share unsavory stories about pooping mid-race, the bravery provided by an anonymous avatar leaves Reddit boards full of them. One runner described passing three people who had stopped less than 10 feet from the trail during a race without porta-potties. Another recounted a friend who had to stop in the middle of a flat, open desert: “I swear everyone within five miles knew he was popping a squat.”

The, uh, bottom line? Shit happens, as Joanna Wietrzyk’s viral race in Beijing made clear. But ultimately, Collier says, doing your business the most environmentally and ethically responsible way on the trails comes down to having a plan.

“It’s safe to assume that poop will be a part of anyone’s race experience and [runners] should not assume that a lack of restroom facilities gives them permission to leave waste or toilet paper wherever they choose,” Collier says. “There should be a plan in place at all levels for how to deal with poop in the least impactful way.”

#85. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

First Highline on Trango Tower: On August 17, Lukas Irmler and Antonia Ruede-Passul of Germany completed the first-ever highline walk on Trango Towers in Pakistan’s Karakoram. They climbed Great Trango Tower to acclimatize before tackling Nameless Tower.

Setting up the 21m highline required fixed ropes and two summit ascents of Nameless Tower. The successful crossing saw Ruede-Passul break her own women’s highline altitude world record, previously set at 5,860m on Ojos de Salado in Chile, while Irmler surpassed 6,000m for the first time.

Following in the footsteps of Norway’s Great Adventurers: Steffen Skjottelvik set out to cross Canada, by foot, dog sled, and canoe, accompanied only by his beloved sled dogs. The Norwegian began his journey in 2023, but when one dog fell ill, he paused in the remote Cree community of Peawanuck. Here he found his home and a way of life that fitted him perfectly. He also fell in love with a local woman and became a second son to the community elders.

His original plan to travel by sled across the Hudson Bay coast changed after wolves killed one of his lead dogs. He decided to canoe the coastline in summer instead.

In 2025, he set off with his malamute Togo and a husky named Bay, facing polar bears, powerful tides, dense bogs, clouds of biting flies, and river crossings. On August 15, exhausted after weeks of difficult travel, Steffen could finally see his endpoint — the town of York Factory across the Hayes River. All he had to do was cross it. Togo survived and made it to shore, but Steffen’s body was found downstream 10 days later.

Where Was ‘Tenzing’ Filmed? Apple TV’s Tenzing recreates the historic 1953 first ascent of Everest, this time with Sherpa Tenzing Norgay at the center of the story. The filmmakers used real alpine environments across Nepal and New Zealand rather than green screens.

Nepal provided locations for Tenzing’s early life in the Lower Mustang, as well as the scenes in Darjeeling, Kathmandu, and Everest Base Camp. New Zealand’s Southern Alps, particularly the Aoraki region, doubled for Everest’s glaciers and icefalls, with the Darwin Icefall standing in for the notorious Khumbu Icefall.

Photographer Encounters Magnificent White Stag: Wildlife photographer Brian Johnston has captured incredible images of a rare white stag, believed to be an albino red deer. Johnston and a friend spotted the stag one windy morning during the rutting season, but it detected them and ran off.

Returning the following day, they found it asleep in a field, apparently exhausted after a night of rutting activity. Eventually, it stood up, giving Johnston the opportunity to photograph it.

Shark Attack Survivor Recounts Losing His Leg While Surfing: Australian firefighter and surfer Mel Ismail was surfing at Glenfield Beach on Australia’s west coast on September 14, when he was attacked by a shark. Sitting beyond the breaking waves, watching a pod of dolphins, Ismail initially thought a dolphin had bumped into his leg. Suddenly, he was dragged underwater and realized what was happening.

He desperately tried to push his fingers into the shark’s large black eye, and it released him. Ismail was bleeding heavily but managed to catch a wave toward shore. Another surfer spotted him and helped him onto the beach. Despite losing his leg below the knee, Ismail is determined to return to the water and start bodyboarding as soon as he can.

Canoe Dig It: Sam Dunning discovered freestyle canoeing during the 2020 lockdown after seeing a video of master paddler Marc Ornstein performing an interpretive routine to music. Amazed by the combination of technical skill and on-water choreography, the New York-based actor and filmmaker began writing Canoe Dig It?, a mockumentary inspired by comedies such as This Is Spinal Tap.

Winning the paddling community’s support was not easy, but at a freestyle canoeing symposium in Ohio, Dunning eventually met Ornstein. Ornstein and his wife agreed to be stunt doubles for the film.

Into Thin Air: This is a good background to the stories we’ve done on Kalie McCrystal, the 38-year-old skyrunner who disappeared on the Matterhorn on September 1. She met a Polish climber on her ascent, and theirs is the last footage of her. It shows her climbing towards the 4,478m summit. Shortly afterward, she was spotted descending the Italian side. Then she vanished.

Mountain rescuers believe she fell between 4,100m and 4,250m, but cannot establish exactly where or in which direction she fell. Despite a thorough search, no clothing, blood, or remains have been found. Her mother and sister eventually accepted that she had died on the mountain.

Climber Awarded Carnegie Medal After Rescuing Hang Glider Pilot: Matthew Clark has been awarded the Carnegie Medal for rescuing a hang glider pilot who crashed into a cliff on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

Clark, a 24-year-old climber and paraglider, had launched from the same spot minutes apart. Clark had just landed when he heard the crash reported over his radio. Reaching the scene with other pilots, he found Parson suspended in his harness around 15m above the ground.

With no walkable route to him, Clark spotted a narrow chimney nearby and free soloed up it, reaching him in about five minutes. Clark cut Parson free, moved him to safer ground, dressed a gash on his knee, and waited with him until a helicopter team was able to extract him on a long line.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#86. Pacific Crest Trail Association Signs New 10-Year Agreement With Government Agencies

The Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA) announced this month that it has signed a new 10-year Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the USDA Forest Service, the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and California State Parks.

PCTA Trail Operations Director Justin Kooyman said in an update posted on PCTA’s website that “the MOU is an important tool that clearly articulates the roles and responsibilities of the PCTA and the federal and state agencies in the maintenance and management of the PCT.

The US Department of Education defines a memorandum of understanding as “a document created between two or more parties explaining how they will work together to achieve a common goal.” It represents a formal but nonbinding agreement.

The PCTA has signed MOUs with federal and state agencies twice previously, in 1993 and 2015. “While the new MOU is an important update, there are not many substantial changes to it,” said PCTA Director of Marketing and Communications Chris Rylee in an email to The Trek. According to Rylee, the most important change is that the new agreement “more explicitly calls out PCTA’s role as collaborative managers to increase the quality of our relationship with agency partners.”

The 1968 National Trails System Act established the framework for collaborative public-private partnerships in the maintenance of national trails, recognizing the role of volunteer organizations and nonprofits in trail upkeep and improvement.

“The PCT thrives because of the partnerships that bring its vision to life. It truly takes a community made up of dedicated volunteers, agencies, and supporters to operate, maintain, protect, and preserve this iconic Trail and the extraordinary values it embodies,” said PCTA Administrator Linsey Steinwachs in the PCTA’s update.

#87. From Groomed Hardpack to Sidecountry, VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports’ H-POWER 89 Is the Resort Ski That Does It All

VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports' H-Power series. (Photo: (c) Kleinmond - Georg Lindacher)

Choosing the perfect resort ski might be the toughest gear decision you make. It’s the ski you’ll use most often, so it better be just right. You obviously want to prepare for the worst—ice, boilerplate, hardpack—but you don’t want to go too skinny and close the door on powder. You need something that carves on corduroy but still retains enough snap and agility to handle bumps and trees. You need a ski that’s durable—you’re definitely not going to skimp on outings this season—and it needs to be up for some occasional sidecountry. Oh, and it has to look cool; that’s non-negotiable.

Is that too much to ask? A few years ago, it might have been. But that’s only because the VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports H-POWER 89 wasn’t out yet.

The H-POWER 89 is the latest brainchild of Marcel Hirscher, an Austrian racing legend with a serious ski obsession. Hirscher started making skis with Red Bull’s backing in 2022. First, he poured his decades of pro experience into making performance piste and touring skis. But now, he’s zeroing in on his true mission: making high-performance equipment for everyone.

The result is the H-Power 89 (and its snappy little sisters, the H-Power 78 and H-Power 68). The H-POWER 89 was developed with the US market in mind and tested on US snow, benefitting from all the same high-tech materials and meticulous testing as the brand’s racing skis, but with a regional focus. The combo ensures a truly versatile ski: immediate power transmission, racecar-smooth stability, and razor-sharp responsiveness all in one sleek package.

The secret is a precisely engineered poplar-beech wood core, reinforced with dual layers of titanal. The H-Power 89’s full ABS sidewalls and racing edges provide superlative grip, letting you execute precise lines even on East Coast ice, while the wider waist provides enough float for a Central Rockies powder day.

But it’s not all about materials and specs. Skiers know that the true heart of a ski is in the overall quality and meticulous craftsmanship that goes into putting the whole thing together. And that’s where VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports stands out. Based in the tiny village of Scheffau am Tennengebirge in the Austrian Alps, the company is small enough to lavish attention on every line of skis it turns out. The planks stay in the press longer, which ensures a stronger bond and more robust performance. And because each line is produced in small batches, quality is guaranteed.

With the H-POWER-89 underfoot, you can’t go wrong. And it might be time to take back that opening statement: Choosing a resort ski won’t be the hardest decision you make this year. In fact, it very well could be the easiest.

At VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, founded in the Austrian Alps by ski legend Marcel Hirscher, we do things differently. We believe in the power of new  and a no-compromise approach to skiing and equipment. Together with  Red Bull, we combine racing  expertise with innovation to create world-class skis for a new generation.
