#88. “Beauty, Breadth, and Epicness”: Colorado’s New, 2,000-Mile Thru-Hike Is Gorgeous and Hard as Heck

Finally finishing the route at Black Canyon of the Gunnison (Photo: Donovan Rice)

An idea struck Donovan “Iceman” Rice in 2024 at the Colorado-Wyoming border. He had just finished the 700-mile Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail and couldn’t get over how much he’d enjoyed it. Rice had hiked the Pacific Crest Trail in 2020 and fell in love with thru-hiking. But no part of that trail, or any part of the New Mexico section of the CDT, resonated with his soul like the mountains of his home state. The scrambling, the alpine ridgelines, fourteeners, and endless side quests had been an absolute thrill for the 29-year-old from Golden.

He reflected at the border, “If there were a 2,000-plus-mile hike that was a longer version of what I just did, that would be my dream hike.”

That moment planted the seed for Colorado’s newest thru-hike, the Great Colorado Route (GCR). Over the next several years, it would grow within Rice’s mind until life presented the perfect opportunity to sit down and build it. He was between jobs and put all of his energy for several months into mapping and planning the route. The result was an epic, 2,000-mile backpacking loop that traversed the breadth of Colorado’s Rocky Mountains.

Rice posing for a selfie near Island Lake (Photo: Donovan Rice)

“[The GCR] goes as far west as Rattlesnake Arches, as far south as Alamosa, as far east as Colorado Springs and as far north as one mile shy of the Wyoming border,” he explained to Backpacker.

When he was finished mapping (or as close as he was going to get), there was only one thing left to do: hike it.

On May 14, 2026, Rice embarked on his journey, starting in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. He wouldn’t return for five months. In that time, he’d gain thousands of online followers who tracked his journey and cheered him on. He’d grow a beard, meet hundreds of new friends, and eventually become the first person to complete Colorado’s newest long trail.

Because it’s a loop, you can start the Great Colorado Route from pretty much anywhere along it. Rice began in the far west and hiked counterclockwise. The trek touches some of the most beautiful national parks and other public lands in the state. Highlights include national parks like Black Canyon of the Gunnison and Rocky Mountain; wilderness areas like the Indian Peaks, Eagles Nest, Flat Tops and Lost Creek; fourteeners like Pikes Peak and the Maroon Bells, and more.

“I really, really liked Indian Peaks Wilderness and the Wild Basin inside of Rocky Mountain National Park,” he said, recalling some of his favorite segments. “And then, I was also a big fan of the Sangre de Cristos and walking directly across Great Sand Dunes National Park—across the dunes themselves.”

In total, the GCR passes through three national parks, two national monuments, all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, 29 wilderness areas, eight wilderness study areas, and accesses 13 Fourteeners, and 47 Thirteeners.

Officially, Colorado has two long trails. There is the famous Colorado Trail, which extends from Denver to Durango and covers 567 miles of the state’s mountain region. There is also the previously mentioned CDT, which starts at the US-Mexico border and follows the continental divide up through New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, and Montana to the border with Canada.

A third route exists, though it’s not technically “official.” The Northern Colorado Route was mapped and designed by another thru-hiker like Rice, named Kevin Silvernale, who established it in 2024. That thru-hike starts in Estes Park and traverses the northern Rockies before terminating in Glenwood Springs.

When Rice was designing the GCR, he reached out to Silvernale. He wanted advice on whether he should make the route as accessible as possible for as many people as possible, or if he should design it more selfishly, to his hiking tastes and mountain preferences.

Silvernale didn’t hesitate. “He was like, ‘Dude, make something that resonates with you. Hike your favorite hike,’” Rice recalls. “And it was really cool to give myself permission to do something a little more extreme.”

Rice warns that the GCR isn’t for first-time thru-hikers or beginners. He tracked 364,000 feet of vertical elevation gain, and “that’s probably an undercount.” He loves scrambling, doing off-trail navigation, and connecting routes that don’t have an official connector. Rice said he didn’t design it to be difficult for difficulty’s sake, but rather because he wanted to experience as much of Colorado’s diverse landscape as possible, without backtracking, doing too many out-and-backs, or road walks. In fact, from the outset, Rice set design rules he wanted to follow.

“The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness,” he said. Beyond pursuing those, the route had to avoid crossover with the CT and the CDT. It also couldn’t have technical rock climbing or require special equipment like packrafts or climbing ropes, and it had to be doable, but challenging for an experienced hiker like him.

Staying honest to those rules kept things very interesting on the trail, he said.

“This whole hike was kind of a scouting mission,” Rice said. He’d find closed trails, or obstacles no other hikers had reported online, and have to problem-solve his way around them. “It was a lot of building the plane while flying it.”

During his four-and-a-half-month journey on the GCR, Rice started an Instagram page and used Corsa Live Tracking for people to follow his progress. And boy, did they. Rice’s Instagram for the GCR has 7,482 followers (as of this writing). If you scroll back to the very beginning, it’s clear how interest in his adventure built over time.

“It was kind of a funny evolution as the trip progressed, where more and more people would start recognizing me,” he said. “It started off as, ‘Wait, are you That Guy?’” As the hike went on, he graduated from being ‘That Guy’ to ‘Great Colorado Route,’ to, finally, ‘Iceman.’ Being recognized, he said, was “a really surreal experience.”

While the hike itself was the reward he sought from the beginning, he said that the heroes of his trip were the small towns dotted along the route. Just about everyone Rice met was stoked about the hike, and many offered support along the way.

“The vast, vast majority of responses I’ve been getting are overwhelmingly positive,” he said.

When he finally arrived back at Black Canyon of the Gunnison on October 1, Rice said he felt a sense of accomplishment that was totally unique compared to his other thru-hikes.

“Not only did I complete this trek, but I created this trek … It definitely made it more awe-inspiring,” he said. “I would say that was probably my primary emotion for the entire trip: this experience of awe and being completely struck with wonder.”

#91. The Only Way to Truly Hunt the Fall Migration Is to Follow It

Published Oct 18, 2026 10:18 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

It’s dark and raining on the Canadian prairie. Most sane people are still tucked in bed or just putting on a pot of coffee. But the group of us getting soaked to the bone setting out decoys and brushing in A-frame blinds in a cut pea field are all certifiable. We’re jonesing for cupped wings, and the only way to get our fix is to wake up before the ducks and geese fly from their roost waters to these grain fields to feed.

The morning is full of the usual anticipation, plus an extra helping. That’s because we’re hunting one of the oldest birds in the world: the sandhill crane, a flying, 4-foot-tall velociraptor with a wingspan of up to 7 feet. At first light their distinctive purrs break the prairie stillness, and we are all now very awake. Their razor-sharp talons dwarf the spurs of any 3-year-old tom. Sandhills have long and pointed beaks, and they aren’t afraid to spear you or your retriever with them.

The first cranes glide into the decoys. Some of us have never hunted them before, but even we can tell that once the sandhills commit, there’s no backpedaling. They are big and clumsy and can’t gain altitude fast enough as we raise our shotguns in unison. Most of the birds tumble from the sky in a tangle of wings and legs, but two sail into the peas. Our guide, Dusty Brown, doesn’t hesitate to stomp through the muddy Saskatchewan stubble toward one of them. The bird spouts a vicious hiss and spreads its wings.

But Brown gives the crane a swift boot right in the chest and it flops back. He finishes it quickly. He has to get the crane to the ground to kill it and protect himself and his Lab, Briley. The second, less experienced crane guide is far more tentative, dancing around the second sandhill like a nervous boxer in the opening round of a fight.

“The first time one stood up and hissed at me, I did the same thing,” says Brown, who has since hunted cranes in Texas, season after season. “I wasn’t sure if it was going to attack me or my dog, and so I was hesitant.”

His experience is the product of chasing the annual waterfowl migration from Canada south to the oil fields of Texas and back north in spring for the conservation snow goose order. The 50-year-old guide has been doing this for more than 20 years. Most core duck hunters undertake similar journeys at some point in their careers, starting in the Prairie Pothole Region in September and calling it in the South come January, stopping at points along the way to intercept ducks and geese.

“When the lakes and rivers freeze up, that’s the end of the season for a lot of hunters because the birds move on,” says Brown. “But for guys like me, it’s just another stop along the way. We never want our season to end. So we hitch the trailer, hop in our trucks, and follow the birds.”

Like so many duck hunters who live a migratory lifestyle, Brown has been infatuated with waterfowl from an early age. A friend’s dad took him on his first hunt, floating a garbage can full of decoys into the marsh, dumping them out, and then coming back for the two boys. They both climbed into the can and used it as a blind while his friend’s father shot ducks. During high school, Brown worked for his dad, slinging pizzas in the bustling flyway of Oregon’s Willamette Valley. He saved all the money he made slicing pepperoni to lease farm ground along the Pudding River. It flooded every year, creating seasonal wetlands for ducks.

The hunting along the river was good enough to last a decade. Brown didn’t start living on the road until his late 20s, when he began buying every goose call he could get his hands on.

“The calls really intrigued me, but I didn’t know anything about contest calling because the world championships in Stuttgart, Arkansas, were 2,000 miles away,” Brown says. “I won the Oregon state goose calling contest in 2001 and became a goose guide at 27 years old.”

That win led to competition calling at contests across the country. Back then you had to listen to live callers to improve (YouTube didn’t exist yet), and that meant traveling from state to state, learning from the best along the way.

By then, waterfowling had Brown firmly in its grasp, and he only wanted to hunt more and see new places. That urge took him up and down the Pacific and Central flyways. The same thing happens to a lot of duck hunters: the early mornings, feathers cutting through wind, tricking birds into the decoys. Some hunters can never get enough, and that’s Brown. He can’t stop. And he doesn’t want to.

“You see a lot of guides who are single because they have devoted their lives to this and a relationship doesn’t play into it,” says Angie Erickson, who hunts with Brown at her Curly Tail camp in Saskatchewan in the fall and spring. “It happened to me. Once you start, it’s an addiction. I hate to call it that, but that’s what it is. I have young twin boys and had to pull the reins in. I was consumed with setting spreads and fooling birds, and I was not spending enough time with my family. When I stopped, it was like going through detox.”

That’s the sacrifice this kind of duck hunting requires. You can lose yourself in the migration, and it pulls many hunters away from the folks they love most. It’s hard to watch hunters with more freedom continue to the next duck camp while you head home and take care of your responsibilities. It can cause jealousy, test friendships, and even end marriages. Brown has seen it happen time and again. It’s the reason, he says, he’s never married and never had children. Because he made his choice years ago, he doesn’t have to choose each season.

Brown won’t be able to pass the knowledge he’s gained as a guide down to a son or daughter, but he does share his expertise with any hunter who’s willing to listen. Unlike some guides who talk at their clients, Brown cares enough to teach his something new. Because odds are they’re not as talented as callers and can’t read birds like Brown.

“Dusty has become one of my best friends in this entire world,” says Hunter Pickett, who began guiding with Brown in Canada and Texas when he was 21. “He’s helped me personally become a better guide and given me the knowledge to kill birds consistently so I can keep doing this for a living. I wake up at 4 a.m. eight or nine months out of the year to go hunt. That’s a great life for a duck hunter.”

Brown’s lessons aren’t patronizing either. When I hunted cranes with him and that handful of other hunters, it felt like old friends sharing a morning together—the way duck hunting ought to always be.

Many guides who travel as much as Brown eventually settle somewhere. They cut back on the number of days they hunt or open outfitting businesses of their own. If Brown has one regret, it’s that he has never successfully worked for himself.

“We never want our season to end. So we hitch the trailer, hop in our trucks, and follow the birds.”

He did try to open his own guide service once in Alberta, with a friend. After years in transit—he’s gone through three Cummins diesel truck engines, which last up to 350,000 miles apiece, in the last two decades—Brown put down stakes. But it was bad timing. Just as the 2001 waterfowl season kicked off, terrorists flew into the World Trade Center. Air travel was suspended for only a few days, but new flight restrictions and fear of another attack caused clients to cancel, and the business went under.

It was a major financial hit for Brown, and it understandably soured him on ever owning another guide service. The COVID-19 pandemic only solidified his stance on never taking that chance again as he watched many Canadian outfitters shutter their businesses due to the extended U.S.-Canada border closure.

“I’ve always worked for someone else,” Brown says. “I think that if I could have started a business here in Oregon, that’s what I would have done. But I just never felt comfortable doing that because we don’t have the bird numbers to make it sustainable.”

Still, not owning an outfit has allowed Brown the freedom to move on when he’s ready for the next adventure. He can’t help that the migration is in his blood. Even at 50, he continues to follow the birds as they make stops along their traditional routes while exploring new spots as migration patterns shift. Brown shows no signs of slowing down.

“I still get excited as we come out of summer and the cooler months are upon us,” Brown says. “You start to see fields full of geese in late August, pay attention to how they act, and I just can’t wait to get on the road—to be there when the first birds come to the grain fields of Canada.”

This story originally ran in the Migrations Issue of Outdoor Life.

Joe Genzel is a contributor at Outdoor Life. Genzel grew up chasing mallards and Canada geese in the Illinois River Valley. But since the only thing left to hunt in Illinois besides whitetails are squirrels, he now spends most of the fall and winter searching for oak and black walnut trees, and walking behind a crazy Russian squirrel dog named Vladimir.

#92. Camino Primitivo Day 14

We woke up early, excited, and ready to go. We threw together the rest of our stuff and headed downstairs for breakfast. We got a delicious honey glazed croissant and a coffee. After we finished breakfast, I bundled up in my coat from Lightheart Gear located in Asheville NC and we headed outside. It was chilly for a while but once we found the trail and headed up hill, it got warmer. After we crossed a bridge and got to a fence, I put my bag down and took off my coat. The trail was lovely too. It was flat and paved road but we passed some pretty views and some interesting trees.

We walked by 2 adorable, short, stubby bulls with long horns behind a fence.

We had a nice, quiet hike up until we reached an industrial park which was noisey. We rounded the corner and there was a little Camino de Santiago market next to a vending machine. We stopped at the vending machine and used our coins to get each of us a Powerade. We entered a park and walked past a huge public Albergue with multiple housing opportunities as we got closer to town.

We crossed the busy road and found the Santiago sign and got my photo in front of it.

We passed by a cute little specialty coffee shop which was called “Shot me coffee” and we stopped for a latte to try their beans. It was nice to have an ice latte.

We continued our leisurely walk through the town and entered the historical building area towards the Cathedral.

We finally found our way to the big, beautiful Cathedral surrounded with people. Tourists admiring the architecture. Pilgrims celebrating the completion of their Camino. Protestors sitting outside the city building across the street.

We got out finishing photo in front of the cathedral before heading to the pilgrim office.

We got on fairly quickly, got our certificates with our Latin names (mine was Mariane and Prestons was just Preston), some souvenirs, and got our pilgrim shells. It was all very exciting. I sat outside the office, unsure how to feel.

I suddenly felt hungry and we went to Camino Curry where Ian and Jane wondered in and we’re surprised to see us! We all had lunch together.

After lunch, we visited the different museums in the cathedral before our 4:45 rooftop tour. We got to walk around the entire rooftop outline of the cathedral. It was gorgeous.

Afterwards, we checked into our hotel, cleaned up, and waited till dinner. We had Galacian wine and cheese with olives and another appetizer of scallops. It was all delicious.

It was a nice way to celebrate the end of the Camino Primitivo.

#93. Weekend Warm-Up: Keep It Burning

Keep it Burning: Making History on the Trango Towers follows Edu Marin as, along with his father and brother, he attempts a second free ascent of Pakistan’s Nameless Tower. He’s after the great Eternal Flame line, created by Wolfgang Gullich and Kurt Albert in 1989.

After failing the previous year, Edu Marin has returned to Eternal Flame with what he calls his dream team. That includes his 70-year-old father, Francisco “Novato” Marin, as well as his brother Alex. Neither has much experience with big-wall climbing or high altitude. However, as Edu explains, “I knew that they would stay until the end.”

It’s a strategy that paid off for the first people to complete a free ascent of Eternal Flame. Two decades after Gullich and Albert created the route, brothers Alex and Thomas Huber free climbed it. Both return for this film, sharing their experience from the first climb.

The three Marin climbers. Photo: Screenshot

They get to base camp at 4,200m and begin acclimatizing and preparing the logistical side of the climb. Managing the weather, the altitude, and the 1,200m of rope to fix adds another layer of difficulty. Then, when the team has settled in to begin the climb, an avalanche hits in the middle of the night.

Everyone emerges unharmed, though shaken. Novato recalls his fear that the avalanche would bury his sons, as they survey their dismantled camp. Everything needs to be dug up, but everything essential is still there, so the trio goes ahead and begins the climb.

They are making steady progress. But at the 6,000m Snow Ledge, they learn that a week of bad weather is heading right for them. While Alex and Novato head down to rest and wait out the storm from below, Edu sits tight.

“If you descend from the wall,” he argues, “you have to climb all the pitches again from the bottom.”

So instead he will sit on this 6,000m ledge, at below-freezing temperatures, for eight days. There’s a weather window that far out, and he plans to take it. This, Thomas Huber says, may be the hardest part of the project.

The sun comes out after 10 days of waiting. Reunited with his family, Edu leads the final ascent.

Edu on a technical pitch. Photo: Screenshot

The weather holds, and, encouraging each other as they ascend the last few meters, all three climbers reach the summit, with Edu completing the second-ever free climb. We see them on top, laughing and embracing, while final cutaway interviews with Novato and Edu discuss what it meant to complete the climb as a family.

“It’s a pleasure to share this sport, and to share it with my sons— there’s nothing better!” Novato says, smiling. “As long as my body allows me, I’ll keep going.”

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#94. Tom Hiddleston, Genden Phuntsok, and Willem Dafoe Reveal Which Climbing Scenes Were Real on ‘Tenzing’

Tom Hiddleston and Willem Dafoe have both seen their fair share of action and drama throughout their careers. They’ve travelled to different worlds in sci-fi thrillers and performed death-defying stunts in action blockbusters. And Genden Phuntsok, the Chinese actor who plays Tenzing Norgay, is at home at high-altitude. He grew up on the Tibetan Plateau raising yaks and horses. But perhaps nothing has compared to the challenges the actors faced on the set of Tenzing, which started streaming on Apple TV on Friday, October 16. This new movie directed by Jennifer Peedom tells the story of Sherpa climber Tenzing Norgay, from his early life as an illiterate yak herder to the first ascent of Mount Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953.

With no previous climbing experience, Tom Hiddleston, who plays New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary, was thrown into the deep end. He trekked to Everest Basecamp. The 45-year-old London-born actor actually learned to navigate crevasses, and climb ice walls and boulders.

Similarly, Willem Dafoe overcame his fear of heights to take on the role of Colonel John Hunt, the 1953 expedition leader. The 71-year-old Oscar-nominated American actor also learned mountaineering skills to bring a level of authenticity to his performance and build camaraderie with the cast.

And while Genden Phuntsok, who stars in the film as Tenzing Norgay, may have had the most high-altitude experience of the three cast members, he had never climbed before making the film. And the rumor that the 40-year-old actor actually practiced his lines for Tenzing with his family’s yaks is true. For the role, he also spent time living with Sherpa mountain guide Phurba Tashi, who has reached Everest’s summit 21 times. Tashi took Phuntsok hiking for four hours a day, every day, according to Outside.

We caught up with Phuntsok, Hiddleston, and Dafoe to hear about their wildest experiences and exposures on set, from witnessing avalanches to actually climbing out of crevasses. Watch excerpts from the interview above, or read what the three actors shared with us below.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Tom Hiddleston: Genden and I had the privilege of literally following in Tenzing and Hillary’s footsteps, as anyone who has trekked to Everest Basecamp has also done.

It was an inspired idea from our director, Jennifer Peedom, who wanted us, as Genden and Tom, to experience the landscape for ourselves. She wanted us to feel the beauty and the wonder of the Khumbu Valley from the pine forests to the rushing rivers over which you cross over metal bridges until that moment when out of the blue sky, these goddesses emerge—the 8,000-meter-plus peaks of the High Himalaya. Ama Dablam, Manaslu, and then eventually Nuptse, Lhotse, Pumori, and, finally, Everest. As you know, if you’ve done the trek to basecamp, you have to take your time because you need to adjust to the altitude.

Hiddleston: Along the way, we met so many Sherpas. Two brilliant Sherpas escorted us: Phurba Tashi, who is the star of Jennifer Peedom’s documentary Sherpa and has summited Everest 21 times. And also Dr. Nima, a high-altitude doctor who was educated at the Hillary School, a school Edmund Hillary built in Khumjung. We got to understand the Sherpa attitude towards these mountains and Everest and also how much both Tenzing and Hillary had given back to those people.

Hiddleston: We saw Everest together for the first time, at the same time. To look up at the magnificence and power of that mountain is to be inspired by such awe and humility. Knowing that we were going to play the first two men ever to stand on its summit felt incredibly resonant and special. We were bonded forever by that experience.

Then we went back to Kathmandu and began filming. But we were also training all the time.

Hiddleston: We did some bouldering in Kathmandu for a couple of days. Then, once we got to New Zealand, where we filmed all the high-altitude scenes, we had the most extraordinary team. You’ll be well aware of Guy Cotter, Hugh Barnard, Barry Blanchard, and Mike Roberts.

Guy Cotter himself has summited Everest six times. The New Zealand mountaineering community is among the most experienced, highly skilled, and capable in the world. We also had a great stunt coordinator in Augie Davis, who had worked a lot with Peter Jackson and knows those mountains.

Hiddleston: Genden and I were taught to ice climb. We were taught about cutting steps and the shared responsibility for the rope, taking turns leading. We learned all about the equipment: the ice axes, crampons, and oxygen tanks. It was amazing.

There’s a scene in the film that really happened. Tenzing and Hillary were cutting steps on the Lhotse Face and they had a great day. They were quite confidently and quickly returning to camp for dinner. As Hillary described it, they were almost running. He leapt across a gap in the ice, but his right foot fell on the other side, the ice gave way and he was falling fast into a crevasse. There was nothing he could do about it, just a free fall into blackness.

Then he felt his rope go tight. Tenzing had made a self-arrest, tied the rope around his ice axe, and Hillary then had what he called the routine mountaineering issue of climbing out of the crevasse.

We did it for real. It really happened to Hillary and it really happened to me. I got dropped into the crevasse in New Zealand. Genden was at the top with the rope coiled around his waist. I had to climb up. I had to generate enough momentum while suspended in mid-air to jam the ice axe into the ice wall and then cut my own ladder of footholds and handholds out of the ice.

The camera was on a remotely controlled jib, but things happened. A sheet of ice that was the size of a single bed dislodged from the lip of the crevasse and fell on my head. You see it in the film and it wasn’t planned.

There was something about the extraordinary experience of being in the real environment that allowed Genden and I to live the experience as Tenzing and Hillary would have done. It was really remarkable, unforgettable, and unrepeatable.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Genden Phuntsok: That really happened and when we were shooting it was all real. We used our bodies to do that and it wasn’t a performance. Of course, we were exhausted. But when I pulled Tom up at the edge of the crevasse, the relationship became like real brothers.

Phuntsok: They are all real professionals and always say to do everything slowly. [They] taught [us] so many important techniques of climbing. They were all always very patient.

Phuntsok: I just tried to find out every detail of what he had experienced and what he suffered all his life.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Willem Dafoe: It’s true. I’ve got a little thing about heights, but the trick is not to look down. One of the most challenging moments was the Lhotse Face sequence, when I was on a very sharp incline. We put a line down, I backed down into it and then I had to come up that wall of ice. I couldn’t look down. By the end of the day, I could, but initially, I couldn’t. So that’s how I deal with it: Just concentrate on what’s in front of you and never look at the depth of things, because that’s when it engages your vertigo or calls to you. That’s how you get over it.

Dafoe: You just learn about what your body can and can’t take, where your abilities lie and where your weaknesses lie. I think that’s one of the reasons people like to challenge themselves: not only to find that little piece of themselves they think is missing, but also to learn about their body and their relationship with their thinking through very difficult physical tasks. You learn a lot about yourself, physically and mentally, and what you can take and what you can’t.

Dafoe: I mean that in a philosophical way. The desire to do something extreme usually comes from trying to find some sort of meaning or trying to come up against something. I think we all have that. It manifests in different ways, but I see it in pretty much everybody.

Dafoe: We had some of the top people in the world because Jennifer Peedom, the director, is from that world. She had wonderful connections through her documentary work and her climbing. She got some of the best people in the world, so we were very safe. They would usually get to the location before us and test for avalanche possibilities and identify where the crevasses were, but sometimes we’d get very close to them. It was usually charted out, so technically, we were very safe. Safety was a big deal, so I never worried about that.

It was more about the physical task of doing things, like cutting ice steps. It was the physical exertion of those things, which you may not see. You see some of it in the movie, but you have to remember that we’re getting dropped off by helicopter for the high-altitude stuff. The helicopters go away, but we still need to get wherever we’re filming. Getting there is part of it, even if we’re not filming along the way. That’s where you enter the story.

Dafoe: I’m an actor who always works from the physical, and I always have since I was young, so I usually try to be ready for a physical challenge. You don’t really know until you get there. As much as there’s climbing, sometimes you lose feeling in your hands and it gets difficult to grip, or you get tired cutting ice steps. A lot of the physical challenge is just enduring difficult circumstances. Being there all day in that kind of weather is challenging sometimes. With a strong wind, it can drive you mad.

You’re climbing, but a lot of the time you’re also sitting around on this very imposing mountain. Where your mind goes and how you help each other are all part of the mix. There’s no trailer to go to, no toilet, nothing to eat. You bring a sandwich, but it freezes in an hour, so it’s useless. You bring it anyway, though. I don’t know why, but we did. It was a great adventure.

Dafoe: The idea is that you get these actions into your body so they become part of you. It doesn’t become the other. You try to create a parallel experience that gives you a key to the real experience you’re trying to inhabit.

For me, the formal training for the climbing was pretty minimal because most of that training happened when we got on location. It’s hard to approximate those things, and the actual weather, conditions, and snow that we didn’t have in the Himalayan foothills, we had in New Zealand when we were shooting the high-altitude stuff.

You could only train so much, but it was mostly about creating camaraderie and a dynamic within the group. That was mostly about trekking in the foothills. That was our training. They would give us rope to work with and teach us some of the things to do with it. But in the end, we had a lot of help with that stuff. You went as deep as you wanted to, and I went as deep as I needed to do the things I do in the movie.

Dafoe: Not so much. I don’t have that kind of ambition to go somewhere really dramatic where the lack of oxygen makes it difficult to move. That’s not my thing. Maybe I’ll come to it, but I loved the experience. As I say, it was a communal experience. To do it solitarily, I don’t think it necessarily turned me into a climber.

Dafoe: Well, it was amazing. There was one scene where we had a basecamp in an area where I’d been shooting the other day. I heard this huge roar, looked over, and saw it come down with such incredible force. Needless to say, you’ve got to see one to believe it. Thank God we were far enough away that we didn’t even feel it, but the roar and the force of it were quite incredible.

I don’t pretend to be a mountain guy because of this experience. I learned a lot, but I’m not that knowledgeable. However, after a while, you could look at some of the snow formations, and I would ask, “Does that look like it’s ready to avalanche?”

#95. Off-Season in the Adirondacks Can Turn on You Fast. Here’s How to Stay Safe.

A hiker ascending Swirral Edge towards Helvellyn in the Lake District. (Photo: Getty/Duncon Andison)

People have written books and made movies about the magic of hiking in New York’s Adirondack mountains, the largest publicly protected swatch of land in the United States at about 6 million acres. But the rugged, high peaks have seen some negative coverage, too—like when a hiker died of hypothermia on a solo hike up Mount Marcy, and the slew of near-daily nonfatal rescues where hikers run out of food and water, or lack sufficient gear, maps, or flashlights.

Many are drawn to the Adirondacks with the goal of becoming a 46er, someone who has summited all 46 High Peaks—traditionally defined as mountains taller than 4,000 feet—and taken on the toughest terrain. As an aspiring 46er myself—I just hit my tenth peak (Big Slide) last fall—I know how unpredictable weather in the region can be and how the trails differ from others in the state and in the Northeast. I’ve also witnessed the influx in traffic to trails post-COVID and have encountered eager, unprepared hikers on my descents.

One late afternoon, while descending Mount Marcy in a downpour after a roughly 16-mile hike, I ran into a group of hikers just heading up. That encounter and others prompted me to talk with search and rescue (SAR), who explained that the publicity of the region can draw in people who are unprepared, leading to higher rescues and recoveries. I asked what advice they’d give to hikers just starting out.

Here’s what they shared on how to safely enjoy the mountains in any season.

The 46 mountains in the Adirondack High Peak region draw people in from all over the state (and beyond) eager. Adirondack Forty-Sixers, Inc., is a membership organization that recognizes those who have climbed all 46 High Peaks since 1925. While passionate, these peak baggers can sometimes push themselves beyond their limits or comfort zone, said Logan Quinn, forest ranger with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation. Quinn has been a ranger in the state since 2013 and situated in the Adirondacks since 2016. “A lot of the people we rescue out of the High Peaks are aspiring 46ers,” he said.

Like many, I’ve long felt drawn to the region, though I didn’t jump straight into tackling high peaks. I spent my first visits exploring local towns, hiking lower peaks, and kayaking, because I wasn’t yet comfortable in the backcountry. My hiking experience has grown alongside my knowledge of safety and preparedness.

Photos from the region regularly trend on social media, said John Bulmer, publisher of Adirondack Mountain News and co-founder of the nonprofit Adirondack Mountain Rescue. Viral photos attract less experienced hikers looking for the perfect shot—especially during leaf peeping season in the fall. “People see Indian Head and a lot of things online, and they want to go and see that, and there’s really no context involved in how hard it was to get there and the navigational skills it takes to take some of these photos,” he said.

In the summer, visitors might encounter sweltering hot and humid days where normally dependable water sources have diminished to a trickle, or downpours and thunderstorms that only impact certain peaks. Come fall and winter, the temperature can drop drastically between nearby Lake Placid and a peak, with whipping winds and unexpected snow accumulation to account for. For those unaccustomed to the region, the seasons can be unpredictable and unruly, especially if you find yourself ill-equipped in the backcountry or atop a bald peak.

“You go out in the winter, you’re not prepared, you’re somewhere remote, your phone dies, your light dies. That’s a worst-case scenario,” said Bulmer, who was also vice chairman of the nonprofit New York State Federation of Search and Rescue Teams that assisted SAR teams. When people come to the range who have hiked other Northeast regions, like the Catskills or New Hampshire’s White Mountains, they’ll often encounter what’s infamously called the “Adirondack mile,” a term hikers use to describe how miles in the Adirondacks can feel much longer and harder than the distance suggests.

High peak trails are more than a century old, sometimes poorly marked, and covered in rocks and roots. They’ll send you straight uphill, gaining a significant amount of elevation over a short span. And if you hike in the melting snow or rain, there’s a chance the trail could become a downhill creek. All of these thing can lead to injuries or blowing through food and water quicker than expected.

“People can get a little overconfident in their abilities, and that might lead them to go out and try a mountain that they’ve done before during a period of inclement weather or during a time when conditions are very bad,” said Sam Fairchild, strategic coordinator and interpretive educator with the Adirondack Mountain Club, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting the state’s wild lands and waterways. Plus, the remoteness of the peaks can be challenging for even experienced hikers, especially if you run out of food or the hike takes longer than planned, Fairchild added.

He pointed to Allen Mountain as a common culprit, an 18-mile hike he said is one of the most remote peaks in the Northeast. The peak made national news in winter of 2024 when an experienced young Canadian hiker went missing on a solo hike. His body was later recovered in the spring.

Outside of unpredictable weather and inadequate gear, experts agree at the most common reason for search and rescue calls is the dependence on cell phones.

“The reliance on phones to do everything—including being your light and being your only form of navigation—causes a lot of issues,” said Quinn. Each of the SAR experts I talked to harped on the importance of bringing these ten essentials as well as being aware of the unique scenarios that might be encountered in the Adirondacks.

They also recommended having additional gear to prepare for an unexpected night in the backcountry or a way to stay warm when waiting for a rescue, especially in winter when hypothermia can set in quickly.

There are resources hikers can check beforehand to prepare, such as the Adirondack Trail Conditions group Facebook group and the DEC website for notices like trail closures, air quality, and weather reports. For new hikers, the Adirondack Mountain Club offers trainings, from things like learning how to read a map to beginner backpacking classes.

The biggest piece of advice SAR experts can give, no matter the skill level, Logan emphasized, is to avoid hiking alone.

“If something goes wrong, you’re in it on your own,” he said. “So, my biggest advice, to those new and experienced, is please don’t go alone to these more remote places.”

#96. I Survived the Taco Bell 50K, Barely

Dan England put his journalistic and ultrarunning chops where his mouth is, consuming a menu item at 10 different Taco Bells over the course of running 50 kilometers. Along the way, he spoke with the Taco Bell 50K race director and dozens of participants to understand the unique allure of this race, which has expanded from a quirky local event to a beloved race format across the country.

I’ve run 100 miles, climbed all 54 of the 14,000-foot peaks in Colorado, owned a heeler, attended at least a dozen death metal shows, and raised a son and twin daughters. But on Saturday, October 3, I  faced one of the biggest challenges of my life: I had to eat an entire Nachos BellGrande eight hours into a 50-kilometer race.

I was already full of Pintos ’N’ Cheese, a Doritos “Locos” taco, several glasses of Baja Blast, spicy potatoes, Nacho Fries, lots of cinnamon things and, for breakfast, a Chalupa Supreme. I’d run 25 miles through some of the best and worst parts of Denver. It was 88 degrees Fahrenheit.

But this is what it takes to finish the Taco Bell 50K. You have to dig deep. You have to go hard. You have to Live Más.

What initially was by the race organizers’ own admission probably the stupidest event they could dream up is now, by numbers at least, one of the most popular ultramarathons in the country.

One of those organizers and this year’s race director, Dan Zolnikov, is flabbergasted at the attention the event has received, even if he still doesn’t quite understand it. Just two years ago, about 250 hungry runners showed up to Denver, the race’s origin, and 120 finished. Last year nearly 750 came to run. It’s turned into an epidemic: Using the Denver race as a guide, many other Taco Bell races have cropped up across the country from Tennessee to California, organized by other runners who want to inspire people.

Maybe inspire isn’t the right word. The goal, after all, is to eat 10 Taco Bell items at 10 different Taco Bells across the course of a 50K.

And yet, maybe inspire is the right word. It’s safe to say that many, if not most, of the 1,200 or so who showed up Saturday had never run an ultramarathon before and would likely never consider doing one otherwise. More than a few didn’t even know that a 50K is, in fact, five miles longer than a marathon. Even more of them had probably spent more time in a Taco Bell than on a trail, running.

I have proof: The longest any of my three running partners had run was a half marathon. And yet, they were among those ready to run farther than they ever had in their lives while eating food you normally consume when you’re drunk or high.

“Back in 2019, the second year we did it, we had 11 show up,” Zolnikov told me, “and I was blown away by that.”

The race is now enjoying a moment. This year, Denver TV stations swooped down upon the event, and instead of shaking their heads, residents were both horrified and supportive of the idea. Hundreds of cars honked at us as we ran, and dozens of residents sat in their front lawns to cheer us on. One group set up their own aid station with small cups of Modelo, which went down smoother than I expected. I hadn’t received cheers like that in a race since the year I ran the Chicago Marathon in 2013.

The thing is, as goofy and fun and ridiculous as the race is, it’s also hard, and that’s probably the combination that fascinates people. The DNF rate, over 60%, is higher than the Leadville 100. Not only do you run a 50K through a major city, one without many cushy trails, a well-marked route or closed streets, you have to stomach all that Taco Bell. And not only are Tums, Pepto, or Rolaids not allowed, if you puke, you DNF.

This is why I was staring down at the Nachos BellGrande at our eighth Taco Bell. Nachos BellGrande is one of my favorite foods. Now it looked like a pile of compost. We’d already faced many other challenges that day, including overworked soda stations that had run out of ice to cool us off, crowded bathrooms (and a strict edict not to go behind a bush), and the cruel pavement pounding our feet into hamburger.

The clock was also working against us: The 11-hour cutoff nipped at our heels all day. We weren’t sure we were going to make it. There was no time to waste.

I took a deep breath with my first gooey bite.

The origin story of the Taco Bell 50K is actually, against all odds, kind of endearing.

The idea started as most good ideas do: on a group long run. This one, in 2018, was with the Denver chapter of Achilles International, which organizes guided weekly training runs and weekend races for disabled runners. Jason Romero, who is blind, had a bunch of ultrarunning buddies, some of whom had guided him in big races.

Heartwarming, right? Yes, except now this turns into a hard lesson of what happens when you allow ultrarunners to go on group runs together. They ran through a Denver farmers market, where one of the runners loved to eat, and they began to joke about fueling up at the most opposite place they could think of. With apologies to the franchise, that turned out to be Taco Bell.

They joked about it for a few weeks, until Romero, using coarse language, challenged the group. Zolnikov plotted out a 50K course through Denver with 10 Taco Bell stops. It’s the same course now, years later, with a few alterations.

The idea was only sort of batshit crazy. Unlike at a road marathon, a good ultramarathon aid station isn’t just stocked with Gatorade and gels—it’s full of real food. This was my answer when my friends, even other runners, called me insane for signing up for the 2026 Taco Bell 50K.

What do you think I eat at aid stations? Salad?

Still, Taco Bell is infamous for challenging even the most iron of stomachs. My Latina wife, who spent several hours on the bathroom floor after one late-night trip, hasn’t eaten it in years. After the inaugural event, Romero admits he and his friends were wrecked and spent far too many hours in a bathroom.

So, against my better judgment, I did what I do when I sign up for any ultra: I trained. Over the course of three months, I ate at Taco Bell an embarrassing number of times. Kelly, one of my best friends and a former co-worker who is “mostly” a vegetarian and had the idea to sign up for it, took several taco trips herself. She also tried to follow a training plan I put together, but her toddler and infant, along with a demanding job, prevented her from completing many of her longest runs, other than a tough trail half marathon.

When I picked her up, at 4:30 a.m., a couple minutes from my home in Greeley, she asked me how I slept before interrupting me and saying her kids screamed at her all night.

We found a place to park close to the start of the race, a Taco Bell with beautiful arches to run through, a design so clever you’d think it was built for the race (it wasn’t). We pulled in at 5:45 a.m. and grabbed a bib from an unmanned table, with Sharpies so you could write your name. Some wrote things like “Beefy Runner,” “Macho Supreme” and “The Little Dog Who Says ‘Yo Quiero Taco Bell’.”

We hooked up with her two friends, tried to use a bathroom at Safeway. Kelly got in, but the men’s line was too long, at least a half-hour wait. This was a theme all day because there weren’t many women running the race: Women are generally smarter than men. The females couldn’t help but gloat at us as they swept past.

“My my my,” one said. “How the tables have turned.”

A few minutes before the huge crowd gathered to listen to Zolnikov’s pre-race briefing, I unwrapped one of my two “big” items, a Chalupa Supreme, an overstuffed fried taco—I decided to start big while my stomach was empty. Last year, they allowed participants to eat during the 7 a.m. briefing, and I figured a few minutes couldn’t hurt. Kelly vehemently disagreed.

Fine. I wrapped up my fried taco and waited for Zolnikov to talk to us about the rules—keep your wrappers, eat two big items, don’t be feral to the Taco Bell workers—safety (don’t run in front of cars) and no shitting in alleys before taking my first bite.

The race had four waves, from fastest to slowest, all by their own determination, and began with AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck,” probably the most appropriate song for this occasion. We were one of the last to line up. We’d stay near that position for much of the race.

Kelly chided me for my serious demeanor as we approached the first stop. Everyone was having so much fun, she said. Yes, I thought to myself, that’s because they don’t know what’s coming. I’d done ultras. They always hurt.

But, OK, fine, let’s focus on the whimsy, for now.

At the first stop, a group of five dressed in tacos practiced cannibalism. The group leader, who had run a 100K earlier this year, found the costumes on Amazon and then made taco hats. The farthest her best friend (also in the group) had run was 6 miles, a smidge less than 50K.

The group of five all grew up together in Tennessee. They were a handful of the hundreds—yes, hundreds—who traveled out of state to take part in the original and hence superior Taco Bell 50K.

I got their names, but I spilled Baja Blast on my phone screen and panic-wiped it with a napkin and erased the note on my phone.

The Taco Bell 50K doesn’t sell race shirts or any merch at all—in this era of trail and ultrarunning commercialization, it’s heartening to see how the race organizers refuse to make a buck off it—so runners, just like the taco worshippers, wore their own fun. Many, if not most, wore some kind of goofy shirt, many with Taco Bell themes. I wore a colorful, button-up skull shirt. Kelly wore a hat that she made, something about how those who get diarrhea from Taco Bell have weak bloodlines. We saw one runner with a Del Taco button up shirt, which made me laugh.

At the third Taco Bell, Kelly ate her Burrito Supreme, so she’d already consumed her two required big items. She thought going big early would pay off. I needed a break after the Chalupa and Doritos taco and ate some small Cinnabuns instead.

Kelly and I had purchased our first four items the day before and kept them in the fridge overnight. This was not only legal but encouraged by race organizers to help prevent us from overwhelming the stores.

But in Taco Bell’s defense, they were ready. Maybe that’s because Zolnikov admittedly harassed many store owners in advance. Maybe it’s because nearly all runners used the mobile app to order ahead, as we did. (Technology is awesome!) Plus, at most stops, there were crates of free bottled water for runners. It was a life saver on a hot day: I was unable to carry much water because my pack was either full of food we carried for the first four stops or the wrappers and containers you have to keep until the end to prove to race organizers that you consumed 10 items.

We get our first taste of dirt, a trail around Sloan’s Lake, a Denver centerpiece, after the third stop, and the route begins to change from questionable urban areas to parks and neighborhoods. It’s actually beautiful.

I pass by a runner who has a plastic bag full of Cinnamon Twists. They will be eight of his meals, he told me. THAT’S CHEATING, Kelly, I say to myself, and kinda bullshit. That’s why they require runners to eat two big items.

We aren’t abusing the rules as much. So far for us, everything is staying down.

At the eighth stop, I use my vast experience at eating when I don’t feel like it, a common problem at ultras, and hork down the nachos. My stomach whines.

I take solace in the fact that I have actually felt better after eating at every stop, not worse. That’s usually my experience in ultras, and it remains true after every Taco Bell stop.

Still, the nachos were tough to swallow. When we start to run again—I’d generously call it a lope—I have a frightening burp, the wet kind that could go either way, like a fart. (In case you’re wondering, shitting yourself is, as far as I can tell, allowed) We agree to walk to let our food digest.

We also continue walking because the real race, as they say, has now started. I have a blister the size of a half dollar on the bottom of my right foot. Kelly says her feet are covered in them. One of Kelly’s friends, Ana, took a digger hours ago and gashed her knee. Everyone is hurting.

A goofy 50K is still a 50K, and many of the back of the pack are experiencing, for the first time, the kind of suffering that comes with an ultra. When I ask a group of 30 in the 10th Taco Bell if anyone has run an ultra before, they all shake their heads.

“I don’t think anyone here has even run a marathon,” says one woman who ran “maybe five miles” for her longest training run.

This is the beauty and brutality of this race. Many of its participants will push themselves harder than they ever have before and will be able to call themselves ultramarathoners by the end. Maybe, and probably, a few will continue. Amanda, Kelly’s other friend, said in the race, “I’m just so grateful to be able to move my body,” which is exactly what an ultrarunner would say.

There are fast people who do this event. Professional runner Sage Canaday runs it every year. This year he came in second behind Aquinas Lasnoski, who finished in 3:44:37 to break Canaday’s course record. (“Running fitness wasn’t there,” Canaday wrote on Strava. “Eating fitness kind of was.”) But this is a race for slow people like me. If you run too hard, your stomach doesn’t have a chance to digest all that food, and again, puking means you’re out.

The only problem with being slow is cutoffs haunt you. This race only has one cutoff, and it comes faster than we expect. We forget that our GPS watches add mileage for everything, even trips to the bathroom, and when we look at the course on our phones, we are unpleasantly surprised to discover that we still have 2 miles to go and only 35 minutes to do it.

When we start to run, our bodies protest in different ways. Our stomachs, thankfully, are fine, but our feet and joints and knees and spirits are beat up. We are tired and hot and ready to be done. But this is what it takes to finish the Taco Bell 50K. You have to dig deep. You have to go hard. You have to Live Más.

We bang out a mile in 11 minutes, and all of a sudden, the arch, that glorious purple arch full of other runners and spectators, appears in our view. We finish with 10 minutes to spare.

We present our wrappers, get a taco sauce packet attached to a gold ribbon for our finisher’s medal, and limp back to the car for the drive home.

The next day, we report how we’re feeling in our new group chat. We’re proud of ourselves: Less than half the field, about 600 runners, finished the race, according to the somewhat official stats.

The consensus is that everyone feels better than they thought they would. (Maybe all that mid-race fueling actually helped with recovery?) It was also more fun than they thought it would be. The underlying message is one that no one wants to say out loud just yet: Maybe we will join all the crazy fools again next year.

Stop 1: Chalupa Supreme Stop 2: Doritos “Locos” taco Stop 3: Cinnabon two-pack Stop 4: Pintos N Cheese Stop 5: Cinnamon Twists Stop 6: Nacho Fries Stop 7: Chicken taco Stop 8: Nachos BellGrande Stop 9: Cinnabon two-pack Stop 10: Cinnabon two-pack

Bonus: Lots of Baja Blast, root beer, red Gatorade, and a bottle of water at each stop
