#109. “We’ll Miss Everything About Him”: Jared Empey Channeled His Grief Into Link-Ups in Idaho’s Sawtooths

Jared Empey (Photo: Courtesy of Steffanie Empey)

Jared Empey an Idaho climber and contributor to Idaho: A Climbing Guide, passed away on July 24, 2026, after a fall on Mount Jefferson (10,495ft) in Oregon’s Cascade Range. He climbed the peak solo and had just reached the summit before the accident. His final message to his wife, Steffanie, was simple: “Top of Jefferson.”

Born in Ammon, Idaho, the second of 11 children, Empey’s life was rooted in family and service. He worked as Kuna’s city treasurer, opened his home to 52 foster children, and was an active member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

The City of Kuna shared a memorial post on Facebook, writing, “Jared has been such an intricate part of our city family that this news is hard to process.” In the same post, Kuna Mayor Joe Stear added, “We are certainly going to miss everything about him. Please keep his family in your thoughts and prayers as they now have to move forward. Until we meet again, my friend.”

In 2017, Empey lost his son, Joshua. Within the grief that followed, he found healing and a connection with God in the mountains, according to a memorial shared by Steffanie. Hiking became a passion, and he often brought his children along, carrying Joshua’s beloved stuffed animal, Pete the Cat, with him.

Empey contributed photographs, trip reports and route information to Idaho: A Climbing Guide, helping document some of the state’s lesser-known peaks for the climbers who came after him. In 2022, he ventured into a remote corner of the Sawtooth Wilderness to link Big Buck Mountain, Peak 8662, and Smoky Peak in an epic, 15-mile day with more that 5,300 vertical feet of climbing. He navigated six towers, a narrowed Class 3 ridge on Smoky’s summit, and became the first on record to make the linkup.

Empey is survived by his wife, Steffanie; his eight children; his parents, John and Susan Empey; and another baby on the way.

#110. Sasha DiGiulian Climbs, Tris, and Writes Books. Here’s Her Secret to Success.

For the past 20 years, Sasha DiGiulian has won climbing world championships, sent big walls from Madagascar to Spain, and pushed the boundaries of what’s possible for women’s climbing—all by age 33. But while DiGiulian has settled into a rhythm in Boulder, Colorado, she hasn’t slowed down one bit. In the past five years alone, she’s launched a nutrition bar company, published a memoir, recovered from five hip surgeries, completed an Ironman 70.3, starred in an HBO documentary, and returned to Yosemite to make the first female ascent of El Capitan’s longest free route, The Direct Line (5.13d). Her secret? Operating in the chaos, not resisting it.

I was at a dinner in Salt Lake City in January 2013 with Reinhold Messner. He flipped over the wine menu and started drawing Bellavista, this 5.14b big wall in the Dolomites. He was like, “This is what you should go do.”

I didn’t have any experience with multi-pitch climbing or big-wall climbing. It’s every guide’s nightmare to hear this, but I was learning how to jumar [use metal ascenders to move upward on a rope] while hanging in free space thousands of feet above the ground, with Edu [Marín] screaming at me in Spanish and me using my limited knowledge of Spanish to figure it out.

I learned so much on that trip being thrown into the deep end … I chose to go [to Spain] instead of the World Games that year. After [Bellavista], I actively chose to stop competing as much and really started to fall in love with big outdoor experiences.

The ability to compartmentalize. You have to be able to put aside everything that’s going on, show up, and do your best. I’m a big Swiftie, so I think of that [Taylor Swift] song, “I Can Do It With a Broken Heart.”

I do about five days of cardio a week, normally a trail run or road biking. I really like swimming, too; that was the impetus for dabbling in the Ironman sphere. I train climbing four to five times a week. On a typical day, I’ll do a [training] session in my garage for two to three hours, then I’ll do about 90 minutes of strength and conditioning. If I’m going outside, I’ll truncate meetings or move them.

[In 2020,] I didn’t know if I’d be able to come back to climbing, or if I’d ever be able to climb 5.14 again. I literally had a panic attack the day before we hiked in because I was so nervous and had so many question marks around it. It was really empowering for me to get to be there with Matilda [Söderlund] and Brette [Harrington]. Rayu was the first stake in the ground of me being like, “Wow, I can still be a professional climber, and I can still push myself.”

I don’t even like to refer to it as balance; it’s just operating in the chaos and seeing what’s the priority, week by week.

I’ve struggled for a lot of my life with disordered eating, especially in my early competition days. The way I got through it was learning how to fuel my body. When I had this massive surgery, two of the only things I could control were how I showed up to [physical therapy] and how I fuel myself … I’ve learned so much about ingredient sourcing, supply chain, and all of these skills I’ve always imagined I’d learn at business school. I feel like I’m getting a small business degree.

Be kind to yourself and be open to change. When we go through these big transition moments, it can be very chaotic and confusing. Taking stock in the day-to-day is important, but so is having that malleability and mindset of, “OK, I don’t know what this next chapter looks like, but I’m going to be open to it.”

This article is from the Fall 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

#113. I Ran Dozens of Trails Over 4 Years to Find the 50 Classic Trail Runs of America

To understand why you undertake something as complex and demanding as writing a book, you need to start at the beginning.

I started running in the fall of seventh grade as a pimpeled, slightly-overweight, late-blooming pre-teen. Middle school wasn’t a kind place for kids like me, but I found solace in the cross country team. None of us were cool. Or particularly athletic. None of us knew how to dance. Or flirt. Or talk to girls. But on the team we found community, and that is just about all you need in life.

I’m not sure why I showed up to the first practice, but, if memory serves, it was a con job by my friend Reed, who we’ll bookmark for later. The two of us grew up in a rural Minnesota county where 90% of the land is public and whitetail deer easily outnumber humans. There were plenty of downsides to living in the literal middle of nowhere, but one upside was limitless outdoor access, including running.

Many of our weekend long runs were on the Superior Hiking Trail, which is riddled with roots and rocks, and generally horrible for running. Our coach made us do it anyway. At the time we didn’t call it trail running. No one did. The “trail” denomination was in its nascence, if existent at all. This was well before large-lugged shoes, pro trail contracts, or the now-ubiquitous cultural catalysts like Strava, UTMB, carb-maxxing, and Scott Jurek memes on social media. You might say we were early adopters, but we certainly didn’t know it at the time.

This might all sound like a poetic genesis for a book about trail running, but that’s not how the real story goes. I didn’t fall in love with trail running then. In fact, I hated it. I quit cross country after a few years and didn’t return to trails until after college, almost a decade later. So, why start with that origin story?

Because my why for returning is also my why for writing The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America.

This is the most straightforward question, so I’ll tackle it first. The Fifty is a beautiful coffee table book that aims to do for trail running what The 50 Classic Climbs did for climbing and The 50 Classic Ski Descents later did for skiing: establish the definitive list of classic trails to inspire generations of runners to come.

Wanting to be sure we picked the absolute best routes, we decided to go a step further than our literary forebears and run every trail on the list, some of them many times. There were quite a few surprises, like the remoteness of the Rogue River, stumbling into bears on North Circle, last minute wildfires closures in the Wind Rivers, and snow on multiple desert runs. There were big bonks and even bigger rallies, an entire grocery aisle of gummy bears consumed, and a grueling solo mission on the longest and hardest trail, Wonderland.

Ultimately, we selected each classic for something unique—stunning alpine views, ethereal geological formations, or important pieces of indigenous history. Together, we wanted the fifty to tell the full story of America’s public lands, both good and bad. Each trail also comes with a story of our experience running it, a mix of moving meditations, physical challenges, and forging deeper connections with friends.

You may notice that I’m using “we” in the section above, which is not by mistake. Writing this book was a team effort and there is no way I would have finished without my co-authors, Rickey Gates and Ian MacLellan. The three of us joined forces almost by accident, but I’m forever grateful that we did.

Not long after moving to Oregon in 2022, I went for a run with my childhood friend and lead con man, Reed, at Smith Rock. Legendary professional skier, Cody Townsend, had just released an episode of The Fifty and, as avid skiers, we spent a mile or three chatting about it. Connecting the dots, I wondered if there was a parallel book about “fifty” trails. I assumed it existed, but a quick Google search on the drive home proved me wrong, so I decided to craft it myself–encouraged, of course, by Reed (who ended up running seven of the trails with me, to his credit).

The first step was recruiting a handful of coconspirators, including Ian, a professional photographer and avid runner who lives in Portland, Maine. The rest eventually dropped out, but Ian’s commitment never wavered. Then, in early 2024, we learned through a friend that Rickey, a professional runner based in Santa Fe, was working on a similar book, so we set up a phone call with him. It was a come to Jesus moment for us—either we were going to team up or we’d be racing to finish. Fortunately, our lists were similar and the vibe felt right, so we agreed to join forces to make an even better book.

The book took Ian and me over four years to write–and Rickey, who started before us, has been working on it for more than ten years! The first year was mostly planning, researching routes, and running a few trails to pressure test the vision. Over the next three years we ran north of 2,000 miles to make sure we picked the very best trails. This meant six to ten trips a year for each one of us. Including travel to–often flights but sometimes a drive if we were lucky–at least a month on the road every year for each of us.

As we were running trails, we were simultaneously researching, writing, and peer editing. Then came finding a book agent and pitching publishers, which I knew nothing about. We were thrilled to get a great offer from Rizzoli, a New York City based publisher known for their beautiful, large format books. It took three rounds of revisions with their editors and another four rounds with the graphic designers to get the layout the way we wanted. Every one of these steps was exciting, but hard earned.

At the same time, the sport of trail running was exploding. Participation has grown by almost 15% year-over-year for the last two decades, with more than 15 million Americans hitting the trails in 2025 according to the Sports & Fitness Industry Association. Many trail runners are seeking adventures outside of the race course, whether it’s new routes in their backyard or far-flung run-cations. Suffice to say, the timing of the book couldn’t be more perfect. Sometimes it’s better to be lucky than smart.

Writing the book has been a journey almost as long as the classic trails within. We began by collectively soliciting hundreds of recommendations from pro runners, local legends, and friends all over the country. From that list, we paired it down using homemade criteria, then ran each trail to be sure they were worthy of classic status. I don’t know the exact number of trails we ran, which might be a good thing.

We had five criteria that trails had to meet to be considered classics. The first three are simple: Can it be run in 24 hours or less? Does it have a clear beginning and end (i.e. no sections of longer trails)? Is it mostly runnable, with little off-trail, scree, or scrambling? Those first few narrowed the list to around seventy. Then came the hard parts. Does it help paint the full ecological picture of the country? And finally, do we recommend traveling across the country to run it?

In the end, our classics range from 19 to 95 miles in length and are spread across 25 states. You’ll find them in the mangroves of the Everglades, the extreme weather of the White Mountains, the lush forests of the Cascades, the tropical beaches of Kauai, and the grandeur of the Grand Canyon, where the Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim route is a lifetime achievement akin to biking Alpe d’Huez or climbing El Capitan.

I can’t answer this for Rickey or Ian, but I’ll try for myself. A four-year project like this book requires an almost insatiable hunger, no matter the cost—late nights, sweat stains, gas receipts, nagging pains, hall passes from my wife, and a few close calls with large animals, to name a few. Why pay that price?

I think back to that kid in Minnesota’s Northwoods who was searching, but never found what he was looking for. I tried a lot of activities growing up—team sports, video games, art classes, and even partying—but none filled my soul. Sure, I ran trails during cross country practice, but I only saw them as workouts. That changed when I moved to the Bay Area and followed friends to the trails in the Oakland Hills and Marin Headlands. It was hard to put into words at first, but easy to feel. I was alive.

I wrote this book for any kid like me who’s searching for that thing that lights them up. There’s a magic to trail running that you can’t find anywhere else. I hope the book inspires more people to get out the door and explore both their local trails and further into their mind. As far as I can tell, there’s no better teacher than a long day running in the woods, and I want to share that gift with everyone.

For those interested, The 50 Classic Trails Runs of America is available for pre-order today and will be published March 9th, 2027. After one hell of a journey for Rickey, Ian, and me, it’s almost here.

#114. We Tested the Best Rangefinder Binoculars for Hunting and Long Range Shooting

Published Oct 16, 2026 5:25 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A correctly tuned ballistic-solving laser rangefinding (LRF) binocular gives shooters and hunters something no other tool can: an extra dimension. Sure, it gives you length, measured in yards and meters. It gives you width, in field of view. And it gives you height, the parabolic curve described by a bullet’s flight.

But the best LRF binoculars give you the additional dimension of time. By putting a ballistic calculator at your fingertips and in your eyeballs, they let you solve a challenging shot in the fraction of a second it takes to push the Range button. Some will even tell you precisely how much time passes between pulling the trigger and your bullet’s arrival at the target.

Some of the new LRF binoculars in our review give you a fifth dimension: omniscience. By applying spatial awareness and predictive analytics, the Shot Probability Analysis tool in Leica’s Geovid Max crunches a variety of inputs and environmental data to tell you, before you pull the trigger, whether you’re likely to miss. Many of the top LRFs in this group project the influence of wind and terrain on your shot.

Bottom line, these are sophisticated digital devices that also must be competent conventional optics built tough enough to handle the indignities of the range and the rough and steep places we hunt. It’s a lot to ask of any sporting good, and it can be hard to know which LRF binocular is for you.

We tested eight leading LRF binoculars, assessing not only their optics, ergonomics and ranging capabilities but also their mobile apps and their ability to digest ballistic data and spit out aiming solutions informed by distance, incline, wind and elevation.

About half the LRFs in this group are more restrained, combining simple laser ranging with a conventional binocular. This subcategory has a lot of options and variation for hunters and shooters who want to ditch their LRF monocular but require a binocular for field observation. By leaving out ballistics solvers and Bluetooth transmitters and receivers, these stripped-down LRF binoculars cost far less than the ballistic wizards that include those features.

At the other end of the price-and-performance spectrum, you’ll pay handsomely for the best of these fully integrated devices, but I’m ready to tell you most are worth it. No other devices in our world truly do it all: crunch ballistic data, provide both-eyes-open viewing and connect to phones and environmental sensors like Kestrels and Calypsos. These LRF binos are required kit for long-range precision target shooters and Western big-game hunters. Here are the best new models of 2026.

With its new BX-6 Range HD, Leupold has not only produced a ballistic-solving binocular that will win its share of long-range rifle competitions, but its best-in-class waypointing capabilities also make it an excellent backcountry hunting optic.

The BX-6 Range HD incorporates the powerful Hornady 4DOF ballistics software, which is quickly taking market share from the OG of the category, Applied Ballistics Elite. By pairing it with the archery-specific Precision Cut Archery software, Leupold has harnessed aiming solutions for both very far and close-in shots. The Hornady software, especially, is smart and its ballistics library extensive, but Leupold’s Control app brings it to life. The app is the best of the dozen or so brand-specific ecosystems that connect ballistic solvers to digital devices. It is fast, more or less intuitive, feature-rich and extremely shareable to any device you choose via QR codes.

Once your ballistic solutions are ported to the optic via the Control app, the binocular becomes a powerful long-range precision tool, every bit the equal of its main rival, Sig Sauer’s KILO10K-ABS HD. As with the Tract, reviewed below, the full library of features that can be projected via Leupold’s vivid AccuView AMOLED display is visually overwhelming. And as the Tract does, the Leupold lets users customize the display to the elements they find most useful.

For most users, the features that make the cut probably include Leupold’s dynamic wind clock, which illustrates the direction and velocity of winds. Making real-time adjustments to the wind call is fast and easy with swift button navigation. The cardinal element of the display — at least in my version — is a distance- and wind-informed hold in big, bold characters that enables fast and precise dialing or reticle holds. Speaking of the reticle, it can be moved around the field of view to the user’s preference.

The Range binocular also has a setting for shooters who use Leupold’s Custom Dial System (CDS), pairing the ranging engine of the LRF to the load-specific click values of custom ballistic elevation dials.

The digital heart of the BX-6 Range is supported by excellent glass. The Leupold’s image is a bit flat, but it’s bright and crisp right to the edges, with very little of the color fringing or greenish hues that dominate the optics of many LRF binoculars. The button arrangement is good, and we mostly avoided the navigational calamities that often result from a six-button layout.

On the other (two) hands, the BX-6 Range HD is ponderously heavy. It clocks in at 41 ounces but somehow seems heavier, maybe owing to its square, brickish build.

We noted a few other deficiencies. It’s nearly impossible to mount the Leupold to a tripod, for instance. The target side of the center hinge is occupied by the laser emitter, so you can’t use a standard tripod stud. And the center bridge is so massive that there’s very little barrel to accept a tripod grip mount. Leupold has attempted to address this by including a strap and plasticky tripod plate, but we got better results using an aftermarket barrel clamp with an Arca-compatible foot.

While we’re handing out demerits, the focus wheel moves just a smidge too freely for most of us.

But if it handles like a brick, the Leupold is also as durable as a brick. Like Leupold’s Gen 2 binoculars, the BX-6 Range HD features interchangeable eyecups, so fitting the binocular to your face is easy.

In addition to its good optics, fast and powerful ranging engine and sophisticated ballistics solvers, Leupold has smartly added a suite of location-based features, building on the waypoint-dropping capabilities of its RX-5000 LRF monocular. That device, you may recall, was one of the first that allowed users to drop laser-guided waypoints on digital maps. The BX-6 Range HD expands digital cartography beyond onX Hunt to include HuntStand and Deercast, along with Google Maps and Apple Maps.

Given the number and utility of its features, its seamless integration with best-in-class ballistics software via a smart mobile app and its optical performance, the Leupold wins our Editor’s Choice award as the top laser rangefinding binocular of the year in a very competitive field.

Tract has been making quiet but steady inroads into the precision long-range shooting world with its TORIC ELR riflescopes. The direct-to-consumer brand now has a very good ballistic-solving LRF binocular to help that scope win Precision Rifle Series (PRS) competitions and make tricky shots on distant game.

The 10×42 TORIC Eagle Ballistics LRF binocular is shooting for the sweet spot in the middle of the LRF category. It costs about half the price of the highest-end binos, it has a relatively modest lasing range compared to its 6-mile peers, and it’s built around a tight, compact frame that fits in most standard binocular harnesses. But inside that chassis is a premium binocular and a feature-rich ballistic solver optimized for the changeable conditions of timed stages and Western big-game hunts.

If anything, the Tract may have a few too many features.

With all the fields activated, the blazingly bright OLED display looks like the heads-up display in a fighter jet, with so many inputs competing for your attention that it’s easy to get distracted, especially during the stress of a competition or a high-stakes hunt. Happily, Tract lets users fully customize the display, turning off elements that aren’t useful in the moment, then switching them back on as needed.

Ballistics solutions are provided by James Eagleman and his PRS-oriented Eagle Ballistics (https://eagleballistics.com/) software, which connects to accessories like wind meters. The app has impressive features, some of which are locked behind a paywall. The app is free to download, but if you’re not a Tract TORIC its capabilities are limited to 100 yards. However, when the binocular synchs users get full app capability (minus the PRS and Advanced Wind modes) for free for 10 days. Every time users resynch the binocular, the 10-day usage refreshes. The additional Eagle Ballistic app features are available for a monthly or annual fee.

The Tract had the second-highest image and brightness score in our test, behind only the Leica Geovid Max. We like the locking diopter controls, the comfortable eyecups, the stand-alone ranging button, and the ability to input wind values in ½ MPH increments. The TORIC recognizes that wind is a confounding factor in long-range shooting and devotes a lot of its tech to mapping and compensating for the effect of wind.

Naturally, it also handles most ranging tasks with ease, including a very useful shorter-range bow mode and near and far ranging modes. The oversized aluminum focus wheel is positioned perfectly for fingertip feathering, and we salute the Tract’s “knobology” for the useful arrangement of the control buttons.

Critics may pan the Tract for its pedestrian 4,000-yard range. We didn’t quite reach that distance, but testers reckoned they’d choose the precision and responsiveness of the 4,000-yard TORIC over units with 10,000-yard range that cost twice as much. The Tract’s very good image, its user adjustability and its compact form factor make the 10×42 one of the best values in this category. The competition-tested software and sheer number of features further drove our consensus opinion that the TORIC Eagle Ballistics LRF Binocular is the going-away Great Buy of our LRF binocular test.

Tract TORIC Eagle Ballistics LRF Binocular 10×42 Specs

Leica has a handy way to telegraph what it thinks of this world-beating laser rangefinding binocular: its color. Flat dark earth is Leica’s designation for its best-in-class devices. The Geovid Pro, in comparison, is olive green.

But there’s another way to tell how good this latest iteration of the Geovid family is: Just look through it. The Leica has by far the highest image quality and brightness scores of our test. Even with a beam-splitting lens that robs light headed to the eye, the Geovid Max records 90% light transmission. That’s remarkable for a laser rangefinding device, especially because optical coatings are often used to boost display visibility at the expense of image resolution. Somehow, Leica has solved this problem.

The display is also improved over previous Geovids: a brighter, “poppier” red MicroLED display that is highly visible even in harsh sun.

The ballistics-solving capabilities of this device are in line with its premium optics. Along with Leupold’s BX-6 Range HD, Sig Sauer’s groundbreaking KILO10K-ABS HD Gen II and the Revic Acura BLR10b, the Leica has all the tools, inputs and connectivity to place bullets with extreme precision at long ranges. It uses Applied Ballistics Professional for the heavy lifting, and once your data is transferred to the device, it’s a cinch to switch caliber and bullet profiles. The Leica Ballistics app is solid if a little Germanic, meaning it’s not always intuitive or particularly useful. That description also applies to Leica’s Shot Probability Analysis tool. It’s a cool way to judge when a target is out of range, but in practice we rarely used it.

The Leica has additional Bluetooth connectivity — to Kestrel environmental meters, Garmin watches and BaseMap Pro — to further customize inputs, make in-the-moment adjustments to aiming solutions and drop waypoints. The Leica’s navigation tools, from tracking features to waypointing, are among the best in the category.

Besides its hefty price tag, we complained a bit about the Leica’s “knobology.” The two operating buttons — for Range and Menu — are a bit too close together for those of us with fleshy fingers, and using the binocular with gloves generated more cursing than ranging. We also found the ranging engine to be slightly slower than the other premium LRFs in the test.

But the reticle/beam collimation was dead-on. The binocular’s balance and ergonomics make it a delight to hold and use in the field, and the image makes it every bit as good as an observational optic as it is as a high-performing ballistics solver. It also has the advantage — seen as a feature by some and a bug by others — of having fewer menu screens and input profiles than its peers. To me, that makes this a very good choice for a do-everything hunting LRF.

The Talon HD 10K is not only a world-class rangefinder and next-level ballistics solver but also part of an integrated system that measures wind velocity and direction. Tethered to Vortex’s Ace Ballistic Weather Meter through the Relay system and informed by GeoBallistics’ powerful software, the Talon is equipped to win precision-shooting competitions and hunt successfully in any landscape on Earth.

The benefit of all that learning is an insanely powerful and precise tool that will elevate your shooting capabilities like no other device.

The Talon HD 10K has some spiffy features that you’ll discover along the way to ringing more steel. Its very busy but customizable display is auto-leveling, which sounds like a small thing until you’ve experienced the head cocking required by many LRF binoculars, especially for users with small faces or those melon-heads among us with wide interpupillary distance. A small button on the underside of the barrel, where the user’s right thumb rests, serves as a menu shortcut, plugging you right into the environment settings. In a fast and practical way, this lets users quickly change wind value and direction, get updates on temperature and humidity and calibrate the compass.

The Vortex also has a feature that I wish other brands would adopt: You can turn off the display when you want, rather than having to wait for it to time out. Press both direction buttons at the same time and the display disappears. That’s a valuable feature for those of us who want to get the distracting red OLED display out of the image when we’re trying to use the binocular for its other job: glassing.

The 12×50 build is big, but it nicely follows the functionality of the original 10×42 Talon HD 10K and gives longer-range shooters and hunters a bit more magnification and a lot more barrel to grip. The higher-power binocular is easily mounted to a tripod with a front-hinge threaded stud. I’d recommend that for ranging in real-world conditions of wind and incline. We found it hard to get ranges beyond about 7,500 yards by hand-holding the 12-power Talon, but anchored to a tripod, it had no trouble reaching out to nearly 10,000 yards.

We can quibble about Vortex’s embed with the GeoBallistics ecosystem rather than powering its ballistic solutions through another provider. I don’t have enough data to claim one system is more precise than the other, but for me, the GeoBallistics system takes a bit more time to learn and relearn, just as I think Vortex has too many in-device screens that require inputs. That slows down its ability to true solutions in the field. But once your ballistics dope is entered in the GeoBallistics app, Vortex makes it a cinch to relay it to the Talon from your phone.

The additional connectivity of the Vortex Relay provides even more inputs to the binocular. Wind velocity and direction, for instance, are delivered instantly to the Talon, revising holdoff and holdover values in real time.

The glass in the Talon HD 10K is very good, but testers noted that it’s not quite as sharp or as bright as that in the Leica Geovid Max, and it’s just behind the glass in the Leupold BX-6 Range HD. But it’s worth noting that the Vortex costs about $1,500 less than either while delivering more magnification in a larger package.

Is the Talon HD 10K worth its street price of about $2,500? For its superior ranging, powerful ballistic solving, optical horsepower and connectivity to the Vortex ecosystem, I think it’s a bargain, especially for our longest-range shooters.

This little powerhouse has much more ranging capability than its compact frame indicates. We routinely got ranges out to 3,000 yards on reflective targets and nearly 1,800 yards on larger trees. And the GPO Rangeguide gave snappy, precise ranges on game-sized targets out to as far as any of us want to shoot at game, around 800 yards.

The little 40mm LRF is also very handy inside 50 yards. With a close focus of 16 feet and the capability to return ranges as close as 6 yards, it’s a great choice for bowhunters. The unit feels tight and durable thanks to its magnesium-alloy chassis.

Not only is the lasing engine powerful, but it’s quick. With some lower-end LRFs, we’ve become accustomed to making a sandwich in the time between pressing the ranging button and getting the return yardage, but the GPO’s feedback is nearly instantaneous, and the scan mode is especially snappy, returning about three measurements per second inside 1,000 yards. That’s especially useful when ranging moving game.

We were less impressed with the Rangeguide’s glass. Some testers noted a blue tint to images and noticeable edge distortion. We also noted a disagreement of about 3 degrees between the reticle and the laser collimation.

We’ve become accustomed to putting up with the ponderous weight of some LRF binoculars as a trade-off for their myriad features and capabilities. The GPO Rangeguide 3200 is proof that you don’t have to trade weight and portability for performance. It’s compact enough to fit just about any harness system and powerful enough for just about any hunting or shooting situation where you don’t need ballistic solutions. Its price, about $1,350, seems fair for the performance and portability it delivers.

There’s nothing fancy about this straight-ahead LRF from Vortex, but for hunters and shooters who don’t want to step up to the company’s ballistic-solving Talon, the Ranger offers very good performance for about a third of the price.

It doesn’t connect to your phone, a ballistics app or Vortex’s celebrated Relay ecosystem, but the Ranger HD 3000 offers very good ranging capability. We routinely got ranges past 2,500 yards on reflective targets and nearly 1,900 yards on fully leafed trees. And it was a cinch to get fast, accurate ranges on just about any target inside 1,000 yards. Its close-in performance should make it a good choice for deer hunters, and the angle-adjusted mode works as well for steep-country rifle hunters as it does for treestand deer hunters.

The glass is about what you’d expect at this price point, and the ergonomics are a little unwieldy — we wanted the focus knob just a little farther forward, and the buttons can be hard to push. But the ranging functions, especially the fast scan mode, are smart and snappy. The GlassPak bino harness is a useful throw-in.

This workhorse of a ranging binocular is a no-frills tool, but the Frontier LRF provides all a hunter needs in terms of ranging modes, including the ability to tune the device for distance versus close-in ranging. The optics are quite good, but tuning the diopter can take a bit of time, a task made more pleasant by the satisfyingly tactile clicks of the adjustment dial.

Priced at about $1,100, the Hawke Frontier is one of a number of fairly priced LRF binos that may not have Bluetooth connectivity to a mobile app or an onboard ballistic solver but offer solid performance for a hunter who wants the basics. Operation is a cinch: Toggle the Mode button to navigate preferences. Hit the Power/Fire button to range. Done. And done.

The magnesium chassis and overall tight build make this a good choice for those of us who are hard on our electronics. We struggled to get ranges beyond about 1,650 yards, but the unit delivered reliable ranging on a variety of targets inside 750 yards.

Athlon has managed to combine a pretty good laser rangefinder and a pretty good binocular to produce a price-point alternative to expensive LRF binos. The new Athlon Argos Pro 10×42 won’t compete with higher-end ballistics solvers, but it’s not intended to. Instead, it offers a 2,100-yard rangefinder that covers the basics, even if the glass makes your eyes water a bit.

The appealing part of the Argos Pro is its price. It’s expected to have a street price of about $400 when it hits retail shelves in early 2027 (MSRP will be closer to $500). But don’t dismiss this LRF bino too quickly. It has a good lasing engine that ranged reflective targets out to nearly 1,800 yards in our testing, and we picked up deer out to nearly 1,000 yards.

The LRF has both line-of-sight and angle-compensating modes, and its close-in capabilities make it a consideration for bowhunters.

The glass is about what you’d expect for the price. We found some edge distortion and color aberration that tend to wash out the image, especially in full sunlight. The black LCD display is hard to see against dark backgrounds. And the unit feels a little flimsy, though we tested a preproduction prototype, so final production models may be tighter.

The Argos Pro has a curious build. The laser emitter aperture is huge — about 30mm — and located on the very front of the center hinge, complicating tripod mounting. Meanwhile, the CR2 battery compartment is on the rear of the focus wheel and accessed through a similarly oversized cap.

But the two-button operation is easy and fast. The laser is powerful and precise enough. And the price puts a competent LRF binocular in the hands of most hunters and shooters.

Laser rangefinding binoculars have to pull double duty. Much more so than LRF monoculars, binoculars are intended as optical instruments. They must be able to render distant targets clearly and in all sorts of light conditions. But their ranging capabilities are equally important. Do they deliver fast and consistently precise distances to targets? Can they also inform a shot based on ballistic software, whether on-board the binocular or delivered via connection to a mobile app?

We put all those capabilities to the test in our field evaluations. We measure units’ best far and close distances at targets ranging from barns to grass, trees, and even deer (though occasionally we used Angus cows as surrogates for deer). We assess their target modes, their optical clarity and brightness, and the visibility of the display in changing light conditions and backgrounds. We further determine whether caliber-specific software is intuitive and useful. And we assess units’ price, warranty, and amenities. We test the maximum and minimum range, and use every targeting mode and menu option. We mount binoculars on tripods to get rock-solid ranging, and we take the units in the field, deploying them both methodically and rapidly at targets of various sizes and distances. And then we pair them to a slave rifle and a ballistic app and judge their ability to improve our shooting accuracy.

We break our 10-point scoring into four general categories: ranging performance, display and optics, features, and value. The average of these categories is the basis of our grades, detailed below.

Ranging performance includes both the maximum and minimum distances the unit is capable of ranging, but also ranging precision and ability to repeatedly range objects of various sizes and textures. The performance score also considers various targeting modes. Display and optics assesses how well the unit “sees” targets, how useful and adjustable the display is to each users’ eyesight and different light conditions, and reticle utility. The feature grade assesses whether the unit connects to a mobile app, or contains a ballistic library, or has on-board sensors. Lastly, our value grade is a measure of whether the LRF binocular is worth its price, and considers its peer group, warranty, and amenities like a harness or carrying case.

The laser rangefinding binocular that gets the highest overall score wins our Editor’s Choice award for the best in the category; the optic with the highest price/value score wins our Great Buy recognition. We also assigned other awards for specific noteworthy attributes.

Our 10-point evaluation adds up to a total numeric score, but we translate those to grades for each submission. Our Ranging Performance grade combines the scores from ranging, accuracy, sensitivity, and processor speed. Our Display/Optics grade aggregates both display and optical quality scores. The Features grade considers amenities, connectivity, and versatility. And then the Price/Value grade is our value grade, which also considers durability.

To earn an “Excellent” grade, the average of that category must be 9 or higher, which is extremely hard to achieve. “Very Good” is an average score of 7 to 9. A “Good” grade is 5 to 7. Our “Fair” grade is 3 to 5, and “Poor” is anything under 3.

Because laser rangefinding binoculars cover the gamut from bare-boned ranging units to fully featured ballistics solvers, you need to determine your use. Are you mainly a whitetail hunter who shoots inside 500 yards? Then any number of units in our test will serve. Do you primarily want a binocular with some rangefinding talents as a bonus? Then select first for optical quality. If you want a unit primarily to deliver range-specific holds beyond 1,000 yards, and as an observational instrument as a secondary talent, then pay special attention to the electronics.

You’ll also want to consider price. These units range in price from $2,700 (the Revic) all the way down to under $1000 (the Burris). Consider your budget, and then stick close to it. Unlike purely optical binoculars (those old-fashioned units that don’t have on-board electronics), rangefinders depreciate in value fairly quickly as new models come on the market with more features for less money than versions that might be only one or two years old.

Next, consider how technically savvy you are. Really. Can you navigate all the steps required to connect your LRF binocular to a mobile app, and then to a library of bullet-specific ballistics? If you can, then you might consider a unit that tethers via Bluetooth to external devices. But if that’s a challenge, then stick with on-board intel.

Pay special attention to brands’ warranties. Electo-optics often have more stringent return and repair terms than brands’ analog optics. If you can find a warranty that delivers 5 years—or even better, 10 years—of coverage for its electronics, consider that a win. Technology in these devices is changing so fast that if your 2026 unit goes down in, say 2028, and you’re still covered, chances are good you’ll get a new, updated unit to replace your old model.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#115. Day 17: The Inner Camino Journey

Thank goodness for earplugs and the fact that I brought them, because despite the snoring, I slept so well. Many pilgrims complained about the snoring, but for me it was a symbol. The choir of loud breathing reminded me of the opportunity to be surrounded by humans of all ages pursuing their own journeys. A community of seekers in a world full of many souls disconnected from their own dreams by daily responsibilities.

I intentionally woke up early because I was beginning to understand the routine that felt best. The most powerful part of it: walking under the morning stars in solitude.

Under the Milky Way, I felt my Saunter of Spirit the most potently.

I got to the first town, Grañón, right as the sunrise made its debut. I bought a coffee from the sweet lady at the food truck cafe and took it down to the steps.

Coffee with the sunrise—it truly doesn’t get better than this.

As I walked out of the town, I caught up to the Basque pilgrim and his companion, whom I hadn’t met yet. I ended up meeting the new pilgrim and walking with him for an hour. He only spoke Spanish and French, so the whole time we communicated in Spanish. It was challenging, but so rewarding. I might not know much, but being able to get to know him with the words I did know inspired me to keep trying.

My Italian brother caught up to me and we walked through several small villages together. I was starting to get hangry and was craving a tortilla, but couldn’t find a cafe selling them anywhere. I followed the compass of my nose and found a panadería. When I stepped inside the door, I was hit with a wave of the smell of fresh, sweet bread. In that moment, I NEEDED one. The shy owner gave me a croissant, and it was the size of my head! That perfect pastry was exactly what I needed to tame the beast within.

Still in pursuit, my tastebuds perked at the sign that read “drinks & snacks”. What I found was greater than I could have ever imagined.

The Inner Camino House was not a cafe or an albergue, but merely a couple’s house that wanted to give pilgrims a place to rest and a moment of home. The husband had done the Camino four times, and the couple got married and honeymooned on the trail as well. He spoke of the importance of going inward and how that’s the solution to so many people’s issues. I couldn’t help but agree and become excited by every word he spoke. Run solely on donations, the kitchen was full of an array of fruits, veggies, sandwich ingredients, pastries, and so much more. He told us to treat it like it was our home, help ourselves, and clean up after ourselves. Before I left, I asked to get a picture with the owner and gave him my contact information for potential opportunities to connect in the future.

As my Italian brother and I left the building, we started to converse about deeper subjects than we’d reached before.

Synchronicities of his previous Camino walk.

After struggling to communicate a week before, our ability to understand each other using three languages was profound.

The brown rolling hills provided no tree cover or greenery to absorb the sun.

The desire to finish the day and find some reprieve was making me delirious, in the best, goofiest way. We were laughing and being slightly crazy. With that, I got my Italian lesson of the day:

il cammino ha bisogno di persone un po’ pazze

“The road needs people who are a little crazy.”

And after saying it roughly 63 times to memorize it, we arrived at our destination: Hostel de Santiago in Belorado.

With a restaurant, bar, and pool on the property, this albergue felt like paradise. It was hard to leave, but after a few hours of decompressing with friends, I got closer to the group of Italians, Brits, and Australians. We did our town chores of groceries and the pharmacy, then spent the rest of the evening together.

I even sprinkled in time to work on the blog. Today I finally got a routine down for the first time since being on the Camino.

I knew my responsibilities of blogging that I wanted to honor.

And I knew the importance to me of spending time with the people around me.

Today, all three of those were honored in their own way. I felt balanced, exactly what I discovered I needed yesterday.

#116. Image of Elephant Carrying Dead Calf Wins Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

Federico Veronesi was following a family of elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he came upon a strange and tragic sight. A female elephant was carrying the stiff body of a deceased calf. The Italian wildlife photographer’s shocking image has become the Grand Title Winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Earlier, we reviewed the runner-up entries for this year, released back in September. One of those entries included Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen’s photo of an orca carrying a deceased calf, which it repeatedly lifted up out of the water. These striking images of animals mourning speak to the contest’s mission. Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum, says it strives to “demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently.”

Other category winners explore the relationship between the wild and urban worlds, document natural beauty, and capture more playful wildlife moments.

Winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category, Alex Visbal’s image shows how artificially dividing a Utah wetland has cut part of it off from freshwater, resulting in pink-producing, high-salinity microbes. Photo: Alex Visbal/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

While images like Visbal and Veronesi’s capture large scenes and massive animals, other winners focus on tiny, hidden natural worlds. Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas of Germany won the Rising Star Portfolio Award for his series exploring the smallest and least noticed animals.

As not all of our readers are as fond of arachnids as I am, we feature Tinker-Tsavalas’ whimsical image of a teensy springtail exploring moss, rather than his portraits of ground crab spiders or harvestmen. Photo: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Below even the insect level are the works of macro photographer Kutub Uddin. He won the Portfolio Award for his series of surreal slime mold landscapes. Like Tinker-Tsavalas, Uddin uses focus stacking to achieve incredible fine detail.

This fruiting slime mold looks like some sort of whimsical, slightly grotesque bonsai. Photo: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Several winners focused on wildlife in non-wild settings. Loren Elliott won the Photojournalist Story Award for his series following the coyotes of San Francisco. There are around 100 coyotes living in and around San Francisco, and their relationship with human residents is close, but fraught.

There were several excellent shots in this series, but I would be failing you if I didn’t highlight this one. These two coyote pups live in a den on a golf course, leaving them plenty of golf balls to play with. Photo: Loren Elliott/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Across the world in Bangkok, common water monitors have also become city dwellers. Seth Forestson won in the Urban Wildlife category for his image of a lizard triumphantly bearing a fish through a public park. In the background, the city skyline rises in dramatic contrast.

Photo: Seth Forestson/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Meanwhile, the Plants and Fungi category winner comes from the weird world of mushrooms. On Mount Olympus, Agorastos Papatsanis used ultraviolet light to reveal the luminescence of Mycena renati. Commonly known as beautiful bonnet, the stems of these mushrooms glow a neon yellow.

Photo: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

The Young Grand Title Winner, who entered in the 11-14 year-old category, is Oscar Whitfield. In Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park, Whitfield captured the efforts of a dung beetle.

Ancient Egyptian cosmology drew parallels between the scarab beetle, pushing a ball of dung, and Khepri, the scarab-headed deity, pushing the sun across the sky. The dung beetle also plays a vital role environmentally. The way they process and bury dung reduces methane production and helps speed decomposition. Photo: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

You can view the full gallery on the Natural History Museum website. Tickets to the full exhibition in London, England are available here.

The full view of Federico Veronesi’s contest-winning image. Photo: Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#119. 8 Completely Normal Things Skiers Do Before the Season Begins

Woman on skis posing at Les Sybelles ski domain, on a blue sky sunny day, with Aguilles d Arves peak in the back, along other mountain peaks. (Photo: Getty Images)

There’s a moment every fall when something noticeably shifts. Maybe it’s the first real storm to hit the high peaks—not just a dusting that melts before the social media team can even post the photos. Maybe it’s the sight of snowmaking guns firing up at your local hill. Or maybe it’s the realization that you’ve spent the last 45 minutes staring at a weather forecast for a ski resort 800 miles away, trying to determine whether a storm will deliver six inches or eight.

Whatever the trigger, you know the feeling. Summer’s grip is waning, ski season is suddenly within reach, and your brain has officially entered winter mode. If you recognize yourself in any of the following behaviors, there’s a good chance you’re already counting down the minutes until opening day. We know we are.

You used to check the weather to decide whether to bring an umbrella. Now you’re monitoring atmospheric river activity, tracking overnight lows, refreshing resort snow reports, and developing strong opinions about the long-range forecast. (You know it’s not accurate, but you just can’t click away.) You’ve learned which weather models tend to be optimistic, which ones are worth trusting, and exactly how deep a base your home hill needs before you’ll believe the season is off to a good start.

The best part is that none of this is remotely unusual among your friends. In fact, they’re probably the ones who sent you the forecast in the first place.

Do you eye every staircase as a training opportunity? Suddenly, every squat counts. Maybe you’ll dust off the resistance bands, start doing wall sits during commercial breaks, or finally commit to that preseason workout you’ve been threatening since April.

That’s because you remember what happened last year: Your lungs were fine, your technique came back immediately, and your quads started screaming somewhere around the third run. But this year will be different. This year, you’ll arrive at opening day with legs of steel and the cardiovascular endurance of a mountain goat.

At least, that’s the plan. Whether you actually follow through is another story entirely.

You weren’t shopping for anything in particular—you were just browsing. Now you’re comparing shell fabrics, debating whether your current skis are still “the ones,”, and deciding between two pairs of goggles marked down during Evo’s anniversary sale. The old ones kept fogging up, anyway.

The annual gear refresh is officially underway. You have 14 tabs open, you’ve read three reviews of the same jacket, and you’ve convinced yourself that the right pair of mittens can solve every problem you’ve ever had on the mountain. (Heated mittens? Yes please.)

Of course, your existing gear is perfectly fine, but that’s beside the point. New gear isn’t just equipment; it represents everything fresh and exciting about the start of ski season. And if you’re going to spend the next five months living in it, you might as well get excited about it.

It starts innocently enough. You see a photo of a dreamily lit European mountain village. You click. You browse flights. You check lodging. You open a new tab to investigate lift tickets—in incognito mode, of course.

Before you know it, you’ve planned a 10-day ski trip to the Alps complete with train transfers, a slopeside chalet, and enough après-ski stops to require a detox when you get home. Then reality arrives in the form of airfare, lodging rates, and the cost of feeding an entire family at a ski resort for over a week. You close the tabs and remind yourself that the local mountain is going to be great this year..

Six inches of fresh snow? Depends. Six inches at a low-elevation resort in warm temperatures is one thing. Six inches of cold smoke on top of a deep base in the trees is another.

You’re no longer impressed by snow totals alone. You want to know the water content, the wind direction, the elevation of the snow line, and whether that storm is going to refresh the north-facing aspects or bake in the sun before you get there.

You’ve also developed an uncanny ability to turn any conversation into a discussion of the impending Super El Niño, and where the early-season skiing might be best this year. You briefly consider becoming a weather influencer, but realize it will cut into your slope time.

It’s not just the skiing you’re missing, it’s the whole kit and kaboodle: The crack-of-dawn wake up call. The thermos of coffee. The first glimpse of snow-covered peaks as you drive into the mountains. The satisfying click of your boots into your bindings. The first chair ride of the day, when the air is cold enough to wake you up and the mountain looks wide open and inviting.

Even the less glamorous stuff sounds appealing. Things like the parking-lot shuffle, squeezing your toddler’s feet into tiny ski boots, and stalking a table at lunchtime.

Don’t forget après. A cold beer, a hot toddy, or a mug of something warm with friends while everyone relives the day’s best turns. In October, even the annoying parts of skiing seem charming. Ask us again in February, when we’re sitting in the red snake of I-70 traffic.

Are you measuring everything in relation to opening day? There are six weeks until the lifts spin. Three weekends until your first planned ski trip. Two paychecks until the season pass bill hits. One more family obligation until you can finally get back to the mountains.

You begin evaluating social invitations based on whether they interfere with skiing. You start mentally calculating how many days you can squeeze in before the holidays. You might even catch yourself saying things like, “We can do that after ski season ends,” as though the next five months are a perfectly reasonable amount of time to wait before fixing the running toilet.

Work calendar? Flexible. Family schedule? Negotiable. Household chores. They can wait. The foreseeable weekends are for skiing, toilet be damned.

This is it. The moment you’ve been waiting for. The first resort announces an opening date, and you react as though you’ve just received a personal invitation to the Winter Olympics. You follow the snowmaking updates, scrutinize every new photo of the mountain, and refresh the lift-status page even though you know perfectly well that nothing has changed in the last 12 minutes.

Will there be only one run open? You bet. Will the snow be a little thin in places? No doubt. Will you spend the first few turns remembering how to ski? Nah. It’s like riding a bike. And just like that, you’re back where you belong. See you out there.

#120. This Bryce Canyon Hike Rivals the Grand Canyon’s Rim-to-Rim Trail—and No One’s on It

Group of hikers trekking through Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah, with rugged red rock formations in view. (Photo: Alex Moliski)

Bryce Canyon might be America’s most spectacular drive-through national park. Visitors pull into an overlook, admire a thousand orange hoodoos, snap a photo, and drive to the next viewpoint. It’s fast food for the eyes: beautiful, looks great on your feed, and over in minutes.

But I wanted more than the Happy Meal. So I shouldered my pack at Bryce Point and headed down the Under-the-Rim Trail, leaving the overlooks and crowded dayhikes behind for an overnight adventure. What I found was another Bryce Canyon entirely, where the landscape becomes something you walk through rather than look down upon.

I expected more of the same orange hoodoos that made Bryce famous. Instead, I wandered through pine forests, sandy hills, and open meadows. The towering formations hadn’t disappeared. They were just above me now, casting unfamiliar shadows across the landscape.

Beneath the rim, Bryce felt less like a geological spectacle and more like a wilderness.

Trail: Under-The-Rim Trail Trailhead: Start: Bryce Point, End: Rainbow Point Distance: 23.60 miles (my GPS numbers) Elevation: 5,167 feet (my GPS numbers) Type: Point-to-point Permits: Required for all overnight trips

The first surprise came barely two miles in. The “Hat Shop” is a collection of odd hoodoos resembling people wearing oversized hats, with enormous boulders balanced on skinny pillars. Whoever named it deserves a raise. But don’t forget to turn around: You’ve already dropped almost a thousand feet below Bryce Point, and the view looking back is one most visitors will never see.

That initial descent is deceiving. About four miles in, you’re at the bottom of the first big drop, but the trail is far from finished climbing. The remaining miles are full of what our backpacking group calls “PUDs,” or pointless ups and downs. Stunning, certainly, but brutal on the legs.

Those PUDs led to an ongoing debate amongst our group: Which is harder, the Grand Canyon’s (currently closed) Rim-to-Rim or Bryce’s Under-the-Rim Trail? I’ve now hiked both, and the similarities are surprising. Both cover more than 20 miles, demand thousands of feet of elevation change, and reward you with spectacular Southwest scenery.

Opinions are split, but I give the difficulty crown to Bryce. Those relentless ups and downs really add up, and so do the endless changing views.

The Grand Canyon might be the undisputed king of desert backpacking, but I think Bryce deserves a place in the same conversation. With flooding, fire damage, and construction disrupting the Grand Canyon’s famous Rim-to-Rim route, this is another adventure worth considering just a few hours north. It’s not the Grand Canyon, and that’s exactly the point.

My favorite stretch came between the Swamp Canyon and Whiteman Bench connecting trails. For roughly two miles, the trail passes through an old burn scar where the forest is slowly reclaiming the landscape. Normally, walking through burned trees feels somber. Here, fresh green growth fills the gaps, and the thinned forest opens up enormous views that the living trees once concealed.

Swamp Canyon Butte and Mud Canyon Butte tower above you, with Bryce’s massive walls rising on your opposite side. Buttes look better from below, if you ask me. This is where you start feeling small—where the park’s big crowds become a distant memory, and the wilderness really creeps in. I thought about the Southern Paiute story of how the hoodoos were formed. “Legend People,” whom the trickster god Coyote turned to stone, were forever frozen in time. Looking up at those towering formations, it wasn’t hard to imagine those figures watching us pass.

Bryce Canyon itself was named for Ebenezer Bryce, an early settler who reportedly described the rugged landscape as “a helluva place to lose a cow.” After navigating its maze of drainages and forests, I understood his frustration—though getting lost in the scenery was precisely why I’d come.

Fortunately, getting an overnight permit is easier than finding Ebenezer’s missing livestock. When we arrived at the packed visitor center, the ranger perked up at the mention of backpacking, apparently excited to discuss something other than the Navajo Loop. They told us we were the only backpackers heading out that week. You can reserve permits on Recreation.gov up to three months ahead, with an in-person ranger check-in required before departure. Bear-resistant canisters are also required, and the park lends them out for free (yes, there are black bears in Bryce). The whole process is very easy, since the trail is still overshadowed by other “bucket list” hiking and backpacking routes in the area.

Campsites are designated, and spacing makes planning important. Swamp Canyon and Natural Bridge are good options for breaking up the route, though neither guarantees equal mileage. You could make this a two-night trip and camp at both, but we were only permitted for a single night. At Swamp Canyon, we found flat tent pads and a designated cooking area.

Water is the bigger headache. Unlike canyon hikes that follow a river, Under-the-Rim crosses long, usually dry washes that finger down from the tall wall. On our trip, the reliable stops were Yellow Creek early on and Iron Spring much closer to the finish. That meant carrying extra water across all those PUDs. Seasonal sources vary, so check with a ranger, treat everything you collect, and consider caching water at permitted trail junctions. Both Yellow Creek and Iron Spring dry up entirely by mid-summer.

Timing is equally tricky. I hiked on April 27, hoping for green forests without the summer heat. I wish I’d waited another week for spring to wake up. Late spring and early fall offer appealing windows, but snow, freezing nights, and summer thunderstorms all deserve consideration.

Bring layers, sun protection, and plenty of water. It was hot during the day and freezing at night. It made for the kinds of mornings where I really didn’t want to get out of my sleeping bag.

Finally, remember that Under-the-Rim is a point-to-point hike from Bryce Point to Rainbow Point. The regular park shuttle doesn’t serve Rainbow Point, so arrange transportation ahead of time. We parked a car at both trailheads to make it easy. NPS offers other options for shuttling from Rainbow Point on its website.

And here’s the funny part: Getting back means driving the same scenic road I’d spent the whole trip trying to escape. There I was, dusty and tired, sitting in national park traffic with everyone else, admiring those same orange hoodoos from the comfort of a car. Only now, I’d also seen them from below.

On the trail, I was a backpacker. On the drive back, I was a tourist. And you know what? There’s nothing wrong with being both. Bryce is a damn beautiful place, no matter which angle you look at it from.
