#121. When and How to Use a Grunt Tube to Call Deer

By Charles J. Alsheimer, Michael Hanback, Natalie Krebs

Published Oct 16, 2026 4:16 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The biggest buck I’ve ever had the opportunity to kill strolled right into range after a simple sequence on my grunt tube. I hadn’t seen the buck, but tried blind calling during a break in the 20 mph gusts ripping through the Midwestern timber. One of the many things I learned from that hunt is that I’d been wasting a lot of time by packing my grunt tube but never actually using it until that hunt. That encounter gave me the confidence to grunt in and shoot two nice bucks in Missouri in the following two years, and I managed to call in a half a dozen other bucks — both out-of-range shooters and younger bucks alike — along the way. And I did it by following the tips below, and breaking some of those rules, too.

While there are plenty of ways to call deer, in this story we’re primarily going to cover when and how to use a grunt call for bucks. That’s why we pulled together advice from some of our best whitetail contributors over the years, plus fresh tips from other diehard deer hunters. Learning how to use a grunt tube effectively isn’t difficult as long as you keep in mind that it’s like any other tool or tactic in the whitetail woods. Deploying a grunt tube might not work, and it can actually screw you up when it would’ve been best to keep your mouth shut. But occasionally, it will help you grunt in and shoot a nice buck you’d never have seen otherwise. Here’s how to do it. —Natalie Krebs

The following bit of information may astound you, or it may just convince you that some wildlife biologists are working too many late hours trying to justify their grants. Either way, here it is: In a massive study at the University of Georgia, approximately 400 different whitetail vocalizations were identified and recorded in a captive deer herd and categorized into 12 different types of calls. A few members of my hunting club don’t have that rich a vocabulary.

That 1988 study remains the biggest piece of published research ever conducted on whitetail vocalizations. Grunts, bleats and other calls are now considered essential tactics. Making them, however, is not as simple as blowing on a tube. For example, a hunter must know the difference between a “tending grunt” and a “dominant grunt” to learn how to use a grunt tube, or he might chase off the buck he’s attempting to call. So how do you make sense of it all? Start here. These four sounds rank among the most important in the whitetail’s vocabulary. Master them and you’ll gain the upper hand in the deer woods.

Fawns, does and bucks all use bleats during fall, but fawns make the sound more frequently than adult deer do. In the first four months of a fawn’s life, its bleat is best described as a high-pitched neeeah sound. By October, however, the fawn’s vocal cords have begun to mature and its bleat begins to resemble that of a doe or a young buck, which sounds like naaah. I’ve watched does and fawns spontaneously bleat while grazing and walking in the woods. On other occasions I’ve witnessed what appeared to be a doe or fawn using the bleat to communicate with other deer from a distance. When a buck hears this sound, he’ll often associate it with a doe group and come to check out its source.

I use the bleat in several different ways. If the action is slow while I’m set up over a doe decoy and there’s no sign of deer in the area, I’ll give off a couple of bleats to see if I can attract a buck that might be within earshot. Or I might use the bleat when I’m on watch and haven’t seen any deer for some time. I’ll bleat two or three times in an attempt to get a buck’s attention. When I bleat in this way, I do it loudly so that the sound will project at least 100 yards in every direction. I’ve also successfully incorporated a bleat call into my rattling sequence. Two or three bleats just before and after the rattling sequence often will be exactly what it takes to bring a buck to the antlers.

On the whole, the bleat is one of the most versatile calls a hunter can use. It works well from September through January and in nearly every kind of situation you’ll encounter.

Bucks that are one and a half years old haven’t matured enough to make deep, guttural vocalizations, so their grunts sound very much like those made by adult does. Because of their similar tone, I group yearling buck grunts and doe grunts together. These grunts sound like someone burping (grrrunt) and are generally short or medium in length and soft to moderate in volume.

Does and yearling bucks use a soft grunt for a variety of purposes, but most frequently it is used as a locator call. In addition, they might give off a grunt during a confrontation with another deer over food. When this happens, the grunting deer’s body language can range from ears pulled back to standing on its hind legs to fight off the intruder. When used as a locator call, this grunt is made as the deer walks through the woods or responds to the vocalization of another deer. Does and especially bucks often give off grunts as they travel during the autumn months.

If I see a buck moving through the woods at a distance, I’ll grunt to get his attention. If he starts toward me I won’t call again unless he stops. When this happens, I’ll call again to try to get him to come back. If I hear a buck grunt (and I haven’t initiated his grunt), I’ll grunt right back at him. If a buck is in the mood to vocalize, you need to try to call him to your location. As with the bleat, incorporating this grunt into a rattling sequence is also a great tactic.

The dominant buck grunt is very similar to that of an adult doe or yearling buck, but with one very distinct difference: it’s much deeper. If you happen to hunt in an area that has a good adult buck population, you’ll want to master this sound. It’s a great call to use on a dominant buck during the heat of the rut. Most mature bucks are very aggressive during this time and it takes very little for them to come running. There are two 160-class whitetails hanging on my office wall that fell for this tactic.

The dominant buck grunt can be used in the same way that the doe/yearling buck grunt is used. But a word of caution: Don’t use this call if you are trying to work a yearling buck. Chances are you will scare him off, because the hierarchy of the whitetail is such that mature bucks harass smaller bucks from the time their velvet is peeled, so that when the rut rolls around, yearlings will often run if they hear a mature buck grunt.

The tending grunt is by far my call of choice during the rut. I’ve never found any call that tops this one for luring in a buck during the tail end of the breeding period. When a buck is with a doe that is in or near estrus and other bucks are nearby, the tending (or dominant) buck will usually make a tending grunt by dragging out a grunt for a minute or longer. Bucks have been known to make this sound for more than five minutes. I once timed one of my research bucks making a tending grunt that went on for nearly six minutes. The tending grunt is of moderate intensity and is a series of short grunts repeated in rapid fashion (one grunt after another, with very little break in between).

The buck that is tending a doe will almost always make this sound when another buck tries to take the doe from him. I like to use this call when the breeding phase of the rut is due to start. When a buck hears it, he knows an estrous doe should be in the area and often will come to check out the action. A tending grunt isn’t foolproof, but it’s as close to the perfect rutting call as you’ll get.

By placing your tongue on the roof of your mouth and making a ticking cadence (while blowing through the tube), you can create a near-perfect tending grunt on this call.

In my opinion the grunt call is the most important innovation under $15 in the history of whitetail hunting. If you’ve piped on a tube for years with little to show for it, you probably think I’m making a rash statement. But I firmly believe that by using these tips to improve your technique, you can grunt in a couple of bucks this fall. One of them might even have a whopper rack.Call repeatedly. In areas in early to mid-October, it can’t hurt to blow half a dozen moderately loud grunts every 20 to 30 minutes. Do this whenever you’re archery hunting in a draw or on a ridge where deer move between bedding and feeding areas. You should also grunt periodically from a stand near a bedding area. Your calls might cause a deer to sneak over to investigate.

Grunt to out-of-range bucks. “Blind calling” can work, but a grunt call really shines when a buck has been spotted. Grunt at every buck you see that is slipping by out of range. If a deer hears you, he should at least stop and look your way.

Get aggressive. Most of the time, after stopping and looking, a buck will continue on his way. Don’t just sit there: Grunt more, and louder. What have you got to lose? It’s a long shot, but your insistent grunts might turn the buck back your way.

Add to the realism. From around November 5 to the peak of the rut, make some estrous-doe bleats with a can-type call, followed by some tending grunts. Young bucks might race in, thinking a breeding show is about to begin. If you’re lucky, a stud might roll in to steal the hot doe.

Grunt with enthusiasm. Many people grunt in a monotone. Don’t. If you sit and blow three or four soft grunts every hour, you’ll probably never call in a deer. But if you put some life into your routine by varying the volume and excitability of your grunts, you’ll have better luck.

Crank it up in the rut. The best calling success occurs around the peak of the rut. This is when bucks are on the prowl, scraping and seeking does. Crank it up by blowing loud, choppy tending grunts every 30 minutes or so. The calls should sound something like urrrrppp, urrrrppp, urrrrppp. Use 5- to 10-second sequences. A buck might come to what he thinks is a rival trailing a doe.

Tone it down post-rut. When the post-rut begins, go back to setting up close to bedding areas and in funnels that lead to food sources and tone your calling back down. A weary buck won’t walk 100 yards out of his way to investigate loud, fancy calls.

Avoid blind calling in feeding areas. Don’t blind-call when bowhunting near crops or acorns, especially early in the pre-rut. Deer are coming to feed in the afternoon anyway, so there’s no need to attract them. Besides, if you call excessively where animals congregate, a doe or a young buck might come over and bust you.

Always pay attention to the wind. One day I grunted at a big eight-pointer. He looked my way and then moseyed off. Twenty minutes later, I heard hooves crunching leaves behind my stand. The buck had circled. Even if a buck moves away, you should watch your downwind side.

Don’t fret about how your call sounds. I’ve heard 10-pointers make wimpy, nasal grunts and 8-pointers grunt deeper than market hogs. The point is: Don’t worry too much about the tone of your grunt tube in October or December. During the rut, however, use a throaty, deep-pitched call; old bucks seem to respond to these best.

Don’t be afraid of grunting. Blow your grunt tube loud enough to get a buck’s attention. On windy days, you’ll have to bear down. Many times I’ve blown a call past its breaking point, sending distorted grunts to bucks 150 yards out; they all stopped and looked. Of course, the closer a buck is, the softer you should call.

Don’t grunt to a nearby buck. Don’t grunt when a buck is within 75 yards and looking for you. He might see you move, or he might not see another deer over there and get suspicious.

Don’t call to an approaching buck. When a buck is walking steadily toward you, don’t call. Grunt again only if the deer loses interest and begins to go in another direction.

Don’t use a grunt tube to stop a buck. When a buck gets in close, don’t fiddle with a call to stop him, not even one of those newfangled hands-free models. Voice-grunt once or twice — something like eck, eck. No matter how bad you sound, a deer will freeze. Draw your bow or aim your firearm before you grunt and be ready to shoot the second a buck stops.

It’s often impossible to call in a buck who knows where he’s going. It’s always worth trying, but don’t lose faith if he just glances your way. Based on my experience, the success rate on bucks that seem to be headed someplace is horribly low, something like 1 in 10. A buck that’s dawdling and moving slowly, however, is something different. Here, my field notes show that at least 50 percent of those deer end up starting toward me — most come all the way in.

Pay close attention to a buck’s body language. This tip is from Jared Mills, an Iowa bowhunter who films his hunts and has the advantage of reviewing the tape to learn more about subtle things many deer callers might miss.

“Let’s say you call to a cruising buck and he doesn’t respond, which is a typical scenario,” says Mills. “In your head you may just be like ‘eh he’s just not in the mood’ or ‘he didn’t hear me’ or whatever. Then [I] go back and study the video and I can see his ears turn back toward me. Well he heard me. A lot of times they’ll mark that location in their head and come back a couple hours later.”

So even when you try calling to a buck and he appears not to pay attention or to be on a mission, don’t discount that interaction. He may circle downwind or he may return later. Be ready when he does.

Simple calls work best. In this respect, calling deer is like calling turkeys or ducks: About 95 percent of the game that’s going to come in will respond to a few basic noises. Rhythm, timing, and volume are much more important than fancy sequences. In fact, you can actually do yourself more harm than good trying the kind of stuff that deer rarely hear except from hunters. In other words, you don’t need to be a master caller to create opportunities. A buck’s attitude is what really determines whether or not he’s going to come to the call. So if he doesn’t respond to the basics and never shows back up — even hours later — take heart: That buck probably wouldn’t have come to anything.

Combine grunting with rattling. Often deer hunters think about grunting or rattling as separate tactics, but there’s no reason you can’t experiment with both calls in the same sequence. Here’s what the research shows about the best times to rattle.

Remember, every calling situation is different. “There’s been plenty of times that we’ve been in a less than ideal setup and called deer right in to us, and there’s been other times where it seemed like the perfect setup with the perfect situation and it still didn’t work out in our favor,” says Zach Ferenbaugh of The Hunting Public, who notes that there’s no one right way to grunt to a buck. “So based off a variety of factors, every time you call to a deer, you may treat that situation a little different.”

Researchers in that 1988 study on deer vocalizations focused on whitetails in the East and South, and they suggest that whitetails evolved their vocalizations to communicate in dense cover. So how well does calling work with open-country mule deer and Western blacktails?

“Blacktails are more aggressive than other species,” said Don Laubach, a Montana game-call-maker and filmmaker whose Deer Talk call was one of the first products to allow hunters to mimic subtle deer bleats. “They’ll roll right in to the right call. It doesn’t seem to have anything to do with the density of the cover. I just think they’re more curious. In fact, I’ve called in a blacktail for a hunter who missed a shot with a bow and flared the deer. I was able to call it back into range just by blowing a series of soft confidence bleats.”

One of Laubach’s favorite tactics for calling mule deer used to be sneaking into the head of a canyon and make a series of low-frequency bleats. If any muleys are bedded in the canyon, they’ll often stand up to locate the sound and hunters can glass the suddenly visible bucks. In the month leading up to the rut, bucks will sometimes walk hundreds of yards to investigate the sound, according to Laubach.

Read Next: Inside the Mind of Dan Infalt, the ‘Big Buck Serial Killer’

Calling generally doesn’t work where deer are continually pressured by hunters or other predators. In fact, one reason deer have relatively intimate conversations might be because they evolved around a variety of predators, and by communicating quietly they were less likely to announce their location. —Andrew McKean

Remember that to successfully grunt in a buck, a lot of pieces must fall into place. Using a grunt tube to call deer is not a perfect science and it may not work in even the best set ups. But trying these tactics in a variety of situations will, at worst, teach you more about deer hunting. At best, you’ll call a great buck into range.

If a hunter wants to use the language of deer to become a more effective predator, he has to tune his hearing by listening to entire conversations of deer. Just as in human conversations, that will require taking the time to listen to some boring dialogue.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#122. JMT Day 12 – Rain Day

We got up, packed, and up to Mather Pass. While eating our oatmeal on top of the pass, we met Real Teal – a section hiker who was really fun to talk with. We ended up discussing her knee problems a bit. She talked about finally finding a physical therapist who actually helped her, and sure enough, it was Blaze (the practically famous physio therapist of the PCT). We also met Roadie and Twinkle Toes – and American couple living in Mexico. We saw thema lot over the next five days, and they were a fun couple

On the descent from the pass, the rain started. It didn’t rain hard at first, so we sang Singin’ in the Rain, and a few other big hits.

By the time we got to the South Fork Kings River crossing (which was nearly waist high last year), the rain was falling a lot harder, so we threw the tent up with the intent to eat and nap while the rain passed.

The rain didn’t pass – instead, it fell harder, and after about an hour, we realized that there was a river running through our tent (mostly under the tent). We quickly scouted for a better site, and then carried my free standing tent to a new site. My Zpacks Duplex has nearly 300 nights of camping, and is beginning to show some age. There are a few (patchable) holes forming in the top, and both zip flies are toast. Mostly, it works out fine, but on nights like this, it was held together by safety pins and a kula kloth.

We ended up with a short day, but stayed pretty dry overall, so not too bad.

#123. Giant Crabs Complicate New Amelia Earhart Search

Researchers hunting for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s plane have followed new clues to a remote Pacific atoll, inhabited by giant coconut crabs so large and active at night that the team sleeps aboard its ship for safety.

In 1932, the American aviation pioneer became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. Five years later, she and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared while attempting to circumnavigate the globe. After leaving Papua New Guinea on July 2, they failed to reach Howland Island, their planned refueling stop. The official account is that navigation and communication problems caused their Lockheed Electra to run out of fuel and crash into the ocean. The disappearance has produced decades of speculation about what happened.

Amelia Earhart beside her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. 1937. Photo: National Portrait Gallery

One long-standing hypothesis, advanced mainly by the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, is that the pair reached Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), about 350 nautical miles southeast of Howland, landed on the reef, and later died as castaways.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University arrived at the uninhabited atoll — part of Kiribati — this week after a 1,500km voyage on their vessel, according to the BBC and Purdue University updates. They are investigating the Taraia Object, an elongated shape in a lagoon first identified in satellite imagery in 2020 and visible in aerial photos dating to 1938.

Some researchers view it as a possible remnant of Earhart’s plane. Others consider it more likely a fallen tree or other debris. This marks the first authorized visit to the island in seven years, and the first to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15 years.

The uninhabited Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean. Photo: Wikipedia

The work, which should take about five days, includes clearing vegetation, scanning for metal, and using dredging equipment to examine the object, which lies only about three meters from shore in as little as 1.5m of water, depending on the tides. Conditions have already limited boat access on some days, though organizers expect an update on the object’s identity within about 48 hours, according to Purdue.

The coconut crab has the strongest pinch of any crustacean. Photo: Reinhard Dirscherl via treehugger.com

The island’s coconut crabs, also called robber crabs, are the world’s largest land-dwelling invertebrates, with a leg span of up to one meter and a body weight of more than four kilos. They can lift objects weighing about 28kg, crack open coconuts, climb trees, and emerge at night to capture live prey such as rats and seabirds, as well as carrion. Expedition communications stated that the crabs’ size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical, so the crew returns to the ship each night.

The same animals appear in theories about what might have happened if Earhart died on Nikumaroro. In 1940, British colonists recovered 13 bones near the remains of a fire. The bones were later lost, though some re-analyses of the recorded measurements have suggested consistency with a woman of Earhart’s stature.

The Taraia Object on a satellite image. Photo: Rick Pettigrew/Archaeological Legacy Institute

In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery placed pig carcasses on a similar island and found that coconut crabs (along with smaller hermit crabs) stripped most of the flesh and dragged bones to burrows in less than two weeks. The crabs are not known to hunt humans aggressively. The primary risk is a powerful defensive pinch from their claws if they are handled or startled.

The survey of the Taraia Object began on Wednesday. The crew established a base camp, cleared overgrown paths, and prepared for their fieldwork.

Previous searches, including one by well-known explorer Robert Ballard, who first located the Titanic, have not produced any aircraft wreckage, and many experts continue to regard an ocean crash near Howland as the most likely outcome. The current team reports encountering some crabs during initial setup but described them as posing no threat to operations at that stage.

The Taraia Object’s survey has begun. Photo: Purdue.edu

#126. Beater Cars, Beer Bellies, and Trash By the Ton. Welcome to Gambler 500.

The Gambler 500 Off-Road Rally (Photo: Alex Pulaski)

A whining growl interrupted my sleep just after 6 A.M. The day’s first emissary—a minibike—darted past, launched from the apocalyptic armada surrounding me. Another dawn for the captains, oft bearded and bellied like Toby Keith in a Frankenstein fever dream, reawakening their doomed creations with WD-40 and a Craftsman wrench.

They are Gamblers with a capital G, living by their own car-centric lexicon and a meager rule set. Mainly: Don’t be a dick. They are gearheads, sharp-witted jokers, iconoclasts who fix broken things—usually internal combustion engines.

On this late June weekend in central Oregon’s high desert, they have congregated, 4,000 strong, as part of a sweeping movement to clean up trash-filled public lands. The weekend Gambler 500 event, also known as the OG 500 or simply Gamblertown, started small in Oregon just over a decade ago. It’s grown into a massive gathering that’s equal parts Burning Man and Baja 1000. Participants modify vehicles of every sort—cars, trucks, vans, and even school buses—into all-terrain adventure machines. Some dress in outlandish costumes. They venture into the backcountry to collect trash, have fun, and experience Mother Nature. Now there are Gambler chapters in every state, blending off-road rambling with environmental stewardship.

Invariably these Gambler events draw allusions to the “Mad Max” movie franchise. The oddest of vehicles—call them hoopties, beaters, or worse—sprout appendages like gnomes or spiders or even propane-powered flamethrowers, and it’s comforting to categorize them via a cultural reference point.

The only problem is that the “Mad Max” films  are packed with insane characters trying to kill one another. Gamblers, while prone to some crazy moments, are battling litter as the enemy, bearing banners for Sons of Smokey, the Gambler 500’s nonprofit wildlands cleanup arm. An app (available to anyone) allows users to mark public-land dump sites, and drivers follow waypoints to remove anything from scattered trash to abandoned boats and recreational vehicles.

No comprehensive report describes the extent or the costs of the trashing of U.S. public lands, though studies hint at the continuing problem. The federal Bureau of Land Management oversees about 245 million acres, primarily in 12 western states; there are millions more acres in state and federal parks and forests. In addition to Gambler-led efforts, agency and volunteer cleanups routinely encounter illegal dump sites—the work of homeless encampments, individuals evading disposal fees, and others.

I had pulled into Gamblertown, in Madras, Oregon, the day before my morning minibike wake-up. Surveying a 60-acre field of mowed and yellowing grain stalks, I noted early arrivals: a desert-tan van budding a trophy buck from its roof and a giant faux cigarette from the grill, another van emblazoned with Pac-Man characters, and a bizarre menagerie of primer-colored cars displaying stickers and spraypainted slogans like defiant tattoos. My plain black 2020 Honda Pilot seemed forlornly out of place—abnormally normal.

A sound I would come to know all too well greeted me: a buzzing minibike, veering around a corner. Its bearded rider wore a colonial patriot’s breeches, a frock coat and tricorn hat. His shouts outdueled the minibike’s whine.

“The shitboxes are coming,” he proclaimed, mimicking Paul Revere. “The shitboxes are coming.”

The Gambler 500 was born in an Oregon bar in 2014 as a cross between a question and a joke: Just how far could a beater car—one costing $500 or less— make it off-road?

“In the beginning it was just me and a buddy saying, “Hey, it will be fun driving some cars around until they die,” said founder Tate Morgan.

About a dozen members of a loose-knit club calling themselves the Gamblers kept the annual tradition going, adopting their own slang like “ABG” (always be gambling) and “pavement is lava”— a reference to staying off-road as much as possible. Their rallies followed preset waypoints; they departed in staggered starts from a suburban Portland saloon’s parking lot.

I met Morgan in the same saloon two and a half months before this year’s event. He’s huge—6 foot 4, 240 pounds—with glacier blue eyes, unruly graying hair and a salt-and-pepper beard. A black bead of motor oil ringed his fingernails. His no-bullshit conversation style is layered with equal parts f-bombs and words like “prescient,” “ubiquitous” and “propensity.”

In a measured voice, he described facing two collisions a decade ago that scarred him and raised questions over survival— his own and his newfound hobby’s. The first was discovering he had testicular cancer. The second resulted from a viral video about the 2016 Gambler 500 event.

The following year, Morgan expected anywhere from a few dozen attendees to a couple of hundred. Instead, 3,000 people showed up in central Oregon. Chaos ensued. Lines. Parking headaches. U.S. Forest Service officers issued tickets for permit violations, and a citation to someone who had abandoned a broken-down vehicle.

All of which left Morgan with a decision: Kill his creation or breathe new life into it. He had grown up in Eugene, Oregon, as a true-believer environmentalist, weaned on activist/author Edward Abbey and his 1975 novel “The Monkey Wrench Gang.” Abbey encouraged others to defend the Earth through “any and every method which may be necessary.”

But Morgan sought to build bridges, not detonate them. If Gamblers wanted to continue experiencing cheap outdoor fun, he decided, they needed to give something in return.

Gathered around their Madras camp, Brett Hrouda, the minibike-riding man under the three-cornered hat, and his friends described their converging paths, how an ancient Subaru earned its nickname, and their succinct plans for this year’s Gambler 500.

“We’re here to pick up some trash and do dumb shit,” Hrouda, 47, said. He lives near Roseburg, Oregon, and splits time as a maintenance director and invoicing manager.

Shenanigans, in his friend Tom Parker’s words. Which is why Parker and his wife, Liz, left the kids at home for the big annual event. Lots of vehicles, dust, and alcohol—especially after dark. They’ve been attending Gambler events for a few years now, including smaller weekend gatherings.

Hrouda tells us he finds peace while driving in the backcountry, “just following dirt roads wherever they go.” Until the trail leads to trash piles, where his patience peters out. The Gambler 500 rings on Tom Parker’s fingers spell out their disdain for litterbugs, with ominous mottos like “Throw trash, catch hands,” and more pointedly, “Kill all litterbugs.”

To be clear, the organization embraces solutions and education—not violence. An event flyer, for example, emphasized “do not engage with or collect trash from active houseless population.”

Liz Parker can see that her children are learning lessons from the adults.

“What I love about this is that our kids are in the habit now of saying, ‘Mom, there’s trash in that ditch,’” she said. “They see it and call it out. We’re passing stewardship on to the next generation.”

Tom Parker, 40, a power-line arborist from Camas Valley, Oregon, paid $350 for his first Gambler car, a Subaru, and pushed it hard for three years. Returning from a beer run, he heard sputtering. The rear-view mirror revealed clouds of black and gray smoke, signifying the Subaru’s impending death.

He traded an old dirt bike for another Subaru—a 1985 GL hatchback chopped down into a makeshift pickup. The car bore no nickname until last year’s Gambler 500, when the Parkers and Hrouda strapped an abandoned sofa and other junk onto the Subaru’s back. Returning to camp, they watched in horror as an animal scurried from the sofa into the cab. It was a rat.

Tom Parker braked hard, skidding. He tried to corner the rat. Liz Parker screamed and struggled to unbuckle, panicked. She wanted out.

“I don’t do rodents,” she said. “There’s nothing worse than trying to bail out of a vehicle and the seatbelt won’t disengage.”

The intruder didn’t survive the experience but is memorialized in the vehicle’s nickname: the Subarat.

An insistent wind whipped dust and toppled the Parkers’ tent. As they righted it, a neighbor appeared, duct tape in hand. Did they have a quarter-inch adapter for a three-eighths drive torque wrench? No. I asked why it was needed.

“We have too many pieces of shit,” he said.

Keeping a collection of misfit motorized contraptions running can be a full-time endeavor, explained my new friend, Matt Vanella. Vanella and his crew had a rickshaw concocted from a scooter, wood and spare parts; a riding lawn mower towing a rickety wooden cart; a trike melded from bicycle and all-terrain vehicle parts, secured by scrap wood and yards of wrapped twine; and a “reverse trike,” consisting of a scooter crossbred with an ATV, supporting a forward-facing rider on a boat seat.

While maintaining this Frankenstein fleet, Vanella said, he and his pals were simultaneously scouting marked dump sites through the Sons of Smokey app. They sought trophy trash to parade into camp. Something big, but not too heavy. Like a fiberglass boat.

It turned out that Vanella and friends—Noah Hilton, John Rushing, Matt Wong and Eric Swanson, all from Oregon—were my camp neighbors. Swanson, 48, a cybersecurity engineer, was the mechanical mastermind.

“When I was in high school, I basically lived in the auto shop,” Swanson told me. “This recruiter came to school, and he asked me, ‘Do you want to be doing this when you’re 50?’ And the answer was no, not as a full-time job. But as a hobby I need that creative outlet that’s tangible, physical.”

Afterwards, Vanella, 42, a facility manager from Albany, Oregon, cajoled me into a ride on the reverse trike. He piloted it from atop the scooter, and  I clambered into the front-mounted seat. No helmets for us. Just Vanella urging me to lean left, lean right to keep us from tipping. Shorts riffling in the wind, I felt giddy, thoughts ricocheting between staying upright and wondering how I would explain a concussion or broken collarbone to my wife.

Making new friends. Laughing uncontrollably at high speed. Doing dumb shit. Was I hitchhiking my way onto the Gambler highway? Judge for yourself: my neighbors recorded the weekend on video.

I found myself in the back seat of their Ford pickup an hour later, bouncing toward a marked trash site seven miles east of camp. Matt Wong, reading from the Sons of Smokey app, called out the turns, while Matt Vanella and the others kept a running commentary. We towed a tilting flatbed trailer. The rough gravel backroads did their best to rock me between the two Matts.

You’re in a Matt sandwich, one of the front-seat wags announced. A Matt-wich, said another. That kind of imagery just writes itself, one suggested faux-helpfully, then asked: Can you actually smuggle all this into your article?

The app had marked our target as “the back half of a truck.” Instead, we found the rusted remains of a semi truck’s front end, including the motor, embedded in the roadside dirt. We figured it weighed almost a ton—far too heavy to lift by hand.

Lacking a winch, Hilton and friends rigged a series of heavy-duty ratchet straps and chains to the metal mass. Inch by inch, they coaxed it up the tilted flatbed. On the ride back, I recalled an old trucker anthem called “Looking at the World Through a Windshield,” and its driver “seeing everything in a little bit different light.”

Well, long strips of rubber that you see Were burnt off of this rig by the likes of me And they’ll rot along the highways in this land.

This big-rig remnant, having rusted on public land for years, rolled into camp on our trailer. An excavator’s jaws clamped tight and tossed it to the ground. Next stop: a metal recycler.

From 2017 on, Morgan worked to establish Gambler chapters across the country. He refused to turn it into a money machine, but sought sponsors to defray costs for the annual event.

Morgan established the Gambler’s non-profit arm, Sons of Smokey, with a mission of facilitating “the collection and disposal of trash from public lands, while fostering a non-partisan movement for stewardship of the outdoors.”

He is proud of what they have been able to do over time—especially collecting more than 6 million pounds of trash.

Rambling around and outside Morgan’s shop in West Linn, Oregon, he described the lineage of his odd collection of Gambler cars, from doorless SUVs to an ugly Saturn and a dilapidated Datsun pickup.

The Gambler event no longer requires participants to invest $500 or less in their cars, but Morgan still embraces the ethic of making something out of next to nothing. That came through as he described applying layers of resin and paint on a car he was given for free.

“It’s like celebrating the shittiness of it,” he said, “because you can never lose if you’re kind of shitty on purpose. Which is kind of the gambler mantra—you know we’re not playing that game of trying to outspend or be faster or bigger or stronger than someone else.”

By keeping event fees low and allowing chapters in other states to use the Gambler name for free, Morgan says, “I got to keep my people.”

“Then by making it about trash and conservation stewardship, I’m also betting that everyone who comes out isn’t blinded by politics or some kind of fucking asshole,” he says. “We might disagree on a lot of stuff, but if you keep that and maybe your hate speech to yourself, it’ll be fine.”

As the morning buzz of minibikes mounted, my nose led me to the neighbors’ camp, where eggs, link sausages and hash browns sizzled. No trash cleanups planned today, they told me—too many maimed machines to repair. The reverse trike’s carburetor kept flooding, and the riding lawnmower’s belt was toast.

Which left me hitching a new trash-hunting ride. I spied a convoy of cars and pickups forming, and an empty seat in a Toyota. The driver motioned for me to hop in. Like many of the Gamblers I met, the driver, Tyler Knudson of Corvallis, Oregon, is a military veteran.

After four years as a Navy helicopter mechanic, Knudson faced no insurmountable obstacles in transplanting a Volkswagen diesel engine into his 1990 Toyota 4Runner. In arcane detail, like play-by-play for a sport I will never comprehend, Knudson recited descriptions of TDIs and ALH engine codes, adapter plates and transversely mounted motors, drive shafts and mounting points.

After a few minutes’ drive and a bumpy turn down a dirt trail, we descended into Willow Creek Canyon. A striking tan-green horizon melded into gray clouds. Until we stopped the cars and could fully comprehend all that waited in the sagebrush.

Up close, it appeared as if a garbage barge had run aground in a storm. Rusting cans. Broken bottles. Mattress springs. A rotting steer carcass. Moldy clothing. A car fender.

One of our convoy members, Colton Baker of Cheney, Washington, tried fitting the scene into words.

“I don’t get how people look at this beautiful view and go, ‘You know, what would be even better? Garbage,’” he said.

Knudson loaned me a pair of gloves, and we all bent knees and began filling garbage bags. Knudson strapped hunks of metal and wood on the Toyota’s roof. Our convoy’s informal leader, Bob Keeton of Port Orchard, Washington, corralled us back toward camp after an hour or so, acknowledging that we had made a dent. But there might be days of trash remaining.

“This whole litter issue is so complex,” he told me. “Some of it is a product of laziness. Some is desperation. To keep my mental peace, I’ve resolved that I don’t care how it got here. I only care where it ends up.”

He likes hunting tires, he said. That afternoon I found him in camp by the dumpsters, his 2003 Subaru Baja piled high with discarded rubber.

“I think it cost me a drive shaft, though,” he said, nodding at the Subaru. “That’s why I brought a trailer—we’re not driving it home.”

Attendees keep camp neat by packing out their own trash or placing  it in the dumpsters. Cars that are disabled are towed out, given away or taken to auto recyclers.

Keeton’s was not the only vehicle that failed to survive the weekend. In camp, a hand-lettered cardboard sign on a green 2002 Saab 9-3 summarized the damage done by trail rocks: “Free: Hole in oil pan.”

Its owner, John McKenzie of Fort Collins, Colorado, had paid $700 for the car the day before in Madras. It returned from a Saturday trail exploration on a trailer. McKenzie’s friend, Russell Caldwell of Mountain Home, Idaho, said that’s pretty much the standard Gambler auto experience.

“We wait to find a good deal on one that needs a motor—something that’s been used and abused and broken, then we bring it back to life,” Caldwell said. “Yeah, then usually break it. Then re-break it.”

Re-creation and recreation. Not unlike Mary Shelley’s descriptions of Dr. Frankenstein’s “whirlwind passions.” When the pressure became too great, the fictional doctor described “bending my steps towards the near Alpine valleys, (seeking) in the magnificence, the eternity of such scenes, to forget myself…”

By the end of the Madras event, the 4,000 in attendance put up some substantial numbers: More than 391,000 pounds of trash collected. Fourteen cars, eight RVs, four boats. More than 2,500 tires.

The organization’s cleanup efforts have won praise from land managers and outdoors enthusiasts. Environmental groups, however, contend that off-roaders—like mining operations and oil drillers—are exploiting public lands.

Jeff Miller, senior conservation advocate for the non-profit Center for Biological Diversity, recites a litany of off-roads degradation, from wildlife habitat to archeological sites to entire ecosystems.

“It’s great that someone is picking up trash, but that doesn’t offset all the environmental damage,” he said. “Off-road driving is a destructive hobby, and I don’t think it has any place on our public lands. That whole road system is the reason trash is there—it’s providing public access.”

Morgan, the Gamblers’ founder, acknowledged that some off-roaders’ actions have given others a bad name. But he says the group’s cleanup results tell a clear story.

“I can’t see any work being done that is more significant and visibly helpful for public lands than what we’ve accomplished,” he said. “I believe that public lands exist to serve all users. But it’s easier to villainize the entire off-road culture than have a nuanced understanding of how other people interact with the outdoors.”

Word of mouth, amplified by the Gamblers’ robust social media presence, continues to reverberate. In July, a friends group of Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument approached Morgan about partnering on cleanup efforts.

“I see trash all over southern Utah, into Arizona and as far south as the Grand Canyon,” said Jackie Grant, executive director of Grand Staircase Escalante Partners. “We occasionally will see something huge—a camper or vehicle—that we don’t have the capacity for. I’m hoping we can come together and make a really big impact on trash.”

Similarly, BLM land managers in Idaho report a “vast landscape that has just been trashed,” with inadequate staff to address the issue. National and Oregon BLM spokespersons said volunteer efforts, including by the Gambler group, are both welcome and “inspiring.”

Scientists tell us that our brains automatically assign individuals into social categories so we can understand their motivations and better predict their actions. But when we met before the event, Morgan had warned against overgeneralizing.

“These are the nicest, kindest people you will ever meet,” he told me. “If you need gas, if you need help fixing your car, if you need a ride to the hospital—these people are there for you.”

This I know to be true. Because a couple of years back, as I knelt beside my Dodge pickup’s flat tire on a roadside, a stranger stopped to help. I asked him about the Gambler stickers on his rear window, and his answers—crazy car fun mixed with cleaning up public lands—ultimately led me to invite myself along for this weekend adventure.

Where I met mostly white men, one of whom offered me a beer and happily explained fitting a fiberglass boat on top of a Buick, dubbing the creation the “Lamboatghini.” I met a woman, 8 months pregnant, behind the wheel of a one-ton Ford pickup towing a flatbed trailer piled high with recovered junk.

And met John Thompson of Burbank, Washington, a longtime Gambler, whose battered, tie-dyed 1993 Oldsmobile Cutlass Ciera has survived 222,000 miles and has been submerged in a pond. Thompson paid $200 for it in 2018, when it was vanilla white and bore some resemblance to a normal vehicle.

“If my 18-year-old self saw me driving this thing now he’d kick my ass,” Thompson said. “But this car will probably outlive me.”

Seemed like nearly every Gambler was determined to pen a new chapter on rising from the dead. As I prepared to leave camp, I found my neighbors huddled with funereal solemnity, clutching beer cans instead of flowers. Their eyes examined the remains.

Behind the riding lawnmower, the crude wooden cart sprawled on its side. Splintered frame boards told a tale: A hard right turn, and Newton’s first law of motion sent the cart—and its occupants, Vanella and Rushing—tumbling. Neither was seriously injured, though Vanella displayed a skinned knee like a war wound.

“I’m kind of happy because now maybe we can throw this cart away,” he said.

But his friends weren’t in mourning – they were plotting. A couple of tie-down straps might reunite the cart and its frame, at least temporarily.

“We’ll get ‘er fixed in no time,” Hilton said.

I wished them well and proffered a round of handshakes. Wheeling the dusty Pilot out of camp, I turned northwest onto U.S. Route 26, passing a station wagon bearing a discarded sofa on its roof. One more load arriving.

After two days of ABG (always be gambling), I held a new appreciation for what lies hidden beyond the asphalt in the high desert’s sagebrush and juniper. I’d seen the weird and the wonderful, witnessed maimed machinery being nursed back to life, donned gloves and filled trash bags, and found hope lurking under a veneer of garbage and indifference.

The snow-topped Cascades and a twisting roadway loomed between me and home, affording a couple of hours to ponder cycles of ruin and renewal, loss and resurrection. Pavement is lava, and I had 93 miles to burn.

Four-time Lowell Thomas Award-winner Alex Pulaski is a former travel editor turned freelance writer. His travel articles have appeared in Afar, National Geographic, The Boston Globe, The Los Angeles Times, The Washington Post, and other publications.

#127. Ultrarunning Taught Me My Marriage Was Over

Allie Kolaski, Ph.D., is a licensed counseling psychologist and the current executive director of Women of the Wasatch, a Utah-based, volunteer-led, 501(c)(3) nonprofit that aims to bring more women, LGBTQ+, and BIPOC athletes into the trail community. Thoughts on running, relationships, and self-discovery? Share your story in the comments.

The first time I ran a 50K in 2018, my fingers swelled.

Maybe from the salt. Maybe because I only learned about electrolytes this spring after eight years of running. All I know is that, at the end, my wedding band felt uncomfortably tight.

I didn’t grow up running. As a kid, I mostly played the classic East Coast team sports. Softball, field hockey. Hours in the pool for summer swim team. By high school, I landed on the crew team. I loved rowing, so, so much. When everyone in the boat is in sync, you can feel it balance precariously on the water. Gliding. Flying. Connected.

I wasn’t talented enough to make a varsity college team, but I walked on my freshman year at Princeton University. I stayed on the team for a year before bouncing around in other athletic pursuits. Teaching spin class, hours of television on the elliptical. Ask me if I’ve watched all the seasons of Grey’s Anatomy (I have).

After graduating from Princeton, I found myself working a job where my exercise came outdoors. Climbing, hiking, mountain biking—or trying to mountain bike, in my case. Years spent exploring hidden corners of the American West. It was a hell of a time, being that free. I was far away from the elliptical.

While adventuring, I also found the man I believed would be the love of my life. For our first date, we drove south to sleep under the stars at Castleton Tower near Moab, Utah. I called a friend the next week: “I think he’s the one.”

We got married in that same Moab desert. It was beautiful, and hopeful, and we were surrounded by love. That was 2017.

In 2018, I stood on the start line for my first ultramarathon.

How I ended up at the start line of a trail 50K, having never even run a 5K, seems like an important aside.

While I’d loved my years of unrestricted adventure, my first year of graduate school put an end to flexibility. I was stressed and short on time. I needed a sport that I could sneak in between the demands of life and that didn’t require a new set of fancy kit. Running seemed to fit the bill.

In preparation for the wedding, I also felt that my casual outdoor hobbies wouldn’t cut it. Like many brides, I agonized over how I’d look in my dress. So, in addition to my casual running, I joined a local gym, lifting weights and learning about functional fitness. Trying to be my best in time for the expensive photos I hoped I’d share with grandchildren.

A few months after getting married, I was looking for fresh motivation. I learned that the head trainer had attempted a local trail 50K a year prior, but only finished one of the two required loops.

I was running more anyway—a park lap or two a week—as graduate school continued to push in the walls. I signed up and roped in a friend to train with me.

I had one request for my husband for that first race. Be at the finish line. Celebrate with me.

The people who know me know well that I don’t enjoy being celebrated or asking for help. Compliments are best received when they are slid to me sideways and when I’m given space to view them in private. The potential finish line fanfare felt unusually exposed.

But it also felt important. Something I really never believed I could do. Even in training for the race, I refused the “runner” moniker. I wasn’t a runner. I hadn’t done X, or Y, or whatever other self-imposed standard. I was just trying to stay reasonably fit, finish 32 miles, and not die in the woods.

At the end of the race, my husband was nowhere to be found.

“I got lost,” he said. The Eagle Scout and mountain guide. “I was on the wrong trail.”

Sitting alone at the finish and watching the 50-mile racers come in and celebrate their runs, I spun my ring on my swollen finger. Eyes big.

I ran another trail race that summer in Idaho. Then a 50K in Zion. A 60K. I snuck in several road marathons, a Thanksgiving turkey trot. I entered the Wasatch 100 lottery, and to my horror, was accepted. So much for a hobby I could fit easily into my grad school schedule.

The Wasatch 100 is an old-school ultra. The racers are still hand-selected out of a bingo ball spinner, and once you’re in, there’s no way out but through. Big mountains, big vert, wild temperature swings, and a coveted belt buckle at the finish.

With my acceptance to Wasatch 100, things got a lot more serious. I hired a coach and started running bigger mountain miles. I ran the Tushars 70K, weeping on the last climb in a thunderstorm, choking down a soggy waffle. The weekends turned into my time for back-to-back long runs. My closest confidants: my running peers.

Suddenly running required a lot of space.

For those who haven’t yet stepped into the insanity that is the 100-mile distance, many ultras allow runners to have a crew. While running itself is an incredibly individual sport (your pace, your body, your suffering, your decisions) the longer ultras recognize that maybe some of that decision-making past mile 50 should be outsourced.

I built out my team, and I asked him to be my crew chief. It didn’t go as I’d hoped.

Still a novice, I went out too fast. I didn’t take in enough salt. I wasn’t fueling well. And my feet fucking HURT. Hundred milers are stupid, and hard, and ridiculous. I texted my crew on the way into the third crewed aid station—Brighton Ski Resort—that this was the worst I’d ever felt IN MY LIFE. At the time, it honestly was.

When I arrived, I expected an inspirational pep talk, but I was just met with annoyance.

He was mad that I was late. Mad to be up for most of the night. Annoyed by the rest of the crew. Gloomy. Distant. He went through the motions—taking care of my sore feet, finding my fuel. But I felt the simmer. It was a feeling I’d had so many times before in our marriage. When it was my turn, I was met with resentment.

It felt like I had run into a brick wall. It hurt worse than my feet.

My dear friend pulled me out of my chair at Brighton, and we got back on course. Her pacing section was short-lived, though, and I went on to DNF around mile 80.

I remember sitting in the dirt, crying big sloppy, overtired tears, waiting for my crew, and my now extremely frustrated crew chief, to pick me up. We never really talked about it again.

Despite the DNF, I kept chugging along. I ran another 50K, a few more marathons. In 2022, I graduated—finishing a Ph.D.

My connection with the running community deepened. It was no longer just a convenient form of exercise in a squeezed world. My time was structured around training; relationships had miles at their core. I volunteered, learned, wrote, and dreamed about running. If I had work travel, I’d look up run clubs. When I had free weekends, I’d sign up for races.

I became a Lululemon ambassador. I joined the board of directors of Women of the Wasatch, a local trail running nonprofit group. I ran 800 laps around a whale sculpture in a traffic circle. Gliding. Flying. It was so fun, and so full.

My world was big again. I was capable of extraordinary things. I was a runner.

To be fair, running did take things. Saturdays disappeared. Vacations often included a race. Some of my deepest friendships belonged to a world he didn’t share. But I was still present in our life. I did the cooking, the cleaning, the dog walking. The finances. After graduate school ended, I also became the breadwinner. I tried to compensate by making sure nothing dropped.

He had his hobbies too, of course. Skiing, mountain biking, canyoneering. I tried my best to champion him. I packed food for his trips with friends. Stretched our budget to accommodate a new ski kit and heli-assisted trips in Canada. Made homemade gifts to celebrate checking off big lines.

Meanwhile, I’d come home from a long run and pretend I’d never been gone. I never expected him at a finish line. I’d sob on my runs, alone in the mountains. I was carrying so much. The mountains held it for me.

When I’d come home with bright eyes, I’d hit that brick wall. Gloom. Anger. Resentment. I squeezed myself into the space he left. I learned to expertly navigate the rocky trails and read upcoming terrain.

I tried to make the expansion of my life cost him nothing, but it was an impossible bargain.

In December 2023, on a trail run in Ketchikan, Alaska, I fell, sliced up my left side, and broke my ankle. Months of pain. Eight weeks in a boot. No running. The disconnection to my community was extraordinary.

At first, I tried to replace running with other activities. I’d come to the start of run club, then drive to the gym to get on the elliptical, balancing on my walking cast. For a minute it was OK; I was entertained enough by the odd workouts people did at the local big box gym. But where there had formerly been so much sky, all I saw now was fluorescent lights.

Without the pressure release, other things came into focus. I was miserable at home. Tired of watching TV while he scrolled on his phone. Tired of feeling lonely. Confused about how the connection with this person I loved so dearly had become so dysfunctional.

As an ultrarunner, I had learned a lot about suffering. How to dig in and push through. How to disconnect just enough from the present moment, while keeping sharp attention on executing the plan. Just eat something! Pain passes. Relationships are hard; it’s just a rough patch. Don’t make decisions at the low point. Keep going. Keep going.

We get genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous lessons about enduring from this crazy sport.

But with a broken ankle, I couldn’t ignore the signals anymore. I was forced to stop even when I’d become so talented at continuing.

Over that year, running slowly returned. Never as quickly as I wanted, and not without big losses. I even donated an entry fee to the Wasatch 100, still too injured to participate in my redemption lap. But after losing so much, and as I exhaled into big mountains again, I found myself less willing to contort into the shapes that would fit.

I was exhausted. Holding up the infrastructure of a dying relationship. Containing my joy. Being met with resentment for the big, extraordinary things I could now envision. The anguish exceeded any late-night sore-feet whining.

When I started running, half on a whim, half forced by convenience, I had no idea.

Running gave me my community. Helped me build goals. Changed my relationship with my body. It showed me how big life can get. How much joy can fit inside of it. The trail world is full of extraordinary places and people and a truly unreasonable amount of glitter. Go watch a finish line, you’ll see the magic for yourself.

Running also gave me somewhere to put my sadness. Taught me how to suffer and endure. The trails and the mountains held my pain. And when I could no longer run, its absence allowed me to look directly at the life I’d become so skilled at persisting in.

On the last day of my marriage, I had a vision. A tiny, glowing ember still burning in the middle of a storm. I cared more about keeping it alive than keeping everything else intact. I refused to keep going.

In the months that followed, I got through the mess of divorce with glitter, mud, and a BQ. I lost friends and found new ones. I fell in and out of love. I was held up by my community, my trails, and the terrifyingly open sky. I was loud and sad and unapologetic and flying toward empty space.

It was another DNF, and I’m still not OK. But I had mistaken endurance for the point, when it never was.

Now at races, I don’t worry about my fingers swelling.

#129. “Even When She Was Scared, She’d Always Try It”: Angela Ha Constantly Introduced Others to the Mountains

Angela Ha, a Sydney-based climber and highliner, passed away on April 27, 2026, after a fall while climbing at Mount Arapiles in western Victoria, Australia. She was several days into a multi-day climbing trip when she fell from the popular Organ Pipes crag. Ha was airlifted to a hospital in Melbourne, and succumbed to her injuries later that evening.

To her friends, Ha was memorable for her fearlessness. Jenny Chen, who met Ha through the Blue Mountains highlining community, remembers her as goofy, warm, and relentlessly willing to try new things. “She really lived her life,” Chen said, “She did what she wanted to do rather than just saying she would. Even when she was scared, she’d always try it.”

Ha devoured outdoor adventures filled every available weekend or afternoon with climbing. In the Blue Mountains, she topped trad and multi-pitch routes at Mellow Bath and Sublime Point. Summer afternoons were spent at highline meetups or slacklining at Victoria Park. “She was always really welcoming and warm,” Chen said. “She was just very easy to be around.”

To share her joy with others, Ha led canyoning and climbing trips through the University of New South Wales Outdoor Club. In 2022 and 2023, she led and co-led climbing trips for beginner and intermediate climbers to Mount York, a popular sandstone climbing area. In March 2023, Ha wrote about spending five days in Kanagra-Boyd National Park with six friends, attempting four canyons as a part of what she called her, “summer of canyoning.” [Editor’s note: ‘Canyoning’ is the more popular term in Europe and Australia for ‘canyoneering.’ Both words refer to the same activity.] In 2025, she co-led a women’s canyoneering trip through Box Creek, teaching rigging and empowering her peers.

Climbing was not only recreational for Ha; it also became a catalyst for big changes in her professional life. After earning a Bachelor of Architecture from the University of New South Wales in 2023, she shifted gears and began studying physiotherapy at the University of Sydney in the hopes of rehabilitating injured climbers.

Chen remembers that her appetite for experience sometimes came with nerves that were easily brushed aside. For Ange, fear wasn’t ever a reason not to go. Ha is survived by her parents, Daniel and Ruby, and her younger siblings, Michelle, Stephanie, and Marcus.

#130. Week 10: Conquering the Four State Challenge and Pushing Through the Pain! [Alyssa’s Vlog]

Alyssa is officially back on the Appalachian Trail after a quick travel detour, and she returned just in time to celebrate two full months of thru-hiking! Kicking things off with a 20-mile day, she wrapped up the remaining four miles of the notorious “roller coaster” before cruising down into Harpers Ferry. However, it wasn’t an easy stretch—she miscalculated her water carry and managed to hike the entire 20 miles on a mere 1.6 liters of water, leaving her incredibly thirsty by the time she reached town.

The real test of the week, however, was the infamous Four State Challenge. Waking up at 3:30 AM, Alyssa set out on a massive slackpacking mission to hike across state lines. While passing iconic sights like the Washington Monument, the sheer exhaustion of hitting the 28-mile mark by 2:00 PM quickly set in. To keep herself moving forward, she had to rely heavily on mental tricks. “I feel like I have to be in the mindset of I’m just never going to stop walking… If I just pretend that I’m never going to stop walking then I’m like well all right I’ll keep walking then,” she confessed from the trail.

By the end of the monumental push, Alyssa’s body was screaming. Her feet were in agony, and she noted feeling something moving in her big toe—likely a loose nail—but refused to look at it until she finished. Despite the pain, she crossed the final state line, officially crushing the Four State Challenge. Now, all that was left to do was eat her leftover Chinese food at the hostel and get some sleep before her “big girl job” interview the very next morning!

#131. Canada Coast to Coast Paddlers Begin Final Stretch

Canadian paddlers Will Vyse and Nolan Aziz — reduced to a twosome after Georges Kirijian left the expedition with an injury — are entering the final stretch of their mammoth 8,000km expedition from Tadoussac, Quebec, to Vancouver, British Columbia, on the Pacific Ocean.

After 184 days, including 34 days in Alberta, they crossed into British Columbia on October 10. This marks the final province of their trip. They have recently been paddling up the Peace River, which they describe as “long and arduous.”  The canoeists have covered well over 6,000km, and both they and their gear look suitably disheveled:

Once they finish with the Peace River, they have a meaty 17km portage to Williston Lake, the largest lake in British Columbia, before taking the southern branch of the Crooked River. After crossing the Continental Divide and completing the Giscome Portage between Summit Lake and the Fraser River, they will take the Fraser through Prince George and down to Vancouver.

Vyse and Aziz originally planned to end their trip in the town of Prince Rupert, but have since altered their route to finish at Vancouver’s Wreck Beach.

“Our reroute maintains a total expedition distance of over 8,000km, and upon completion will still be the longest ever recorded single-season canoe trip,” Vyse and Aziz wrote on social media.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#135. The 8 Best Ski Helmets of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: Our expert testers wore 36 helmets at resorts across North America and Europe as well as on backcountry ski tours. They crowned the Sweet Protection Switcher 2Vi MIPS as the best ski helmet overall for its comfort, goggle compatibility, and venting. For a helmet around $100, they recommend the Smith Rodeo MIPS that’s also the most eco-friendly out of the bunch.

Protecting your noggin is non-negotiable. Luckily, ski helmet design has come a long way in the last few decades, and there’s no excuse—not even style—for skiing with an uncovered dome.

Unlike skis, helmets aren’t something most of us build a quiver around. One helmet should cover almost every day on the mountain—a powder day in January or a spring session in April. That, however, puts a little more pressure on choosing the right helmet. If you’re gonna wear it all winter, you better like it.

Our team of testers in the Tetons, Sierra, and Cascades put 36 lids to the test last season, evaluating each helmet’s performance on resort storm days, sunny spring ski tours, and everything in between to bring you the best ski helmets of 2027.

Sizes: Small/Medium, Medium/Large, Large/XL Weight: 560 g Key technology: 2Vi, MIPS, Occigrip turn-dial

Pros and Cons + Excellent venting + Comfortable, adjustable fit + Compatible with a variety of goggles – Ear pads were too thick for some

Testers voted the Sweet Protection Switcher 2Vi MIPS the best overall helmet for its comfortable fit, excellent venting, and versatility between the resort and backcountry.

The Switcher 2Vi MIPS helmet features Sweet’s 2Vi platform, which includes a shock absorbing inner structure paired with integrated impact shields to absorb energy in areas of potential high impact. Fit and comfort was ideal—with a rear dial that’s easy to cinch and ear pads that are unfussy to remove, this helmet let testers with various head sizes dial in fit and comfort. The Switcher 2Vi is sleek and easy to slide under a hood during a windy lift ride, and airflow is top notch thanks to top and front interconnected vents that can be opened—something our testers appreciated while spring skiing at Grand Targhee Resort on a 40-degree March day.

Their only complaint was the earpads, which some called unnecessarily bulky. Still, if you’re looking for a solid all-rounder to check most boxes, the Daymaker is your lid. “If I was heading out on an international ski trip and could only bring one helmet, this is what I’d bring,” said one tester after a winter of traveling to Japan and Europe.

Sizes: S-XL Weight: 550 g (medium) Key technology: Comes in MIPS and non-MIPS versions; also features Smith’s Round Contour fit designed specifically to minimize pressure points for round heads Lab Score, Cooling: 5 (Static Air); 4 (Wind)

Pros and Cons + Half the price of more tricked-out helmets + Most eco-friendly helmet we tested – Vents don’t close – Plastic goggle holster and chin buckle feel flimsy

It’s not often you find a MIPS helmet for around $100, which is why the Smith Rodeo feels like a sneaky score. One tester called it an “all-rounder” and praised its versatility while skiing the park one day and backcountry the next. “This is a super simple helmet that’s lightweight and has heaps of style,” said another.

Despite being designed for round heads, even our testers with bigger, oval-shaped heads had no complaints, thanks to generous adjustability and a spacious, high-cut injection-molded ABS shell, which is designed to handle heavy-duty impacts and resist denting.

One of few helmets made with a majority of recycled materials, the Rodeo has the low-profile look of a retro BMX helmet and is best suited for those who want style first, bells and whistles second. Ear pads are easily removable for warm spring days or park riders who wear goggles underneath their helmets. It has 10 good-sized vents, but you can’t close them in a blizzard; they’re permanently open. The Rodeo paired well with the oversized goggle look that’s trending now.

Sizes: S-L Weight: 417 g Key technology: MIPS, Ripcord 360 Fit

Pros and Cons + Magnetic buckle works with gloves + Cozy ear grommets pop out + Easily adjustable vents – Less subtle, more of a statement

When comfort reigns supreme, testers found themselves reaching for the Pret’s updated Lyric 2 helmet time and time again. “So comfy, I almost drove home in it,” said one tester after a blustery day of storm skiing at Crystal Mountain in Washington.

The toasty ear grommets provide a welcome respite from chilly days on the hill, and when the sun shows its face, a single lever throws open the front and upper vents for optimal airflow. The ear grommets pop out too, whether you’re looking for a spring look or are just someone who prefers no ear flaps.

The chin strap’s magnetic buckle, which snaps together with the most satisfying click, was a crowd pleaser. “I’m not sure why every helmet ever doesn’t have the magnetic buckle,” said one Wyoming tester. “That is now a must-have for me.” Pret helmets definitely have a signature look with fun, contrasting colors—some love it, but it was a little much for our testers who prefer a more understated look.

Sizes: XS/Small, Medium/Large, XL/XXL Weight: 530 g Key technology: MIPS Evolve, Recco, Twiceme NFC Medical ID

Pros and Cons + Extremely comfortable + Unique rescue technology – Expensive – On the heavier side

POC’s Obex BC MIPS helmet proved its merit both in and out of bounds, racking up hours at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort and on Teton Pass. Testers loved the comfortable fit, full coverage, and easy venting, with one tester noting: “This is a pretty ideal one-helmet solution.”

Technically billed as a backcountry helmet, testers agreed it felt more like an everyday resort helmet you could also take touring. That’s likely because of the weight—while it wasn’t overly bulky, it was actually the heaviest helmet we tested (heavier than the standard Obex), so we couldn’t justify billing it as the best helmet for a long tour. “This was the perfect helmet for skiing in and out of bounds at Jackson Hole since it felt solid and protective while lapping the tram, but slid easily into my helmet carry for short bootpacks,” said one tester.

One feature sets the Obex BC apart from any other helmet: The Twiceme NFC Medical ID is a chip inside the back of the helmet that allows you to store an emergency contact and medical info, designed to support rescuers in the field. Hopefully it’s a feature we never have to use, but adding safety-minded features to our gear is something that we’ll always give a thumbs up.

Downside? Spending $300 on a helmet can be hard on the wallet, but technology like MIPS, Recco and the integrated medical ID system made a hard case for spending a little more on potentially lifesaving features.

Sizes: S-L Weight: 506 g (medium) Key technology: MIPS, plus Scott’s 360 Pure Sound Tech & Recco technology for superb noise detection Lab Score, Cooling: 4 (Static Air); 2 (Wind)

Pros and Cons + Super comfortable thin yet cushioned liner + Excellent moisture management + Clean, streamlined style – Could use some venting up top

While some helmets have a thick lining that takes on sweat like shag carpeting, the Scott Flow Pro MIPS’ sparse, unobtrusive padding inside made it ultra-comfortable on everything from storm days at Alta to spring skiing at Mammoth. And while other helmets cause pinching or pressure points, this well-cushioned lid fit like a dream even on oval-shaped heads.

Thinly padded ear covers let sound in better than other helmets. The liner material is thermoregulating and kept testers from overheating—but most wished for a few more vents. The only adjustable vent is on the front rim of the helmet. “Not sure why it’s called the Flow helmet. It’s got minimal venting,” one tester said, while another added that “the vents were small but effective.”

Sizes: S-XL Weight: 380 g Key technology: AMID, Holo Core, 360° Fit System

Pros and Cons + All-day comfort + Classic look + Lightweight yet durable – Ear flaps aren’t removable – Minimal venting

When six testers came back from the hill raving about the Atomic Four Amid Pro Helmet, we suddenly understood why all the athletes on Atomic’s freeski team wear it. It’s not flashy or overly feature-laden, but testers loved the classic look, comfortable fit, and rock-solid design.

As the lightest helmet in our test—and with a sleek design that slid easily into a pack or helmet carry—the Four Amid Pro became testers’ go-to backcountry helmet. Featuring Atomic’s proprietary impact protection and Holo Core design—an extra crumple zone to dissipate forces in a fall—this helmet also checks all the safety boxes. Fit was easy to adjust with the back dial and slid over a hat, gaiter, or both. “As comfortable on long bootpacks as tram laps,” said one tester.

While the helmet only has eight small, fixed vents, testers said the lightweight design made up for that, managing heat build-up well. The main complaint was that while the washable liner is fully removable, the ear flaps and liner are all one piece. Most testers said they wished they could remove the ear padding, and a few took a pocket knife to the liner to free up airflow.

Sizes: S-XL Weight: 550 g (medium) Key technology: MIPS, Koroyd, AirEvac, BOA 360 Fit System

Pros and Cons + Outstanding venting + Comfortable fit + Large size run – Expensive

An updated version of one of Smith’s bestselling helmets, the Vantage 2 impressed us with its clean look, comfort, and ample venting. “It’s almost like a convertible for your head,” said one tester after an unexpected 50-degree ski day at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort.

Dual vent switches allow you to open and close the vents on the top and side of the helmet independently, even with gloves on: “Confirmed, you can do this while skiing,” said one Washington tester. The intricate venting system gave this helmet the best airflow of any other lid we tested—throwing the vents open on a slushy spring day and sealing everything up for January storm skiing gave us ample versatility throughout the season. A durable Koroyd shell provides sleek, lightweight protection for resort days, cat laps, and the occasional ski tour. The BOA dial at the back made micro adjustments easy, and the goggle loop is easy to unhook without removing gloves.

The Vantage 2 is on the pricier end due to key technology like MIPS and Koroyd material that optimizes energy absorption by creating crumple zones to reduce the risk of injury on impact. Budget-conscious skiers might opt for something else, but you get what you pay for: premium fit, comfort, and safety features a step up from the rest.

Sizes: S-L Weight: 436 g Key technology: MIPS, Fidlock chinstrap

Pros and Cons + Seamless goggle integration + Multiple independent venting ports + Magnetic chinstrap buckle – Not as compatible with non-Glade goggles

The dreaded forehead gap is about more than just style—no one likes to get brain freeze when frigid air blows straight at their forehead lap after lap. Testers loved the helmet and goggle integration of the Boundary MIPS, which provided a seamless seal while hotlapping the resort.

The Boundary syncs up nicely with all of Glade’s goggles, and while there is no unwanted forehead venting, there are tons of welcome top and side venting for spring days on the mountain. The helmet vents (which operate independently) lined up perfectly with Glade goggles, which prevented fogging on a steamy 35-degree day at Grand Targhee, Wyoming. Another fan-favorite feature: the magnetic chinstrap. “Just say yes to magnetic chinstrap,” raved one tester after a few weeks of testing in the Tetons. “I think this should be mandatory on all helmets,.” said one tester.

The only major downside is that this helmet is designed to integrate seamlessly with Glade goggles, but not with others, leaving a few testers to feel “boxed in” to their goggle choice.

A well-constructed snowsports helmet should last you a few years, depending on the number of days you ski or ride and how many big crashes you take. If your helmet has been dented or damaged or seen years of heavy use, it’s probably time for an upgrade.

Most of the helmets we tested come with MIPS, which stands for Multi-Directional Impact Protection System, a layer of lining between the shell and foam that allows the helmet to rotate on impact, reducing rotational forces to the brain in the event of a big tumble. Some brands have developed their own proprietary technology that offers similar safety protection as MIPS. If you’re purchasing a new helmet, we do recommend seeking out a lid with multi-directional impact technology.

When it comes to fit, it can be helpful to try helmets on in person in a store to ensure the sizing works for your uniquely-shaped head. If you’re buying online, measure your head circumference with a soft tape measure just above your ears and about an inch above your eyebrows and look for helmet sizing that fits that range (most helmet brands use centimeters in their size ranges). You don’t want excessive movement or extra space in your helmet, but you also don’t want pinching or squeezing. Every helmet we tested has a micro-adjustable knob on the back to get a more precise fit. All helmets should fit with other goggle brands, but we’ve found the best fit (read: no gap on the forehead) tends to be when you purchase a helmet and goggles from the same brand.

In terms of temperature control, helmets with insulating lining or a layer of fleece run warmer than others that are more barebones on the interior. If you run hot, also look for lots of controllable vents.

Our testers wore helmets inbounds at resorts across North America and Europe as well as on backcountry ski tours. They are based in Jackson, Wyoming; Teton Valley, Idaho, Seattle, Washington; and Mammoth Lakes California, and traveled extensively throughout the winter, testing these helmets across the mountain west and even in the Alps. After multiple days on snow with each helmet, testers evaluated each helmet for comfort, fit, venting, versatility, and any other stand-out features.

Lily Krass Ritter is a freelance journalist and ski guide based in Victor, Idaho with work featured in The Ski Journal, SKI, Powder Magazine, Freeskier, Teton Gravity Research, and Ascent Backcountry Snow Journal. She spends winters backcountry skiing in Grand Teton National Park and riding lifts at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, with the occasional trip to the Alps (for the food, obviously).
