#136. How a Missed Turnaround on Mt. Shasta Turned a Dayhike into a 36-Hour Survival Situation

Mt. Shasta (Photo: Mimi Ditchie Photography via Getty)

How Backpacker reported this story: Writer Sam Anderson spoke with the Forest Service program manager for Shasta’s climbing rangers and the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office to learn about how two dayhikers ended up spending 36 hours stuck high on California’s Mt. Shasta and the mission to rescue them.

Two hikers from Salt Lake City had a close call on Mt. Shasta this week after a missed turnaround and a wrong turn forced them to spend an unplanned night exposed to 15-degree weather.

The Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office (SCSO) received a distress call at 10:20 p.m. on Monday, October 12. A 19-year-old male and 20-year-old female were underequipped to safely wait out the night at their location, about 11,000 feet up Avalanche Gulch. They’d begun their day at 4 a.m. at the Bunny Flat Trailhead with no plans to summit, alongside a male companion who did plan to summit.

According to Sage Milestone, public information officer for the SCSO, the group had been on their way to Mt. Rainier when they made the spur-of-the-moment decision to climb Shasta.

Their route was dangerous from the beginning: Avalanche Gulch’s terraced scree ramps are loose and crumbly without snow and ice to consolidate them. Along with that advisory, the pair had also ignored a recommended turnaround time posted at the trailhead. On their way up, Milestone said, the pair ran into their friend who had summited as he descended; he advised them to turn around at Red Banks, located at 12,800 ft. Unfortunately, the pair did not reach that point until around 5 p.m., five hours past the posted turnaround of noon.

Now separated from their companion and stuck in rapidly-dropping temperatures with inadequate clothing, they followed officials’ advice to keep descending to maintain body heat.

The group again contacted emergency services at 2 a.m. to report that they had reached Helen Lake at approximately 10,400 feet. Shortly thereafter, their phones died.

Rescuers scrambled in a first-light operation involving air and ground operations. Ground searchers and air crews with CHP Air Operations first scanned the upper reaches of Avalanche Canyon. Around 9 a.m., they located two hikers, who turned out to be unrelated to the search and in no need of help.

On the ground, crews tried another approach. Beginning at Horse Camp, a large cabin at 7,880 ft. on one of the mountain’s most prominent trails, which the hikers had already passed on their way up, they descended into nearby Cascade Gulch.

While rescuers didn’t necessarily think Cascade Gulch was the most likely place to find the missing climbers, searching it was a matter of diligence, Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center, said.

“Cascade Gulch is a common place for people to end up if they get lost on Avalanche, but it’s usually only when the trails are covered,” Meyers said. “When trails are exposed like they are now, you can just follow the main drainage to hit any of the trails back to Bunny Flat.”

However low-percentage, the decision paid off. Rescuers in Cascade Gulch heard shouting around 4 p.m. Soon they had located the two hikers, who were uninjured and managed to descend safely with help.

According to rescue crews, the hikers confirmed they had passed Horse Camp on their way down. How they got lost from there remained unclear.

“The trail from the cabin to Bunny Flats is a superhighway,” Meyers explained. “It’s the baseline recommended day hike for anyone of any experience level on that area of the mountain, so it’s really well-marked and very wide. We’re still scratching our heads about how they missed it.”

While Milestone said “there were red flags from the get-go on [the hikers’] attempt,” he noted that officials were grateful the climbers followed rangers’ advice to keep moving down the mountain to stay warm, and that they believed the pair had learned from their experience.

The rescue follows multiple similar incidents on Mt. Shasta during the past month. One badly injured hiker was airlifted from Horse Camp on Sept. 11 after attempting a glissade at high altitude, injuring his feet, and crawling back down most of Avalanche Gulch. And three young hikers endured a long rescue in early September after using AI to plan their summit bid via the Clear Creek route.

#137. “Walking 800 Miles Was the Quick Part”: The Making of the HAYDUKE Thru-Hiking Docuseries

In 2023, four thru-hikers set out on the Hayduke, an 800-mile route through the canyon country of southeast Utah and northern Arizona. There is no trail to follow, and they hiked after a record snow year. Andy Laub, Elina Osborne, Zelzin Aketzalli and Peter Hochhauser carried four cameras and came home with 20 terabytes of footage.

Three years later, that footage is HAYDUKE, a four-part docuseries streaming on Camel’s Cabana. Andy and Elina co-directed it. For The Trek, they interviewed each other about walking it, filming it, and what it took to turn that mountain of footage into a story.

ELINA: You’ve worked on other documentaries and hiking projects. What sets this one apart? Did something about this experience change how you approached the story?

ANDY: We were making a trail film without a trail. That alone gave HAYDUKE its flavor.

With As It Happens: Pacific Crest Trail and THRU: The Pacific Northwest, I’d filmed adventures on American long trails. Each had its own personality, but there was generally a path. On the Hayduke, we took that same approach to filming a lived dirtbag experience, only now we had to figure out the path ourselves.

And we showed up in 2023. A state of emergency had been issued, as record snowmelt raced through the canyons we navigated. An already wild route became something else entirely. As we said out there, every day felt like an EPIC, a lifetime, and that experience really shaped the story.

ELINA: There are some pretty intense moments in the series. How do you create emotional impact without sensationalizing what happened?

ANDY: For me, the key was giving those moments room to live. The stakes were already there. They didn’t need heavy music cues or fast cutting.

Like when Z gets caught in quicksand in the Escalante. You and Peter are helping her, and Peter starts being sucked down too. I’m about 20 yards back in the reeds. We’d made a pact: if you can help, help. If you can’t, film. That shot runs for close to a minute. The emotional weight is in what’s happening, so the edit needed to let us stay with it.

But showing the intensity also meant showing how we worked together. We weren’t just stumbling from one dangerous situation into another. We were constantly reading the landscape, assessing independently, sharing what we saw, and deciding how to move forward. Like a family of ants, we were small yet mighty.

ANDY: When you first signed on, what did you imagine we’d make, and how different is that from the story we’ve finally released?

ELINA: When I got your email at the end of 2022 and agreed to jump on board the Andy (and Peter) train, I knew that whatever we made together would be beautiful. Seeing what you and Peter had made on THRU: The Pacific Northwest blew my mind.

The level of production and coverage that only a filmmaker and thru-hiker could accomplish changed what I saw as possible on a long, self-powered journey. I imagined it would be a story of four people coming together to experience something beyond any thru-hike they’d done before.

The story we released was exactly that, but much more layered. I didn’t think the theme of losing my Mum would be so central to how I approached it. And I remember we agreed from the outset: no to the episodic format! Yet here we are.

ANDY: What was it like returning to the hike year after year while making this? How did your relationship to those memories change?

ELINA: We were four people who hadn’t hiked as a team before, in high-stress situations that were literally life or death, which meant interpersonal conflict. There were a lot of moments of tension. I have vivid memories, not all captured on camera, where I truly questioned if completing the Hayduke was worth it. Did I even want to be here? Was this level of risk worth getting to the end?

My relationship to those memories softened. I don’t think they became romanticised, but I returned to them with a bigger-picture perspective. We included some of these scenes, but maybe not as many as we could have. They felt far less central to the story we were trying to tell.

ELINA: We made a conscious decision to leave out a lot of specific location names. Why was that so important, and how did it affect the story?

ANDY: We kept the names we couldn’t avoid and left all others out. Part of that was wanting to help protect these places. But it also felt truer to anchor the story to our experience rather than pin every moment to a map.

ELINA: How does carrying a camera change the experience of a thru-hike for you?

ANDY: On the Appalachian Trail, taking pictures wasn’t a priority. We finished with disposable cameras. I took maybe 100 photos across the whole hike, yet I treasured every one.

By the Pacific Crest Trail, I’d been working in network adventure TV, yet it was films like 180° South and filmmakers like Jimmy Chin that really inspired me to bring a camera and capture dirtbag adventures cinematically.

On the Hayduke, that meant 8-9 pounds of equipment, plus the energy it takes to use it. Every bend and conversation caught my attention. I loved it, but trying to capture so much eventually wore me out.

When we thought the gimbal died in the Grand Canyon, part of me was relieved. I needed my remaining energy to just get through. But when it miraculously turned on the next morning, my spark returned. I’d already accepted I’d film less, so every shot thereafter felt like a bonus.

And that’s the camera-on-a-hike conundrum. Whether I’m carrying a disposable camera or nine pounds of it, I keep coming back to the same thing: the hike comes first. The hike is the muse, and the camera is a paintbrush.

ELINA: You’ve hiked the Hayduke. You’ve endured 800 miles of its toughest terrain and a real test of will. How on earth do you begin sinking your teeth into 20TB of footage?

ANDY: Well, it turns out walking the 800 miles was the quick part! Haha.

We brought home hundreds of hours of material from 4 cameras, your recorded journals, and audio of nearly every dinner and siesta we had out there.

It took six months to review 80% of it, everything up to the final 12-day stretch in the Grand Canyon. I built a nearly 300-page outline and color-coded clips in Adobe Premiere in an attempt to memorize the footage. I can’t weave a story unless I know what I’m weaving with.

Then I took a year away for other projects and fundraised for HAYDUKE’s post-production. When I got back to its edit, festival deadlines meant I started assembling before I’d reviewed the Grand Canyon footage. Reviewing and editing at the same time was intense!

Our first cut was feature-length. It had story and flow, but we both felt it left too much heart and personality on the cutting room floor: the things that make a long hike beautiful : )

So, with a clearer structure, two years of perspective, and another long walk across Death Valley, we took a deep breath and reopened it. You rewrote the script, and I spent 7 months revisiting hundreds of hours of selects and reworking it. In the end, the three year process helped us move past the film we knew how to make and discover something entirely new.

ANDY: Your writing helped give all that footage direction. How did you begin finding the moments that could hold this enormous adventure together?

ELINA: The beauty in both of us having hiked and filmed was that we both knew what we captured out there. We both knew what it was like to experience the Hayduke. The inner world of each person is something I didn’t experience.

But it was clear from the outset that some stretches held far more weight in terms of story, whether that was the level of risk, the people we encountered, or moments of awe. You did the due diligence of labelling a lot of these in the project file. The key was then knowing how to string them together into not only a cohesive A-to-B journey, but a story with several character arcs.

ANDY: You were used to making films on your own. What was hardest about letting someone else help tell a story you were also living?

ELINA: I think with most creatives, we don’t want people to see our rough drafts: the versions that are awful, that don’t make sense, that are almost unreadable. It was hard to let go of the fear of being seen as bad or incompetent. But in this process, it was necessary. It was necessary to bounce ideas, to go back and forth, to trust the process, and trust each other.

ANDY: It wasn’t until after the hike that we decided your writing would carry the series, and it goes much deeper into your personal life than anything you’d made before. What did it feel like to take that on?

ELINA: It was terrifying. I felt complete imposter syndrome. I felt a huge weight in doing justice to each person’s story, while also letting an audience into my own mind. Sometimes it’s a lot easier to hide behind the camera and let others’ voices carry the story. This time I understood that if I were to narrate a four-character series, I also needed to be someone who expressed their own vulnerabilities.

The kinds of stories that stay with me are the ones where the artist has been most vulnerable. I understood this in theory, but doing it in practice is a whole other thing. I constantly doubted how much was too much, or too little, and how much space my own thoughts could take up next to everyone else’s story. It helped having you encourage me throughout and have faith in my writing. That assurance, and a gentle push to dig deeper, let me open up more than I would have in isolation.

It was also the first time I asked someone to read over my work. My incredible sister, who is a writer, read through my final scripts. Her questions and feedback improved the final piece tenfold.

ANDY: What was it like returning to memories of your Mum through three years of writing, revision, and reflection?

ELINA: I probably cried a lot in the first drafts. With grief, the pain first hits like a tsunami. It pulls you under, and every other element of life feels irrelevant. As years pass, the pain subsides and comes in smaller, less frequent waves. Initially, digging back into that pain to bring it into my writing was draining. But the more I wrote through it, the more I could write from a place of excitement and joy in telling this story.

It truly clicked when I read Things Become Other Things by Craig Mod. He tells stories of walking through rural Japan to his friend who had passed away. The premise was sad, but the execution was filled with levity and whimsy and joy. It’s hard to imagine experiencing those highs again when you lose someone so close to you, but in time you learn that you will. And it’s what they would have wanted for you anyway.

ANDY: HAYDUKE was originally a feature-length film, but we both felt something was missing. What did doubling the runtime and making it a four-part series allow us to find?

ELINA: We realised the feature film was missing the spark. The magic! It missed the nuances of each person, little moments that felt big to us. Doubling the runtime gave us room not only to develop more of each character and their arc, but to let the project breathe. It gave us the space to let the audience feel moments as we did ourselves when we were out there.

ANDY: For three years, there was always another version to write, scene to review, or problem to solve. What does it feel like to finally set this project free?

ELINA: HAYDUKE has felt like a phantom limb. Something I could feel, something I knew existed, but to everyone else in my life, there was nothing to be seen. To talk about a project in the hypothetical for three years, and for it to finally be out in the world, is release. It’s freedom. It’s an exhale.

The journey of making it has been the most challenging and rewarding thing I’ve ever done. And regardless of what happens with it, however it’s received, I feel content knowing we put everything we possibly could into getting it out into the world.

HAYDUKE is streaming now on Camel’s Cabana.

#139. Russians Give Up on the Khumbu Icefall; Will Try Everest West Ridge Instead

The first steps on a lonely Everest were daunting for four Russian climbers, who tried and failed to cross the Khumbu Icefall. They adapted quickly, heading up to the Lho La instead and setting up camp at that high pass at the base of the West Ridge.

Andrei Vasiliev, Natalya Belyankina, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Valery Sipilov set off from Lobuche on their first round up the mountain last week. Their original plan was to attempt the Khumbu Icefall, which has no ladders or ropes at this time of year. They set off at 5 am on October 9, looking for a way through the maze of seracs and crevasses.

“At first glance, it appears to be pure, unadulterated chaos,” Sergey Kondrashkin later wrote. “Yet on closer inspection, one can discern distinct sections. We opted for the central section, which seemed somewhat more solid — though ‘solid is a relative term…At least, it was easier to envision a viable path here between the seracs, snowfields, and ice walls.”

The recent snowy spell that hit Nepal filled many of the crevasses but also had a downside: loads of hard trail-breaking through deep snow.

Kondrashkin reported they crossed the most difficult terrain with only a few ropes in some sections and mostly moved as a roped team of four. “Time and again, I broke through the surface, sinking in up to my waist or even my chest,” he wrote. “By the end of the day, we reached an altitude of 5,700m, with still 500 vertical meters to go to the top of the Icefall and the biggest crevasses on the upper part.” They planted their tent on a small, flat platform.

“Conditions did not improve on the following morning,” Natalya Belyankina reported. “We ran out of steam on the second day, having gained only 100m in elevation after six hours, so we decided to head back down.”

The Russian team in the Khumbu Icefall on Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

However, they had food for four days, so instead of returning to Lobuche, they retraced their steps across the Icefall in three hours (they had spent one day and a half going up) and pitched the tent right below the high pass known as Lho La.

That was their second potential route. The Lho La is the col between Khumbutse, a lesser peak that rises to the left, and the characteristic pyramidal peak known as Everest’s West Shoulder. Lying on the border between Nepal and Tibet, it gives access to the very long West Ridge to the summit. It is also the route that Jost Kobusch will attempt in two months’ time. The German is on his fourth attempt to solo Everest in winter.

The Russian team’s tent in front of the wall leading to the Lho La between Nepal and Tibet. Photo: Natalya Belyankina/Instagram

Progress up the Lho La was fast, unlike the Icefall. The team completed the mixed terrain of the 600m wall in a single day, then pitched their tent on the col. On the fourth day, they scouted the terrain above and went to the base of the West Ridge, before returning to Lobuche for now, Alpymon reported.

The Russian team on a lonely Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

The climbers loved the experience of being completely alone on Everest. “Groups of trekkers only make it as far as that famous rock — joking, laughing, and congratulating one another,” Belyankina recalled. “Just yesterday, near the Everest Base Camp rock, a young man was playing the saxophone. It sounded wonderful. But once we cross a couple of moraines, that’s it — we’re all alone on the mountain.”

#141. I’ve Been Lifting and Running for a Decade. Here’s the Workout Routine That Helps Me Excel at Both.

Thanks to a decade of personal experience with hybrid training, Outside Run contributor Adam Meyer knows all about the challenges of lifting and running. To get the best advice on scheduling lifts around key runs, he interviewed Katie Cyrana Hillery, a physical therapist and RRCA-certified running coach, and Mike Thomson, a certified running coach and personal trainer.

Every runner has heard by now that more time in the weight room can lead to better running performance. It sounds counterintuitive, but I’m living proof that anyone can benefit from it. I’m 6’-5”, 215 pounds, and I’ve been lifting and running side by side for the last ten years.

My current week includes four lifting days on an upper/lower split, a functional fitness session on Wednesdays, and a total of about 25 miles of running, plus the weekend active recovery days where I go hiking with my family, bike with my kids, or incorporate mobility work.

Research shows that strength training can improve running performance and help prevent injury. The challenging part, though, is knowing how much to do of each without one impacting the other. Where does leg day go when you have intervals on Tuesday and a long run on Saturday? What happens to your squats when your mileage peaks? Put a heavy lift in the wrong spot, and your next workout will likely pay for it, along with your recovery.

To sort it out, I spoke with Katie Cyrana Hillery, DPT, OCS, CSCS, clinical director at Evolve Physical Therapy and an RRCA-certified running coach, and Mike Thomson, a certified running coach and personal trainer at Life Time. Here’s how these experts recommend you design your week that allows room for both.

For years, my instinct was to spread out my intense training days throughout the week. These days, my Tuesday would include running intervals in the morning and a lower-body lift that afternoon, then nothing heavier than upper-body work until my long run on Saturday. It took me longer than I’d like to admit to stop feeling guilty about “wasting” a rest day by not touching a heavy squat. However, both coaches recommend the opposite, and say you should stack the hard days together so your easy days can actually be easy.

“What I recommend is you keep the hard days hard,” says Thomson. “So, on speed and tempo days you do your runs in the morning and lifts in the afternoon, ideally. If you must, do your lifts right after the run.”

The reason behind this is that lifting soon after a workout is better than lifting the next day when your legs feel heavy and compromise running performance. Put into practice, if your Saturday long run is the priority, that could mean intervals in the morning and a lower-body lift that evening on Tuesday, with nothing heavier than upper-body work from Thursday on.

If two strength training sessions a week is all you can manage, you have to make them count. How? Hillery suggests training one leg at a time.

“Prioritize single-leg strength, as running is a purely single-leg sport,” she says. “Exercises like split squats, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, and step-ups can support single-leg stability.”

On weeks where work or travel knocks me down to two sessions, I prioritize single-leg work over anything bilateral. It’s less satisfying than a heavy back squat, but it’s kept me out of the physio’s office more than any other change I’ve made.

Thomson recommends starting with the big compound lifts, including squats, lunges, deadlifts, pull-ups, and dips. Then, fill the back end of your strength session with injury-prevention movements like Poliquin step-ups, lying hamstring curls, and core exercises.

Every runner’s body and goals are different, but here’s an example of my two-day-a-week strength training split for reference only:

During a running base season (the training phase focused on building aerobic endurance), scale back on your strength training volume without cutting load. Do fewer reps and sets, or train less often each week, without decreasing the weight.

“Whereas in the base phase of training one should be trying to gain strength, during peak mileage and race prep actively, the focus should be maintaining strength,” Hillery says.

My lifts don’t get lighter in the five or six weeks leading up to a goal race, but I stop doing accessory exercises, and I go down to two lifting sessions per week instead of four. It’s a hard mental adjustment when you’re used to chasing PRs in the gym too, but it’s the difference between showing up to race day fresh versus burnt out.

I used to worry about this myself, especially early on when I’d read about “specificity” and figured all that time under a barbell was working against my running. A decade in, my times have only gotten better as my lifts have gone up, not the other way around.

If you’re still worried that lifting will make you bulky or slow, Thomson has heard it before. “The idea that strength training will slow you down is misinformation. I don’t know a single D1 college program that isn’t getting their athletes to lift and run.”

“Getting stronger can improve running efficiency, meaning the same running pace can feel easier and require less effort,” Hillery says. “It also allows your muscles to produce more force, which can translate to better performance on hills, accelerations, and in speedwork.”

After ten years of hybrid training, I no longer think of lifting and running as competing priorities. They’re both just training and fundamental to my fitness. The week I described up top that includes four lifting days, a functional fitness session, 25 miles of running, and active recovery on weekends, only works because I stopped treating strength as an add-on to my running and started treating it as part of a long-term plan.

Experts recommend stacking your hard training days, protecting your easy days, and adjusting volume before you reduce load when your running mileage peaks. Do these things, and lifting stops being something that competes with your running and starts being the thing that lets you keep doing it, injury-free, for years to come.

#143. This Fastpack in Washington Is an Ideal 24-Hour Adventure

Trail Runner Community Engagement Editor David Gleisner spent 24 hours fastpacking (and successfully not freezing through the night) in the Chiwaukum Mountains of Washington.

I watched the stars disappear until there was just one left, directly overhead, a pinprick of white in the pale blue sky.

When that last speck disappeared, I knew it was time to get up. I shook the frost off my ultralight quilt, deflated my sleeping pad, and grabbed my pack, walking over to our al fresco dining room up on a high clearing. As the rest of the group started to stir, the morning sunlight descended on the surrounding mountains, a welcome reprieve from the cloudy conditions of the day before.

The day before, 10 of us set out from the Icicle Creek Trailhead, deep in the Chiwaukum Mountains of Washington. Led by trail runner and climber Jenny Abegg, a local of nearby Leavenworth, our mission was to fastpack up to Lake Edna in the high alpine, camp for the night amidst the fall foliage, and run back down to complete a 20-something mile loop. Everything we needed would be carried in our packs, and we aimed to travel as light as possible.

We were here for a press trip to preview Patagonia’s upcoming Mountain Movement collection of lightweight, no frills gear for big days in the mountains. So I was expecting a chill, party pace jaunt up some beautiful trails.

My last experience in these mountains came in starkly different circumstances, four months into a northbound thru-hike of the Pacific Crest Trail in 2023. I remembered endless climbing and  descending to lush river valleys only to ascend right back up to alpine ridgelines on unrelenting switchbacks. Surely, though, it felt so hard because I had 2,3000 miles in my legs and 30 pounds on my back. This time, I expected it would be much easier.

We made good progress initially among the ferns and moss of the low country, jogging over rocks and roots and fording ice-cold creeks. The group, composed of trail running media, athletes, and representatives of Patagonia’s trail running apparel team, got along well, sharing stories of trail runs past.

Then, we started to climb. Our pace slowed to a steady power hike as some of the group pulled out poles and others used hands on knees for added momentum. Conversation quieted, too, as we focused on continual upward motion amidst bright red maple. In due time, the blissfully uncrowded trail opened up to views of cloud-covered peaks. We each added a layer or two among the patchy snow of the high country, continuing to traverse the scenic ridgelines until the summit of 7,316-foot Cape Horn came into view, signaling our destination.

After cresting one final pass, we entered the basin of Lake Edna around 3 p.m., meeting up with four other members of our group who took a shorter route. The only other person at the lake was a man with a rifle slung over his shoulder for bear hunting, we learned. Luckily, we were all wearing bright colors.

Without much to set up—we didn’t have tents, after all—Jenny eyed the ridgeline above the lake with the keen eye of a mountain athlete. “Does anyone want to tag that?” she asked the group. I’m not much of a climber, but I’m also not one to say no to an adventure. “I’ll join!” I replied.

Jenny, a Patagonia employee named Jess, and I hiked and scrambled our way to the summit of Cape Horn. From the summit, we could see the rest of our crew down by the lake, and the lone hunter’s tent over the next ridge. But with clouds shrouding the ridge, Jess and I left the traverse to the expert (Jenny) and headed back to camp.

Clad in matching puffies, we set up camp stoves to boil water for backpacking meals and hot tea, cozy comforts in the chill of the misty evening. When we were done swapping stories over dinner, a group of us decided to set up the “cuddle puddle.” We deployed our sleeping pads and quilts in a sardine-like arrangement, lining up next to each other to share body heat. The sun set, the night quieted, and, aided by Nyquil I brought along for a lingering cold, I drifted off to sleep.

The next morning, we learned that the cuddle puddle had proved useful, as those campers who opted for solo spots looked worse for wear after a restless, cold night. Don’t be afraid of a little body heat, people! Our lightweight Patagonia puffies kept our upper bodies toasty warm, but some had opted for minimal lower layers to save weight, and a 40-degree-rated quilt can only do so much. We fired up the stoves again for morning coffee and breakfast, slowly getting our bodies and brains working again.

Jenny offered us redemption on the ridgeline now that conditions were clear and she had the beta. This time around, a group of seven of us headed back up Cape Horn with our belongings on our backs. My Brooks Cascadia Elites got an experience they were not designed for as we scrambled across sharp granite ridges, tagging unnamed summits as the wind whipped around us. Eventually, when it was time to descend back to the trail, I learned I’m not as confident a descender as I previously thought. We stutter-stepped and slipped our way down the dirt and foliage until, mercifully, we made it back to singletrack.

The rest of the day was comparatively lovely, descending back down 5,000 feet in dappled sunshine to Icicle Creek. After fueling with the remainder of my Nerds gummy clusters, I made it back with the perfect amount of remaining food: none. All told, I notched 22.5 miles with just over 7,000 feet of climbing and descent in the 24-hour expedition.

While our trip leaders didn’t take it easy on us, we were game for the challenge: We logged the ninth-fastest Strava segment on the ascent, according to Jenny. The gear held up to the test, too. My pack stayed secure and comfortable even as I carried 10 to 15 pounds. My shorts and sun hoodie breathed and flowed with me as I moved, while the midlayers and puffies kept me insulated when I stopped. Everything I brought with me served a purpose at some point over the 24-hour trip, and by the time we got back to the trailhead, I had just a couple gummy worms left.

The organizers promised an “unforgettable route.” Between the foliage, conditions, and new friends, this trip delivered.

#145. “Everyone Around Him Was His Best Friend”: St. George’s Climbing Community Fondly Remembers Dan Smith

Daniel “Dan” Smith, a climber and arborist from St. George, Utah, is remembered by his friends for his warmth, openness and creativity. A lifelong resident of Southern Utah, Smith spent much of his time exploring the desert through his art and climbing.

Smith died by suicide on June 1, 2026. He had lived with the effects of a traumatic brain injury since he was 12, when a skateboarding accident left him with seizures and disrupted sleep. In 2025, he opened his own tree-trimming business, aptly named Tree Smith.

Carson Olmsted grew up with Smith and remembers less about any particular climb than the way his friend made the people around him feel. “Everyone around Dan was his best friend, even if he had just met you,” Olmsted said. “There was something about the way he interacted with people that made you feel immediately comfortable and accepted.” Olmsted said that Smith also loved photography and spending time with his wife, Lexi Jensen.

Friend and fellow climber Michael Eardley recalled one particularly cold winter climb in Pine Valley, when Smith gathered his friends around a fire in below-zero temperatures to talk about what they were grateful for. “He genuinely cared about people, and I think that was one of the things that made him so special,” Olmsted said.

After his death, friends and family gathered at Contact Climbing Gym in St. George to celebrate his life.

“He was an amazing climber, but climbing was only one part of who Dan was,” Olmsted said. “He loved being outside, pushing himself, experiencing new things, and sharing those experiences with the people around him.”

#146. 5 Tips to Get the Most Out of Your Fall Backpacking Trips (Without Freezing Your Buns Off)

The seasons are a-changing, but that doesn’t mean you have to stop a-hiking. In fact, I would argue that fall is the best time of the year for backpacking: fewer crowds, crisp weather, and the added spectacle of the color change combine to make October and November my all-time favorite months to hit the trail. (Hiking after peak colors have come and gone is also great, because fewer leaves means more views through the trees.)

However, the colder weather, shorter days, and (in some areas) added excitement of hunting season mean you need to take a little extra care in prepping for autumn outings. Planning a fall backpacking trip isn’t rocket science: this article will cover all the main extras you’ll want to consider.

Mid-September in the Canadian Rockies is already getting cold enough for early snowstorms.

Weather is, in general, both the most challenging and the most rewarding aspect of fall backpacking, so this will be the longest section of the article.

Fall is a time of transition. The summer heat is fading into the long, cold sleep of winter, and that can translate to erratic weather. I’m from Virginia, where it can be 90 degrees on some October afternoons, and then dip down to freezing a few nights later.

READ NEXT – Best Sections of the Appalachian Trail To Hike in Fall

Such temperature swings are often even more dramatic in the mountains, where changing elevation can add or subtract additional degrees quite rapidly.

This is likely common sense, but hikers should keep in mind that “fall” conditions come at different times (and different intensities) depending on the location. If you want to time your trip for peak color change, don’t base the dates on the color conditions in your hometown at 150 feet above sea level.

The best leaf-peeping conditons might occur weeks earlier up in the mountains, especially further north. Peak fall colors typically occur sometime in September in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and Maine, for instance, while the foliage change may not touch my hometown in Virginia until early November.

Similarly, don’t let mild conditions at home lull you into a false sense of security when packing for an overnighter in the mountains, where the weather may already have turned chillier. The broad rule of thumb is to subtract about 5 degrees Fahrenheit from the temperature for every 1000 feet of elevation gain.

Pay extra attention to this in fall: the difference between 80 degrees at the trailhead and 65 degrees at the ridgeline in summer is less challenging than the difference between 45 degrees at the trailhead and 30 degrees at the ridgeline in November. In cool shoulder season weather, you should always be mindful of the risks associated with temperature change. If it’s raining down low, the last thing you want is to get yourself soaked before climbing up into subfreezing conditions.

In big mountain ranges and further north, you should be prepared for freezing weather and early-season snowstorms as early as September.

Simply put: in fall, you need to be prepared for a wide range of conditions. You may still encounter some hot days depending on when and where you’re hiking, but your summer backpacking kit likely isn’t going to be enough for the cold nights.

Layering is crucial for backpackers, especially in the shoulder seasons. Having a few extra lightweight garments you can shrug on and off throughout the day will help you to stay comfortable across a range of conditions.

If you’re looking for gear inspiration, check out the packing lists of some Triple Crown thru-hikers. Most of them start in early spring, which has similar temperature considerations as fall, so this will give you a sense of how other hikers approach the issue.

As a certified Cold Person, these are the items I always bring on fall backpacking trips to ensure I stay comfortable on cold nights:

Sleeping bag: I require at least a 15-degree comfort rating (if the sizing works, opting for a women’s 15-degree bag usually ensures you’ll get one that’s comfort-rated to the advertised temperature). In shoulder season I prefer the draft control of a traditional mummy sleeping bag rather than a quilt. The REI Magma 15 was my go-to, but REI no longer makes the warmer women’s version. Nowadays I have the Feathered Friends Lark 10, which is excellent but expensive.

Inflatable sleeping pad:  R-value of at least 5 recommended. I use the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XTherm, the latest version of which has an R-value of 7.3. Nice and toasty. Another trick is to layer a foam pad underneath your inflatable to boost the ground insulation even more. That’s more for winter trips where you’re camping on snow or frozen ground, but can be an inexpensive way to warm up a summer sleep system.

Clothing layers: Midweight merino wool base layers and thick wool mountaineering socks for camp, plus a good beanie and knit gloves. Good puffy and rain jacket. I do not normally carry rain pants unless I anticipate a lot of rain or snow.

I also never hike without my ultralight Montbell Tachyon wind jacket and pants. Very optional, but they don’t weigh much and I find they really help take the edge off the cold.

Stove/cooking setup: Hot camp coffee or hot chocolate on a cold fall morning is, for me, one of the greatest joys of life and no amount of ultralight propaganda will ever part me from my MSR PocketRocket and titanium pot. Hot food and drinks encourage me to stay adequately nourished and hydrated. If I somehow end up getting really cold during a hike, they can also help warm me up quickly before hypothermia has a chance to set in.

From the summer solstice on, the days start getting shorter. By the end of September, the nights are longer than the days. The change in daylight hours from one day to the next will be more pronounced near the September and March equinoxes and at more northerly latitudes.

You’ll want to bring a decent headlamp and possibly a battery bank to keep it charged, depending on the length of your trip. If you still want to pull really big miles, be ready to do a bit of night hiking at one end of the day or the other. On the flip side, if enjoying daylight hours at camp is important to you, you’ll probably want to shorten your daily mileage accordingly.

Even in late fall, most of us can still put in a normal complement of miles without needing to hike by headlamp by simply maximizing the daylight hours: that means get up and start hiking early in the morning, and don’t dillydally too much at breaks. I’ve always been of the school that prefers to start the day early and arrive at camp early, and that strategy serves me particularly well in the autumn months.

If you’re out on a long hike that will span seasons, it can be interesting to watch this change in daylight as it develops, and it’s something you’ll have to keep in mind with your planning as you hike further and further into fall.

Southbound on the AT in October = a good time to wear blaze orange.

In many regions, fall means hunting season. Every locality has different rules for hunting season, so the best thing to do is check the regulations in the area where you’ll be hiking to find out whether this is a risk. To be safe, it’s always a good idea to have some blaze orange clothing in the fall: it doesn’t weigh any more than regular clothing, after all, and that extra visibility could save you if there are some hunters out and about while you’re hiking.

This is a simple one: there’s not much more to say about it from a hiking standpoint.

As southbound Triple Crown hikers can attest with dismay, many seasonal businesses that cater to hikers will close after the summer season ends — maybe even as early as Labor Day in some cases. Hiking in the off-season has many advantages, but it does mean you probably won’t get to partake in much trail magic, and some beloved hiker hostels, restaurants, and shuttle services will already be closed for winter.

This can even be the case in popular hiking destinations: I’m hoping to get out for some fall backpacking in Shenandoah National Park next month, for instance, and I already know I won’t be able to count on a hot meal or snacks from the Wayside restaurants and camp stores, as most will be closed for the year by then.

Moral of the story is, it’s always a good idea to confirm whether businesses will be open before factoring them into your autumn lodging, resupply, or shuttling plans. Off-season hikes generally demand a somewhat higher level of self-sufficiency than summer treks.

Even though fall hiking is amazing, the trails are in general a lot less crowded in autumn than they are in the summer months. The aforementioned cold and dark of fall are deterrents for many, and of course people in general just find it easier to take time off from work (and, for obvious reasons, school) in summertime.

For those who do have the flexibility, gear, and fortitude to backpack in the fall months, this solitude can be a major reward. Trails that are crowded with visitors in the summer might be nearly empty by early November, and you might find yourself with popular camping areas all to yourself at night.

I just mention it because not everyone likes or is comfortable with that degree of solitude. If nothing else, it’s good to be mentally prepared for it. If you’re hiking alone, you may want to bring a book or something to fill up the hours in camp.

All this being said, beautiful fall weekends, especially around peak color change, can still translate to big crowds. Just like with the temperature change, you really do need to be prepared for a range of conditions when it comes to trail crowdedness in the fall.

Despite the 1,600 words I just wrote about special considerations for fall backpacking, it really is not something to be scared of, and is even accessible for beginners. The very first backpacking trip I ever took as an adult, as well as my first-ever solo overnight trips, all took place in mid- to late fall.

The difficulty, of course, will vary depending on where you plan to hike. Backpacking in November in the Rocky Mountains or the High Sierra could be more akin to an extreme sport with a high likelihood of wintry conditions, whereas backpacking in November in the southern Appalachian Mountains is quite approachable with a little extra gear and planning.

In my opinion, backpacking is the ideal way to enjoy what I consider the best season of the year. As long as you’re prepared for quieter trails and colder weather, there is no reason you can’t continue happily logging miles well into the autumn months.

#147. Wildfires Force Closure of Carstenz Pyramid for the Season

All around the world, natural disasters are hampering climbing expeditions. The latest case is a series of uncontrolled wildfires in Papua that have doomed the fall climbing season on Carstenz Pyramid.

The region is facing severe, widespread forest fires that have blanketed the island in a persistent thick haze. The air quality and visibility have reached levels that make transportation, logistics, and climbing operations impossible, according to local outfitter Tropic Adventure Papua. Apparently, the effects of the El Niño phenomenon, known this year as the Super Niño due to its extraordinary intensity, are to blame. It has brought a prolonged drought and extremely dry air, diminishing hope for the rain needed to extinguish the fires.

By the time the situation became unbearable, the first groups of foreign climbers had reached Timika in Papua, but no one made it to the top during this season, which is now officially canceled.

Outfitters have already shared the news with their clients and are now placing their hopes in 2027.

“Our thoughts are with the local communities affected, and we’re hoping the fires are brought under control soon,” Garrett Madison posted on social media. Instead, they have set the dates for next year, with two trips in March and October.

Tragically, the situation in Papua is only a fraction of a major environmental catastrophe. Wildfires are sweeping through the Indonesian archipelago and affecting Malaysia and Singapore:

The harm caused to the fragile Indonesian ecosystem is incalculable. In recent days, a viral video of a young orangutan rescued from a treetop where it tried to escape with burned hands and feet has drawn attention to the disaster. In fact, a significant number of primates were evacuated by rescue services in Borneo. Some of them were returned to the forests as the fire receded last weekend, according to the BBC.

The intensity of the fires in Papua and the air quality can be tracked live here.

At 4,884m, Carstenz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya in the local language) is the highest point of Oceania and considered one of the Seven Summits. Located in Central Papua, and with a tropical climate, Carstenz can be climbed at any time of year. However, summit options increase in the less rainy months, from February through November.

Outfitters apply for permits twice a year. Political unrest has often kept climbers away in the past, and major mining operations limit ground access. Climbers are typically airlifted to Base Camp instead of trekking through the jungle.

#149. Think NRL and PRS Can’t Help You Shoot Your Classic Hunting Rifle Better? Think Again

Published Oct 16, 2026 9:15 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

At Outdoor Life we believe that hunting and competitive shooting go hand in hand. In my younger years, that meant honing my shooting fundamentals behind a service rifle at 200, 300, and 600 yards. Today, it’s NRL Hunter, PRS, and NRL-style rimfire matches.

I’ve seen, and written a lot about, how it’s helped improve my shooting in the field, but we do get feedback from self-described “normal hunters” who just want to hunt with their classic rifle, and don’t find all the gadgets, gizmos, and high-tech guns appealing, applicable, or useful.

But even if you have no interest in competing, there are still lessons to learn from those competing at the highest level in these disciplines — and techniques that can help you shoot the rifle you already have better than ever.

The most common deficiency is the tendency for hunters and shooters to blade their body. That means that your shoulders are angled, and not perpendicular to the line of the bore. Often, a shooter’s non-shooting shoulder will be rotated forward, and the stock rests on the shoulder to the rear. This is commonly referred to as being “bladed.” The problem can be fixed by getting your body square to the butt of the rifle, so that the recoil impulse runs straight back.

Even in light-recoiling, braked competition guns, high-level shooters notice a distinct difference in how much their sight picture moves — which makes spotting impacts more difficult and slows down follow-up shots. When your body is rotated out of square from the rifle, stability is more difficult to attain and the force of the recoil from, say, an old Winchester .30/06 will cause both the rifle and your body to shift out of position. If you’re shooting a classic-style hunting rifle, it’s usually unrealistic to spot your shot impacts, but properly positioning your body will help ensure that the rifle settles back onto target after recoil.

This change of position might feel awkward at first, especially if you’re used to shooting with the rifle coming across your chest. You might also need to move your scope rearward to get the proper eye relief. But from the bench, prone, sitting, or standing off shooting sticks, getting yourself square with the gun will increase your stability and your ability to run your rifle decisively and make quicker follow-up shots when you must. If you’ve come up with old-school offhand positional shooting techniques, you’ll still likely be more accurate with slow, single shots in a traditional bladed position because torso twisting and tucking the support elbow adds stability. However, if your offhand shooting is at ranges of 100 yards or less, or you commonly hunt driven game, a squared-off position will help you control your body and rifle better, and you can more easily run your bolt from the shoulder without breaking position.

As you’re trying this out, pay attention to how your rifle reacts under recoil — it can give you clues as to how you can improve your position. If your rifle tents to jump to the right (for a right-handed shooter), your body might still be too bladed. The rifle will follow the path of least resistance under recoil, and if your sight picture jumps to the left, you might be pressing too hard onto the comb with your cheek.

The first introduction I had to a modern shooting grip came in 2009 from my buddy Richard, who was a Marine Scout/Sniper. Until then, I’d always wrapped my thumb around the grips of my bolt action rifles, using a firm handshake’s worth of pressure to control the gun. Richard pointed out that, by resting the thumb atop the tang or alongside the grip, you can greatly reduce the torque or twisting force you’re putting into the gun.

This technique has become much more common in the years since, and modern precision rifles are exclusively designed with this style of grip in mind. Preferences vary, but you’ll see lots of vertical or near-vertical grips on modern gamer guns.

Even if you’ve got a traditional grip on your rifle, you can use this modern technique to improve your stability and control. Rest your thumb atop or alongside the top of the grip, but don’t apply much pressure with it. I find that using the middle and ring finger of my shooting hand to firmly hold the grip allows me to press a harder-recoiling gun straight back to my shoulder while allowing my trigger finger to be relaxed and apply gentle rearward pressure.

The best grip pressure for your rifle will depend. On a 25-pound PRS rig, a lot of shooters only want to use enough pressure to control the rifle and break the shot cleanly. On a light hunting rig, you’ll need to secure it more firmly. Shooting editor John Snow and I often refer to this as “driving the rifle.” Mastering this will take practice but, just like shooting position, once you establish a grip that controls your rifle without putting torque into it, your stability, trigger pull, and accuracy will improve.

Many hunters, especially those using a bolt action, will break position, bring the gun away from the shoulder, then cycle the bolt. This puts you at a disadvantage in a couple ways.

First, if you break your shooting position while chambering an additional round, it becomes more difficult to see what’s happening down range and get back on target quickly. In a PRS match, this will cause you to lose track of the target and, often, time out on a stage. In the woods, those precious seconds can mean the difference between a decisive follow-up shot and losing an animal. If everything goes as planned, you won’t need a follow-up shot. But sometimes you will, and setting yourself up for success will be a net benefit for the average hunter.

If you utilize what we’ve already discussed, and build a stable position, squared up behind and controlling the rifle, you can run the bolt while still maintaining your sight picture and position. A .270 or .30/06 might temporarily blow out your sight picture, but you’ll still be back on target much more quickly than if you break position to chamber another round. Again, it’s unrealistic to spot your impacts with many of these rifles, but you at least want the gun to settle back onto target after recoil. You’ll maintain better awareness of what’s happening downrange and be ready to break another shot if needed.

If there’s a single support tool that can elevate your performance with any given rifle, it’s the modern lightweight shooting bag. There are many different designs, but we often default to the Shmedium-sized Armageddon Gear Game Changer. This waxed shooting bag, when paired with a lightweight fill like Git Lite, is incredibly useful, and you don’t need to add anything to that beautiful old museum piece you’re toting around the woods. No screws, adapters, or ARCA rails necessary.

Most of us have used various sorts of bags for support on the range, but once you learn some of the basics of utilizing these waxed canvas bags, you’ll wonder how you ever lived without one. Tree limbs, fence posts, rocks, glassing tripods, and many other impromptu rests become rock-solid shooting platforms. There are just a few things to know and practice.

There are good reasons why lots of the design elements that have been honed in competition are finding their way to hunting rifles. But if you don’t like that, it doesn’t mean that you can’t benefit from the refined techniques that are helping top level shooters achieve incredible accuracy and consistency. It can be humbling and uncomfortable to change how we do things, but these techniques are proven to work. If you want to improve your shooting and increase the certainty that you have while hunting, you’d be well-advised to pay attention.

#152. Cloud Seeding Has Promised More Snow for Decades. Can This Tech Startup Deliver?

A fundamental caveat holds the ski industry together. The business generates more than $58 billion a year, employs roughly 75,000 people, and offers an outdoor escape for over 50 million skiers and riders in the U.S. annually—if there’s snow.

With climate change, winters are becoming warmer, shorter, and less predictable. The 2025-’26 season was a painfully clear example of that across the West. The historically low snowpack wasn’t just a bummer on the slopes, but also into summer as wildfire and drought followed. Increasingly, ski resorts are leaning on artificial snowmaking and new technologies to ensure their snowpack is skiable all winter.

One California tech company, Rainmaker, claims it can help. This venture-backed startup is making bold claims about its weather modification systems and big moves to partner with Utah’s ski resorts. It’s aiming to deliver subscription powder days to mountains across the state starting this season.

“This tech is very well suited to protecting our winters and extending the ski season,” Augustus Doricko, Rainmaker’s founder and CEO, told SKI. “Rainmaker can make more snow for these winter resorts to ensure that the industry continues to exist and is less volatile between these boom and bust years.”

Doricko, a self-described “26-year-old mulleted tech guy,” started Rainmaker in 2023. It already has over 100 employees and is operational in five U.S. states, working with state governments, the agricultural industry, and the ski industry. Snowbird Resort is the company’s first ski area partnership—and according to Doricko, he’s in conversations with numerous others across Utah and beyond. When we spoke, he even mentioned the possibility of cloud seeding at the 2034 Salt Lake City Winter Olympic Games.

That goal is still years away. In the meantime, Doricko wants to take Rainmaker’s technology mainstream. If it can deliver on its promises, it could be a game-changer for the ski industry.

However, some climatology experts are skeptical. Even with the best systems and latest tech, reliably inducing snowfall over a specific area is a type of magic no one’s mastered in 80 years of trying.

General Electric discovered glaciogenic cloud seeding in 1946, and the process hasn’t really changed. It requires two basic ingredients: Really cold clouds and an ice-nucleating agent (commonly, silver iodide). When released into super-cooled areas of existing clouds, the nucleator mimics ice’s crystal structure and kickstarts a chain reaction as water starts freezing to it. The effect snowballs within the cloud, and eventually those frozen particles start falling as precipitation (read: powder).

Many resorts, including Vail, Aspen, Winter Park, Telluride, Wolf Creek, Deer Valley, Park City, Palisades Tahoe, Snowbird Ski Resort, and others, have experimented with cloud seeding—to mixed results. Most of those resorts ended their cloud seeding operations after just a few seasons.

Rainmaker claims its advantage over previous cloud seeding operations is twofold. In the past, cloud seeding deployment methods were either ground-based or required airplanes to circle continually. Rainmaker, by contrast, has built proprietary drones, engineered specifically for the task. The “Elijah Drones,” as they’ve been dubbed, are cold-resistant, can fly for 60 minutes, weigh about 50 pounds, and are equipped with cameras and state-of-the-art weather monitoring systems. They are flown using laptops and designed to target the coldest parts of a cloud. When they’re positioned, silver iodide flares in custom-built steel tubes ignite, releasing the chemical particles as the drones hover in place.

The second advantage is even more essential to Rainmaker’s business model. It’s also what draws the most skepticism from experts. In the past, cloud seeding operations, whether ground-based or aerial, couldn’t prove their operations actually worked. Doricko compared it to flying a plane and throwing magic beans out the window. If it snows afterward, who’s to say your beans caused it? Well, Rainmaker claims it can.

“As of January, we became the first and only company in history to unambiguously prove and measure in real time how much of the snow was coming from our operations,” Doricko said, referencing experiments Rainmaker ran in Pendleton, Oregon, in January 2026. Using Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD), Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES), and polar-orbiting satellites, Rainmaker validated how much precipitation it induced “with measured effect.”

“[Cloud seeding] has been a lot of quackery for a long time, but the fact we can measure it—it’s the whole enchilada,” he said.

That Oregon research program was a major success. But the real proof of concept happened later in August. At the end of a four-month research program in Homer, Alaska, Rainmaker demonstrably created 19 million gallons of rain over the Kenai Peninsula. SKI was there with the company, visiting Rainmaker’s research program just days before it happened.

SKI traveled to Homer toward the end of Rainmaker’s research operation in late August, 2026. It was warm and cloudless. As Gus Buck, the research operation Program Manager, explained, the conditions were terrible for cloud seeding—as had been the case all summer.

“We’ve mostly been geared towards finding points of failure, so we can really have a high-functioning drone come this winter,” he said. Without substantial clouds to seed, most of the research team’s testing had been focused on troubleshooting, debugging, and dialing in the drone designs.

On our flight day, we were up before dawn. The Rainmaker team held a briefing in the living room, discussing the weather, what to expect, the locations they’d deploy from, and who was going where. Then everyone broke, loaded into the trucks, and took off in different directions.

Admittedly, the testing SKI observed was pretty mundane. Rainmaker operators flew the drones up, targeted a cloud, and then hovered in place, monitoring, watching, and taking notes. When the batteries ran low, or their connection got spotty, they landed, fixed the issue, and repeated the process. The drones weren’t even loaded with the silver iodide flares.

That changed, though. Days after SKI visited, weather moved in on Homer: clouds built up, cooled down, and conditions ripened for seeding. Rainmaker launched its drones, this time equipped with silver iodide flares, and fired them up. The resulting experiment made national headlines.

“We produced 19 million gallons in three hours with two, but really just one drone,” Doricko told SKI. “We were able to unambiguously detect our seeding signatures in two clouds.”

While 19 million gallons of rain might sound like a lot, context matters. That precipitation fell over 100 square miles, equating to roughly .01 inches of rain. Converted into snowfall, that’s just .1 inches—a marginal deposit no matter how you slice it.

“That [Homer] case really didn’t produce that much precipitation,” Bart Geerts, a climatologist and professor of atmospheric science at the University of Wyoming, told SKI. Geerts has been involved with cloud seeding operations and research since 2011. While he admits Rainmaker’s results are notable, he isn’t sure they’d work when scaled up.

Geerts pointed out that small clouds, like the two Rainmaker seeded in Homer, make seeding signatures easy to detect. They’re also just big enough to induce precipitation. However, in more substantial storm clouds, that becomes harder, even with advanced radar and satellite systems.

“For the big snowstorms, the slammers, we have absolutely no idea whether cloud seeding could enhance the snowfall,” he said. “[There’s] just too much going on inside those clouds to be able to tell if it’s making a difference.”

That’s a big reason why most ski resorts don’t cloud seed, he said. “It’s very difficult to quantify.”

Furthermore, he pointed out that supercooled clouds often form in regions like Homer, on Alaska’s Kenai Peninsula. But in places like Utah, Colorado, and Wyoming, they’re much rarer—providing fewer opportunities to seed clouds.

“The places where you want [cloud seeding] in the drier regions, interior mountains, it’s going to be a lot harder to do,” he said.

Geerts was skeptical of Rainmaker’s technology claims, but he wasn’t afraid to call the company a “game changer” in other regards.

“It’s a game changer in terms of the company’s business model … And it’s a game changer in terms of the size of the company. It’s much bigger than pre-existing cloud seeding companies,” he said. “But the impact, as I have said, remains uncertain.”

That may be true, but Doricko said ski resorts are already expressing interest in Rainmaker’s product. While the company has yet to implement its drone operations at Snowbird Resort, its first official resort partner, that’s coming—and very soon.

“Between Snowbird, the other mountains around Utah that you can imagine the names of, a couple now in Colorado, and one in California, I think that Rainmaker will have a handful of partnerships with different ski resorts where we’re doing drone-based snowpack enhancement ops before the winter’s out,” he said.

That’s ambitious. And his long-term goal is even bigger. Doricko wants to work with the state of Utah ahead of the 2034 Winter Olympic Games to buffer the snowpack and put Rainmaker’s name on a global stage. He referenced China’s cloud seeding operations ahead of the 2008 Summer Games, which helped prevent rain at the opening ceremony. If Rainmaker could do the opposite and help make Utah a winter wonderland for 2034, it would be huge for Doricko and his company.

“That would be a really, really cool thing to talk about,” he said.

Rainmaker has a lot of work ahead if it aims to partner with as many ski resorts as Doricko referenced in our interview. Whether it will have the weather impact its marketing promises remains to be seen. Skeptics like Geerts aren’t holding their breath. But for skiers and riders everywhere, Rainmaker’s promises offer a glimmer of hope in an uncertain future.

#153. Cyclist Beats Pony Express Horseback Record

Lachlan Morton has completed a 3,217km bicycle journey along the historic Pony Express route from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California.

His time, 6 days, 21 hours, 15 minutes, beat the fastest recorded horseback mail relay from 1861 by 19 hours and 45 minutes.

Pony Express Trail. Photos: Top, Lachlan Morton/Instagram. Bottom: Shutterstock

Morton crossed eight states, negotiating remote desert tracks, the Great Basin and the Sierra Nevada. He encountered freezing conditions, fierce headwinds, and sections of barely discernible trail where he had to push his bicycle.

Unlike the original Pony Express, which changed riders and horses, Morton cycled the entire distance himself. However, he used different bicycles and had a support vehicle carrying supplies.

Morton is an Australian professional cyclist whose career spans elite road racing, gravel competition, and ultra-endurance adventure cycling. Rather than focusing solely on traditional racing, he has become widely recognized for long-distance challenges.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.

#154. Do Hikers Need an Off-Season? A Burnt-Out Backpacker Makes the Case.

Hiking high in the mountains (Photo: Lauren Berger)

At the end of every racing season, my high school cross-country coach laid down the same strict decree: Two full weeks off. No runs, no light jogs, no cheating. I hated the rule. I spent those two weeks pawing at the gates, desperate to keep moving for fear that I’d lose my fitness.

But last month, as I blearily packed my bags for yet another day in the mountains, I found myself wishing more than anything that Coach Stasko would appear on my left shoulder and tell me to take a break. Then, I told myself to snap out of it. It’s just hiking, I reminded myself. Hikers don’t need an off-season.

For many endurance sports, a designated off-season is a crucial time to rest, heal nagging injuries, and give the nervous system a break from the endless cycle of prep and exertion. Most trail running coaches advise their athletes to take two to six weeks off of running at least once per year, especially after completing a demanding objective. Runners often follow that period of total rest with several months of unstructured outdoor time or cross-training. Cyclists and triathletes are known to take even longer—sometimes up to two full months of rest before they start their cross-training. But what about hikers? Does taking long walks through the woods count as an endurance sport?

In 2021, German researchers tested a group of walkers before and after they hiked 60 miles over a 24-hour period. What they found surprised them: the group’s post-hike health markers were similar to those of ultramarathon finishers. Admittedly, that’s a long way to hike in a single day. But those results indicate that periods of low-intensity, long-duration exercise can create muscular and metabolic stresses similar to high-intensity running events. Even if you’re not doing grueling, single-day forced marches, extended hikes leave a lasting impact. Do enough of them, and your recovery plan might need to resemble that of an ultramarathoner, too.

Physical exhaustion isn’t the only thing an off-season break can solve. Like fatigue, mental and emotional stress can be cumulative, and forcing yourself to take structured breaks from a sport gives your brain time to reset. Regular off-seasons are one of the keys to keeping hiking sustainable as a lifelong hobby. Prolonged rest is also one of the most consistently prescribed fixes for athlete burnout—the very thing I was experiencing when I realized that hike prep had begun to inspire more dread than joy.

So, I asked myself a question for the first time since the 12th grade: What would Coach Stasko do? The answer was obvious: He’d take a break. He’d go drive his mustang and see his friends and update his Facebook page and do all the other things a cool, aging, earringed cross-country coach did. He’d chill out, reconnect with other hobbies, and give his legs all the time they needed.

So, that’s what I did. I confess I didn’t stop hiking entirely, but I did put a moratorium on long hikes above treeline, and I cut the time I spend on my legs each week from four days to just one.

Those changes have made all the difference. Over the last month, I’ve started to feel my stoke come back. Now when I think about hiking, I feel more curious than tired. Which, as far as I’m concerned, is a sign that it’s working.

So, do hikers need time off? Physiologically, it depends on your training load. But mentally, it all depends on you: If you feel like you need a break, you probably do. Here are a few symptoms that could mean it’s time for a proper off-season. If any of these apply to you, it might be time to step back and focus on other things for a while.
