#165. ‘Overboard!’ We Went Hunting in a Hurricane, and Barely Survived a Night at Sea

Published Oct 15, 2026 3:55 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

This story, “Hurricane Hunt,” appeared in the March 1954 issue of Outdoor Life.

As a newsman here in south Georgia, I’m sure I get to see many more hurricane warnings than the average citizen. I’m equally sure sighting one of these warnings on a teletype machine means more to me than to the average newsman. Each time I see one my mind races southward across the wire-grass flats and pine slopes of Georgia, across the cypress swamps and cabbage-palm hammocks of north Florida to a day when I punched a cash register instead of a typewriter.

I needn’t mention the year. If you’re an adult and read newspapers or listen to the radio, you’ll remember the incident before you read much farther. It was autumn, and I had just opened a sporting-goods store in east-central Florida. Considering my brief tenure, I had made a great many new friends in the St. Johns valley, if one can think of so slight a depression as a valley. One of these new friends was Hutch Newsom, a huge, lithe, tough, pleasant fellow of about 40 who knew the coast like the porch of his home. And I was to meet him this day, a September 17, the eve of my birthday. Many years have passed since birthdays meant much to me, as birthdays, but that date has leaped out at me every year since.

In the grayness that should have been sunrise that morning, dark clouds sagged baggily over the very treetops, bulging as if ready to split under their liquid weight.

Normally I wouldn’t have seen this dreary vista. I’d have been asleep. But this morning an air of foreboding awakened me, and my little fishing barometer was already descending past the 29 mark. Aircraft known as hurricane hunters had for three days kept constant watch over what had become a monstrous cyclone, centered near the Bahamas somewhere east of my home in West Palm Beach. It was moving northwest, toward Jacksonville.

The storm worried me for two reasons: Hutch had offered to take me on a marsh-hen hunt this day, along with Ed Howe, a fat little Palm Beach insurance salesman. Second, a sizable crack somewhere above the main show window of my store was expected to admit a lot of water if it rained while the wind was easterly.

By noon the sky seemed lighter, but a fresh wind kept patches of dust swirling in the street. Sharp gusts under the rear door of the store scattered papers on my desk. I tested the ventilator windows for security, and spent a futile hour looking for the crack over the show window.

Hutch called at noon. “Everything ready?” he asked.

“Sure,” I said, noticing through the window that people had begun to gather in little groups up the street, out of the wind, or to walk hurriedly about their business. “What about the weather?”

“Well,” Hutch said, “looks sort of raw. But this wind will roll the water in like nobody’s business, and you’ve got to have high tides to get marsh hens. Makes ’em flush easy.”

During the time I’d been in Florida I’d never hunted marsh hens. I was anxious to try it. Still, I knew Hutch was venturesome. He was the kind of smiling, stubborn-chinned fellow who didn’t look as if he were afraid of anything — and wasn’t. Then I said, “That little bet I made about my average on these slow birds is hereby withdrawn, in this wind, but I’m willing to tackle ’em, if you say.”

“Storm warnings are out up to Cape Hatteras,” Hutch answered, “but looks like we’re going to miss most of it here.” His deep bass voice was reassuring, and I said I’d expect him at 3 o’clock. It would take us nearly an hour to get across the causeway to Palm Beach and up the strand to the fish camp where we’d get a boat. Hutch had said we’d pole along and scare birds from the grass tops.

I didn’t go home for lunch. I told my wife I was rushed at the store, because I didn’t want her to talk me out of going. Actually, none of the clerks were busy. The only places doing any business were the coffee shops, and building-supply houses where customers were buying nails and sheeting to batten down against the blow. I ate a tasteless sandwich and kept going out to look at the clouds which still seemed lazy but which somehow passed quickly.

I called Ed, and he said he’d be ready, if unwilling. All the time I kept remembering pictures of the Miami hurricane of the 1920’s, of the huge ship blown ashore in Biscayne Bay park and stone houses reduced to the rubble you can still find in the lush weedery of Miami’s suburbs.

Ed called back. Wasn’t the hunt called off?

I told him no, that we still planned to leave at 3 o’clock. When he demurred, I suggested he tell his missus he was going out to see a prospect, and promised to buy a $2 loss policy on one of my guns. Ed chuckled and said he was game, but his voice, already a little thin, seemed a little thinner. In addition to the storm, he was concerned about his wife who was overdue with their first offspring. Ed was the youngest of us, with a pink, round, Peter Rabbit face, and was surely no outdoorsman. But he’d said such a hunt would give him something fresh to talk about with prospective clients.

Just before 3 o’clock I called my wife again and told her I was going over to Palm Beach and wouldn’t be back until after dark. That was indeed true, but I should have told her I was going hunting.

And why not? The storm wasn’t coming anywhere near, and I’d been out hunting at all hours for years. Yet I had a little feeling of guilt. I dismissed it when Hutch pulled his Model A Ford up to the curb.

I threw in my waders, gun, two boxes of No. 6 shot, and climbed in. I almost asked Hutch to wait while I went back into the store to get a couple of life preservers; but then I decided I was getting all worked up over nothing.

At Palm Beach, Ed waddled out to the car with a raincoat, sou’wester hat, boots, moccasins, a huge hunting knife, a field coat, and about the worst stovepipe of a shotgun I’d ever seen. Hutch noticed me gawking at the gun, but he winked approvingly. “Ed’s got the right thing for a salt marsh,” Hutch said. “Spray and mist just eat up a good gun in no time flat. Took a fellow once who insisted on carrying a pretty automatic. Three weeks later we went on a deer hunt and he couldn’t pull back the bolt. So we went back home an’ I took it apart an’ shook out enough salt crystals to churn up a jug of ice cream that same afternoon.”

Hutch wasn’t kidding about the salt. I thought of my nearly perfect Parker and was glad I had decided not to wipe off the heavy grease which had preserved it all summer.

As we drove up the strand north of the famous Florida resort, Ed worriedly kept looking up and down the sound. His chubby forehead was creased, and a sort of hunted look darkened his eyes.

“What’s the matter, Ed?” I kidded, hoping to cheer him. “Got some poor insurance risks for the storm?”

“No,” he said almost in a whisper. “It’s just Lucy.”

Lucy is Ed’s wife. After a moment I said, “The hunt isn’t that important. If you’re worried about her and the baby, for heaven’s sake let’s go back. You don’t have to be a nitwit just because Hutch and I are.”

Ed slowly shook his head. “Maybe it is important,” he said. “Nobody ever knows just what is. If talking about hunting marsh hens helps me sell insurance, it may be more important for me to be here than back at Palm Beach. I couldn’t stop the hurricane, even for Lucy.” His jaws were set as solidly as a tent rope in the rain.

I saw Hutch glance down at Ed, over the match he was chewing, and in Hutch’s eyes was a new, surprised respect for the little man wedged between us.

The water in the sound looked different. Waves were larger than I had ever seen them and they seemed to carry farther. The crests reached from shore to shore in a steady, driving rhythm. They looked slow, but when they hit the steep inshore beach they pounded heavily, lashing high into the air, whipping over the lower part of the road. But Hutch drove on, humming a juke-box tune.

A mile short of the fish camp, the road hit a low spot where seas had once washed out the fill. It had never been properly rebuilt. Sea water was flowing across it. Hutch stopped the car, put on his waders, and carefully tested the depth. He seemed satisfied.

I wouldn’t have tried it, but Hutch chugged right on through. The bottom felt shaky, and we stopped on the far side to see if a wheel on the chronically ailing vehicle might be loose. As we got out of the car there was a peculiar gurgling noise, and we saw the roadbed at the spot we had crossed dissolve in a sandy froth.

“Nothing to worry about,” Hutch shrugged. “I think we can get through after the hunt, when the wind dies.”

There was no other road. I looked at Ed, found him looking at me, hard.

At the fish camp all the boats were pulled out and staked down with their bottoms up. Kinley, the man who ran the camp, was boarding up windows and was surprised to see us.

“Bang-bang!” Hutch said, pointing his forefinger and clicking his big thumb. Hutch had known Kinley for years. “We want some meat.”

“You mean you’re going out in this?” Kinley asked. But he was already starting down to the landing where he took the lines off a 14-foot plywood skiff. I figured that was a pretty good endorsement of Hutch as a boatman.

When we put the skiff in the water, here on the lee side of the strand, it lay as if in some farmyard pool. The water was unusually clear, and very low. Darting minnows scooted away. But I saw Ed was looking across the sound where even in the grayness we could see a mass of angry whitecaps.

“Hens all gone across by now,” Kinley stated. “Nothin’ doing on this side with low water. You got a good kicker, ain’t you?”

Hutch took the little five-horsepower outboard from where he kept it clamped to the scarred door of the car. Kinley grunted. “Good lookin’ little kicker,” he said, but he seemed to emphasize the adjective little, as he looked from the motor to the whitecaps.

Straight across from the camp, a peninsula jutted out so that it was only about half a mile distant, but on each side of the shore the mud beaches swept away westward from the peninsula’s weathered, sandy point. “Hadn’t we better just go straight across to the peninsula, and work the shores from there?” I asked. “Then we could get ashore if the motor failed.”

Hutch laughed. “Could. But wouldn’t find no hens until we got to where the wind’s piled the water up in the marshes, way over yonder.” Watching Ed, he added, “We’ll try it your way, though.” Ed’s face seemed a trifle blue, and the wind wasn’t that cold.

Our trip across to the point wasn’t bad. We pulled up into a creeklet and tied the boat to a mangrove bush. Spreading out across the finger of land, we began to wade through the scant marsh, hoping to kick up enough birds to persuade Hutch not to take the boat farther downwind. High tide ordinarily would have covered all but the grass tips here, but the wind had blown the tide up along the west shore.

Suddenly something flushed in front of me — a gray-brown bird whose speed increased rapidly. Hutch downed the bird as it angled toward him, retrieved the thing, and motioned for us to come look.

“The book says this one’s a clapper rail,” he explained. “There are at least three kinds of marsh hens: sora, the little bird they shoot in Georgia and Ca’lina; the Virginia that they shoot farther up the coast, and this one, the biggest of the lot.” The bird was as large as a grown crow. Its flesh felt soft.

We started on, and suddenly a sharp gust of wind blew my cap off. I reached for it, and before I could get it on my head, it began to rain, tiny, stinging drops almost as fine as mist, blowing nearly parallel with the ground.

It became impossible to keep one’s eyes open, traveling in the direction we had taken, and we reversed our course. On the way back toward the boat I bagged two birds and Ed missed an easy one. The rain grew heavy, drops becoming as large as buckshot.

Then, magically, the sun came out. Bright, hot on our necks where rain still trickled down. The rain stopped entirely, and the wind slackened.

We got back to the boat and were unloading our guns and thinking we had been fortunate to kill three birds under the adverse conditions, when the skies began closing in again with a blackness that suddenly turned the whitecapped water to ink and old lace.

Ed said abruptly: “I don’t like it.” He squinted as he looked back the half mile toward Kinley’s camp, and when I followed his gaze I saw, creeping out from the shore, a massive series of ripples on the water that began to break upon themselves and throw spray into the air, hiding what looked like a figure waving wildly on the beach by the camp.

Hutch cast off. The boat drifted rapidly southwestward while he prepared to start the motor.

Ed called to him and pointed. When Hutch looked, the calm left his face. All at once it seemed leaner, and his morning whiskers stood out clearly. He pulled the starter rope and the motor roared dependably.

“She’s gonna be rough when she first hits,” he said, shouting now because the wind was a new force that flattened Ed’s sou’wester against his forehead and, once, made a toot like a horn in my gun barrels. Hutch headed straight into the wind and opened the motor wide. It had a high-pitched, soothing whine.

The heavy sea had not yet reached us, and the little motor drove the boat steadily forward toward the landing. Nobody said “Guess the squall changed course.” It was unnecessary. We all knew that, somehow, this was the first blow of the hurricane, the biggest in years, a capricious hurricane that had deserted its path to wreak unbelievable havoc on the Palm Beach area.

Our bow went up on the first wave with a lurch that threw Ed halfway out of his seat. He got busy and bailed. Several smaller waves passed, and we could see one ahead bigger than the first. Right then we felt a terrific jolt, probably a log floated off by the wind, and the quick scream of an outboard motor that has sheared a pin. Before Hutch chopped the throttle the boat was broaching into the wind.

Ed grabbed an oar, but it was as if he were paddling with a toothpick. The boat was already broadside, and I heard myself yell: “Get another pin!”

Hutch didn’t even look up from his flailing oar. “No wrench, no pins,” he shouted. All of a sudden he dropped the oar and grabbed the gunwale. He was cartwheeling out as he shouted hoarsely, “Overboard!”

I didn’t have to turn to know he was looking into the big wave. I grabbed the anchor rope and rolled out headfirst.

The wave hit just as I shook water from my eyes. I saw Ed, clawing at the buckles of his raincoat, pitched out of the boat as it went up on its beam. The top of the wave slid under the boat, carrying Ed with it.

When the wave had passed I saw Ed swimming awkwardly, the chin strap of his sou’wester cutting into his throat, and I knew he was still trying to get rid of his coat. Hutch saw him too and yelled, but his words were lost in the wind.

The boat lurched and I stretched out my body toward Ed. I felt my foot bump him, and then he caught it and pulled himself within reach of the boat. I took a turn of the anchor line around my right hand and passed the loose end to him. It was slick and hard as a greased cable.

The boat was right side up again now, two thirds full of water. Hutch was working his way along the gunwale toward us when Ed began trying to climb into the boat. Hutch caught at him, pulling him back, and Ed was fighting him. “No good!” Hutch was shouting. “And get your clothes off — it’s going to get worse!”

It did, almost before Ed got rid of his coat. The rain came again, blinding, choking, cold. Half of it seemed to be wind-whipped sea water, but I think that was because the boat’s pitching kept me under the salt water half the time. Hutch got the motor unfastened and let it go before the stern sank.

The rain came again, blinding, choking, cold. Half of it seemed to be wind-whipped sea water, but I think that was because the boat’s pitching kept me under the salt water half the time.

The boat didn’t sink though it got full of water and once turned completely over, but it pitched so it was impossible to hold on. We finally managed to get close together on the same side in the manner of an outrigger, constantly working to keep the boat upright, clutching each other and the rope. Once, with my head under water, I thought whimsically of my treasured Parker shotgun and Ed’s old relic, and admitted mirthlessly that now one was no better than the other.

The rain increased, became a vertical river blotting out vision and sound until it seemed impossible to tell where the rain ended and the sea began.

Time passed. I couldn’t guess how much. Finally I didn’t even care, didn’t care about anything except holding on so I could get my head above water part of the time. I sensed Ed and Hutch were still with me but I couldn’t be sure, and I wondered about my wife and Lucy’s baby.

I discovered I was seasick and must have been for some time. Horribly sick. Even through violent air maneuvers and a good many years at sea I had never known anything like this. Gasping for breath, I inhaled sea water and became sicker, if possible. But I held on, because I couldn’t turn loose. I thought once, in a fleeting logical moment, that if I survived this my hands would show rope burns for weeks. Sometimes the rope would slacken, as if Ed had been torn loose; then it would tighten viciously with his weight, and seasick as I was I couldn’t help thinking how bad it must be to be having a baby in a hurricane.

Once, or maybe it was twice, a bright sun shot through that awful rain. I was aware of its brilliance; I couldn’t actually see it. Up, down, skidding sideways half underwater. Then over again, and over, and over again.

My legs? Something was beating on them and I wondered, with a moment of groggy horror, if they were numb and a shark or barracuda was at work.

Something was beating on my legs and I wondered, with a moment of groggy horror, if they were numb and a shark or barracuda was at work.

Then there was pain. I kicked, mostly to see if they were still there, and felt something solid. I kicked again, and this time it tore the calf of my right leg. I extended a foot, and felt it dragging over something brittle and rough. It dragged for several seconds before reason came to me — oyster shells.

We were dragging over oyster shells, and the way we’d been drifting those could only be on the mainland shore, a wild, uninhabited salt desert that ran for miles along the sandy muck.

Then there were no more oysters. We were swept on again. My spirit died. And then — more oysters, higher this time, cruel, pleasant things cutting at my hips, banging my thighs. But at the speed we were drifting they would cut me to pieces! I made myself turn loose the anchor rope.

That was no better. Beaten about alone in that water, the shells would have killed me. But the boat overtook me, pounded at me as if asking me not to leave it. I mustered enough sense to crawl up on the gunwale. My weight pulled that side of the boat under water, but I lay half-drowned and thankful for the meager protection. I wriggled toward the stern and pulled a limp Ed partly into the boat too, even before I realized the boat was hung on the oyster bank. Ed had knotted the rope about his wrist. I found Hutch’s legs under me, and then his face. The rain seemed a shade lighter, but it didn’t matter, and I remember wondering if it was only Hutch’s body I was holding.

Read Next: Frozen Terror, One of the Greatest Survival Stories of All Time

We pounded on the shells. I knew, presently, that the bottom of the boat was nearly gone, and tried to protect my knees by lying over a thwart. The beating brought Hutch to life, too, for I suddenly found him helping me, trying to protect Ed. Then we were loose and drifting again, drifting into mangrove trees, pounding against their springy limbs.

The boat wedged fast. Hutch and I dragged Ed into the swamp until we bumped into a threshing palm tree. The three of us huddled in the torrential darkness with our backs to the palm, not even thinking of our cuts.

Then the body chemicals that had kept us fighting to live played out. We fell into nightmarish, exhausted dozing. We could feel trees crashing down about us, the sharp report of their cracking trunks piercing even the wind.

When I was fully conscious again I went through the torture of standing erect. Rain still fell, but now it was only a drizzle. The wind no longer shrieked. It was a fresh breeze under a gray dawn sky.

The palm was still there, cracked in its roots, leaning at a crazy angle, its top awry. Everywhere were splintered and fallen trees. The brush was flattened and rivulets of water ran back toward the sound, which was now miraculously some 100 yards away down a sloping bank.

We fell into nightmarish, exhausted dozing. We could feel trees crashing down about us, the sharp report of their cracking trunks piercing even the wind.

Hutch sat with his back against the palm, eyes puffed and closed. I touched his shoulder. He opened swollen eyelids, and after a moment a faint smile tried to crack his chalky face. He nudged Ed, and Ed woke up painfully. He looked at Hutch and at me but no one spoke. Then Hutch said, “Hell, we’ll be late for breakfast.”

Ed tried to answer but failed. Then he tried to grin but that failed too.

My knees would barely support me. They were flimsy, yet so stiff they felt as if they belonged to someone else. My right pants leg was gone and among the smaller cuts an ugly gash puckered at me from the calf. Hutch seemed unhurt beyond a twisted knee, but Ed, stripped naked, was a mass of small cuts and bright greening bruises that made an awful background for ridges of clotted blood. He said suddenly: “I’ve got to get to Lucy.”

“We’re on the west shore,” Hutch answered indirectly. “Better start headin’ west; there’s a railroad runs a mile or so in.”

We staggered behind Hutch for an hour until we found a set of rusty rails and Hutch said, “We’ll go south. That’s toward home, anyway.”

Two agonized hours later we came to Kenny, a little station 10 miles north of West Palm Beach. The agent put us into his car, and when I woke up I was home, and my house was unharmed.

The phone lines were down so my wife drove Ed home. She was back before I got to sleep, reporting Ed — rapidly recovering — was all mouth and a new papa. Most of the houses away from the water were safe. The hurricane had headed for the interior and Palm Beach was already clearing its debris.

It was more than two weeks before I heard from Hutch Newsom again. He came into the store and bought a package of shear pins and a grappling hook, and we discussed my water-ruined show window. “One thing I was right about, anyway,” Hutch said sheepishly.

“What’s that?” I asked, suspiciously. My leg still hurt.

Read Next: How I Almost Drowned During a Coast Guard Rescue in a Freak Storm

“I said we’d get that car back across the wash when the wind died. Well, I got it back — today. I’ve got it layin’ all over the back yard. Want to go marsh-hen huntin’ tomorrow, when I get it put back together?”

“No thanks,” I said. “I’d rather stay home and have a baby.”

#166. Jordanian Man Trekking 23,000Km From South Africa to Siberia

Saddam Al Alaya is almost a year into his attempt to walk 23,000km from Cape Town, South Africa, to Magadan, in Russia’s Far East. The 35-year-old Jordanian left Cape Town on January 1, 2026, on a trek that he estimates will take three years. He covered the 5,500km to Rwanda in nine months, so he is on schedule.

This year, Al Alaya has already passed through South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Tanzania, Burundi, and now Rwanda. He expects to transit 18 countries in all, including his home country of Jordan, which he will cross from south to north.

Al Alaya grew up in Wadi Musa, beside Petra, and began guiding tourists around the famous archaeological site and the nearby canyons when he was about 16. He continued to guide while working for a business degree. He conceived the idea for this long walk in 2021, and spent almost five years organizing it.

Al Alaya meets a supporter. Photo: Facebook

Like so many adventurers, he wants to give his project a social angle, but Al Alaya seems particularly good at this. He founded an organization called Hike With Me, and many of his social media images show him glad-handing officials, walking with local people, or visiting regional schools. He often carries a white flag, symbolizing peace.

Al Alaya has official sponsorship from several Jordanian ministries, national organizations, and Jordanian embassies in various countries along the way. These have helped him with visas, security, and logistical support, according to the Jordanian News Agency.

Meeting some local people. Photo: Saddam Al Alaya

#169. Animal Attack Roundup

We usually hear about animal attacks that happen to hikers, tourists, and other visitors to an area. But it shouldn’t be surprising that most victims are the villagers who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here is a brief summary of the incidents worldwide in the last few days.

Hippo sinks family canoe, killing three — DR Congo

A family canoe on Lake Tumba. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

A mother and two of her children died when a hippopotamus reportedly rammed their wooden canoe during a nighttime crossing of Lake Tumba. Four family members were aboard; only one survived.

Mary Thandi, 35, and her 15-year-old daughter Esther suffered serious abdominal injuries when a hippopotamus attacked them near the Thiba River in the early evening of October 10.

They were returning home with two other people, who escaped. Both victims were hospitalized. Their current condition is unknown.

George Mbae Kalubira, 60, was fatally injured after encountering a wild elephant while searching for pasture for his goats around 5 am.

A snake catcher (not the one in this story) with a cobra. Photo: Shutterstock

A snake catcher died after being bitten in southern India. Initial reports in local press did not mention the snake species or how the bite occurred.

Police said the boars initially attacked the people at the front of the group, then charged the others. The three surviving victims suffered minor injuries.

Ishu Kumar, five, was reportedly bitten on a finger near a hand pump at a local childcare center. His family alleges that staff failed to arrange immediate medical treatment and sent him home. Neighbors later advised taking him for a ritual treatment, but he died.

Angry villagers then blocked a highway with the child’s body, demanding an investigation.

Charlette Gonsalves, 51, was bitten by a venomous snake in her kitchen early one morning before sunrise. Her family initially did not recognize the injury as a snakebite.

She was transferred between three hospitals as her condition deteriorated, but died the following morning.

A 44-year-old man was cutting grass near a pond in Đồng Tháp Province when a green snake bit his hand.

According to Vietnamese reporting, he became dizzy within three minutes and began vomiting blood approximately 20 minutes after the bite. He developed serious blood-clotting abnormalities and swelling extending toward his elbow.

Doctors administered antivenom and plasma. He survived.

The victim began vomiting, lost consciousness, and developed severe cardiovascular and neurological complications. He died approximately 83 hours after the bite.

#172. Kae Ravichandran Is So Much More Than Just a Boston Marathon Champ

Journalist Emma Zimmerman met Kae Ravichandran—the first nonbinary champion of the Boston Marathon—while reporting at the All the Above Trail Fest in Western, MA. Ravichandran sheds light on the complicated reality of being a transgender runner for whom the sport is an outlet of joy, freedom, and self-expression, and also judgement, confinement, and grief.

When Kae Ravichandran won the 2023 Boston Marathon, no one told her she was a champion. No tape was held up for her, and no reporters greeted her at the finish line. She strode across the yellow paint on Boylston Street and slowed to a walk, as any finisher might. Ravichandran had just claimed victory in the Boston Marathon’s inaugural nonbinary division, but she would receive no prize money. She would have no podium ceremony. Few people would even know her name.

“I don’t think I was particularly infuriated,” she told me over a video call in September 2026. For the most part, the anticlimactic experience just felt “really weird.”

In the years that preceded that race, Ravichandran had faced a conundrum all too familiar to trans athletes: She could continue competing in the male division, the gender she was assigned at birth, hide her true self, face the mental repercussions, but see her athletic achievements taken seriously by the public. Or she could begin hormone therapy, live in alignment with her identity, and be considered—at best—a representative of a movement.

By 2023, she had made her decision. She started hormone therapy and began racing in the nonbinary division (at the time, she used she/they pronouns, though she’d eventually shift to she/her as she grew more comfortable in her identity as a woman). She then joined a group of LGBTQ+ athletes to successfully advocate for a nonbinary division at the Boston Marathon.

When she crossed the finish line, she was a winner with nothing to show for it, save for a plastic vase engraved with the words “Boston Marathon 2023,” mailed to her home in Vermont two months later.

When Ravichandran and I spoke, three-and-a-half years after her historic win, she was a 28-year-old medical resident in pediatrics at the University of Vermont. It was 7:30 p.m. and she had just finished a shift in the pediatric ICU. She was surprisingly alert, if relaxed in demeanor. She wore a loose ponytail, wisps of dark hair escaping into curlicues at her ears. Her words were earnest, though slow and deliberate; she seemed careful to choose the right ones.

When I asked about her choice in medical speciality, any caution disappeared. “I know that I myself would have really benefited from a gender-affirming pediatrician growing up,” she said. “I’m just hoping to be that person for somebody else.”

Kae Ravichandran grew up in Westford, Massachusetts. The child of immigrants, her mother came from Kuwait and her father from India. Her parents were raised in “fairly conservative” families, backgrounds that informed their reactions to her gender expression. “They didn’t totally understand it,” she reflected.

As a child, Ravichandran excelled in school, particularly in the sciences. She cherished her collection of dolls “before [her] parents found them,” she added. Her favorite was a figurine of Daphne from Scooby Doo, clad in a purple dress with long hair flipped at the edges. Upon seeing the doll, “I was like, oh, I want to be this when I grow up. At that point, I did not realize it was going to be really hard.”

Her free time was spent among clusters of friends, predominantly girls. In preschool and early elementary, they played with dolls before graduating to shopping, baking, running, and outdoor adventures. Ravichandran’s parents didn’t approve of her playmates, or of the feminine manner in which she expressed herself. “I was often told, ‘those girls are such bad influences on you’,” she said.

If Ravichandran lacked acceptance at home, she found it in her high school cross country team. The kids were quirky and from diverse backgrounds. They laughed often, despite the physical demands of the sport. No one blinked when Ravichandran arrived at practice wearing form-fitting clothing and shorts that revealed her thighs.

She went on to compete on the cross country and track teams at Case Western University in Ohio. Her teammates celebrated her gender expression, albeit in quiet and understated ways. Members of the women’s team invited her on shopping trips, encouraging her to try on the feminine clothing she admired. They decorated her hair before parties and invited her to pasta dinners before home meets. Toward the end of college, she began using they/them pronouns.

All the while, she excelled on the race course, competing as a valuable member of the men’s team. She often finished among the top seven runners and received All-Academic honors in the University Athletic Association. Ravichandran straddled two worlds: in one, she excelled as an athlete on the men’s team. In the other, she expressed her true identity. “When you’re a college athlete, you want to be the best that you can be,” she said. “But I had this other truth that was really eating away at me.”

It was the late 2010s, and transgender athletes were beginning to receive more media attention, most of which was critical. Ravichandran remembered reading about Lia Thomas—a collegiate swimmer and the first openly transgender athlete to win an NCAA Division I championship—and the hostility she received. She understood that seeking eligibility on the women’s team would require considerable time, work, and medical treatment. Would she even be allowed to compete? “I decided, at that point, to prioritize running over the feelings that were eating away at me,” she said.

She graduated in January 2020—three months before the pandemic hit the U.S., spinning the country into lockdown and Ravichandran back to her hometown. In Massachusetts, she was 600 miles from the friends she’d made in college who honored her identity. She stopped running. But as the pandemic ebbed and flowed around her, she moved closer to Boston for a medical assistant job, and began living with housemates who used her correct pronouns. Suddenly, she felt an internal pull back to the sport.

When Ravichandran moved to Vermont for medical school in 2021, she signed up for her first marathon.

A few miles into the Hartford Marathon, she heard a familiar voice. She glanced toward the sidelines to find a handful of faces she recognized—their mouths wide with excitement, shouting her name. Her college friends had traveled all the way from Ohio, just to surprise her. “I think, having a family that doesn’t accept part of who I am, having a chosen family is really important,” she said. “It’s especially common in queer communities, especially queer communities of color.”

These were good days: Ravichandran kept her chosen family close, if not in proximity, then in spirit. Their voices were just a phone call away as she logged miles on Vermont country roads. She ran a 2:36 marathon and a 1:11 half-marathon. She was training to become a doctor—a long-held dream. But she was still racing in the men’s division, feeling something jabbing inside of her, reminding her: none of this was enough.

At the 2022 Boston Marathon, that feeling grew too sharp to ignore. That year, the nonbinary division had yet to be instated, and Ravichandran registered for the men’s race. As she crested Heartbreak Hill, something inside of her gave way. “I was like, ‘I’m just gonna run to the top of this hill and then be done, because I don’t want my name associated with a male gender,’ and I just walked off and got a ride to the finish line.”

After the race, Ravichandran began gender-affirming hormone therapy and shifted to using she/they pronouns.

Not long after the 2022 marathon, Ravichandran connected with Jake Fedorowski, author of The Guide to Nonbinary Inclusion in Running, who was leading efforts to push for a nonbinary division at the Boston Marathon and other races. She began collaborating with Fedorowski and a group of other runners passionate about inclusion. She contacted race directors throughout New England, asking for nonbinary divisions. On Boston Marathon weekend in 2023, she met some of the runners with whom she’d collaborated at a shakeout run. All of them were buoyant over their successful advocacy. “There were so many tears of trans joy. It was something I had not totally experienced [until] that point,” she said.

But when she looked back on that day in Boston—and its aftermath—a few painful memories clouded the joy.

Following her win, the Daily Mail put out an article, sharing photographs from Ravichandran’s teenage years, “before I had socially and physically transitioned,” she said. Soon, she was tagged in a plethora of angry tweets. She received direct messages over Instagram, including from people “telling me to kill myself, because 41% of trans people kill themselves,” she said, alluding to data by the Trevor Project that shows 40% of transgender and nonbinary youth seriously considered attempting suicide in 2025.

But not all attention was hostile. Ravichandran was also invited to present at schools and organizations. In Vermont, she stood before a room of elementary school students and issued a hard-hitting question: “Do you consider banana bread to be bread or cake?” The children quarreled, unyielding in their opinions: bread, cake, bread, cake.

“Does it really matter if it’s bread or cake if it tastes really good?” she asked. It was a metaphor for gender, of course—the boxes society squeezes people into; the anger that ensues when someone doesn’t fit.

Undoubtedly, Ravichandran was no longer just an athlete. To some, she was a cause for hate speech. To others, she was a symbol of a larger movement. While she didn’t mind the latter classification, it didn’t come without a layer of grief: “I have always been so jealous that cis runners can just run in races without the larger social ramifications,” she said.

Not long after the 2023 Boston Marathon, Ais Oisín was searching for athletes to recruit for their transgender and nonbinary running team, Transcenders. Oisín, cofounder of the team, typed phrases like “trans and run” into the search bar. Suddenly, an Instagram profile appeared. The handle: @transrunnergirl. It was Ravichandran.

The two began talking over the phone—discussing Transcenders, queer community-building, and Ravichandran’s experience as a trans woman of color in both medicine and running. “I think we really connected on this earnest level,” Oisín said. Soon, Ravichandran was traveling from Vermont to New York’s Hudson Valley on weekends when her schedule allowed, attending Transcender’s first Queer Track Meet, or simply visiting with members of the team.

The first time I met Ravichandran, she was standing shoulder-to-shoulder with her Transcenders teammates at All of the Above Trail Fest in Western Massachusetts, a celebration of queer runners. She seemed at home among her teammates, some clad in black singlets with the words “Transcenders” across their chests—calm and smiling, even in the minutes before running a 20K.

“Sometimes it’s just radical to exist,” Oisín said. “Kae goes beyond that. She’s visible in places that are not comfortable to be visible.”

Early in medical school, Ravichandran expanded her advocacy work beyond running, helping transgender kids gain access to safe and healthy lives. She began volunteering as a medical staff member at Camp Outright, a residential summer camp focused on queer and trans youth. At camp, she discussed safe practices for binding and tucking, and how kids can talk with the adults in their lives about gender-affirming care.

While the term “gender-affirming care” is often used in reference to surgery and medication, in reality, it spans much broader. A 2025 study published in JAMA Pediatrics found that less than 0.1% of transgender and gender diverse minors receive puberty blockers or hormone treatment. A 2024 study found that 97% of adolescent breast reductions—the vast majority of gender-affirming surgeries—were performed on cisgender boys. For young people, gender-affirming care can also mean mental health resources, haircuts, and clothing that helps “make your body the way you want it to be shaped,” Ravichandran said—all resources she discusses with campers.

To Ravichandran, the topic of trans kids’ health cannot be understood in isolation from sports: “Preventing trans youth from participating in sports is a public health issue as well as an equity issue,” she said. As of June 2026, 29 states had banned trans youth from playing sports in alignment with their gender identities, decisions with ramifications that extend far beyond simple belonging.

“Trans youth participate in sports at a much lower rate than cis youth,” Ravichandran said, “while things like chronic pain, depression, and anxiety are much higher in trans youth.” Indeed, a 2020 study published in JAMA found that transgender individuals face significantly higher rates of both mental and physical health conditions than their cisgender peers. Ravichandran wondered how many of these conditions could be partially prevented if kids had access to gender-affirming physical activities.

But alongside her wishes for inclusion in sport, Ravichandran remains acutely aware of the struggles inherent to existing as a transgender athlete. She recalls the aftermath of the Boston Marathon and countless other times when running, which is “the most liberating thing in the world,” became a means of confinement.

“I remember at camp one year I asked some kiddos how they felt about sports,” she said. “They said, ‘I don’t want to be the next Lia Thomas.’”

#173. 5 Essential Rules for Hunting Mature Bucks from the Ground

Published Oct 15, 2026 3:08 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Depending on the circumstances, sometimes I bowhunt whitetails from the ground. It’s not necessarily more effective most of the time, but then again, there are days when it’s the best expediency, especially if I’m hunting where I don’t have stands up, or there’s not an abundance of suitable stand trees in the right places for a climber.

Hunting deer from the ground isn’t a new concept; Native Americans managed to do it successfully for centuries. And back in the heyday of Fred Bear and other pioneers of modern bowhunting, climbing a tree to hunt from a stand was hardly a common practice. It’s no more difficult taking a shot at a deer from ground level than it is when you’re 25 feet up in the air. Depending on the amount of intervening limbs and branches, sometimes it’s better to shoot from the ground than it is from an elevated position. Either way, if you move when a buck is looking in your general direction, his peripheral vision is likely to pick you up. If you move or draw when he’s looking the other way, or behind a tree, you’re likely to pull off a decent shot.

The day I killed my best bow nontypical, I was stretched out on the trunk of a large tree that had been blown down by a storm, with my back resting against the root wad.

The day I killed my best bow nontypical, I was stretched out on the trunk of a large tree that had been blown down by a storm, with my back resting against the root wad. It was early in the afternoon of a sleepy autumn day after most of the leaves had fallen and gone crunchy, and I was stationed about 25 yards up the ridgeline from a well-worn trail. There were rubs here and there, and I was scanning the steep ridge I was on, as well as the ridge opposite mine, to catch sight of what had made them.

As you probably know by now, rutting bucks will cruise high trails in the early afternoon when the thermals are still rising in hopes of picking up the scent of an estrus doe below them. I was hoping to get a shot at one of these walk-about bucks. I had posted a doe-in-estrus dripper—made by Whitetail Research Center, incidentally—on a branch behind a large tree on one end of the trail so that I would have the chance to draw undetected, and did the same with a second dripper where the trail moved away from me; I didn’t know from which direction a buck would approach, if at all.

I nocked an arrow and propped my bow up against the tree. I had already scratched all the leaves from around the bow so that I wouldn’t make a lot of noise if I rolled down from my comfortable perch to take a shot. Fifteen minutes after lying down on the tree, I heard a deer approaching from behind me. Screened by the root wad, I quietly rotated off the tree, picked up my bow and waited. Within several seconds I saw the buck; it was big-bodied with a non-typical rack that we later scored at 154 inches and change. Shooter, I thought.

The buck walked up to the dripper, sniffed it for a moment, and moved on. By then I had drawn the string. As the buck walked by, I bleated. It kept moving. I bleated again and it didn’t slow down. I shot it through the lungs as it walked and it ran about 40 yards, stopped and looked back, went all wobbly and fell.

A number of things had worked in my favor: I had good cover, I could see and hear a long way, I had positioned the drippers in strategic locations and I was upwind from the trail the buck was using. Perhaps most importantly, the rut was on and bucks drop their guards when they’re hunting for does. Still, I put myself in a position to succeed if certain things went my way. In that case, they did; usually, whether I’m up a tree or on the ground, they don’t.

The important takeaway from all this is that ground-hunting is a viable alternative to stand hunting. Nowadays any number of good ground blinds are available for hunters to use, but they inhibit a bowhunter’s mobility during the sometimes chaotic days of the rut when does and trailing bucks seem to be going in all directions. In such cases, using natural cover is a better option.

Jim Brush of Galesville, Wisconsin, and George Mann of Opelika, Alabama, are two of the best ground hunters of modern times, and both have been featured in Outdoor Life. Brush, who’s bowhunted on every continent and has a 14,000-square-foot museum of big-game trophies at his house to show for it, did most of his deer hunting on his 1,000-acre farm in Buffalo County, Wis., near the Mississippi River. His favorite technique was to take a fold-up chair in the woods, get in a blowdown, rattle antlers during the rut, and wait for a trophy buck to come along.

For a number of years, Mann held the state archery record buck in Alabama and his name has appeared frequently in the records books of the Pope & Young Club for a variety of game. One of Mann’s favorite ways to hunt deer was to clear some shooting lanes in a place with well-worn deer trails, then set in a chair at the hub of the shooting lanes. A few years ago, in Outdoor Life, an article about Mann was accompanied by a photo of him decked out in bowhunting regalia and sitting in a chair in an Alabama swamp. Incidentally, many of his big-game trophies can be seen in a special annex called the Mann Wildlife Learning Center at the Montgomery Zoo.

Brush and Mann had their own ways of doing things, usually dependent on the limitations of the regions where they hunted, but they shared a few common denominators that were critical to their success. The most important and fundamental rule to ground hunting is that the wind must be moving in a favorable direction relative to the bowhunter’s position, and a deer’s likely line of approach.

Hilly woods or swamps with lots of folds, ditches, and creeks are best for ground hunting. The overgrown border or fence line adjacent to a field or food plot likewise can be good. If the cover at ground level is too heavy with palmettos, hollies, or other evergreen cover, vision will be limited and in that case it’s best to hunt from a tree stand. The main green cover on Brush’s farm is cedars and a few hollies; on Mann’s property in east-central Alabama, it’s palmettos, magnolias, young pines, and cedars.

There’s not much wiggle room for wiggling when you’re hunting on the ground. If you’re under, say, 18 years old, maybe a camp stool will work, but if you’re like most of the rest of us, a well-padded camp or dove chair with back support is a better option. Just make sure that you can draw your bow from a sitting position without banging it against metal arms or an inordinate amount of movement.

You can’t sit in the open. Presuming you have a folding saw with you, cut out a roomy bowl in a fallen treetop near a well-used trail or scrape line and sit there. In the woods, the best ground blind of all is a big cedar whose branches have been lopped off near the base and up the trunk to the proper level. Once you’ve cut out a fairly wide niche, you become virtually invisible. The remaining cedar branches help stifle your scent, too. Wherever you hide, and not counting wind direction, the most important consideration is back cover; that is, there must be something to screen your body so you’re not skylined. This is especially critical when you set up at a higher elevation that affords you a good view of the surrounding terrain. If it’s late evening, try to find a shallow, dry gully or creek bed, preferably with stumps or blow-downs that you can get next to or behind. When you position the chair and sit down, you should be able to see the surrounding woods just above the bank.

The very best time to hunt from the ground is when the rut is at its peak. Bucks will temporarily abandon much of their natural caution and wander around in unfamiliar territory searching for does. Of course, it’s also possible to hunt bucks successfully any time in the fall or winter around feeding zones such as patches of oaks, picked cornfields, or food plots.

Be prepared to move; if a buck is chasing does around the bedding area on the opposite ridge, figure out a way to get over there and set up when things quiet down. A good traveling pack might include a compact binocular, folding saw, snips, 10 feet of camouflaged blind cloth for a backdrop, and a rangefinder, plus a small chair and your regular hunting stuff.

Hunting at ground level gives a bowhunter a nice break from sitting in a tree stand for hours and waiting or something to come by. Then, too, some bowhunters simply aren’t physically able to climb up and down a tree to a lock-on, or use a climber.

Related: The Whitetail Tactic Most Hunters Abandoned — and Why It Still Works

Jim Brush, in the upper Midwest, and George Mann, in the Deep South, hunted different regions in different climates, but they shared fundamental rules and observed them to good effect. Most importantly, perhaps, nobody told them that they couldn’t hunt whitetails successfully from the ground. They believed that they could do it, and then they went out and proved it.

This story first appeared in OL on August 15, 2015.

#174. Why I Quit Climbing

There are certain moments in your life that divide everything into “before” and “after.” That was one of mine.

I remember the impact. It was October 1, 2020, and I was attempting an all-gear ascent of Crank It (5.13+ R/X), a slippery, 40-foot granite testpiece in Boulder Canyon, Colorado. I had gotten past the crux and was trying to keep it together for the pumpy finish. Next thing I knew, I was hitting the ground from 30 feet up, directly onto my butt. I remember knowing immediately that something was wrong. Not just physically, and believe me, I wish that pain upon no one—but perhaps something more. Maybe this was the sign that something wasn’t right with my identity as a whole. It’s tough to say. I remember the strange stillness afterward—the kind that comes when the adrenaline wears off and you are left alone with the reality of what just happened. I woke up in the middle of the night in so much pain and had to remember it was all real.

I had spent most of my life learning how to be comfortable with being uncomfortable. I climbed things that scared me. I climbed things that scared other people. I sought out the routes that seemed too dangerous, too difficult, too ridiculous to be worth it.

And then one day, my body reminded me that there was a price for that.

Eventually, I went back to the route. Going back was more than returning to climbing. It gave me a reason to keep moving. After breaking my back, climbing became a kind of proof that I hadn’t lost myself. That I was still me. That my body could heal. That fear hadn’t won. You can see that in my film.

“I clipped two, bitches!” I screamed at the camera after finally clipping the chains on May 16, 2022. The route description in the guidebook was correct: it really ain’t over until you clip the chains. And by doing so, it meant I was done with my (literal) backbreaking, two-year project. One where I had to learn how to keep direct eye contact with my biggest fears and still keep climbing. It was more than a send to me: it was freedom.

My old friend Nina Williams had been one of the first people to visit me after breaking my back. She had brought a big bag of assorted comfort gifts while I lay there in a back brace. One of them that stood out was a container of vitamin gummies. She put a sticky note over the label that said, “Very glad you are…” I pulled back the note to uncover the brand of gummies: “Alive!”

After I sent, I remember scream-singing “Dangerous Woman” by Ariana Grande on the drive home. I remember the celebratory drinks (barely) and flood of messages congratulating me. One was from Nina; it hit hard remembering how far I had come.

Now, with Crank It finally put to rest, I could get back to hunting down the next big project. At the time, I thought I was finding my way back to the thing I loved. Looking back, I think I was finding my way back to the person I knew how to be. Because eventually I had to admit something to myself that was uncomfortable in an entirely different way: I didn’t just love climbing. I loved the danger.

I loved the parts that made people’s eyes get wide. I loved doing the things that seemed impossible or irresponsible or just plain crazy to everyone watching from the ground. I loved approaching the unapproachable. I loved feeling so in the moment because anything less than that would mean consequences. It was the only time I’ve felt truly present.

I had made a name for myself climbing things that no one else wanted to climb. And there was something intoxicating about being the girl who would. And I’m not going to lie: the applause was part of it. The recognition was part of it. Being told that you were brave, that you were fearless, that you had done something extraordinary—it gets into your bloodstream.

When your identity is built around doing what other people won’t, it becomes very difficult to imagine who you are when you stop. So what do you do with the girl who loves scaring herself? At some point, you tell her that she probably won’t be happy climbing unless it’s that way.

I had reached a point in my early thirties where the life I had built around climbing no longer felt like the life I wanted forever. My parents wanted something different for me. A family. Stability. A life that wasn’t constantly balanced against the possibility of injury or death.

And, quietly, I wanted those things too. But to be honest, I hadn’t felt attracted to anyone for a couple years. A family felt like a far-away dream.

In June 2022, the summer after I sent Crank It, I started rehearsing a route called Dangerous Acquaintances (5.12a X) in Eldorado Canyon. I went out to it all the time, sending it on toprope seamlessly. Old Molly would’ve been chomping at the bit to line up a real lead attempt. But that’s the thing: It couldn’t just be an “attempt.” In the past that hadn’t always stopped me. But as I lowered down in the dark after sending it on toprope with a weight vest on, I wasn’t already thinking of who could belay and who might want to film and what the weather might be like in the next week.

I guess I didn’t realize it at the time. But this happened with multiple prospective projects. I couldn’t find “the one” again.

Then, coincidentally, I met somebody. At first, it was slow. Then, fast forward six months later, I was getting my mom’s engagement ring resized. I have always been an all-or-nothing person. When I believe in something, I don’t know how to give it half of myself. So I gave that relationship everything.

I thought I had found the next chapter. I thought maybe this was what came after climbing. Maybe this was the life I had been working toward all along. A person to come home to. A future to build. Something bigger than myself. I thought this was my happily ever after.

One night in Vegas, my friend Bill Ramsey sat me down over drinks and warned me of the potential that I was headed to not being a climber anymore. He could tell my focus was elsewhere. He even mentioned that we probably wouldn’t be as close if I stop climbing. We both are obsessive people, and climbing was what our friendship had been based on. He just wanted me to be careful in investing so much in this new relationship, and to not give up on something that was part of me.  I thought he was being ridiculous and didn’t understand that my life was changing for the best.

Meanwhile I was still doing climbing events and promoting my film. One of these events towards the end of 2024 was the American Alpine Club’s Bishop Craggin’ Classic. There was an afterparty rave at a bar in Bishop. I walked in rocking a bright blue puffy jacket and shiny silver pants. As the music blared, I made my way through the crowd, then saw a familiar face in the distance. I ran and yelled, “Nina!”

She turned toward me and we hugged. I hadn’t seen her in years. Looking at my old friend, I felt a strange combination of nostalgia mixed with guilt for losing touch with the person I used to be. And then I swallowed those tears back in pride for continuing down the path I was going, farther and farther away from her and climbing. My relationship and new proposed life had taken hold of my focus. I felt like I needed to focus all my energy on making sure it didn’t fail. There was no room for climbing. Even if what I thought was the right path was gradually tearing me apart.

In place of climbing came late nights, parties, and a culture I hadn’t really been part of since college. And, honestly, I loved it.

There were small things cracking that I didn’t think much of at the time. I liked to sleep in. Maybe my mind needed it. Even when we had nowhere to be, my boyfriend would get frustrated when I stayed in bed past 10. I kept sleeping in anyway. It seems insignificant now, but I remember the arguments about it—the guilty feeling that something as harmless as how I spent a Saturday morning could become a problem.

I remember girls filming us dancing at concerts because we were the “cutest couple ever.” I was in my happily-ever-after era. I was having fun. I was falling in love. I thought I had finally found the person I was going to experience all of it with.

At Thanksgiving in 2024, my boyfriend shook my dad’s hand and charmed the hell out of my parents. He told my friends he wanted to marry me. He introduced me to his mom and later told me she thought I was “the one.”

He loved non-climber Molly. That mattered to me more than I realized.

For so long, climbing had been the easiest way for people to understand me. My achievements came first. My identity as a climber came first. And here was someone who, I thought, was choosing me without any of that. Just Molly.

Or at least, that’s what I thought. By the time I started seeing what was really happening, climbing was the last thing on my mind.

Infidelity is such an obvious reason to leave someone. A clean line in the sand. A thing you can point to and say: this is where it ends.

I think part of me believed that walking away would be too easy. This was my person. I had already imagined the future. I wanted to fight for my love, not admit that I had been wrong about it.

So I pretended to believe the lies. I swallowed the things that didn’t make sense. I pushed down the questions. I told everyone I was fine. Women warned me about him. I blocked them.

We were long-distance, and distance made it easy to explain away the things I didn’t want to see. A missed call. A strange story. Another red flag I could fold neatly into the growing pile of things I told myself didn’t matter.

In March 2025, I moved to Denver to live with him. Shortly after, I got a text I couldn’t ignore. A woman reached out and told me she thought she had been dating him for the previous six months. While he was shaking my dad’s hand in Florida, she told me she had been watching his dog. She had no idea at the time he was visiting my family.

I broke down at dinner with him and his cousin. I had just moved across the country to build a life with him. And even then, as devastated as I was, some part of me still thought I had to try to make it work.

But something had changed in me. I started searching. Not because I wanted to find something, but because I needed to know whether I was crazy for wanting to leave. I searched for clues. Then I found them. Photobooth pictures of him kissing other girls. Underwear in the laundry hamper. Things I could no longer explain away.

It became a vicious cycle: find something, break down, promise myself I was done, then find a reason to stay. My hair became part of that cycle, too.

I have had trichotillomania since I was 12, and stress makes it worse. During this period, I started pulling more and more. One night, in front of our friends, he looked at me and said, “I think you’d be such a bad mother because you pull out your own hair.” I called my parents crying.

At the same time, my film was traveling around the world with the Banff Mountain Film Festival. It was an honest film about my mental health, something I had spent years learning to speak about openly.

At the European premiere, the announcer asked me onstage, “What’s next for you?” I told her I wanted to settle down and have a family. The crowd cheered. I remember running offstage and straight into my boyfriend’s arms as everyone celebrated the idea of the life I was supposedly moving toward. I still miss that feeling, like everything was falling into place.

Maybe I wasn’t risking my life on the rocks anymore. But I was still risking it. And I definitely wasn’t climbing.

Then, after another fight over something I had found, he said, “I just don’t think I can be with someone who has a mental disorder.”

After everything I had been through—everything I had put into my film, everything I had publicly opened myself up about—this broke something in me.

In April 2025, I had accepted an award from a nonprofit for my work helping break the stigma around mental health. He had been there beside me, my date, watching me be recognized for turning something I had once been ashamed of into something I could speak about openly.

He had seen me at my most vulnerable. And now he was telling me that vulnerability made me unworthy of being loved.

I had spent years in climbing learning how to endure pain, fear, and exhaustion. I knew how to look at something terrifying and convince myself to move toward it. But I didn’t know how to recognize what was happening to me when the danger wasn’t on a wall.

In July 2025, I opened a box from my storage unit and found a mismatched pair of climbing shoes. The left one was from Crank It. The right one was from China Doll. Two of my most proud achievements.

I had saved them without knowing why. I hadn’t climbed in a year. I remember looking at those shoes and feeling something I couldn’t quite name. Shame, mostly. They belonged to a version of me that felt impossibly far away.  I threw them into a box of stuff I didn’t know where to put, and moved on.

“It’s hard to see the label when you’re inside the jar,” my friend said to me while I was on the phone crying to her again. She said it in a way that made me understand how deep I was in all of it. Because the main question on everyone’s minds was, “Why don’t you just leave?” But climbing out of the jar still felt impossible.

There are parts of this story that are harder to admit than others—not because they hurt the most, but because they force me to confront who I was when I was barely surviving. Over the course of six months or so, I lied to my parents, slept through entire days, and almost missed my grandmother’s funeral because I couldn’t get myself out of bed to make my flight. I stayed up all night pulling out my hair, one strand at a time, until I could barely recognize myself in the mirror. I wore a wig to hide the bald spots. I stopped eating. I partied more than I should have. I stopped caring whether I ate that day or drank too much; I had no sense of purpose left. I was looking for anything that could quiet the feeling that my life was coming apart. I was in survival mode, and I was barely holding myself together.

That September, I sold and gave away all my climbing gear. Crash pads, ropes, quickdraws, cams, all of it. I couldn’t even look at it anymore without a feeling of shame. I still wonder if my friends who I gave my ropes to knew how bad I was spiraling at the time. Or if they were just excited to get nearly brand new gear.

But I kept the Crank It shoe and China Doll shoe, as well as the few gear pieces I ripped when I broke my back. Tucked them away in a small green drawstring bag and saved them for a time when I could maybe look at them with compassion for myself and my journey.

The final straw wasn’t a big fight. It was much quieter than that. It was a chilly September night and we had just gotten back from dinner. I realized that what was happening between us was no longer something I could fix by trying harder. I had become so consumed with proving that I was worth staying for that I had stopped asking whether this was a life I wanted to stay in. I was exhausted. I didn’t stop caring immediately either, but this was the moment I said goodbye–and actually meant it. And I left the state of Colorado altogether.

But leaving him didn’t magically fix my problems. In an attempt to regain my independence, I moved on my own to an area of Tampa, Florida that I thought would give me a fresh start. Instead, partying—which had been my love language with my ex—became a way for me to cope. I quickly fell into unhealthy habits in Tampa and found myself surrounded by people who were caught up in the same lifestyle. Before I knew it, I felt stuck and didn’t know how to get myself out. By January, I had spent all the money my dad had given me to start over on partying.

One day in December 2025, I got a knock on my apartment door. I put on a beanie to hide my bald spots from my hair-pulling and cracked open the door in a T-shirt and underwear. Several policemen stood there. Turns out, I had slept for three days straight after being drugged at a restaurant by a guy I was interested in. My family was beyond worried and sent the police for a wellness check.

I got to a point where everything in life felt like a burden and a chore. I put off everything. Why didn’t I have car insurance? Not because my family wouldn’t help me out financially to get it, but because I felt like it was too much of an anxiety-provoking task to accomplish. My parents so desperately wanted me to get a job, but I could barely get out of bed, let alone stay awake for normal hours. Depression sleepiness is so overpowering. Every time I had to do something like go to the grocery store, every cell in my body would tell me to take a nap instead.

This March, I checked myself into an inpatient mental health treatment center in West Palm Beach, Florida. For 45 days, my phone was taken, I lived on a strict schedule of all day therapy, cameras watched my every move. I remember the staff doing a search of my bags when I got there and taking my shoelaces. “Why can’t I have my shoelaces?” I asked, genuinely confused. They just looked at each other. Naïve girl.

At the treatment center, I went to so much therapy that sometimes it felt like therapy was my full-time job. I talked about things I didn’t want to talk about. I cried about things I thought I had already moved past. I tried to understand how I had gotten there and, more importantly, how I was going to get somewhere else. But mostly, I got bored. I started ordering boxes of beads and making bracelets for the girls in my unit. I wrote letters to people in my life. I wrote in my journal a lot. I counted down the days until I could try to be a normal person again.

At one point, they showed my film at the treatment center to my unit. My eyes got teary at the end. I missed that girl. The girl who, even though she had her own issues, took something incredibly traumatic and turned it into something beautiful. Everyone was so impressed, and they reminded me that if I could get through something like that, I could get through the darkness I was going through now as well.

There is a strange humility in having to rebuild your life from the ground up. For so long, I knew exactly what I was supposed to do: Train. Climb. Push harder. Take the risk. When in doubt, run it out. Brush off the close calls. Try again. Do something bigger next time. I understood that language.

But rebuilding a life doesn’t work that way. There isn’t always an anchor to clip to confirm you’ve accomplished something. There isn’t always a route description telling you to watch out for this section and look for the good hold coming up. Sometimes, the biggest accomplishment of the day is simply choosing not to go backward.

After the inpatient treatment ended, my parents convinced me to move to the same city as them—Naples, Florida—so they could help me get back on my feet.

Two months later, in August, I was sitting in my new therapist’s office when they suggested I check out the new Central Rock climbing gym in Fort Myers.

For the first time in a long time, I didn’t cringe at the idea. “Maybe I will,” I said, and I actually meant it.

It had been two years since I’d last climbed. The only shoes I had left were the right one from China Doll and the left one from Crank It. On August 29, 2026, I pulled them out from my new closet in Naples and drove to the gym.

My mom came with me, which was sweet of her. She just watched me climb. But it was nice to not feel alone in returning to something that had carried so much emotional weight in the past. Climbing for the first time in two years made me feel like I once again had a weight vest on. I knew what to do, but just couldn’t do it.

My hair was now short and brown, so people didn’t recognize me. But there were still people in rental shoes who were impressed with how I could do the V3s on my first try. My mom’s face lit up when other climbers complimented my technique.

It felt strange to be exercising again. I was so out of breath. I was definitely scared to commit to certain moves because my body felt so heavy and I was worried it might bother my back to fall again. But it also reminded me how good the after-climbing feeling can be. When your forearms are so tired that opening and closing your hands fully is difficult. I left feeling exhausted, but also psyched for the first time in a long time.

As of September, I have been to the gym a handful of times and plan to keep going. I want to make friends. I’ve spoken with the gym about showing my film and doing a Q&A, where all proceeds will go to a meaningful cause related to climbing and mental health.

“Look how much you’ve healed,” my therapist said to me during one of our recent sessions. I hadn’t pulled my hair—a habit I’d kept since age 12—since I went to the treatment center in March. Sitting there with my new, short hairdo, I smiled and teared up. Happy tears.

I’m still mending. Some days I feel like I’m making enormous progress. Other days I feel like I’m holding the same broken pieces I’ve been holding for months, wondering if they’ll ever fit together again.

But there is one thing that keeps me going: the sense of chasing what’s next. I don’t know exactly what “next” is yet. For someone who spent most of her life chasing very specific goals, that’s uncomfortable. But I’m beginning to realize that not knowing doesn’t mean I’m lost.

I know I want to help aspiring athletes. I want to take what I’ve learned from a life spent chasing difficult things and give some of it back. I want athletes to understand that their worth is bigger than their performance, their accomplishments, their sponsorships, their grades, their rankings, and whatever it is they’re being applauded for that day. I want them to know that they are allowed to change. I know that because I am changing, too.

And I know that I am becoming a climber again. That part of me didn’t die. Even though I’m only able to climb for about an hour before my forearms give out, and climbing V4 gets me winded, I am climbing.

But by returning, I hope I am becoming a different climber. I don’t want to climb because I need to prove something. I don’t need to prove that I’m fearless. I don’t need to prove that I can handle more pain. I don’t need to prove that I’m the girl who will go where nobody else will. And I certainly don’t need to risk my life so that someone else can tell me I’m brave.

I want to climb because I love climbing. That’s it.

For the first time, that feels like enough. Maybe that’s the strangest part of all of this. After spending so many years trying to find out how far I could push myself, I’m now learning that strength can look like something completely different.

Sometimes strength is walking away. Sometimes it’s admitting that you are broken. Sometimes it’s letting your family come get you. Sometimes it’s sitting in a therapist’s office and saying the thing you’ve been too ashamed to say out loud. And sometimes it’s waking up without a plan and deciding that you’re going to find one.

For so long, I focused on how to handle the idea of falling from dangerous places. Told myself if I just held on harder and longer everything would be ok. I never learned how dangerous it could be to stay there. I didn’t know that the next thing I loved would break me in ways climbing never had. And I certainly didn’t know that I would have to build myself again from the pieces. But I am. Slowly. Piece by piece. Move by move.

I will tie back in. Not because I have anything left to prove, and not because I’m trying to become the girl I used to be. But because she was never the whole story.

#175. New Flash Floods Disrupt Trekking Routes in Nepal

A flash flood has cut off parts of the Manaslu Circuit in a fresh blow to Nepal’s tourism industry.

This time, the flood hit the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district. While not as catastrophic as the glacial lake outburst flood in the Langtang Lirung area in late August, the flooding is still severe. A landslide caused the river to swell suddenly, washing away houses and bridges and damaging a hydropower plant, the BBC reported. Authorities have not recorded any fatalities, but some farmers remain unaccounted for.

The Bhudi Gandaki River flows south from mountains in the Manaslu region, and the flood severed the popular Manaslu Circuit in several sections. The Chum Valley is currently isolated after bridges were washed away. According to the Manaslu Conservation Area Project (MCAP), all trekkers in the area are fine. The Tourism Times reports that helicopters are airlifting some tourists back to Kathmandu.

“We have decided to cancel our Manaslu and Tsum treks for this autumn season based on advice from local authorities and our internal risk assessments,” Roland Hunter of The Mountain Company told ExplorersWeb. Instead, they are offering clients a trek through Upper Mustang followed by a crossing of Thorong La, the highest point on the Annapurna Circuit.

Poor weather also closed Thorong La for weeks after a snowy spell hit Nepal’s mountains. However, the trail recently reopened, and trekking groups have crossed the pass over the last five days. “There is a trail through the snow on the pass, and after sunny weather the snow has consolidated, reducing the risk of avalanche,” Hunter explained. “The road has been washed away lower down near Chame, although the trekking trail has been repaired so it is passable for trekking groups.”

Hunter said that many trekkers are now diverting to the Annapurna Circuit, and he presumes it will be busier than ever for the next few weeks.

The Tourism Times also reports damaged trails on the Tashi Lapcha Pass, a high-altitude trekking route connecting the Rolwaling and Khumbu regions. Tashi Lapcha is one of the most challenging sections of the Great Himalaya Trail (GHT) and includes rock scrambling and fixed ropes that are currently damaged. The paper shared a report from IAM Trekking Guides:

The damaged section lies along the approach to the David Lama Bivouac shelter at Upper Jabo. Trekkers and climbers must use the fixed ropes and carefully scramble across the rocky terrain to proceed. The loss of footholds in such a steep section can increase the risk of a fall, particularly for groups carrying trekking or climbing equipment.

A damaged passage at Tashi Lapcha. Photo: IAM Trekking Guides

Those intending to hike in the area should ask their local trekking operators and tourism offices for updated information. According to India’s weather services, the monsoon officially left Nepal yesterday. Nepal’s peak trekking season begins now and lasts until the end of November.
