#178. Why a Hunter Is Leading the Fight Against Colorado’s Right-to-Hunt Amendment

Published Oct 15, 2026 2:33 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

As Colorado’s voters consider a ballot question next month that could enshrine hunting and fishing as a constitutionally protected right, proponents and opponents of the measure are accusing each other of political meddling.

The twist? Both sides claim to represent Colorado’s hunters and anglers.

The question on the ballot is titled Amendment 83. If passed by 55 percent of Colorado voters on Nov. 3, it would create “a constitutional right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods, including all species of fish and wildlife managed by the state except for non-game species, endangered species, or any species that is illegal to hunt under federal law.”

The ballot measure further establishes “hunting and fishing as the preferred means of managing fish and wildlife populations.” You can read the relatively short paragraph in is entirety here, along with text of the other five constitutional amendments on the November ballot.

But Amendment 83 has drawn an especially stark contrast between two types of Colorado’s hunters, with each claiming that the other is misrepresenting the interest of both the public and Centennial State hunters and anglers.

On the one hand: those who claim that the loss of any hunting and fishing tradition accelerates the future loss of others that underpin the American system of wildlife management. On the other: those who claim that “throwback” practices such as trapping and predator management are outside of the mainstream and turn non-hunters against other, more socially acceptable, types of hunting and angling.

The rift between these tribes was on full display last month as the main opponent of the constitutional question claimed election malfeasance by proponents of A-83.

Eric Washburn, a political consultant, self-described avid hunter, and lead agitator of the No-On-83 campaign, has accused the Colorado Wildlife Council of using public funds to electioneer on behalf of a previous constitutional initiative, the 2024 Proposition 127 that would have banned hunting for mountain lions, bobcat, and lynx. That ballot measure was defeated by voters, possibly because of electoral interference by the Colorado Wildlife Council, says Washburn and co-signers in their petition.

Washburn claims that the public education campaign overseen by the council — it’s funded by a $1.50 surcharge on hunting and fishing licenses, which generates about $3.5 million annually — is masquerading as a political action fund. Though the election in question is two years old, Washburn’s petition to Colorado Parks and Wildlife calling for a suspension of council funding was granted earlier this month by CPW Director Laura Clellan, who has pledged to conduct a full review of the council’s engagement in political matters.

Washburn’s group is called Colorado Hunters & Anglers for Sensible Wildlife Management. One of the main in-state groups advocating for passage of A-83 is Coloradans for Responsible Wildlife Management, and many of its leaders helped pass legislation that created the Colorado Wildlife Council in 1998 for the very purpose of taking politics out of questions of wildlife management.

The tensions pulling at Amendment 83 are broader than this specific constitutional question. Both sides represent wider constituencies that are using this election to define the future of hunting and fishing — not only in the rapidly-urbanizing state of Colorado but, by extension, the rest of America. Still, it should be noted that Washburn’s constituency is far smaller than the wave of sportsmen support for A-83. Nearly all organized hunting and fishing groups have come out in support of it, including the influential Colorado Wildlife Conservation Project, the state’s largest coalition of hunting, fishing, and wildlife conservation groups.

“Hunting and fishing are integrally woven into the fabric of Colorado’s outdoor heritage and provide meaningful ways for families to connect with nature and harvest healthy, sustainable food,” says Gaspar Perricone, chair of the CWCP. “Amendment 83 preserves those opportunities into perpetuity while ensuring wildlife management remains in the hands of the professionals responsible for conserving Colorado’s fish, wildlife, and habitats.”

Colorado is the latest battleground in efforts to elevate hunting and fishing to constitutional right. Twenty-four states offer some constitutional protection to hunting and fishing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Some states, like Vermont, granted this right nearly 250 years ago. Florida, where 67 percent of voters approved a ballot measure in 2024, is the latest state to grant constitutional protections to hunting and fishing.

Florida’s hunters and anglers owe the electoral success to the International Order of T. Roosevelt, which has made its main priority the passage of these constitutional questions. The group’s website notes that it is actively working in more than a dozen states to pass similar constitutional protections for hunting and fishing.

But it’s an open question, even among lifelong hunters and anglers, about whether their activities are a privilege granted by state agencies that can be taken away if participants violate its laws and tenants, or whether they’re a right guaranteed by the constitution.

In Colorado, the ground campaign to promote Amendment 83 has fallen largely to veterans of Colorado’s recent wildlife-management battles. These include Proposition 114, which narrowly passed in 2020 and required CPW to reintroduce wolves to Colorado, and Proposition 127, the 2024 ballot question that would have banned hunting for mountain lions, bobcat, and lynx if it had passed.

One of those veterans of the Centennial State’s wildlife wars is Dan Gates, a lifelong trapper and executive director of Coloradans for Responsible Wildlife Management. Gates is also a former chairman of the board of the Colorado Wildlife Council, which was created after two devasting — at least for traditional hunters — ballot questions in the 1990s. The first closed the spring bear season and ended the use of bait and hounds to pursue black bears. The second banned the use of foot-hold traps in Colorado. Together, those ballot initiatives signaled changing times in a rapidly urbanizing Colorado.

The Wildlife Council was one response to these changes. The legislation that created it authorized a portion of sportsman’s license fees to educate Colorado’s non-hunting public about the access, habitat, and infrastructure funded by Colorado’s hunters and anglers. One of the council’s most successful media campaigns, Hug a Hunter, showed a blaze-orange-clad hunter receiving an unexpectedly warm hug from a hiker. Later campaigns promoted science-based wildlife management as the most durable approach to sustaining habitat and populations of both game and non-game species.

It’s that campaign that Washburn’s petition seeks to disable. In an interview, Washburn claims that the council’s work went beyond public education to electioneering. Citing research from the anti-hunting Center for Biological Diversity, Washburn claims the council actively campaigned against the lion-hunting initiative in 2024, using public funds to do voter research and polling, and enlisting personnel from CPW to encourage voters to oppose Proposition 127.

“Then, in a remarkable example of self-defeating candor, [the council] congratulated themselves on running a campaign to defeat Prop 127,” says Washburn. “It’s a little like Al Capone going on Facebook and boasting that he just robbed a bank.

“If you want to understand the problems with the council, look at the 1998 legislation that created it,” says Washburn. “It was created out of politics, in reaction to those 1990s-era ballot measures. Furthermore, the council’s 2022-25 strategic plan talks explicitly about protecting ballot measure votes on issues that have to do with wildlife management. This isn’t an education campaign. It’s a political campaign designed to achieve a political result.”

But Gates maintains that it’s become impossible to separate the political from the educational. He vehemently maintains the council’s work is not electioneering. Its role is to remind everyday Coloradans who hike, float, and walk their dogs that much of the state’s abundant wildlife, open spaces, and habitat was created, protected, and funded by the state’s hunters and anglers.

“The dominant message of the council has been what could be called ‘The Science of the Wild,’” says Gates. “It has promoted the need of science-based wildlife management as the best tool to maintain our wildlife resources in perpetuity. We’ve polled the public to confirm that’s a resonant message. Is that ‘electioneering’?”

Gates says the resonance of the council’s message is frightening to anti-hunters because it effectively reaches the majority of Coloradans: those who don’t actively hunt or fish but don’t oppose the activities.

“They have figured out that if they sit idle and let that message continue to be disseminated, then they will continue to lose at the polls,” says Gates. “The only way they can prevail is to shut the messaging down — that’s the Wildlife Council — and then turn around and go after individuals and organizations that are supportive of science-based wildlife management.”

Gates includes Washburn, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Colorado Hunters & Anglers for Sensible Wildlife Management as either anti-hunters or as “infiltrators” who claim to be hunters and anglers but who are opposed to traditional science-based wildlife management.

“These antis have studied our playbook, and now they’re working systematically to take the head off the hammer and the handle off the screwdriver,” says Gates. “It’ll be so that we still have our traditional tools, but we won’t be able to use them.”

To support that conclusion, Gates cites a demand in Washburn’s petition to CWP that would prohibit the council from doing any outreach that promotes the role of hunting in wildlife management fully six months before an election.

“That would mean we couldn’t have any outreach beyond April in election years,” notes Gates. “That’s electioneering, effectively silencing what has been a popular and effective public-education campaign that simply promotes the role of hunters in science-based wildlife management.”

Gates says Washburn’s petition is a first volley in an attempt to discredit and then defund the Wildlife Council.

“If they can shut up a statutorily mandated $3 million program because of a single citizen’s petition, then it will give [anti-hunters] the confidence to go after other pillars of the North American model of wildlife conservation,” says Gates. “And it will stop other states from adopting their own versions of our Wildlife Council.”

Washburn chafes at the notion that he’s not a bona fide hunter or angler.

A founder of the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership, professional member of the Boone and Crockett Club, and avid hunter, he claims that A-83 would provide a constitutional basis to overturn voter-approved bans on trapping, wildlife contests, and bear hunting. Rather than bolstering support for traditional hunting practices, the constitutional amendment could make sportsmen and women pariahs in the public’s eye and invite further ballot initiatives.

None of the other states that have passed constitutional amendments protecting the ability to hunt and fish have had specific hunting methods outlawed by the voters, as Colorado has.

If A-83 now protects “traditional” methods of hunting and fishing, could those voter-approved amendments banning leg-hold traps, bear baiting, and wildlife killing contests be resurrected?

“We think the ethics of fair chase and the North American mode are things to be proud of,” says Washburn. “They’ve created a lot of support for hunting in Colorado, which is great. If this amendment passes and you suddenly enshrine all these ‘traditional’ methods in the constitution, you risk overturning bans that have been established over the past 40 years by Colorado’s citizens and the state wildlife commission.”

That end-run around voter-approved initiatives could inflame Colorado’s electoral majority, those voters who generally support hunting, says Washburn.

“Colorado’s society is becoming more urban,” notes Washburn. “If [A-83] passes, the public can rightly say ‘we put these restrictions in deliberately, and now they’re bringing back practices that we already rejected?’ To me, that’s a much bigger threat to hunting in Colorado than instituting a bag limit of two per day for furbearers.”

That point has been roundly refuted by the Colorado Wildlife Partnership Council, which notes that passage of A-83 would not bring back those voter-rejected practices. Sources stress it would take subsequent legal action to resurrect leg-hold traps or spring bear hunting, and there’s little judicial precedent for it.

But Washburn is further troubled by A-83’s language mandating hunting and angling as preferred methods of wildlife management.

“I’m a hunter. It’s a big part of my life,” he says. “But there’s a lot more to wildlife management than just hunting and fishing. The preferred method of managing beaver is not to hunt or trap them. It’s to conserve as many as we can if we want to hold more water on our landscapes. When it comes to bighorn sheep, preferred management may be disease research. With deer and elk, the preferred management may be understanding how to curb CWD.”

If Amendment 83 has languished under the weight of a combative congressional mid-term election and the sheer number of constitutional amendments on Colorado’s ballot, the hunting and angling industry has awakened to the risk it poses for traditional sporting methods.

Just this week, the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation’s political action arm contributed $125,000 to support the ballot measure. Also this week, the sport-fishing community came out in support of the initiative, noting that angling has contributed $2 billion to Colorado’s recreation economy in 2022 alone.

The economic argument may sway Colorado’s non-hunting voters who can’t parse what they consider small differences between proponents and opponents of Amendment 83.

Read Next: Grizzlies Are Killing Far More Livestock in the Rockies Than Wolves

“The Colorado Wildlife Council actually anticipated this moment,” says Gates. “The council was intended to use a small fee from sportsmen to show a changing demographic in Colorado the benefits of hunting and fishing, to include the $7.5 billion industry that supports 25,000 jobs.”

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#181. A Human-Powered Journey Around Norway

Bad weather has forced Norwegian Jonas Holm, 27, to alter his 5,500km human-powered attempt to circle Norway.

Holm took a year off from his construction job and set out from southern Norway in late April, beginning in Svinesund on the Swedish border. He planned to paddle nearly 3,000km north, skirting Norway’s coastline as far as Grense Jakobselv, near the Russian border. From there, he would travel south through Norway, Finland, and Sweden with his dog, Rago.

Jonas Holm during the kayak section of his journey. Photo: Jonas Holm/Padling

However, difficult conditions forced him to stop paddling south of Bodø in northern Norway, a little over halfway to Grense Jakobselv. On his website, Holm says he wants to avoid feeling pressure to reach particular places by particular dates, instead focusing on experiencing the landscape. With constant wind and rain, he decided the remaining fiords could wait until next spring.

Holm’s tracked route so far. Photo: Jonas Holm

Holm won’t sit on the couch until he can complete the coastline. Rather than wait months for better weather, he has stored his kayak and will begin the second segment of his journey: the 2,500km trek south from Grense Jakobselv. After a quick break at home to dry his clothes and gear, Holm recently drove north to Grense Jakobselv and set out with a backpack and a companion. Rago, his Alaskan malamute, is even carrying some equipment. As winter arrives and snow accumulates, Holm plans to eventually transition from walking with a backpack to skis and a pulk.

His exact route is unclear, but he will roughly trace Norway’s eastern border, though he mentions crossing parts of Finland and Sweden on his way back to his starting point in southern Norway.

You can follow Holm’s progress through the live tracker on his expedition website.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#183. The “Sleep Monster” Was No Match for Katharina Hartmuth at Tor des Géants

Germany’s Katharina Hartmuth won the 2026 Tor des Géants in 67 hours, 10 minutes, and 9 seconds—breaking her own course record by over 13 hours. She also finished third overall and closed the gap to the men’s CR to just 1.8%. She credits the huge leap forward with fearless pacing: “I used to hold back in races, I think I was afraid of failing. I realized if I wanted to actually improve and find my potential, I had to take more risks and be willing to fail.”

Katharina Hartmuth watched man after man pass her on the second big climb during Tor des Géants, a grueling 330-kilometer (205-mile) race through the Italian Alps. She let them go and silently said, “I’ll probably see you again.”

Hartmuth, 31, who’s landed on podiums at UTMB, Hardrock, and the trail running world championships, was right. She saw every single one of those men again.

She won the women’s race by over 13 hours and finished third overall—becoming the first woman to race her way onto the overall podium at one of the most difficult and competitive ultra-ultra distance races in the world.

Her time of 67 hours, 10 minutes, and 9 seconds bested her own women’s course record by 12 hours and was the sixth fastest in the run’s history. She narrowed the gap between the men’s and women’s record to just 1.8% as she finished just 75 minutes behind men’s winner Jia-Ju Zhao of China, who also set a new course record.

Closing that gap was the biggest motivation for Hartmuth, a German who lives in Switzerland, where she earned a PhD in climate science. After her first run at Tor in 2024, she looked at the men’s times compared to the women’s and she knew women could get closer.

“The gap was way too big,” Hartmuth told Trail Runner. “My top goal going into this year was to narrow it as much as I could.”

She thought 75 hours was definitely possible, 72 on the perfect day. But 67 hours?

“If you would have told me 67 hours was possible, I’d have said, ‘Yeah, okay, who do I think I am?’ The great Franco Collé won it three times and ran it in 66 hours, so I’m certainly not going to get anywhere close to that time.”

To think about what it means to run 67 hours at Tor de Geants, consider this: The course travels 330K, or 205 miles, through the Italian Alps, traversing 79,000 feet of climbing along the way. That’s like stacking two Hardrocks back-to-back, albeit at a slightly lower altitude, and adding yet another 16,000 feet of elevation gain on steep and rugged terrain. But the stats don’t do this iconic race, which started in 2010, justice, said Stephanie Case, who’s raced Tor four times and won it in 2015.

“It is truly a mountain expedition, and it requires you to navigate over extremely technical terrain through multiple days and nights on very little sleep,” Case said. “To run quickly and safely under these conditions takes incredible skill. This is not a long UTMB—it is a whole different kind of adventure.”

“I still cannot wrap my head around how difficult this race is, and I have attempted it twice,” professional trail runner Alyssa Clark added. “Every climb is the hardest climb of another race.”

It’s hard to comprehend just how hard Tor is unless you experience it, Hartmuth believes, but since she had experience on the course, she had some ideas about how to shave time.

When Hartmuth won the women’s race in 2024, ultrarunning superstar Francois D’Haene won the men’s race in 69:08:32. She made a list of where she saw opportunities for improvement, which included more efficient aid station transitions, a smarter sleep strategy, and developing better fatigue resistance for the end of the race.

And, above all else, she went into this year’s run looking to take some risks.

“My first Tor was all about enjoying the adventure and getting to the finish line,” she said. “This time, I wanted to take more risks and I knew I would either fail—or the result would be exceptional.”

It was a love of the mountains that hooked Hartmuth on trail running. As a graduate student in Switzerland, she would hike into the Alps and see runners out on the trails, but she couldn’t imagine doing that herself. Instead, she started volunteering at races and loved supporting runners. She still couldn’t fathom the idea of running an ultra-distance race, but she decided it would be fun to give it a try.

She discovered that, not only was she perfectly capable of finishing, she could also finish quite well. She won her first race, the 65K at the 2018 Innsbruck Alpine TrailRun Festival, and continued to log impressive results as she raced more. But no matter how well she ran, it was never the competition that drove her. She loved running because the mountains are where she’s found the greatest joy. And because trail running is what brings out the best in her.

But earlier this year, Hartmuth reflected on her races and wondered if she was actually getting the best out of herself. She usually races on the more conservative side and picks off runners in the later stages. When UTMB saw some of the wettest and coldest weather in the race’s history in 2025, Hartmuth worked her way up the field to finish third. But despite her many impressive results, including two UTMB podiums, she thought she might have more to give.

“I used to hold back in races, I think I was afraid of failing,” she said. “I realized if I wanted to actually improve and find my potential, I had to take more risks and be willing to fail.”

She credits her Hoka teammates, including 2026 Western States runner-up Francesco Puppi, with inspiring her to be bolder. As she heard about their approaches and saw their results, she felt moved to try the same strategy.

“I wanted to see what would happen if I went faster from the beginning and kept pushing for as long as I was feeling good,” she said.

“Feeling good” being relative, of course.

At Tor, her feet started hurting in the first 10K. The days were hot and the trails were dry, debris got into her shoes, and her socks were soaked with sweat. The chafing got so painful around the halfway mark that she couldn’t imagine finishing.

She slept for just 15 minutes on the second night and had to face the “sleep monster” on the third. She was hallucinating and couldn’t remember what she was even doing on the trail. She asked herself, “Should I keep following the flags?”

But, as she got deep into the race, her legs still felt relatively good, considering they’d scaled the equivalent of two-and-a-half Everests. So she kept pushing. She ran many of the climbs she’d hiked during her first attempt in 2024 and she stayed within minutes of the second place man, Switzerland’s Jonathan Schindler.

Her fueling strategy kept her energized; she ate pasta at most aid stations and could stomach gels until the last descent. And she leaned on her training and experience when the going got tough. For the last year, she’d trained herself to run on tired legs and a tired brain, working to increase her fatigue resistance and uphill running capabilities, and she trusted herself to work through her lows. She’s certainly had plenty throughout her career.

Hartmuth has been open about her mental health struggles and she’s dealt with a slew of injuries in the last few years, including knee surgery after getting hit by a car while biking and sudden vision loss that left her unable to see the trail during Hardrock.

“I think one of the biggest things is just believing that you can do it and not being too afraid of what will happen,” she said. “Of course, there will be problems, but I knew I could take care of them when they came up, I didn’t want to spend time and energy worrying, I wanted my mind to be focused on pushing.”

When she got to a 6-mile gradual climb just before the 300-kilometer mark, she remembered walking nearly the entire thing in 2024. She told herself, “Of course you don’t want to run, but your body can still do it and you can make up so much time if you keep running.”

The third night was the biggest question going into the race.

“I was pretty sure I would have a better second half but I couldn’t imagine being able to push the whole time,” she said. “It’s so different from an effort like Madeira or the Bob Graham Round FKT, when you’re done in less than a day.”

But on the third night, she was still moving well and every time she did the math to estimate her finish, she was getting faster. She surpassed every greatest hope for her finish time and knew she was about to become the first woman on the overall podium.

“I didn’t feel pressure, it just gave me wings and I wanted to see how much more time I could take off,” she said.

Hartmuth’s performance continues a recent trend of women redefining what’s possible at the 200-mile-plus distance. Women are about 10% slower than men over the course of a marathon, an analysis of 60 marathons found. The data looks similar in 100-milers At the Western States 100, the gap between the men’s and women’s course record (both set this year) is 12.3%, similar to UTMB’s 11.3%. Meanwhile at the sixth edition of the Cocodona 250 this May, Rachel Entrekin broke the overall course record.

“I’ve thought a lot about what women have been achieving in the sport and I’ve gotten confidence from what others have been doing. Maybe it’s a bit like the 4-minute mile and you just need to see it happen.”

When she crossed the line in Courmayeur in a record-setting time and closed that gap with the men’s record to 1.8 percent, it didn’t feel like the end of anything.

“It just excites me a lot because I think I’m just getting started and I see so much more potential for myself,” she said. “Of course I know that there will be races where I fail, but I feel like I just started to unpack this box of potential and I’m excited to keep going.”

#185. I Spent 5 Years Bowhunting One of the Biggest Nontypical Bucks Ever. Then My Buddy Killed Him

Published Oct 15, 2026 12:39 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “A Five-Year Stalk,” originally ran in the August 1963 issue of Outdoor Life. The buck remains the 26th largest nontypical whitetail of all time, the fifth largest nontypical whitetail ever taken by a bowhunter, and the second largest nontypical whitetail ever taken in Nebraska. The buck taped out at 284 5/8 inches (gross) with a net score of 277 3/8, according to the Boone and Crockett Club (although Pope and Young recorded them as 279 7/8). The antlers are now owned by Bass Pro Shops.

The first time I saw the deer I made myself a promise. I’d hunt him until I hung that strange and magnificent rack on my wall, no matter how long it took, unless another hunter killed him first. I didn’t guess then that I was taking on a five-year assignment and the most fascinating outdoor quest of my life. Before I was through, I’d have a liberal education in the almost incredible wariness and stealth by which a big whitetail buck survives the hunting seasons.

I met him first in October 1958. I was hunting in my favorite area, on the farm of a friend, Dan Thomas, along the Platte River south of Shelton, Nebraska, 30 miles northwest of my home in Hastings where I worked as a salesman for a meat-packing house. I was carrying a 57-pound bow and three arrows. I’m 36, took up bowhunting seven years ago, and have not used a gun for deer since.

I had crossed a cornfield, on the watch for fresh sign, and had stopped at a fence to look over an adjoining alfalfa field and the timbered river bottoms beyond. Ready to move on, I saw a band of five or six whitetails break out of the timber and run straight for me. The lead buck was tremendous. I had seen nothing like him.

His rack was big and massive, and was the queerest, most deformed set of deer antlers I had ever looked at. There were heavy, spraggly points, long and short, growing from the main beams in all directions. Strangest of all, he had two long prongs curving out and down on either side of his head between eye and ear. They extended below his jaws, giving him an odd, lop-eared appearance.

I knew I was looking at a dream trophy, a nontypical whitetail big enough to go well up on the record list, with antlers the like of which I could never hope to see again. At that, I didn’t realize how good he really was.

A deer trail crossed the fence where I was standing, but I was in the open. So I risked a couple of careful steps back and sank down on one knee in a clump of weeds, an arrow nocked and ready.

The buck was 50 or 60 yards away, still coming like the wind, when he suddenly swerved. I had the wind, and to this day I don’t know what alerted him, unless he had seen movement when I backed up or didn’t like the looks of the weeds that hid me.

He cleared the fence 70 yards from me and stopped, looking directly at me. I knew he wouldn’t come closer, and I couldn’t resist a shot. But the arrow sailed under him. He whirled and ran, leading his bunch in a big circle back into the bottoms.

I retrieved my arrow and started to follow his track. But I knew it was useless, so I went back to my car. I had no interest in any other deer that morning.

Then and there I named him Mossy Horns. I know it sounds corny, but with that irregular rack and those two long tines on each side of his face, it fitted him. I vowed I’d keep after him until that wonderful head was mine.

I knew I’d have a lot of competition. I was not the first hunter who had seen him, nor would I be the last. Stories had circulated in that neighborhood for two or three years, among bowmen and gun hunters, of a big buck with an unusual rack. I had heard them but had discounted them as tall tales. Now that I had seen him, I realized none of the stories had done him justice.

I hunted the river bottoms along Dan’s farm until the bow season closed after Christmas. I had half a dozen chances at lesser deer, but on each occasion the memory of that freak rack kept me from shooting. If I filled my license I’d be through. If I waited, I might get another chance at him. I saw him twice more, but at a distance both times, and then the season ended.

I had hunted alone that fall, but when the 1959 season opened, Gene Halloran, a retired farmer, and Charley Marlowe, a Hastings advertising executive and the only member of our Oregon Trail Bowhunters Club who had killed a deer with a bow up to that time, joined me. I never like to wish partners bad luck, but I couldn’t help hoping neither of them would get the buck I was after.

By that time Dan had his own reasons for wanting the big deer killed. Two years before Dan had planted 50 young spruces for a windbreak about 30 yards from his house. For some reason, the big buck had taken either a marked liking or dislike to them. He tore them apart with his antlers and hoofs and killed every one. There was no question what deer had done it, either, for he left his tracks all over the place; no other whitetail in those parts could have made them.

The Platte bottoms in that area are covered with a dense mixture of cottonwoods, brush, willow tangles, weeds, and grass, and are dotted with countless islands, some small and easy to get to, others big and surrounded by deep water. Many places that can be reached early in the fall become inaccessible later when the sloughs and channels are half-frozen. A belt of wild country with farmland on either side and the shallow river winding through the center, those bottoms are a deer hunter’s dream.

Halloran, Marlowe, and I built tree blinds in half a dozen places, nailing up small platforms 10 to 20 feet from the ground, depending on the trees we put them in and the height and thickness of the surrounding brush. Such blinds are a big help to the bowhunter, since they get him up where deer are not likely to smell or notice him. In the kind of country we hunt, they are close to essential. The cover is so dense it is almost impossible to stalk deer. We have to figure their routes and habits from their tracks and then wait them out.

Unless alerted by movement, whitetails rarely look up. They are used to danger on the ground and look for trouble at that level. They don’t pay much attention to a platform or a motionless hunter waiting overhead. Getting into a tree above them often means the difference between a long shot and a shot at good bow range—or no shot at all.

For all our preparations and many hours of hunting, the long archery season was slipping by without our glimpsing the big buck. I was resigning myself to the fact that he had moved out of the area or might even be dead. We’d had no word of a hunter taking him, but there are always poachers as well as natural misfortunes.

Marlowe finally got a good doe and quit hunting. Gene and I kept at it, but I had about given up hope on Mossy Horns. Then, one November evening, I saw him coming extremely cautiously down a slough 150 yards away. Unless he changed course, he’d walk past me beyond range. He stopped twice at the edge of thickets to watch and test the wind. So far as I could tell, his antlers were identical with those he’d carried a year before. I concluded I had learned something many hunters don’t know. Apparently nontypical whitetails remain in that category all their lives, growing a rack substantially the same shape each year.

I waited until he was beyond me, with a thick screen of brush between us, and then started the most careful stalk I’d ever made. A hard wind was blowing, and he was heading into it. By keeping off to one side with brush between us, maybe I could close in for a shot.

I tiptoed after him for half a mile. He stopped several times, and each time I waited. Three times he rubbed his antlers vigorously against a bush, and while he was doing so I sneaked closer. I had him in range twice, but there was too much brush in the way.

Finally he stopped again, at the border of a thicket, alternately standing quiet and alert, then fighting a bush with his hard and polished antlers. I inched in until I was 25 yards away and was slipping around a willow clump to shoot when a dry twig broke under my feet.

The buck didn’t look, stomp, or snort. He went out of sight in the brush in one crashing bound. Well, I reflected, no deer lives to reach that size without learning all there is to know about avoiding danger.

I saw him once more that year, on the last evening of the season, as I was coming up from the bottoms at dusk. The light was almost gone, but I made out the white throat patch of a deer, and then the huge antlers of Mossy Horns took shape in the gathering dark. He was standing in the open, out of range, calmly watching me. I stopped to stare at him, and when I moved he whirled, and his upflung flag waved derisively, then faded out of sight at the far side of the field.

“O.K., Mossy,” I muttered under my breath. “Next year it will be different.” It would have been, too, but for a piece of typical deer-hunter impatience and a blunder on my part.

That fall of 1960, our hunting party grew to four. Del Austin, a warehouse manager from Hastings and an enthusiastic convert to bowhunting, joined Marlowe, Halloran, and me.

I had kept track of the big deer all summer. Dan saw him about every three or four weeks, never far from his hangout on the Platte bottoms, and when the season opened on September 10, we all believed we had his habits figured out.

There was one particular spot in which I had faith, the corner of a cornfield bordering the bottoms. I had found his fresh tracks there three or four times toward the end of summer and concluded it was one of his regular crossing places. So I built a blind in a nearby cottonwood and resolved to stay in it until he came along.

I waited in that blind every chance I got for seven weeks, growing more and more impatient. Then, one cool afternoon toward the end of October, two bucks strolled out into the corn 200 yards down the fence. They were far from matching the deer I wanted, but they were good whitetails and I yielded to temptation. As soon as they were out of sight in the corn, I climbed down and started after them. I was pussyfooting down a corn row 70 yards from the tree when something made me look back. Mossy Horns was standing under my platform looking hard in my direction. Apparently, he wasn’t sure what I was, but he walked slowly away until he got my scent, and that was that.

About a week later, Charley Marlowe was in a tree blind when four deer walked past him at good range. He drove an arrow into a young buck, and it ran out into the corn and dropped. Before Charley could climb down, the big deer stepped out of the brush 30 yards away, stood broadside, blew a couple of times, and ran back toward the river. Marlowe’s license was filled, but he admitted afterward he was glad when the deer skedaddled.

“A man can stand just so much temptation,” he told us with a dry grin.

Before that season ended, I had another chance. I was back at my stand in the cottonwood, and my wife Velma, who has bowhunted as long as I have, was in a smaller tree about 50 yards away. We waited all afternoon, and dusk was deepening when I started to climb down. Just then I heard a twig break, and there was the big buck, head lifted, ears pointed ahead, taking short mincing steps. I had never seen an animal more alert.

I FROZE and let him walk under my tree and beyond it. Then I drove my arrow at his shoulder. I heard it hit, a good solid thunk, and he flinched and bolted. There was a woven-wire fence nailed to the tree Velma was in, and he crashed into it so hard he almost toppled her off her platform. Then he was gone.

We could find no blood, and by then the light was so poor we decided to go up to Dan’s house, kill half an hour over a cup of coffee, and come back with a flashlight. That was as long a 30 minutes as I can remember.

We found the feathered end of my arrow not far from where the deer had crashed into the fence, but that was all we found. There was no blood or any other hint of what had happened. I was haunted the rest of that season by worry that I might have killed him—that he might have crawled into a thicket to die without our ever finding his magnificent rack. The last week I filled my license with a 160-pound, three-point (Western count) buck, my third deer and the first with a bow.

Nothing happened the next summer to relieve my fears that I had killed Mossy Horns. For the first summer in three years Dan failed to see him, and we resigned ourselves to the likelihood that if my arrow had not finished him, time had. From the size of his rack when I first saw him in 1958, we concluded he’d be at least eight years old.

The next season didn’t have quite its usual appeal for me, and as it went along and my luck stayed bad, I felt less and less enthusiasm. Charley and Del each killed a nice doe — Del’s first deer — and my wife got a four-pointer. Gene was laid up temporarily from a heart attack. I kept on hunting alone, but my heart wasn’t in it.

The season was three quarters over and snow was piled in deep drifts on the bottoms before I got a chance at a deer. Late on a bitterly cold afternoon, I was back in the same tree where I had shot at the big buck when I spotted a button buck coming through the willows 100 yards away. Then a bigger one walked into sight behind him, and bringing up the rear was the deer I had given up seeing again.

My heart did a somersault. He was walking warily and craftily, turning his head from side to side to work that enormous rack quietly through the brush. It looked no different from when I had seen it last, except that it seemed bigger. The tangle of stubby points stood out like overgrown thumbs, and the down-curving prongs on either side of his head were at least a foot long. In spite of the icy wind, I started to sweat.

The two lead bucks turned out toward the corn, but the big fellow stayed in the willows. Halfway between the brush and the field, the smaller bucks tried to get through a deep snowbank but couldn’t, and they finally turned away from me to go around it. Now the big deer followed. It was as if he remembered that cottonwood of mine and was avoiding it.

While the three were picking their way through a clump of trees at the far end of the cornfield, half a dozen does came out of the willows single file, walked under my platform within six yards of me, and started to feed. The two smaller bucks came down along the edge of the field and joined them, but Mossy Horns hung back in the timber. It was almost dark before he ventured into the corn, and then he stayed well out of range.

That was the only time during the 1961 season that any hunter laid eyes on him, but at least we knew he was still in the area. I gave him up finally, and filled with a four-pointer.

Dan had a field of milo that he didn’t get around to harvesting that fall. A herd of whitetails fed there all winter, the big buck among them, and early in the spring, on the bottoms not far from that field, Dan had the rare luck to find his shed antlers lying close together. Next to the head itself, that was about as good a trophy as a man could ask for. The tips of several points were missing, but one down tine measured 11 inches, the other 13 (one still carried a ring of dried velvet), and the rack was the most impressive any of us had ever seen. I had proof now of every claim I had made about this deer for four years.

The story of that find has an interesting sequel. Last spring, some six months after Mossy Horns was finally killed, we learned that Max Wilkie, a farmer living about two miles from Dan, had found another set of shed antlers from this same buck four or five years before. The down-swept tine on the left side is broken off about three inches from the main beam on this set, and the right one is short, but from the shape and points there is no question that the rack belonged to a younger Mossy Horns.

In the summer of 1962, I decided that if I couldn’t get to the big buck, I’d try bringing him to me. I spent weeks cutting deer trails through the heavy brush of the bottoms, in places where I had seen him most often, and building tree blinds overlooking them. Then, a month before the open season, I cleared out to give him and the other whitetails a chance to get used to them.

Two other partners joined us that fall, Kenny Whitesel, a farmer living near Hastings and one of Nebraska’s top bowhunters, and Charley Marlowe’s 16-year-old son Chad. That made six in the party, and each of us had his heart set on Mossy Horns. I was beginning to worry on one score. Would his head still be the trophy it had been in the past? Unless we were wrong, he was not less than nine now, and bucks carry poor racks in their declining years.

I got the answer to my doubts before the season was many weeks old. A new interstate highway, I-80, was being built through our hunting grounds on the north side of the Platte, and the north channel had been temporarily dammed. Walking the dry river bed one afternoon, I saw unmistakable tracks where the big buck had gone up the bank into an alfalfa field. I tracked him to a willow-grown island, jumped him, and got a good look at his antlers as he crashed away. They looked as big as ever.

I avoided that island from then on, not wanting to drive him out of his bedding area, and I also shunned the trails he was using. I saw him twice the next week. The first evening I was in a tree where a runway crossed a big slough. Just before dusk, four or five does walked under the tree, and then a four-point buck followed, stopping beneath me to rub his antlers on a bush. The big deer showed up right after that, but he moved off without coming close enough for a shot. The next time he was even more cautious, sneaking out to the edge of the brush downwind from me and then vanishing quietly.

SEEING NO MORE of him for a week, I searched the river bed again, found his tracks on a trail he had not used before, and built a new blind. I had a hunch it was now or never. Bowhunting season would close November 2 for nine days while riflemen took the field. Mossy Horns had grown to a legend in that neighborhood now. A lot of hunters wanted him, and I doubted he’d survive the gun season.

An hour before dark, my first evening in the new blind, I saw him slip out of thick willows on an island and head my way. He crossed the dry channel, entered the brush below the bank on my side, and came on until he was only 15 yards from me. I had deer scent sprinkled around the base of the tree, the wind was in my favor, and I was sure it was all over but the shooting.

The deer had other ideas. He stopped in brush so thick I could barely make out his outline. Nothing that has happened to me in a lifetime of hunting shook me up the way the next 10 minutes did. They seemed like 10 hours. Neither of us moved a muscle. Although a deer is not likely to look up of his own accord, he is almost sure to detect the slightest motion, even in a tree overhead. Finally the buck turned, bounded up on top of the bank, still in thickets where no arrow could get through, and started to walk around my tree. The wind had died, and everything was so quiet I was afraid he’d hear my pounding heart.

He halted where a fence came down to the river, not 20 feet from my platform, and I wanted to try for him the way a strangling man wants air, but I knew better. If I muffed this chance, I couldn’t hope for another.

He tortured me for another 10 minutes, finally clearing the fence and walking out into a field of alfalfa. He was 45 yards from me when he stepped out of the brush, and I sent my arrow at him instantly. It sang just over his back and whacked into the ground beyond him. He was back in the thicket in one long jump.

WE WERE HUNTING every possible minute now, knowing the bow season would soon recess. On the last afternoon in October, Halloran, Whitesel, and I got to Dan’s place early, hurried to the bottoms, and chose our stands. Del Austin and Charley Marlowe left Hastings after work, knowing they’d have less than an hour to hunt but counting that worth the trip.

Del had planned to use one of my blinds but couldn’t afford to waste time looking for it. So he put up a small, portable platform he’d brought, a rig that could quickly be hung in a tree. Before he climbed up on it, he poured buck lure around the tree and trimmed away some willow tops that might interfere with his shooting.

There was only room to stand on the platform, and Del hadn’t hung it quite level. His legs ached and he couldn’t change position, but he stuck it out as long as there was enough light for shooting. At last he gave up, clipped his arrow back in the bow quiver and took out a cigarette before climbing down.

As he opened his lighter, he heard a crashing 50 yards upwind, and then the biggest deer he’d ever seen broke out of thick brush. In the fading light, Del could not see the horns clearly enough to identify the buck, but he realized that this was a buster whitetail and that its guard was down, maybe because of the deer scent around the tree. That can be a powerful attraction for a buck at the peak of the rut.

The deer came at a dead run, stopping once and half turning as if looking for something, then coming again. He skidded to a stop, broadside, 20 yards from the tree, and Del drove a broadhead in behind his front leg. The buck whirled, plowed into the brush, and was gone. Del heard him stop briefly 40 yards away, and then walk on through the dry leaves.

Marlowe, Halloran, Whitesel, and I got back to Dan’s about dark. We waited an hour, then started out with flashlights to look for Del. We met him halfway to the river, listened to his story, and went back with him to search for the deer. He was still not sure it was Mossy Horns, but from his description I had very little doubt.

We found the trail easily. There was a lot of blood, and before we had followed it far we found the broken arrow, snapped off 10 inches above the head. That meant a hard hit with deep penetration. We trailed the deer through brush and slough grass for three hours, and by then our lights were giving out and the blood sign was down to a few drops or a smear every 30 to 40 yards. At last we lost it altogether. Del tied his handkerchief on a bush to mark the place, and we went home to wait for morning.

I DIDN’T SLEEP MUCH, and at daylight I was back. I picked up the trail and had followed it another 100 yards when I heard Del and Dan coming. We spread out, and the next time I saw Del he was crouched down with his bow at full draw. But after a few seconds he eased off and motioned for me to circle in from the other side. Then I saw the deer lying in a clump of willows, antlers tangled in the brush. One look was all I needed. Del had killed the buck I had hunted for the past five years.

The signs of age were plain on him. He was gray around the face, his loins were sunken, and he carried hardly an ounce of fat. From what I know of meat animals, I estimated he was 60 pounds lighter than he’d been in his prime two or three years before, but still he dressed out at 240. His rack was less massive than the shed one Dan had found, but it was still a terrific trophy. He was as stout-hearted as ever, too. Del’s arrow had done a clean and thorough job, yet he had run nearly a quarter of a mile after he was hit.

Measured by Glenn St. Charles of Seattle, an official measurer for the Pope and Young and Boone and Crockett clubs, his rack scored 279-7/8 points. The Pope and Young Club is concerned with recording trophy game shot by bowmen, and this deer’s antlers exceed its existing record of 186-2/8 for a non-typical whitetail by nearly 100 points. Even more impressive than that, his rack is the third biggest recorded for a nontypical whitetail and the biggest ever claimed by a hunter. The two top heads in this category score 286 and 284-3/8.

But the late Grancel Fitz, writing in the most recent edition of Records of North American Big Game, published by the Boone and Crockett Club in 1958, said of them: “In the nontypical whitetail class we know nothing of the two very old and strikingly similar specimens which stand at the top, except that they are Texas bucks from the old-time Buckhorn Saloon collection in San Antonio … But both of these remarkably symmetrical freaks are far ahead of any other trophies in their class.” And certainly Mossy Horns was way ahead of the next buck on the nontypical whitetail list, shot in British Columbia in 1905 and scoring 245-7/8.

We could find no sign of my shot of two falls before, even when we dressed him, and the only guess we could make was that my arrow had struck one of the down-pointing tines alongside the buck’s neck and broken its head off without drawing blood.

We dragged him across the bottoms to the edge of the fields, and I stayed with him while Del and Dan went back after Del’s car. I had a lot to think about all the miles I had tracked him, the many times I had seen him, the shots I’d had and missed. Until the previous night, I had always kidded myself that I’d be the hunter to down him. I suppose because I had hunted him longer than anyone else and thought I had earned the right. I won’t say I wasn’t jealous of Del’s good luck, for I’m afraid I was. But at the same time, next to taking that tremendous rack myself, nothing could have pleased me more than having it fall to a hunting partner, a fellow bowhunter, and a sportsman who deserved it on every count.

Read Next: These 2 Record Whitetail Bucks Changed Bowhunting Forever

Turning that angle over in my mind, I felt better. And then I had another happy thought. The big buck had left plenty of sons there on the Platte bottoms. Some of them were bound to turn out big, and somewhere among them there might even be a nontypical rack something like his.

#186. Controversy Continues on Dhaulagiri as Expeditions Called Off

After Manaslu, Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er this season with no summits. The rope-fixing team says they stopped working for safety reasons, but some climbers suspect other motivations and describe a tense atmosphere.

Paul Clarke of Australia — who had been waiting at Camp 2 for five days — shared his frustrations with ExplorersWeb. Clarke had just learned that the rope fixers had stopped working above Camp 3 and were retreating. He described a lack of motivation among the Sherpa rope fixers after VIP clients with Seven Summit Treks, the company in charge of fixing the route, had called off their summit attempt. Soon after, all 20 climbers waiting at Camp 2 were told to return to Base Camp.

“Makalu Lakpa came through the lower camp this morning after the decision had been made,” Clarke said. “It was a pretty uncomfortable atmosphere, and I think everyone understands just how badly this has affected the rest of the teams on the mountain.”

Clarke’s outfitter, 8K Expeditions, sent a Sherpa team to retrieve their gear and tents from Camp 3 at 7,100m.

A helicopter lands at Dhaulagiri Base Camp. Photo: Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

Makalu Lakpa Sherpa is leading the 14 Peaks Dhaulagiri Expedition, one of the two largest teams, together with its sister company, Seven Summit Treks. Today, he posted a message explaining that increasing winds on October 10 resulted in a higher risk of slab avalanches on October 11, when his team was due to attempt the summit. He says that is the only reason his team returned to Base Camp.

In an unusual remark, Lakpa stated that he looks after his own group and cannot be held responsible for “other teams’ summit ambitions, climbing strategies, or rope-fixing arrangements.” He also noted that the rope-fixing work was assigned to Seven Summit Treks, not his team.

Finally, he spoke out against climbers who had expressed their disagreement yesterday:

To those criticizing our decision from a distance, I ask you to understand the actual mountain conditions before passing judgment. Assessing risks firsthand and making decisions that determine whether a team returns home safely is very different from commenting on social media.

Guides working for Lakpa’s company and for Seven Summit Treks have posted messages on social media supporting his decision. Benny Lieber, an American guide working for 14 Peaks, posted his assessment of avalanche risks on the mountain:

A post on Dhaulagiri conditions by Benny Lieber on Instagram. Photo: Benny Lieber/Instagram

Chhang Dawa Sherpa, leader of Seven Summit Treks, argued that the weather window was too short, given that a summit push would take “several days.” The plan was to move up to Camp 3 on October 11, reach the summit on the morning of October 12 (with October 13 as a buffer day), and return to Base Camp the following day.

Chhang Dawa, a director at Seven Summit Treks, posted about Dhaulagiri’s weather forecasts. Photo: Chhang Dawa/Instagram

Still, these explanations have not satisfied some climbers. Their biggest frustration came from watching the mountain in perfect, windless weather (though a wind plume eventually grew on the summit, according to Benny Lieber).

“From my perspective, one of the biggest frustrations is how badly the weather window appears to have been misread by Makalu Sherpa,” Paul Clarke said. “The strong winds and poor climbing conditions yesterday were not a surprise, since we had all been watching the forecasts for days, and winds in the 40–50kph range had been clearly visible well in advance.

“Despite that, Makalu Sherpa sent the rope-fixing team and his VIP clients higher on the mountain yesterday in conditions that were obviously going to be difficult. That has left climbers from multiple other operators stranded by a decision they had no control over. The consequence is that the rope-fixing team has now come back down, the VIP clients are no longer continuing [a helicopter was waiting for them as they arrived in Base Camp], and we have just been told that all our expeditions are over.”

Vincere Zeng of Singapore also shared her pòint of view with ExplorersWeb. Zeng has summited seven 8,000’ers, and was the first Singaporean woman to summit K2 and Annapurna. “I attempted it [Dhaulagiri] last autumn as well, so I was fully aware of the risks involved, which is why I had been monitoring the weather closely every day,” she said.

Zeng explained that her group was aware of high winds on October 9 and 10, and therefore waited at Camp 2. They planned to attempt the summit today, on October 12, in the morning. “We also considered Oct 12-13 as a possible buffer, as the next strong wind cycle was forecast to arrive around the afternoon of Oct 14,” Zeng explained.

“What I did not understand was why the 14 Peaks team chose to move toward Camp 3 (~7,000m) on Oct 10, which was the windiest day in the forecast, and then cancelled the rope fixing based on the conditions they encountered that day,” Zeng said. “From our side, we hoped we would at least have the opportunity to assess conditions during the originally planned Oct 11-12 window.”

Both Clarke and Zeng said that the 8K Sherpas who went to Camp 3 yesterday to retrieve equipment reported good conditions to that point.

“Of course, that does not mean conditions higher up, particularly around the traverse and summit slopes, were necessarily safe,” Zeng noted. “But it was one reason I hoped conditions could be reassessed once the forecasted wind had passed, especially as we still had time to do so. Instead, we were informed that the expedition was cancelled before we had that opportunity.”

Vincere Zeng (with green down suit) waits at Camp 2 in good weather last weekend. Photo: Vincere Zeng

Zeng explained she was “absolutely prepared to turn around if an assessment showed that conditions were unsafe.”

Clarke confirmed that all commercial expeditions on Dhaulagiri have called off their attempts. With the big teams pulling out, there is no manpower to launch another commercial-style attempt.

“At this point, nearly all of the teams have already packed up their Base Camp operations, and almost all of the climbers have flown out by helicopter, either yesterday afternoon or this morning,” Clarke said.

One team, however, has no intention of leaving. Andrzej Bargiel’s expedition, which includes a significant support team and film crew, is still hoping to summit and ski down the mountain, as he explained to fellow climber Xenia Santha of Hungary today.

“We wish Andrzej [Bargiel] the best of luck,” Clarke said. “If he can continue and summit, it will obviously provide another very clear picture of what the conditions on the mountain were actually like during this window.”

Risk assessment is always a tricky issue on commercial expeditions. Climbers pay large sums of money and expect every possible summit chance. It is often hard to explain when conditions are too risky, considering that factors include avalanche risks and wind, but also group sizes, the skills and endurance of guided climbers, complex logistics, and the disastrous consequences of a wrong decision.

However, in this instance, it is the lack of choices rather than the conditions that has frustrated climbers. Ironically, commercial expeditions on big mountains are more interdependent that ever, but communication between them, and sometimes with their clients, can be poor.

“As a client, I have no exact knowledge of the rope-fixing arrangement or collaboration agreed between the different outfitters,” Zeng said. “As we were a relatively small team with less manpower [8K Expeditions], we were to some extent dependent on the main rope-fixing team and whatever cooperation had been agreed between the operators. So, once the main fixing effort stopped, in practical terms it also affected our ability to continue.”

“Seven Summit Treks and Makalu Lakpa are now, from our perspective, trying to justify the decisions that were made by saying the weather was the reason they stopped,” Clarke concluded after reading the posts by Makalu Lakpa and Chhang Dawa today. “Based on the forecasts we had been watching for days, what we saw ourselves, and now the reports from climbers and Sherpas who were actually higher on the mountain, I simply don’t agree with that explanation.”

Large expedition operators sometimes react only when climbers openly share their experiences and thoughts, and their reaction is often to try to stop the dissemination of news from the mountains.

Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha, said media coverage had caused tension. Santha received a text message asking why she and Clarke had been speaking to the press. “I found that quite surprising; we have only spoken publicly about what we experienced firsthand and about decisions that directly affected our expedition,” Clarke said.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#187. Less Than 24 Hours After Becoming First to Repeat 5.15d, Jakob Schubert Tells Us What It Took

Jakob Schubert after making the world's first 5.15d repeat on 'DNA' in the Verdon Gorge of France. (Photo: Michael Piccolruaz)

In the near-decade since Adam Ondra established Silence (9c/5.15d) in 2017, the world’s hardest sport grade has remained only theoretical. Since then, four more climbers have proposed routes at the grade, but none had been repeated. That just changed.

On the afternoon of October 10, Austrian climber Jakob Schubert made the second ascent of DNA (9c/5.15d), a 55-meter route in France’s Verdon Gorge. French climber Seb Bouin made the first ascent of DNA in 2022. “I’m really happy,” Schubert told me over the phone the next day. “I would never trade this story for anything.”

With DNA, the 35-year-old Schubert has become both the first climber in history to repeat a proposed 5.15d route, as well as the first to climb two. His line B.I.G., in Flatanger, Norway, was the world’s third 5.15d proposal in 2023. Since Schubert has aligned with Bouin on his proposed grade, this also makes DNA the world’s first confirmed 5.15d route.

Schubert has tried every 5.15d except the newest line at the grade, Jorge Díaz-Rullo’s Café Colombia. He told me that DNA feels harder than his route B.I.G., and could be the hardest route at the grade. Partly, however, this is because of how height and reach-dependent DNA is.

“It’s a very morphological route,” explained Schubert, who stands 5’9”. “The shorter you are, the harder the route gets. At some point, it would probably be impossible. I’m only borderline tall enough.” Both DNA and B.I.G. rely on power endurance, but Schubert thought that the climbing on DNA felt more technical. “I’ve never done these crazy kneebars before,” he explained. “You really have to learn them on DNA, otherwise, certain moves are just impossible.”

Schubert said DNA felt similar to B.I.G., and he felt it’s certainly a 5.15d climb, but the projecting process was more daunting, due to the complex beta. “There’s so many more small, hard sections you need to learn,” he explained.

So although the route took Schubert fewer overall redpoint attempts than B.I.G., he invested far more time in preparation. In the end though, he said difficulty at the sport’s highest grade is largely subjective. At least at this early stage in the grade’s evolution, it’s almost impossible to say that any one proposed 5.15d line is harder than the other. All the 5.15ds are hard, they’re just hard in different ways.

“I think every [5.15d] climber would name a different route as the hardest for them,” Schubert observed. “Adam would maybe say B.I.G. I would feel like, ‘Whoa, Adam, you’re crazy. B.I.G. is the easiest for me.’ Adam would say for him, Silence is the easiest, for sure. Seb [Bouin] would say DNA is the easiest.”

As Schubert made the first 5.15d repeat in history, some 180,000 people were watching. He livestreamed his DNA ascent on YouTube, just as he did with B.I.G. back in 2023. In fact, you can find all of his redpoint attempts on the route over the past several days on YouTube.

But Schubert said that although livestreaming offers an intimate look at what a 5.15d ascent looks like, he noted that by the time he’s doing redpoints, he’s already put in the hardest work.

“Some people read ‘ninth live attempt’ on YouTube, and think this is basically my ninth try on the route, which is obviously far from the truth,” Schubert said. Since first trying DNA in 2024, he has put in at least 30 days on the route spread across multiple trips. But underlying these 30 sessions is also a deep bedrock of training and planning.

“You don’t see all the work that I’ve put in before I even did any redpoint tries, all the mental preparation I’m doing every day between tries, even on rest days,” he said. “I’m thinking over and over about the route, climbing it in my head, thinking about very small details that I could change … It’s a lot of work to get to this point.”

The DNA projecting experience, he said, was also made far easier by Bouin’s transparency and the footage of his first ascent. “We had the video from Seb, and he did a crazy job checking out the perfect beta for the route,” Schubert said. “I had to change a few [pieces of beta] because I’m way shorter than him, but I could copy a lot of beta, which saved a lot of time.”

Schubert, who has won more IFSC gold medals than any male climber in history, and podiumed at both Olympic Games, is likely the world’s most accomplished male competition climber. He said that the pursuit of perfection is precisely what makes projecting a route like DNA, compared to competition climbing, so meaningful to him.

“I could never climb this perfectly on a competition route, because it’s an onsight attempt,” he said. “That’s the cool thing about projecting. You can get to a point where you feel perfect on the wall, and that’s so amazing to achieve.”

The top comment on Schubert’s YouTube send video came from Adam Ondra, who congratulated him on his success, but also on his ability to handle the pressure of the livestreamed attempts. But Schubert told me that although livestreaming added some pressure, overall it actually made the send more enjoyable. He also clarified that he was the one who wanted to livestream his attempts—not sponsors or anyone else.

“It filled me with so much happiness, reading all the comments of people enjoying being part of the process,” he said. “It made [the climb] even more of a special experience.”

Schubert’s YouTube followers certainly seemed to agree. “I stopped everything to see the attempt, and I´m so grateful [for] the emotions you made all of us feel!” wrote one commenter. “Thanks for reminding me what a human being is capable of,” said another.

“I VERY rarely shout at the screen when I’m watching sports … but I did on this occasion when you stuck the crux move,” typed a third.

Uncut footage and livestreamed ascents are becoming more commonplace in hard sport climbing and bouldering. Scottish climber Will Bosi, for example, was also livestreaming his attempts on Silence this week. (Schubert is the only climber so far to livestream a successful 5.15d ascent.)

However, there is an equally well-established trend of the world’s best climbers intentionally working hard projects away from the spotlight. Some even keep their sends close to their chest for months afterward. Sean Bailey didn’t publicize his ascent of Duality of Man, another proposed 5.15d, until nearly a year after he clipped the chains. Shawn Raboutou took months to announce his V17 proposals Megatron and Alphane.

But Schubert said that as a professional climber, he sees himself as not just an athlete, but an entertainer. He wants to reduce the barriers between himself and his fans, climbing as transparently as possible.

“It filled me with so much joy,” he said of the response to his DNA livestream. “It felt like I got a lot of people even more psyched on climbing, inspired people, and that makes me really happy [because] I feel that’s also part of my job as a pro climber. We are, after all, like singers or actors or artists. We are trying to inspire people and get them psyched, and make their life better.”

I was somewhat reluctant to ask the guy who just climbed what is perhaps the world’s hardest route, “What’s next?” but when I did, Schubert admitted that he certainly has ideas. He tentatively plans to travel with Ondra to project Exodia, the world’s hardest proposed boulder problem (V18), first sent by Elias Iagnemma in Italy last November. He also hopes to work the Stefano Ghisolfi route Excalibur (5.15c).

Schubert did seem reluctant, however, to set his sights on another 5.15d, even in the distant future. “I don’t know how many more times I’m going to try [5.15d],” he said. “There’s a lot of effort and time you have to put in. It’s also a tough mental process.”

After all, only a few other routes proposed at the 5.15d benchmark exist in the world. Projecting them would entail multiple trips, each likely weeks long, which Schubert admitted is a time commitment he’s not sure he wants to make again. He’s also gunning for a third showing at the Olympics, in Los Angeles in 2028. “That’s something I obviously have to work hard for, which means a little bit less time for huge projects like this,” he said.

Then he paused. I was reminded that I was talking to him less than 24 hours after he clipped DNA’s chains. “Like I said, I have a feeling like maybe DNA is actually the hardest [5.15d] for me and the process could get a bit easier,” he said. “So we’ll see.”

#190. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Adventure Has No Retirement Age: Adventure is continuing well into the ninth decade of life for a growing number of paddlers and hikers. Ninety-one-year-old Dale “Greybeard” Sanders only took up extreme endurance challenges at 80. Since then, he has paddled the Mississippi River from source to sea twice, completed the Missouri River Race, and this year reclaimed the record as the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail.

The challenge of competing and breaking records keeps him going, but not everyone is chasing endurance records. For Wendy Eden, 77, the goal is just to be out in nature and to keep exploring her beloved Canadian wilderness on her own. That means adapting her approach as she gets older.

I Hitchhiked From Sydney to Perth: Aston Brown describes his experience of hitchhiking across Australia from Sydney to Perth. He sees hitchhiking as an opportunity to surrender control and connect with people he would otherwise never meet.

Far more common in the 1970s and 1980s, the practice plummeted in Australia because of its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who targeted hitchhikers. Now it is starting to pick up again, as online communities and social media introduce it to a new generation.

Brown recognizes that hitchhiking carries dangers and that his experience as a man does not reflect the risks women traveling alone face. Yet his journey left him with a sense of connection. He spent three days and 1,900km traveling with Neil, a 79-year-old widower, on a four-month road trip around Australia. He also met a Zimbabwean family who had left the U.S. because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns, a retired tractor enthusiast, and Doug, head of Australia’s national science agency, who invited him birdwatching to see one of the country’s rarest birds.

She Had a Will To Live: A 72-year-old hiker survived six nights in the wilderness after falling 30m down a steep embankment. Mary Beth Granbery was on the Cabin Creek Trail near Mount Shasta in California when she fell.

She had set out on a multi-day camping trip and was expected home within four days. When she failed to return, friends and family raised the alarm. Rescuers found her camper van at the trailhead and launched a search. They found her one day later, at the bottom of the embankment. Despite suffering injuries from the fall, dehydration, and hypothermia from the cool nights, Granbery was still conscious when the rescue team reached her.

Across Madagascar To Find The World’s Last Lemurs: Geena Truman and her husband took a 2,500km road trip across Madagascar to search for lemurs. In a rented 4×4, they set off from Antananarivo. On the RN7 highway, they drove through rainforest, highland rice paddies, canyons, and desert, encountering rare species including golden bamboo lemurs, ring-tailed lemurs, and Verreaux’s sifakas.

Leaving the highway, they ended up on rough tracks with tricky river crossings, mud pits, and routes so difficult to navigate that they hired a local guide, known as a pisteur, to find their way.

Driving through Madagascar’s iconic baobab trees towards Tsingy de Bemaraha and Kirindy Reserve. Photo: Geena Truman

Grand Ole Roadtrip: In the summer of 1976, six young climbers piled into a blue Ford van and drove west to tackle Wyoming’s Teton Range. That first trip to the Tetons saw them face loose rock on the Enclosure Ice Couloir, a terrifying slide down the Skillet Couloir that nearly carried two of the group over a glacier’s edge, and two separate encounters with violent thunderstorms that left them clinging to exposed rock.

At the heart of all of this was the Grand Teton Climbers’ Ranch (GTRC), an affordable base for mountaineers. It offered more than a cheap bed: It was a place to meet climbing partners, exchange stories, and recover from the day over shared meals. Today, the GTRC remains one of their favorite places on Earth.

Renate Powell Completes Munro Round in Barefoot Shoes: Renate Powell has completed her second round of Scotland’s 282 Munros, this time in barefoot shoes. The keen hillwalker turned to minimalist footwear in her forties when an old skiing injury left her knee in constant pain.

She started by walking just 100m a day, then spent more than a year gradually building up to take on a Munro in her barefoot shoes. Fourteen years after first trying them, she continues her long-distance walking, without the knee replacement that was initially suggested.

Climbing the Cuillin Munro in barefoot shoes. Photo: Gillian Parker

Mad, Bad and Dangerous To Know: Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, has been living with Parkinson’s for seven years. He’s been out of the public eye for two years, and his current state is uncertain.

Fiennes spent much of his life building a remarkable expedition career after serving in the military. His 1979-82 Transglobe Expedition saw him and fellow former SAS soldiers Charles Burton and Oliver Shepard complete a 60,000km circumnavigation using surface travel, crossing both Poles.

He later completed a 2,170km unsupported ski crossing of Antarctica with Mike Stroud, and attempted to reach the North Pole unsupported five times. After severe frostbite during a 2000 expedition, he famously amputated his own dead fingertips with a fretsaw. This article plots out the timeline of his extraordinary expeditions.

A Climber Has Now Called For Help Three Times in 2026: Two climbers had to be rescued on September 22 after becoming stranded on the 500m White Dyke scramble on British Columbia’s Edge Peak. The pair set out at 8:30 am, but later that afternoon, with only three hours until sunset, the less experienced climber was too exhausted to continue.

After two hours attempting to rescue themselves, they activated a Garmin SOS beacon. This is the third time one of the climbers in the duo has had to be rescued this year. Rescue veteran Brent Boulet warned that social media seems to be drawing less experienced people onto technical routes. He stressed the importance of realistic timing, turning back when necessary, and knowing a climbing partner’s capabilities before setting out.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.
