#193. What It Took to Kill the Biggest Buck of My Life

Published Oct 15, 2026 9:39 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

He was the most impressive buck we had on the farm that year, maybe any year, and I knew just where he lived. Or, at least, I thought I did. There’s a marshy creek that runs down the west side of the property, and that creekbottom transitions to a 100-yard-wide stretch of hardwoods that border a hayfield. The buck lived in the creekbottom and patrolled the hardwoods for does as they made their way up into the field.

I knew this because my hunting buddy Josh Dahlke and I had the whole area rigged with cellular trail cameras and we’d been monitoring the buck since August. Most of the photos we had of him came from a camera we’d set over a scrape in the timber, within 20 yards of a stand. This was a set that Josh and I had talked about for years, that he’d scouted the previous fall, and that we’d then hung together in the summer.

It was November 6 now, and I was parked about 300 yards away from that very stand, waiting in the predawn darkness. I wanted it to be light enough to slip through the woods without a headlamp but dark enough that I’d be in the stand and ready before legal shooting light.

With just the right amount of light, I left my truck and walked straight across the hayfield as quickly as I could. When I hit the edge of the wood, I stopped. Somewhere back there, probably, was what I hoped would become the biggest buck I’d ever killed. I’d spent months thinking about this deer and planned my work and family schedules around hunting him. I didn’t know if I would have a chance to kill him this morning. But I did know that by entering these hardwoods now, I would certainly risk blowing him out and ending my opportunity to hunt him for good.

In other seasons, on other big-game hunts, I’ve traversed dangerously steep mountain terrain, where a misstep could mean a deadly fall. I felt that same combination of fear and thrill now, peering into the dark woods. One swirl of wind, one misstep, and all could be lost. It was certainly not a life-or-death situation, but in this moment, it kind of felt like one.

And this is what any good adventure relies on: clear and substantial risk, plus the promise of an irresistible reward. Over the next several weeks, we’ll be publishing a series of adventure stories here on OL+. You can also read these features now through our iOS, or Android apps or on Apple News+. The risks in these upcoming stories are often physical and obvious (like freezing to death on a mountain), but they can also be intangible (like blowing a rare opportunity on a limited-entry bull tag). The rewards can be exotic (like the horns of a massive argali ram) or they can be rooted in personal history (like a single perfect archery shot after a decades-long bowhunting career).

The truth is, you don’t need to travel to far-off lands or climb the highest peaks to have a true hunting adventure. You just need a deep passion for the sport, and you must be willing to put that passion on the line.

I certainly felt like my deer season was teetering in the balance as I tiptoed toward that stand. My heart raced with every calculated step. My ears strained for the telltale sound of a deer bounding away through the darkness. But by the time I reached for my climbing sticks, I still hadn’t spooked a deer.

I climbed as quickly and quietly as I could, pulled up my bow, nocked an arrow, and looked up to see a deer walking toward me. It was a buck, and it looked like a pretty good one. Was it him? On impulse, I turned toward the deer, and he spotted the movement. He was 30 yards out and obscured by brush and darkness. But even so, he didn’t look as large as the buck I was hunting. I prayed that he wasn’t.

“He stopped briefly behind a small tree, but all the panic was gone. A summer’s worth of dedicated practice overrode any thought or feeling now.”

I reached for my binocular as he turned and slipped into heavier cover and disappeared. He didn’t fully spook, but he didn’t give me a good look either. Was that it?

I’ve interviewed serious deer hunters who have made deep sacrifices to hunt a single trophy buck. I know hunters who have ruined relationships and set back their careers to go all-in on hunting a giant buck they’d become obsessed with. Sometimes these stories end happily, with the hunter killing his buck and then coming back down to earth. Sometimes they don’t. I hadn’t been so extreme with this buck, and I’d never consider myself a big-buck trophy hunter, but I could feel myself slipping in that direction now. I had passed smaller bucks that I would have happily shot in previous years. I’d skipped out on time hunting with my dad and uncle to chase this buck, not to mention all those evenings missed with my wife and 2-year-old daughter.

I thought about all this over the next two hours as the sun climbed over the hardwood canopy. But eventually those thoughts were interrupted by a distant grunt. I looked north to see a massive, gleaming rack 100 yards away in the timber.

“Oh God,” I whispered aloud, overtaken by a moment of panic.

I stood slowly and clipped my release onto the D-loop with a shaking hand. The buck marched directly at me. At one point he disappeared behind a giant oak tree, but I could still see his shadow on the forest floor, closing the distance quickly. Somehow this made me even more nervous.

By the time the buck got to 40 yards, I’d regained some composure. If the deer broke to my right, he’d get downwind of me and surely spook. If he broke to my left, I’d get a good, close shot at him. The buck angled left, and I came to full draw.

He stopped briefly behind a small tree, but all the panic was gone. A summer’s worth of dedicated practice overrode any thought or feeling now. He stepped from behind cover, only 20 yards away, and my arrow zipped behind his shoulder. He ran for 60 yards, stopped, and fell over dead. I watched him for a long time through my binocular. Then I sat down and soaked in one of the best moments of my deer-hunting life. The adventure was all over.

This story originally ran in the 2022 Adventure Issue of Outdoor Life.

#196. 7 Odd Deer Hunting Tactics You’ve Probably Never Tried But Should

Published Oct 14, 2026 6:56 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’ve probably heard about all the standard deer hunting tips and tactics by now. Target pinch points and funnels during the rut, mind the wind, monitor major food sources, so on and so forth. But what are the secret tactics that real hardcore whitetail hunters are using? You know, those oddball deer hunting tips that don’t typically get covered in articles. Turns out, there are quite a few.

Take for example, my friend Eliot Strommen. When he glasses a whitetail buck crossing a field of alfalfa or wheat, swaggering alone or trailing a doe, he watches where the deer enters the timber, then eases downwind into position as close as he dares. The longbow hunter stands behind a tree, picks up a stick and starts cracking logs and whipping brush. He picks up his right foot and paws one, two, three…then with the left, one, two, three.

“If you watch a buck paw the ground or scrape that’s the sequence they use,” says Strommen, who wraps up his routine by pinching his nose and cutting loose a whiny grunt-snort-wheeze with his voice.

The idea is to sound like an inferior buck in the brush, one that is roaming around a mature deer’s space and getting on his nerves. “After making all that racket, I’ve had bucks run up to within 30 yards of me, wild-eyed and hair raised,” he says. “They stamp and snort, it’s pretty wild.”

His tactic might seem odd to some, but it works. Here are a few more tricks you have probably never tried before, but should this season.

One late October morning I smoked an 8-pointer with my muzzleloader. His hocks were black as clumps of coal, and he reeked so badly I almost choked as I opened him up . Pop, pop, pop in the leaves. I peeked up and saw a 10-pointer boring down on me, eyes ablaze and tines held low.

The intruder marched to within 20 yards. I crouched behind the dead deer and shivered. The buck stopped, stared, detected no threat and turned and swaggered away.

It was one of my wildest hunts ever and it taught me something. For a week or so in the late pre-rut, dominant bucks looking to mix it up are drawn to the musk of one another. Play off that and set a mix of buck urine and/or tarsal near your stand. If you can hack the black hocks off a buck your buddy shot earlier in the week, do it.

Hang wicks with buck scent or hocks near your post and be on your toes, especially if you’re hunting on the ground. A crazed, 200-pound buck homing in on the musk of what he perceives to be a rival is one bad dude.

You don’t have to wait until gun season to get out of a tree and stalk. One November day bowhunter Don Kisky left his Iowa farmhouse with 5 steps in his pocket and a small lock-on stand on his back. He’d been seeing little deer movement from his best stands the last few days, and it was time to change it up.

“When bucks are locked down with does and breeding them or getting ready to, many of them aren’t in their core areas anymore,” he says. “That’s why the woods seem to go dead and your stands go cold. Many bucks and their does are away from the main timber, out in a grassy ditch, brush pile, cedar clump or other out-of-the-way spot. They won’t move for several days, so find them and go to them. The bucks are so focused on their doe that their guard is down, and if you stalk right you can get super close.”

Kisky climbed an oak tree that day, glassed the CRP ground for an hour and spotted a big 11-point curled beneath a cedar tree across a pasture. The buck, tongue lolling, looked exhausted from chasing and breeding his doe.

Kisky wasted no time bailing out of his makeshift observation post. He got the wind, stalked for nearly an hour, closed to within 20 yards, drew his bow, rose up over a grass patch, and nailed the 162-incher.

Even when Kisky is sitting in one of his best tree stands and spots a buck tending or bedded with a doe, he doesn’t think twice about climbing down if the situation is conducive to a stalk.

“Most bowhunters that spot a buck with a doe like this are reluctant to move,” he says. “They sit there second-guessing and miss out on a golden opportunity. Look things over and make a plan. If the wind, terrain and cover are right for a stalk, don’t be scared to get out of your tree and go make it happen.”

One season in Illinois I saw a 10-pointer, his rack would go 170 if it was an inch, coming on a trail, moving right to left, upwind, strolling with his head down, the way you want a buck to walk into killing range. He was 60 yards when I stood and clipped the release to the string. It struck me and I smiled, “I am going to kill a Booner with my bow.”

At once the buck stopped, wheeled and leaped into the brush. I got to looking around and wondering when it hit me, “He smelled me at the point where I had walked across that trail 3 hours earlier.”

Ever since, I have never stepped foot on or near a deer trail. I always parallel a trail well on the downwind side of it. When I have to cross one, I take a few steps back, take off and jump as far and high as I can. Sounds silly and a little overboard, but by launching you leave no scent on the trail or several feet off to either side of it. I’ve seen with my own eyes that it makes a big difference.

Read Next: 3 Totally Normal Tactics Deer Hunters Used to Think Were Really Weird

One of my mentors in the 1990s was Jack Atcheson Sr., a renowned hunting consultant and taxidermist who has hunted on 5 continents and shot as many head of game as any man on earth, from Cape buffalo to elk to sheep to all the varieties of North American deer, and some big ones.

One time on a pack-in hunt for mule deer in Wyoming, Jack told me we were going to still-hunt the entire week, and he was going to teach me how to do it.

“I’ve been hunting deer for 20 years,” I reminded him with a smirk.

“Yeah, but this week you’re going to learn how to do it right.”

On day one, we split apart about 200 yards and still-hunted west toward our landmark, a towering crag. I arrived in an hour, sat on a log and waited. Two hours later, in creeped Jack.

“Two bucks, one a big 4-point, and a small herd of elk,” replied. “You?” he asked with a sly grin.

I had jumped one doe, and I got Jack’s message loud and clear.

For the next 5 days we hunted side by side, creeping up mountains and down drainages, stopping often to scan wide with our eyes and glass tighter into the cover. Every 100 yards or so, we’d stop, turn, creep back 50 yards and re-scan the terrain where we had just come from.

On the last day, that is how I found and shot my buck.

“Every person I’ve ever hunted with, and there have been many hundreds, moves way too fast and never looks back,” Atcheson told me. “Still-hunt as slowly as you can for 50 yards, and then slow down some more for the next 50. Stop often, always beside a tree that you can use as a rifle rest if you need it. Every several hundred yards, fishhook back and look where you came from. You’ll see and shoot a lot more bucks that way.”

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season

Dr. Grant Woods is not only one of the top whitetail biologists in America, he’s also a hard-core bowhunter. That’s why I put so much stock in his research, from the routine to the, well, strange.

The Missouri researcher has captured and analyzed hundreds of thousands of trail-camera images over the years, with many of the best shots coming at scrapes doctored with a variety of scents and lures. So what’s the best scent to attract bucks to scrapes?

Woods has found that both mock scrapes created with human urine and pre-existing real scrapes doctored with pee produce the most buck sightings and, get this, the most mature buck sightings.

“It happens more often than random chance can account for,” Woods says. He and other scientists note that mammals like deer and bears are likely drawn to human urine out of curiosity of the smell, as well as the salt therein. Forget that pee bottle you’ve been fiddling with for years.

One day I scouted a 50-acre woodlot and found a dry, shallow creek bed running through the length of it. I walked the ditch until I found the spot where several deer trails converged and crossed it. The next morning the deer would be coming back into the woods to bed from alfalfa to the north, and the wind would be out of the west. Perfect!

Before dawn I found a spot on the east side of the pinch point, lay down and dozed until sunrise. I perked up and kicked back against the ditch bank, so just the top of my head was showing. The leaves were down, and I could see well to the north. As the sun got higher, the deer started coming. The first two animals walking on the trail were bucks, a fat 8-pointer followed by a bigger 10.

With the bucks 100 yards out and approaching, I rolled onto to my knees, stayed crouched, nocked an arrow and put pressure on the string. The 8-pointer stepped behind a tree, and I didn’t wait. When he dropped down into the ditch to cross it, I ran an arrow through his lungs. He ran up and out of the ditch, but he didn’t go far.

You don’t find this type setup very often, but when you do, you’ve got one of the best spots ever for an archery ground attack. The ditch or depression should be only about 3 feet deep, so you can lie back, watch, roll onto to your knees and draw your bow and kill a deer when he eases into the ditch or walks parallel to it.

Read Next: 101 Best Deer Hunting Tips For the Rut

Illinois hunter Dan Perez hasn’t killed dozens of 150-inch-plus bucks by being shy. When the weather turns brutal and the creeks freeze solid in the Midwest he rolls into his best spots with his bow or gun, pack, tree stand — and a sledgehammer.

“If you crack open some moving water near a crop field, you can have fantastic action,” he says, “especially if it’s been a dry fall and there’s not a lot of standing water around.”

One time a few years back, Perez dropped the hammer and battered a big hole in a frozen creek near a cornfield, then hung a tree stand on the east side of it. When he returned 2 days later on a northwest wind the joint was littered with tracks, rubs and scrapes, and it stank of rutting deer. Between 1 and 3 p.m. 5 different bucks followed does in for a drink. At 4:30 he drew his bow and whacked a 10-pointer coming to the only open water for a mile.

#197. Kyrgyz Climb 'Eternal Flame' Route on Nameless Tower

On September 28, a Kyrgyz team made its country’s first ascent of 6,239m Nameless Tower.

The expedition was led by Mikhail Mikhailov, known for his role in the 2004 North Face ascent of Jannu, which earned a Piolet d’Or, and for the 2009 first ascent of Peak 6134 on Minya Konka with Alexander Ruchkin, according to Mountain.ru.

Other members of the Nameless Tower group include Mikhail Danichkin, Timur Akbashev, Aidar Akbashev, Zarina Kutanova, and Aleksei Pototsky. The Kyrgyz team carried out the technical climb of this soaring granite spire, one of the Trango Towers, via the famous Eternal Flame route.

Nameless Tower. Photo: Timur Akbashev/Mountain.ru

Eternal Flame is one of the most celebrated big-wall routes in the Karakoram. It was first climbed in September 1989 by Kurt Albert, Wolfgang Gullich, Christof Stiegler, and Milan Sykora on Nameless Tower’s South Face. The original climbing route is roughly 650m long, on a vertical wall with a total height of about 1,000m. It was graded VI, 7b+, A2.

The route combines sustained hard granite climbing with the altitude, logistics, and objective hazards of a 6,000m Karakoram peak, which is why it has remained a major objective for both free climbers and traditional alpinists. The Kyrgyz ascent adds its country’s name to the short list of teams that have summited by this classic line.

#200. Dhaulagiri: Rope Fixing Halted For Unclear Reasons

About 20 climbers from several teams had planned to start their summit push on Dhaulagiri today, and conditions couldn’t be better: bluebird skies, low wind, and setting snow. So why are climbers stuck at Camp 2? And why are they so angry?

“We are…stuck here at Camp 2 waiting for the route above us to be fixed,” Paul Clarke of Australia texted to ExplorersWeb this morning.

As Clarke explained, the Sherpa team from Seven Summit Treks assigned to fix the route on Dhaulagiri this year refuses to lay ropes on the last sections above Camp 3.

“From what we are being told here at Camp 2, SST’s VVIP clients are no longer planning to climb higher,” Clarke said. “As a result, the company has little motivation to continue fixing the route for the remaining climbers.

The rope-fixing team had laid ropes until some 400m above Camp 3 earlier last week. The SST leader, Makalu Sherpa, shared his latest update on Friday. At that time, he reported everything was going well. The rope-fixing team made good progress while the clients waited at Camp 2. Neither SST nor 14 Peaks Expeditions has updated about Dhaulagiri since then. There have been no safety concerns reported during the current push.

In recent years, 8,000m peaks have been fixed either by a dedicated team assigned by the Expedition Operators Association of Nepal or by agreement among the companies on the mountain. They assign the rope fixing to a team of volunteers, whom the other operators all chip in to pay. Most 8,000m clients these days lack the skills to climb on their own and depend entirely on fixed ropes (and a packed trail) prepared by Sherpas.

The assigned rope-fixing team may stop for safety reasons, such as bad weather or risky conditions. We are waiting for further statements to clarify the situation. For now, unless a different group of Sherpas takes over, there will be no summit push.

This has frustrated those like Clarke and his climbing partner, Xenia Santha of Hungary. The pair patiently remained at Base Camp during the storm two weeks ago and have been at Camp 2 for five days, waiting for their moment. It’s mid-October, and there will probably be no further opportunities for them.

Today, Anni Penttila of Finland posted a text in Finnish on Instagram that translates to:

“Nothing came of it this time, either. It’s so disappointing that there’s really nothing to say at this point. Everyone turned back to Base Camp today.”

Anni Penttila’s story today from Dhaulagiri.

As the clients all retreat, Andrzej Bargiel remains at Base Camp with his large support and film team. The Polish skier intends to climb and ski down Dhaulagiri without oxygen. He has already skied eight other 8,000m peaks in that style, including Everest.

#201. ‘I Was on the Clock.’ Ohio Bowhunter Gets Permission for Just 30 Days, Tags Giant on the Opener

Published Oct 14, 2026 4:22 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Central Ohio is a well-known big-buck haven, and Daniel Schwartz knew exactly where he would be hunting the afternoon of the Sept. 26 opener.

“I had a good history of an older, mature buck from camera pictures,” Schwartz tells Outdoor Life. “I figured the deer was six years old, and although there were other big bucks in the area, he’s the one I wanted opening day.”

Schwartz says he had the green light to bowhunt the farm for only 30 days, so he felt pressure to tag a deer during that time.

“That’s why I named him ‘Timer,’ because I was on the clock to get him,” says Schwartz, a businessman from the town of Marengo.

Schwartz had hung a lock-on stand on the edge of a bean field, and it was positioned ideally for a northwest wind.

“But as we got closer to opening day the weather forecast changed and we were going to have a southwest wind,” Schwartz says. “I went into the area and hung another stand on the bean field that would be perfect for a southwest wind, which is what we had on opening day.”

Late the afternoon of Sept. 26, Schwartz and his cameraman buddy, Dylon Gandee, used electric bikes to quietly access the farm. They parked in cover and climbed 16 feet up to the two stands they’d set in the same tree for the afternoon hunt.

“I was hunting a trail where Timer was coming out of a bedding area and into the beans to eat. Some other deer came into the beans that afternoon, and some big bucks. But about 7 p.m., Timer stepped into the field and offered me a 32-yard shot.”

The deer wasn’t fully broadside, and Schwartz says his arrow hit a touch high. But when Schwartz and Gandee climbed down, they found Schwartz’s arrow had passed through.

They also found a faint blood trail where the buck had disappeared into woods back toward his bedding area. The men decided to back out and return at 9 p.m. to trail Timer.

“My buddy Jacob Mosher came back with Dylon and me, and we followed the blood trail into the woods. Timer only went 30 yards into the timber, and we found him dead.”

Schwartz took Timer to Toby Hughes, a Buckmasters master scorer in Caledonia. Hughes scored the 16-point buck with 22-inch inside spread at 180 inches.

Schwartz will have his buck mounted by a taxidermist, and a video of his hunt for Timer is on his YouTube channel.

Read Next: ‘I Was Shaking.’ Georgia Hunter’s First Archery Buck Could Be the New State Record

During his hunt for Timer, Schwartz saw another giant buck he called Toby. Schwartz figures the deer is four years old, and plans to return to hunt him next year.

#204. Weekend Warm-Up: Sending Ivindo Falls

Gabon Uncharted: Sending Ivindo Falls follows a crew of young kayakers, as they attempt to paddle 150km down the Ivindo River’s many rapids, gorges, and waterfalls.

The four kayakers are what the film’s narrator calls the “top of the crop.” After taking a moment to admire this charming malaphor (I think our narrator has combined “cream of the crop” and “top of the class”) we meet the Send team. Leader Adrian Mattern of Germany spent years planning their trip to Gabon, bringing with him the talkative Dane Jackson, patient Kalob Grady, and Bren Orton. Orton signed on with the shiny-faced, inevitably short-lived optimism of a youngster in 1914 headed for the front, sure of being home by Christmas.

“Apparently,” the narrator notes, “no one told him what he was getting into on this trip.”

Once on the ground, they load up their supplies and set out on a long stretch of flat water. Struggling along behind, we meet the film crew, an interesting behind-the-scenes look at the process of filming a professional, well-funded adventure documentary. Filmmaker Olaf Obsommer, photographer David Sodomka, and narrator David Arnaud do everything the Send team does, backward and in heels. Or, no — I’m thinking of Ginger Rogers.

Obsommer was part of the first team to scout the river by kayak in 2007. They portaged past most of the rapids for safety. Nowadays, better kayaks and the ability to scout ahead by drone will, hopefully, let them complete what he started.

At the first of four whitewater sections, Kongou, they settle in to take the rocky labyrinth piece by piece. If they take the wrong branch, they’ll be heading over a 25m waterfall.

Adrian is entranced by Kongou Falls, and only when the team delicately sit him down and explain that he would very likely drown, which would be awkward, does he agree to move on. Photo: Screenshot

They work their way down the river looking for rapids that will not kill them immediately. On the way, they get advice from Juste Parfait Zangonga, a local expert, on how to not be killed by elephants, gorillas, crocodiles, vipers, or hippos.

The next rapids, Mingouli, are less maze, more rollercoaster. The Send team can finally start living up to their name. Between first descents, they paddle past a family of elephants and get devoured by insects.

First descent down a tricky section of Mingouli. Photo: Screenshot

Kouata Mango, section three, is where Mattern finally gets to send a massive waterfall. The team agrees that this one is less likely to kill him badly, and over the side he goes.

Tsengue Lelendi, the final set of rapids, rounds out the trip. The laconic Kaleb takes a look at one particularly rough section and tells our narrator that the rapid is unrunnable. The rest of the team spends a long time debating it, anyway. Lo and behold, he’s right. After scouting with drones, mapping every angle, and discussing the route at length, they agree to skip a section of the rapid. The chain will still have just a few missing links left.

“A part of this river will remain untouched,” Arnaud concludes, “as it should, probably.”

#205. 23 Hunters, 46 Deer, and a Record-Book Buck: Inside a Classic Mule Deer Camp

Published Oct 14, 2026 2:32 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “Buckskin Bonanza,” appeared in the September 1961 issue of Outdoor Life.

During most of that raw and bitter afternoon, I followed a mule-deer track which was hard to believe. The sharp prints were nearly as big as the palm of my hand.

Sometimes the prints were distinct in the snow that had fallen a few days before. Elsewhere they vanished as the biting wind blew snow across them. My ears and fingertips were numb, and the farther I traveled, the more elusive became the trail. Several times I almost gave up, but these were the biggest deer tracks I’d ever seen.

“I’ll cross just one more ridge,” I promised myself, thinking of the long hike back to the jeep. “Then I’ll turn back.”

I trudged ahead and found the tracks again, 100 yards or so beneath a low ridge. I followed them slowly toward the crest, trying to keep the snow from crunching too noisily underfoot. Just under the crest I paused to catch my breath before peering over the top. There, not 200 paces away, my deer was standing and watching his back track. He was even bigger than his hoofprints suggested.

As carefully as possible, I raised my .270 behind the trunk of an aspen. Using the tree as a rest, I held the crosshairs of my scope squarely on the big animal. He had five points on each side, and the rack was thick and heavy. But even as I counted the points, I caught movement in a clump of trees beyond the buck. It was another muley almost as big as the buck I’d followed. Then suddenly the landscape before me was alive with deer.

Just by panning my scope from left to right, I saw six more deer — all within good range of my .270. Each was the kind of beautiful trophy that deer hunters dream about.

I studied the herd a long time, perhaps too long, trying to pick out the best rack. Several bucks began to drift away. The biggest ran. I never did pull the trigger; the deer season wouldn’t open for two more days.

Finding these bucks was the result of a pre-season reconnaissance made especially to locate the big ones. I carried the rifle only because this country was also good for bears and lions, on which the season is never closed.

Though I saw no bears or lions, in a few days of wandering across the West Tavaputs Plateau of northeast Utah, I found enough deer for a lifetime of hunting. It’s a region that more and more sportsmen are bound to find.

This Tavaputs country came to my attention in a roundabout way. First I noticed in the official Utah Fish and Game magazine that a record kill of 128,000 deer had been made in the state during 1959. A similar score was predicted for last year. That 1959 bag of mule deer was the largest anywhere in the nation. Even more important to me was the unusually large ratio of trophy heads. I’m always looking for new and better deer-hunting areas, so I filed this information away.

In the spring of last year I traveled to Utah to fish and explore some remote parts of the Green River country. That’s when I met Jim Hurst, who leads an exciting, sometimes perilous, life. He’s a bush pilot whose best customers are uranium prospectors, petroleum scouts, and sportsmen. Jim also flies the mail to remote ranches, and every year he participates in river rescues on such wild stretches of river as Desolation Canyon on the Green and Cataract Canyon on the Colorado. Many boatmen owe their lives to him.

One day we were flying over Desolation Canyon, and Jim pointed a finger toward the trackless landscape to the west.

“That’s great deer country,” he shouted above the motor’s roar. “The best I’ve ever found anywhere.” That rang a bell; I remembered the magazine report.

Next day Jim introduced me to Ray (Budge) Wilcox who operates a vast cattle ranch in the middle of that West Tavaputs Plateau. Thereafter Budge and I carried on a lively correspondence right up until deer season.

“Why don’t you be our guest?” Budge had written during the summer. “Plan to arrive a week before the season. Deer are easy to get, but with a free week to scout around, we can get a line on some bucks as big as our yearling heifers.”

He didn’t have to elaborate. I arrived in Dragerton a week before opening day, and Budge and his oldest son, Don, were there to meet me. We drove 30 miles across steep and upside-down country to the Range Valley Ranch, which is co-owned by Budge, Don, and Don’s younger brother, Waldo. Besides the cattle operation, they entertain hunters for a reasonable fee. They furnish meals, transportation, lodging, guide service — the works.

There are several ways to contact ranchers, and these will work almost anywhere in the West. One is by local inquiry — around farm and ranch-supply shops or around cattle auctions. Another way is to write to the local chamber of commerce, to the state fish and game department, or to the county agricultural agent. This last man really knows his way around.

The cost of your hunt depends on how the rancher operates. For instance, will he let you set up your own camp somewhere? Can he accommodate you if you want room and board instead? Conceivably a hunt, exclusive of licenses and transportation, could cost you as little as $25 for a small party. On the other hand it could cost as much as $200 per person for the whole season. A Utah nonresident license is $40.

The layout at Range Valley is actually two ranches. The first, or winter, ranch is a picturesque spread deep in a red and blue rock canyon formed by Range Creek. The elevation is about 8,000 feet. It’s in this vicinity that the Wilcox cattle herd in winter. Although the Tavaputs region is extremely dry, several clear, cold springs keep Range Creek running the year around. I recall when I arrived, the sagebrush in surrounding meadows was fragrant, and giant cottonwood trees all along the river were as bright as nuggets of gold.

Don told me some interesting stories about the Mokies, a civilization of cliff dwellers who long ago inhabited the area. Tradition has it that they seldom grew more than four feet tall. Their tiny “apartments,” granaries, and crude pictographs still exist on nearby canyon walls.

Also still in evidence are drawings made later by Indians. They seem to show that rattlesnakes, deer, sheep, and bears lived in the valley in those days; today only the sheep are missing. Still later, the valley was a hiding place for outlaw Butch Cassidy’s Wild Bunch. The first homesteader was an army deserter from Fort Duchesne to the north. His shack and hay derrick are still standing.

The second, or summer, ranch is breath-taking in its location on a canyon rim 10,000 feet high. Almost from the cabin door a canyon falls away in a dizzying, near-vertical slope. But behind the main building stretch thousands of acres of rolling plateau. It’s a mixture of sage and grass upland laced with strips of quaking aspen. Together, the summer and winter ranches comprise the finest of mule-deer range.

Budge and I stopped long enough at the lower ranch to drop Don off there. Then we continued up to the summer camp where we’d do most of our deer reconnaissance. I’d thought the driving was tough enough on the way to the lower place via a winding road and a wind-swept 10,000-foot pass. But it was like turnpike travel compared with the road to the summer camp. I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a weak heart.

This trail is a thin strip dynamited out of sheer cliff in places where even a bulldozer couldn’t operate. It has 12 switchbacks to climb 2,000 feet in less than a mile. And since it’s impossible to turn a jeep around on several of the switchbacks, you have to back up part way. Budge drove in four-wheel drive.

When we were about halfway to the top, wet snow began to fall. We finally arrived, after constantly skirting the edge of oblivion, and I had a new respect for both my host and his vehicle.

I also had a tremendous appetite for the extravagant T-bone steaks that Pearl Wilcox, Budge’s wife, prepared on our arrival. Waldo and his wife Julie joined us for dinner.

That night I slept with visions of deer running up and down the cliffs.

In the morning, the West Tavaputs Plateau was a blinding white. Five inches of snow had covered the high country during the night, but the storm had passed and the sky was deep blue from horizon to horizon. We could see that no snow had fallen at lower altitudes, at least not in Desolation Canyon.

Budge and I enjoyed a breakfast big enough for four men, pulled on heavy jackets, and went out into the cold.

“We’ll take the jeep,” he said, “and sashay straight across the plateau to get you acquainted. After that, we can separate and cover more country.”

“Sounds sensible to me,” I said, “but I’ll need a little time to get accustomed to this altitude.” I live in Columbus, Ohio, where it’s only 500 feet above sea level; two miles higher made quite a difference.

“Just take it easy at first,” Budge advised. “But carry your rifle, because lions like to run after a fresh snow. You might see one.”

The jeep coughed and sputtered several times before starting, while I scraped a crust of snow from the windshield. Once we were under way, Budge said, “I think you were mighty wise to get here early — especially with this new snow. I figure the biggest bucks will be more bunched up than ordinarily at this time. They’ll be harder to find, but when you do find them, you’ll know how to save plenty of footsteps once the season opens.”

During the next few days we covered plenty of Utah’s most air-conditioned real estate, both by jeep and on foot. On southern exposures, some of the snow melted; on northern slopes, it remained. It was a pleasure to reconnoiter the land with Budge. He has spent all of his 58 years in this part of the West, and he loves it. We saw plenty of deer.

We found one spot where a lion had stalked a small band of deer and then had waylaid a forkhorn buck not long before we discovered the kill. On another occasion we had a close look at a pair of golden eagles. At dusk on still another day, I saw a spectacular scene I’ll never forget. In an irrigated alfalfa field above the winter ranch buildings, we counted 65 deer at one time. I’ve traveled widely in deer country, but can’t recall anything to match this.

There was just one disappointing note: Among all those muleys were only two or three bucks in the true trophy class.

The big herd, though, was a welcome sight to Budge, for he’d have 23 hunters coming to the ranch on the eve of opening day. His 16 bowhunting guests had scored 100 percent during an earlier archery season. And now he was optimistic about the rifle season.

The dates of Utah’s deer season vary from year to year. Generally, though, the bow season opens October 1 and runs for two weeks. The rifle season opens toward the end of October, often on the third Saturday or third weekend.

Since I wanted to see more really big deer, I returned to the high camp next day to continue my exploration. Experience and a strong hunch told me that the biggest bucks would still be in the highest country despite the snow. That’s how I happened to follow that one big track I mentioned earlier to the six big deer on Monument Knoll, where the elevation is about 10,500 feet. That’s also how I found still other big bucks in the same area the next morning while Budge went into Dragerton to pick up his party of hunters.

It’s always exciting to spend the eve of opening day in a deer camp. Of the 11 California hunters who arrived at the upper camp, even those who’d scored in their own state’s deer season were full of expectation. They oiled rifles, swapped yarns, and made a few friendly bets on the biggest buck. Then they all retired early.

Next morning Pearl Wilcox was the busiest person in camp. She fried enough bacon and eggs and made enough hotcakes to feed everyone in the county. With these calories under their belts, the Californians scattered to every corner of the plateau before daybreak. I headed straight for Monument Knoll and wasn’t too surprised to find Budge going the same way. Two other hunters joined us.

“Let’s surround the area,” Budge suggested, “and stillhunt it until noon.” As an afterthought he added, “Then I’ll get the jeep and pick up the deer.”

He was mighty optimistic, I thought, as I went my own way. But so was I.

I’d no sooner separated from Budge than I found the fresh tracks of eight or nine deer heading for lower altitudes, but I didn’t bother to follow; all were obviously small animals. Instead I continued along a contour, climbing occasionally to the rounded summit of Monument Knoll. Suddenly a fine muley buck and I were looking at each other less than 50 paces apart.

For a moment I stood flat-footed. With a mittened hand, I fumbled for the safety on my .270, a Remington Model 721 with homemade myrtle stock. I tried to find the deer in my scope. The buck stood and watched. It wasn’t until my scope’s crosshairs were wavering on his neck that he bounded off, but only to stop and stand motionless 50 yards farther away. I aimed again, but lowered the rifle. He was a good buck, but not up to what I was looking for.

I’d just started on my way again when there was a shot not far to my right. I hurried that way and found Budge just under the ridge dressing out a bragging-size muley. Its rack looked as big as a rocking chair. Budge first saw the fat six-pointer silhouetted on the skyline; immediately it broke and ran. It didn’t even flinch when he hurried off the shot.

“I was sure I missed him,” Budge said, “until I found big splotches of blood on the snow.”

Somehow the deer ran far downhill, even though hit with a solid chest shot. I helped Budge finish dressing the critter and then moved on again. The happy rancher wished me luck and repeated, “I’ll meet you here at noon.”

Monument Knoll seemed to be loaded with outstanding bucks. A quarter of a mile from Budge’s kill, I picked up a fresh, unusually large track and decided to follow it.

That was a good decision as far as Owen Strand of Hawthorne, California, was concerned; I pushed the deer right past the spot he’d selected to scan the surrounding country. He needed just one shot to tumble the buck into a steep canyon. It was an extremely handsome, heavy-antlered buck. The deer was so big that even with its entrails removed, the two of us couldn’t begin to drag it up the steep slope. Actually it was to require a major effort by eight hunters later on to drag the deer back to the canyon’s rim. There it could be reached with a jeep.

That afternoon I had Monument Knoll to myself. The morning’s shooting hadn’t made the muleys thereabouts any less jittery. I spotted three good bucks at extremely long range, but they evaporated before I could even begin a stalk. I decided to hunt more slowly, more deliberately. I saw other deer far away. But before I realized it, afternoon was becoming early evening. The sun dropped behind the purple badlands in the west, and I turned to head back toward Budge and the jeep. All at once I was exhausted both mentally and physically.

I’d concentrated so hard all day that at first I thought I was only seeing things. But there it was again — a flick of movement in the aspens across a long draw. I held my rifle against an aspen to steady it, and carefully studied the spot through my scope. In the rapidly fading light, a splendid buck muley took half a step forward and looked straight toward me. Here was the buck I’d dreamed about so long, but my dreams hadn’t included such impossible conditions.

The buck was 300 to 400 yards away. Besides, he stood in second-growth aspen with little more than his neck, rack, and rump showing. When I stretched out prone in the snow and tried to steady my sights on the dim and distant target, I had serious doubts. The crosshairs wouldn’t stop wavering.

Then I took a deep breath, held it, and squeezed off a shot. The buck staggered, lurched downhill, and fell. I found him 360 paces from where I fired.

I’d been hunting for a trophy muley like this one for 10 years. It had six points on each side, and I estimated it weighed 250 pounds, maybe more.

I’d barely finished field dressing the deer when I saw lights come bobbing over the ridge behind me. A few minutes later Budge was shaking my hand. He seemed even more pleased with the world than I was, and he had good reason.

“All the fellows had deer practically coming out their ears,” he said. “Everybody got at least one.” (Utah’s limit was two deer per hunter: one buck, one doe. Even extra permits were available in some areas).

Naturally there was a celebration in camp that night. For me, the rest of the hunt was pure clover. I didn’t care about bagging a nontrophy deer, so I took photos and jeeped down to the winter camp where 12 other hunters were having a great hunt. By noon of the second day, the 23 hunters on the spread had bagged 46 deer, a score hard to match. There were many fine trophies. Largest of all was a slightly amazing five-pointer collected by Jim Poore, a Los Angeles attorney, at the high camp (see photo). The main antler beams were as thick as my forearms, and a quick job with a tape measure indicated it would make the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book.

For Don Wilcox the hunt meant plenty of hard work; he helped most of the hunters skin, cape, and quarter their deer. But for everyone else, it was mainly an adventure to be long remembered.

By the Same Author: I Was Floating One of the West’s Great Trout Rivers. Then the Governor Dropped in on His Helicopter

Besides bagging a winter’s supply of meat and a year’s supply of hunting stories, they hunted in magnificent country. They traveled across improbable landscapes and stumbled across ruins of an ancient civilization, which few other men have seen. Some found delicate Indian arrowheads, and others found a welcome change of pace from the smog and the grind of life on the West Coast.

But all were elated that they’d discovered Utah deer hunting. They voted to try it again this year.

#208. Impact Velocity, Not Energy, Is What Hunters Should Pay Attention To

Published Oct 14, 2026 12:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When I was a kid, and in the preceding decades, a hunter’s maximum effective or ethical shooting distance was determined by their ability to simply hit the target. With the tools of the day, that meant flat-shooting, fast cartridges gave hunters potentially longer effective ranges. Eventually, in the effort to more accurately predict effective distance and reduce the risk of wounding loss, we began to combine the raw potential to hit the vitals of the animal with an estimated kinetic energy value at that distance. Various formulas and guidelines for minimum effective KE values have been pressed out to the masses.

For example, some outdoor writers have  recommended a minimum of 1,500 foot-pounds of energy for an elk. But as we’ve developed better tools for rangefinding, measuring velocity, and mapping bullet-drag profiles, impact velocity has become the top consideration for predicting terminal ballistic performance.

As our rifles, bullets, and shooting gear have evolved, hunters have done their best to make accurate predictions of their effective range. For a long time, the limiting factor was simply whether or not you could realistically hit an animal in the vitals with your gear. This drove development of faster, “flatter-shooting” cartridges which offered some forgiveness in trajectory and range estimation.

As rangefinders and personal chronographs became more common and optics improved, shooting accurately at distances beyond 300 yards became more common, too. And, in an effort to ensure that our bullets packed enough punch at distance, we used ballistic coefficients to estimate retained energy along with estimates on how much energy was necessary to kill our quarry reliably. Hunters have been working out similar formulas for a long time — all with the goal of being more effective and, consequently, more ethical. One example is the Taylor Knockout Formula, which essentially calculates a bullet’s momentum and factors in bullet diameter.

In the last decade our gear has improved even more dramatically. We have superbly shootable rifle platforms and chronographs that are utterly reliable. Bullet manufacturers have the tools to precisely map out drag profiles for their bullets — not just rely on a G1 or G7 ballistic coefficient — a value that changes depending on the projectile’s velocity at a given moment. Couple that with excellent rangefinders with onboard ballistics and environmental sensors, and we have what we need to make very precise shots at distances beyond what was realistic only a decade or two ago.

Being able to reliably hit your target is still of the utmost importance when figuring out your effective or ethical range. But we’ve progressed to the point where we can account for trajectory, and downrange kinetic energy doesn’t mean much. The biggest predictor is the impact velocity and what a particular bullet will do at that velocity.

Kinetic energy has been, and still is, a calculated value that causes hunters to swoon in favor of bigger and faster cartridges. The problem is that KE alone doesn’t really correlate with the damage a certain cartridge will produce or its effectiveness at killing game. Similarly, Taylor’s formula might work well if we’re talking about brain-shooting elephants with minimally-expanding or solid bullets. But it isn’t useful for a wider variety of game, shots, or with bullets that instantly change diameter when they strike an animal. Those are much less predictable. Even the usefulness of sectional density as a predictor is debatable because the sectional density of an expanding bullet changes as soon as it impacts flesh and begins opening up.

Because no two bullet wounds are exactly alike, and each situation is unique, there isn’t a universal tool to predict exactly what will happen. Energy values and formulas have been a “best effort,” and aren’t bad, but they include a lot of noise that doesn’t contribute to our understanding. Many hunters will pick a combination with higher energy than another option, thinking it gives them an advantage. If you’re not considering things like bullet construction and terminal behavior, and the game you’re shooting, you can wind up with a setup that actually creates a less-substantial wound cavity than a different combo with less energy at impact.

We still don’t have a perfect way to predict what will happen when our bullet strikes an animal. But because our tools have become better and more precise, we are seeing many hunters focus on impact velocity as a primary factor in their bullet’s effectiveness at distance. We can accurately predict a bullet’s impact velocity at a given distance and condition, and don’t have to rely on the velocities printed on the box. Many contemporary hunting bullets are also tested to determine their behavior at any given speed, so you generally know exactly what to expect — and when a shot is too far.

When a bullet strikes with a velocity between its maximum and minimum design limits, the terminal effectiveness doesn’t vary much. A softer bullet traveling way above its maximum design limit can result in less penetration, while a bullet impacting at too slow of a speed might not expand enough to cause an effective amount of trauma.

A good practice for supersonic rifle cartridges is to keep your impact velocities at 2000 fps or above.

There are certainly bullets — especially cup-and-core style — that will work adequately below that, but generally any hunting bullet will function well and do a lot of damage at that speed. A ballistician once told me that in his testing, 2000 fps seemed to be the threshold at which terminal effects became significantly more dramatic. Whether you call this hydrostatic shock, hydraulic effect, or something else, a 2000 fps impact velocity is predictably going to result in the bullet working well.

Astute hunters will point out that the same correlation among similar variables could be seen from combining bullet construction with kinetic energy. This is true, but the mass component doesn’t add much value in predicting terminal performance. Ultimately, it renders down to the velocity component at bullet impact, and how a particular bullet will behave at that velocity.

Considering impact velocity and bullet construction isn’t a universally accurate predictor of what will happen. But right now, it’s the best and simplest way for us to limit ourselves in pursuit of quick and clean harvests.

We can’t always account for every factor, but we can predict how our bullet will generally behave, and the speeds at which it will function. Impact velocity can vary depending on distance, but also on factors like elevation and temperature. It’s especially important for those using shorter barrels. For example, an average 6.5 Creedmoor load from an 18- or 20-inch barrel can fall below its effective velocity inside 400 or 500 yards. When this is the case, a hunter might be able to hit the animal, but if the bullet isn’t working properly, or doing the damage it would at 2000 fps, the results might be disappointing.

Read Next: Why Small Cartridges Are So Effective for Big Game

As you’re preparing for hunting season, practice enough to determine your effective distances and how well you can shoot in varying wind conditions. Utilize different positions and do everything you can to improve your marksmanship fundamentals. But don’t forget to take a closer look at your bullets, the speeds they were designed for, and what your impact velocities will be at varying ranges.

#209. Russian Team Moving Up on Everest

The only team currently on Everest has set off across an untouched Khumbu Icefall. There are no ladders or ropes at this time of year, and everything ahead of them is uncertain.

Earlier this week, the Russian team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina acclimatized toward the Nuptse shoulder, to the right of the Khumbu Icefall. Heavy snow slowed them, eventually forcing them to stop for the night at 5,650m.

Nuptse in the sun, with the Khumbu Glacier at the base and Everest’s West Shoulder on the left. Photo: Russian Everest Expedition 2026

Returning to their quarters in Lobuche, the team focused on rest and pondered their options. “We are considering two alternatives: either going up across the Khumbu Icefall or trying the West Ridge via the Lho La, the mountain pass to the left of the Khumbu Glacier that leads to Everest’s west ridge,” they said. Jost Kobusch has attempted the West Ride/Lho La route several times in winter.

The Russians have now chosen the first option. “We’re heading up, attempting to get through the Khumbu Icefall,” Vasilief told Mountainclub. “We’ll see how things go from there.”

The team plans to spend six days on the mountain and has not confirmed whether they will attempt the summit or complete another partial trip.

#212. EHD Outbreaks Are Killing Deer in Three States. Here’s What to Know

Published Oct 14, 2026 10:56 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Virus-carrying midges are hampering deer season in South Dakota, where an outbreak of epizootic hemorrhagic disease has prompted South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks to issue deer license refunds.

Hunters can voluntarily turn in their South Dakota deer licenses for a full refund if they planned to pursue game in one of 16 counties along the Missouri River. The state also withdrew 62 unsold licenses. It had already closed nine southeastern counties to mentored, youth, and apprentice deer and switched statewide archery and muzzleloader licenses to buck-only for 2026.”

South Dakota’s EHD outbreak started in July and continued through an unusually warm September. Heavy rain left mud holes, which are hot spots for the biting midges that carry EHD. Whitetails often hang out in the same spots. There’s no cure for the bite-transferred virus, but a hard freeze would kill the midges and help stem the spread.

The state-wide count of deer reported dead from EHD climbed from 196 as of the commission’s September meeting to 407 in October; 31 of them have been lab-confirmed EHD deaths. This total is slightly higher than all the 2025 season.

“A lot of our reports have come from the month of October,” said South Dakota Game Fish and Parks senior wildlife biologist Byron Buckley, as reported by the South Dakota Searchlight. “That could be because we are seeing the disease a lot more or that there’s just a lot more people on the landscape.”

Wisconsin faces the same problem, but with increased mortality likely due to higher-density deer herds and less exposure to previous outbreaks. The state has logged roughly 2,300 reports of sick or dead deer with signs of EHD this fall, with 1,300 of those in Washington County alone. A map showing case locations concentrates the outbreak in the southeastern portion of the state.

Farther west, Wyoming biologists are monitoring an EHD outbreak, too. They’re also following bluetongue, a closely-related midge-borne virus that can kill deer and is especially hard on domestic sheep. Whitetail deer and pronghorn in the Casper and Glenrock areas of the state have several EHD cases.

EHD is not contagious between animals and affects only ungulates. People and pets can’t contract it. Wild game — including deer, elk, pronghorn, and bighorn sheep — infected with EHD usually spike a fever within seven days of being bitten. The biters, smaller than mosquitoes, are known as biting midges or no-see-ums. When the midges transfer the virus to mammals, the fever isn’t necessarily obvious, but other symptoms can be.

Sick animals can suffer from swollen heads and necks. They may also become weak and lose their fear of humans. That’s what hunters are seeing now. Infected deer usually seek water, and are frequently found dead near seeps, ponds, creeks, and other bodies of water.

“We’ve seen a lot of deaths along the river,” Janet Milek, Wyoming Game and Fish Casper Region public information specialist told Your Wyoming Link. “We’ve had a lot of reports from fishing guides and agricultural water users.”

Read Next: Cow Manure from Serial Polluter Blamed for Killing 11,000 Bass, Trout in Iconic Maryland Stream

Fortunately, EHD isn’t 100 percent fatal and most affected animals, some of which will not show symptoms, recover. Acute infections can cause death within 24 to 36 hours, according to Wyoming Game and Fish.

#215. Trekking and Packrafting 700Km Across Northern Siberia

Two Russian explorers have completed a journey of about 700km across the remote Putorana Plateau in northern Siberia. During their expedition, they encountered drought conditions, wildfires, and a brazen bear that raided their food supplies.

Danil Barashkov and Sergey Malykh set off in early July. They flew to the small town of Svetlogorsk in northern Siberia, before taking a motorboat up the Kureika River system toward Lake Dupkun. On July 7, they started on foot across the Putorana Plateau from a nearby scientific research base.

A mountainous region between 67°N and 70°N in the Arctic Circle, the plateau is the size of Great Britain. Featuring some 25,000 lakes, it is the second-largest store of fresh water in Russia after Lake Baikal. The men set out with 40kg packs and entered the plateau’s remote eastern section, expecting to use packrafts for most of their journey. Instead, they found drought conditions, with water levels too low to paddle, and even drinking water in short supply.

“There was almost no rain all of June. So we ended up like this: ‘I’m standing on the pavement, wearing skis.’ We arrived with our packrafts, and there was no water,” Malykh told Russian news site NGS24.RU. Though water was scarce, the mosquitoes remained. “I’ve never seen anything like this before: you lift the lid of the pot, and there’s a layer of mosquitoes floating around. Yeah, we definitely had no problem with protein.”

The pair found very dry conditions early in their trip. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Their original plan was to cross the plateau and continue to the settlement of Khatanga in northern Siberia. However, the exceptionally dry conditions forced a change of plan. Instead, they crossed toward the upper basin of the Kotuy River, 300km of hiking that sometimes required shuttles to move their gear. They covered only 15km per day and realized that their trip would run longer than their initial six-week plan. But this slog paid off; from the Kotuy, they could finally use their packrafts.

Barashkov and Malykh had a few scary bear encounters. In one instance, they almost walked into a sleeping bear, and in another, a curious bear only retreated from their campsite after coming as close as 15 meters — and after ignoring their shouts and a shot from a flare gun.

A bear that didn’t come too close. Photo: Danil Barashkov

However, the worst instance came after they cached some food. A bear had found the supplies and was still eating them when they returned. With hundreds of kilometers still to travel, Barashkov and Malykh couldn’t afford to lose everything. They collected their bear deterrents and managed to briefly scare the bear away before hurriedly packing what remained of their food into their backpacks and escaping downwind.

Over the next three weeks, they used packrafts to travel 400km and their luck improved. They found plentiful berries and caught fish in the river to supplement their remaining food.

Their arrival at Chirinda in the second half of August marked the end of their expedition after around 60 days. Yet forest fires forced the pair to remain in the village for another 10 days. Wildfires swept through the surrounding tundra forests and smothered the area in smoke, grounding flights.

Wildfire smoke near the village of Chirinda. Photo: Danil Barashkov

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#216. Cow Manure from Serial Polluter Blamed for Killing 11,000 Bass, Trout in Iconic Maryland Stream

Published Oct 13, 2026 7:24 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A six-mile trout stream in Maryland just lost roughly 11,000 fish, including brown trout, bass, river chub, and minnows, among others. The suspected cause? Cow poop from an upstream dairy farm.

Twenty-five species of fish going belly up were reported on Sept. 30 along Basin Run in Cecil County. Most of them settling on the river bottom rather than floating on top, according to one resident. The fish kill demonstrates why violating stream protections has real-world impacts on people and wildlife, at a time when the federal government continues to roll back Clean Water Act protections.

“I’ve never seen that many dead fish in that stream,” a Cecil County resident told the Cecil Daily. “I saw large fish, smallmouth bass, minnows. I saw eels. They’re a pretty strong species.”

Basin Run flows into Octoraro Creek, then the Susquehanna River and the Chesapeake Bay. This isn’t the first kill in the creek. Ashley Bowley, founder of Protect Basin Run, is compiling state inspection reports in the area that are potentially caused by Kilby Farm. Kilby Farm has already been accused of discharging pollution, including manure, into Basin Run.

“This has been happening for years,” says Bowley, referring to those inspection reports.

The Maryland Department of the Environment is investigating the fish kill. The agency sent officials to the farm Sept. 30, but they were denied entry. They returned on Oct. 1 and 5 and were granted access both times.

The preliminary cause of the current fish kill is listed as pollution due to overflow from a manure lagoon. Previous allegations include fermented feed, milk, and manure piped toward the creek and improper disposal of dead cattle.

“These violations are unacceptable,” said Jay Apperson, Maryland Department of Environment spokesperson. “We are taking this issue very seriously and have already obtained a preliminary injunction from the court barring this facility from discharging pollution into the waterway.”

The public agency and private farm have a history that goes back several years. In 2018, the state awarded Kilby Farm $1.85 million through its Animal Waste Technology Fund. That money was to retrofit a digester that turns manure into biogas to generate electricity and heat for the operation. The farm, which has about 400 dairy cows, was again awarded grant money in 2021, part of a state grant to Sustainable Chesapeake paid for equipment to help the farm’s digester produce more heat in cold months. Then the relationship waned.

In August 2025, the farm reached a settlement with the state, paid a $50,000 penalty and agreed to stop discharging into the creek. The discharges continued, the state alleges, and it sued this spring. A judge ordered the farm to stop in June. A contempt hearing was held Oct. 13, the outcome of which was not available by press time.

Pennsylvania farmer Ben Flahart, along with his wife and another dairy-farming couple from Pennsylvania, bought Kilby Farm in 2017. They also deliver milk produced by their dairy cows through Kilby Cream. Last month, Flahart’s attorney told The Baltimore Banner the state is not accounting for a tributary that is polluted before it flows through the farm then into Basin Run.

Related: ‘This Would Have Serious, Real-World Impacts.’ Why the EPA’s Rule Change on Water Protections Would Be a Disaster for Fish and Wildlife

Basin Run used to be stocked but is now considered a self-sustaining fishery known for brown trout. It is classified by the state as Class III-P, which means it’s cold enough to support wild trout. It’s also considered Tier II for high-quality water that comes with special protections against degradation.

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#219. 10 Reasons Why Late October Is the Best Time to Tag a Mature Buck

Published Oct 13, 2026 5:24 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A big-racked buck stands from his bed, stretches to shake off the afternoon jitters, and turns to a rub near his bed. Walking over to it, with neck swelling strong, he tears that cedar to shreds. Then he turns down the trail to hit another.

Eventually, he makes it to a watering hole, and after that, nears your food plot, which is placed strategically in the timber. Around sunset, he steps into that clover-laden clearing and starts plowing through the greens. Before long, you’re at full draw; all that’s left is to make a perfect shot.

Related: The Best Access Tool for Deer Season Is Already in Your Garage

That’s the power of a late-October deer hunt. There are many pros and only a few cons to hunting the last week of October. More and more expert hunters confess that late October—not mid-November—is the best time to kill a specific mature target buck.

Here are 10 reasons why the last week of October is the best time to kill a big buck.

So, you’ve scouted a buck all season. He’s still on the property you hunt. But as soon as the rut kicks in, he might not be. It’s not that his home range will shift dramatically, but his pattern around his core area will likely change.

Plus, by the heart of the rut, he won’t be predictable at all.

If you still have a big buck on camera, and you’ve invested time figuring out where and how to kill him, late October provides the best window for success.

Whitetail research shows that daytime movement gradually increases throughout summer and fall, peaks during the rut, and tapers off into the late season. For those with a rut that peaks in early to mid-November, late October is an excellent time to fill that buck tag.

If you know where a deer is living, and there’s still a pattern to hunt, get more aggressive now. The buck is likely spending a little more time moving during daylight each day. Increased daylight movement simply means greater odds that the buck will pass by your stand when you’re there.

A buck’s testosterone levels peak during the rut. Because of this, whitetail bucks tend to be more aggressive. Of course, hormones peak in November, but by late October, testosterone levels are on a sharp incline, nearing the top.

As noted above, this leads to increased daytime movement. It can also translate to a false sense of confidence (and security) for a deer to travel. Plus, because the rut is so near, that buck might begin searching for does.

Sticking with the testosterone theme and more aggressive behavior, bucks are more vocal. They also start posturing and even fighting. Deer in general are being very social now and will continue to be so for several weeks.

Knowing this, be aggressive with your deer hunting tactics. Use calls, such as bleats, grunts, snort-wheezes, grunt-snort-wheezes, and more. Hit those antlers together and mock up a big buck fight. Display a decoy and use deer attractants to bring that mature buck into bow range.

Because the rut is still at least a week (or maybe longer) from really starting, most bucks aren’t on the run in search of does just yet. Instead, they’re close to home and spending time in their core areas.

Thankfully, these deer are still following predictable bed-to-feed patterns. Hunters who’ve scouted and know where a big one lives can deduce where it’s bedding, feeding, and traveling. Connect the dots and choose stand locations accordingly.

White oaks are among the most favored foods for whitetails. They’ll march past cornfields, corn piles, and almost all other deer food sources to reach a producing white oak tree. It’s deer candy, but nutritional, thanks to lower tannin (tannic acid) levels.

Because of this, white oak acorns don’t last long. (Also, due to the lower acidity, the “shelf life” isn’t as good.) Therefore, by late October, a lot of the white oak acorns are cleaned up. Hunters should scout and find the white oaks with remaining food. That’s where the deer will be. Their favorite dish is condensing into tighter spaces.

Cold fronts spark deer movement. Late October cold fronts get big deer on their feet.

Of course, the day of the front can be good. However, the day before the front arrives and the day after it passes are the best windows. If the cold air remains, the hunting can be good for several days after the front hits.

Unless there’s a clear pattern on a big deer, and the entry route access is foolproof, most of us don’t hunt mornings during the early season. However, the late-October pre-rut is a solid time to start hunting mornings.

Deer are starting to move differently on the landscape now. Furthermore, they’re getting back to bed later, making those morning sits more viable. During this window, there’s a greater reward to accompany the risk of spooking deer while walking into the stand before daylight.

Those with a traditional mid-November rut should see 90 to 95 percent of does enter estrus during the 11th month. That said, 5 percent, or perhaps slightly less, could enter estrus in late October. That’s action most hunters completely miss because they aren’t there to see it.

Of course, you can’t count on this event to fill your tag, but it’s one to keep in the back of your mind. It can turn a late-October bed-to-feed hunt into the first buck-and-doe chase of the year. When a doe does come into estrus early, it’s not uncommon for her to have multiple bucks in chase mode. That just might be the ticket to the monster you’ve been watching.

Most deer hunters save their vacation time and brownie points for the heart of the rut. For many hunters, those days are burned during November. However, by that point, every bowhunter in the woods (and some crossbow and gun hunters, seasons depending), are in trees, too.

Read Next: 101 Best Deer Hunting Tips For the Rut

That’s exactly why you should start in late October. Take your “rutcation” before everyone else and get the jump on the competition. Sitting in late October can reduce the pressure and give you the best chance of big buck success.

#220. Superniño Weather Threatens Aconcagua Season

The Aconcagua climbing season is approaching, but the threat of unstable conditions linked to this year’s superniño is causing headaches for expedition operators, guides, climbers, and rescue teams.

Temperatures on the surface of the Pacific Ocean are so high that the weather phenomenon usually known as El Niño (the boy) has become a superniño for 2026. Warm, wet air from the ocean can result in massive precipitation inland, and for Aconcagua — South America’s highest peak — that means lots of snow.

A graphic illustrating increasing temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.

Argentina’s meteorological service forecasts a colder, more humid spring than usual, both in coastal areas and in Patagonia, the location of Aconcagua. Authorities in Argentina’s mountain province of Mendoza are issuing weather alerts that warn of flooding and intense snow. Several mountain passes are closed and neighboring Chile is also enduring intense rain and snowfall. The webcams at Portillo ski resort, 27km from Aconcagua, show winter-like images.

The effects of the superniño may unfold over several months. It will surely change conditions in mountain areas by the time the Aconcagua season starts in November for trekking groups, and on December 1 for climbing expeditions. Local guiding companies fear that snow-covered trails and flooded rivers may isolate lower camps. Further up the mountain, climbers might have to progress on icy ramps instead of scree slopes, and deal with significant avalanche risk.

Given the circumstances, park authorities will wait before announcing when the season will begin. Local media suggest either December 5 or December 15 as tentative opening dates.

“The [super] niño will reach its maximum intensity in December, when the temperature of the Central Pacific Ocean will be +2.7°C higher than normal,” meteorologists told La Gaceta.

#223. We Tested the Best Budget Trad Bows: These 5 Affordable Bows Shot Surprisingly Well Against a Custom Recurve

Published Oct 13, 2026 5:00 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

When I was 14, I made a red oak board bow in my parent’s garage. The bow cost about $10 to make, and it had jarring handshock. Even though that cheap bow wasn’t a great shooter, it got me in the door and I wouldn’t have been able to learn the basics or take my first steps in archery hunting without it. I’ve since made better selfbows and owned many of the best custom bows. But I’ve returned to my humble roots to test the best budget trad bows on the market.

All of the bows proved to be nice shooters and absolutely capable of killing game ethically. Here’s what I found from testing these budget trad bows and comparing them to my custom Wengerd Ibex which costs north of $2,500.

I’ve been shooting the Sage Elite II for a few weeks now and it’s been just as impressive as the original Samick Sage, with a few key upgrades. It now has limbs that truly bolt down, an improved limb pocket, and a better grip. My Sage Elite II also shot a few fps faster than my original Sage in the same draw weight.

The bow has an even draw to about 28 inches. After that point you can feel it stacking and, at my 30-inch draw, it feels like you’re pulling into a wall. Based on my shooting, this 62-inch model is ideal for people with a 26- to 28-inch draw length. After the shot, you’ll feel some residual vibration, but it’s not uncomfortable to shoot, either.

I’d describe the Sage Elite II as an honest shooter. It’s not going to punish you unfairly for a bad shot and it’ll reward your good shots. It’s not exceptionally forgiving and it’s far from being as enjoyable to shoot as my custom bows, but it’s the best bow I’ve in its price bracket. It’s ideally suited for new archers because you can buy it with low-draw weight limbs and steadily increase in draw weight by buying new limbs for a reasonable price.

There are a ton of bows that are very similar looking to the Galaxy Sage because this design was so ubiquitous for many years. Some of those other options are less expensive too. But I would caution anyone against buying a Sage clone off Amazon because I’ve seen those companies pop up and then disappear. One example is the Tachyon recurve that I reviewed two years ago. Today that bow is now longer available on Amazon and I can’t find a website for the company. Spending an extra $30 to $50 is worth it for the customer service you get when you buy from a known company that’s based in the U.S. If you need support or you need a replacement down the road, they’ll still be there to help out.

The Grizzly G62 is a 50s-style recurve with long working limbs and undeniable cool factor. The long limbs make it smooth to my 30-inch draw length and the short riser keeps this bow lightweight. I throughly enjoyed shooting it throughout testing. It’s an easy bow to recommend for archers who are looking to step up from a Sage but aren’t ready to drop more $1,000-plus on a new custom bow. The entire Bear Archery line of recurves are worth considering as they’re all time-tested designs and the bow you choose ultimately will depend on your personal preferences.

The Grey Dawn was a real surprise in this test. The cheap longbows I’ve shot in the past were plagued with uncomfortable grips and horrible hand shock. But the Grey Dawn is an exceptionally pleasant bow to shoot. The draw is smooth to my draw length, it feels very stable at full draw, and I shot excellent groups with it during accuracy testing. The only change I would make is to take a rasp to the grip to flatten it — a personal preference thing. This bow would be a great choice for indoor competitions, 3D archery, and hunting. I like it so much that I’m considering hunting with it this year.

Like the Sage, the Ghost is an “honest shooting bow.” If I lost my focus, it let me know about it with an errant shot. It didn’t give me much help for a mediocre execution, but my good shots stacked together. The Southwest Ghost didn’t need string silencers to be quiet enough for hunting and it had very little handshock — just some residual buzz. The Ghost’s draw starts off easy and it has noticeable stack as it gets to my long draw length. If you’re around a 28-inch draw, however, it’ll likely be very smooth.

In accuracy testing, the Mesa was very consistent and it was easy to shoot accurately. One downside of this bow is that it’s easy to push shots left or right due to its low-mass weight. If I were going to hunt with the Mesa, I’d put a bow quiver on it to weigh it down.

The Mesa has very little vibration and felt stable at full draw. It has an excellent draw cycle for a longbow and it felt comparable to custom longbows I’ve owned in the past. It’s another great bow at a relatively affordable price.

If you spend 10 times the price of a Galaxy Sage Elite II, do you get a better bow? Yes — definitely yes. That’s like asking if a $100 Vortex Triumph binocular is better than a $1,700 Zeiss SFL. It’s not a fair fight. The real question is, how much better is the performance for the price?

My Wengerd Ibex is about 10 fps faster, significantly smoother, more accurate, and overall more pleasant to shoot than budget alternatives. Custom bows offer more than just performance benefits. You get to work with a craftsman to choose a bow’s length, woods, limb materials, and a specified draw weight at your draw length. The hand-made aspect and the materials is why custom bows cost more.

But I wouldn’t recommend that a new archer buy a custom bow. It’s much better to learn proper form and develop your taste in bows — with the options I tested above — before committing. They won’t hold you back in terms of accuracy for the time being, and I’d persoanlly be completely comfortable taking all of them in the woods this fall. When you’re ready to step up, take a look at used custom bows. A used bow is typically 50 percent the cost of a new custom bow, and it’s a great way to try before you buy.
