#263. It’s Never Too Late to Learn to Hunt

Published Oct 11, 2026 11:09 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

More than 11 years ago, I moved to Glasgow, Montana, in order to be closer to my daughter after her mother and I separated. In a small town like this, where it seems like everybody hunts, I got asked all the time if I did. “Not yet,” I’d say. “I’m waiting for the right person to show me how.”

Sometimes I felt like the only adult male in this town who didn’t hunt. I’d always had an interest in it, but I guess I missed out on being taught when I was a kid in Ohio. Then life started up, and it was just one of those things that I never got around to.

It’s not as though I lacked contacts or invitations, but most of the people who might have taken me hunting don’t do it the way I thought I wanted to. A lot of them drive around until they see something, and then they shoot it not too far from the road. I’m not saying everybody is like that, but I wanted to hunt what I guess I’d call the “right” way — walking and stalking an animal that doesn’t know I’m there, and feeling like I really earned it.

My day job — actually, it’s my night job — is working as a custodial engineer at our local middle school. I go to work at about 3 p.m. and work until midnight or so. Andrew McKean, Outdoor Life’s hunting editor, is at the school a lot; he coaches the middle school’s track and cross-country teams, and I’ve known him for a while. Our kids are in the same grades, and we’re friends on Facebook. I’ve seen posts from his hunts, and it seemed like he does it the way I’d like to. Maybe because he’s a coach, I thought that he’d be a good teacher. I thought about asking him a few times, but every time I got close, I’d get cold feet. We’re both busy, and I didn’t know how he’d react to a guy about his age asking him to be a teacher.

I finally popped the question last spring. I was actually pretty nervous — like a middle school boy asking a girl to a dance. I asked Andrew if he’d be interested in teaching me how to hunt. I think he was taken aback by the question, but he said he would, and that we’d figure out all the details before the fall deer season.

The truth of it is that I thought Andrew would get as much out of teaching me as I’d get out of learning, and that’s exactly how it played out. I passed the local Hunter Education class, probably the only 48-year-old who took it, and got a rifle — a Remington Model 700 in .30/06 that Andrew helped me pick out. He also guided me through the other gear I’d need: a scope, sling, bipod, ammunition, and binocular. I spent a good bit of time over the summer with that rifle, and learned how to shoot pretty well. Andrew was busy with his job and his kids, so he didn’t get a chance to teach me about shooting as much as either of us would have liked, but as it got closer to hunting season, we spent more time together at the range, and I think Andrew was happy when he saw I was a pretty good shot, and safe with the gun.

Andrew said he knew of some pretty good mule deer country we could hunt, and we agreed that we’d try to keep shots inside about 250 yards. I practiced a lot with my rifle, and got pretty comfortable shooting at that distance, although I really didn’t know how it would go when I didn’t have a solid bench to shoot off of.

The first day out, we encountered some deer — ­including a nice buck — but they managed to get away before we could really settle in for a shot. It was a ton of walking, but there’s something about the way we did it — trying to sneak up on deer, and just hiking and glassing — that really suits me.

One of the unexpected things about hunting is that you can go as fast or as slow as you want, and it was fun glassing deer and figuring out a way to get closer to them. I was eager to kill a deer — I guess Andrew was anxious for me, too — but the cool thing is that we had time to talk and laugh and joke around. I was still nervous, but my nervousness and uncertainty about how it would end somehow made it even more exhilarating.

And I was learning things all the time, including about how not to skyline myself on a ridge, and about how to use dry stream beds to hide in. Andrew even taught me how to belly-crawl when we got close to deer. I have a bum knee from an old ski injury, and that slowed me down, but I got pretty good at being sneaky.

On our second day, it all came together, although not before we had all sorts of blown opportunities. I missed a chip shot at a little buck. Andrew was cool about it. He said everybody misses, and it was something I just had to learn from.

Not 30 minutes after that miss, I spotted a buck bedded up a coulee, and Andrew had me figure out how to stalk up on it, keeping in mind the wind direction and the terrain. Somehow, it worked out, and I crawled to within 250 yards—243, to be exact—and waited for the buck to stand up. When he did, I shot and connected, and that part of the hunt was over. Andrew showed me how to field dress the buck, and we dragged him out together.

As we were getting my buck out, I kept thinking to myself, Why did I wait so long to do this? There are lots of reasons, but one is that I didn’t really know how to start, and I didn’t have anybody to show me the way to do it right. I think a lot of people are like me — interested and eager and capable — but they don’t know how to take the first steps.

People, including Andrew, have asked me why I want to hunt, and I guess it’s because of the meat. Natural protein. Andrew is wired the same way. That’s why he hunts, and he showed me how to skin and then how to butcher my buck. We trimmed and wrapped the meat in his kitchen, and he showed me the different cuts and how to cook them.

I was pretty nervous taking the meat from my buck back home. My wife isn’t all that jazzed about venison. But I cooked the backstraps for my 49th birthday dinner, and it was just perfect. Tender, tasty. Everybody in my household raved about the meat, and now they want more of it.

That helps make my case that now I need to go elk hunting. And that I need to teach my teenage daughter and my 8-year-old son how to hunt. One of the things Andrew impressed upon me is that now that I’m a hunter, I have an obligation to teach somebody else how to hunt. That makes sense. And I have a feeling I’m going to have just as much fun being a teacher as my kids will being my students.

This story first appeared on Outdoor Life on Jan. 19, 2018.

#264. The Story of Earl Denman, Tenzing Norgay’s Forgotten Everest Partner

In the famous photograph of Tenzing Norgay standing on the summit of Everest on May 29, 1953, he holds his ice axe aloft, strung with flags. What you can’t see is the wool helmet under his hood. It had been left to him by a Canadian named Earl Denman, who six years earlier had convinced Tenzing to join him on a doomed, poorly equipped, illegal attempt on the mountain from Tibet.

Jennifer Peedom’s new film, Tenzing, recreates the triumphant 1953 conquest of Everest, with Genden Phuntsok in the title role, Tom Hiddleston as Edmund Hillary, and Willem Dafoe as expedition leader John Hunt. Denman’s name doesn’t appear in the cast list.

I first came across Earl Denman in 1997, in Jon Krakauer’s Into Thin Air, which describes him as a “poverty-stricken Canadian engineer” who “somehow” talked two Sherpas, one of them Tenzing, into accompanying him to Everest in 1947. Denman had written his own account of the attempt, Alone to Everest, published in 1954 and long out of print. The photograph facing the title page shows a lean man in a pale hooded smock on what looks like a ship’s deck, a coil of rope beside him, staring into the distance. With the hood pulled up and tied under his chin, he resembles a cross between Lawrence of Arabia and John Cleese.

Earl Denman was born on December 11, 1914, at Tod Inlet on Vancouver Island, Canada, where the Butchart family, founders of the famous Butchart Gardens outside Victoria, B.C., ran a cement works. His father worked there as an engineer until rheumatoid arthritis left him unable to walk. When Earl was about four, the family returned to England, as he later put it, “in the forlorn hope of gaining relief for a completely paralyzed father.” His father was bedridden for “seven painful years,” Denman wrote, nursed by Earl’s mother, and the family’s savings were “whittled away to nothing.”

According to Denman’s great-niece, Lisa Jones, the boys were sent to live with other people while their father was ill. Earl went to a couple named Topps at Heckington Fen in Lincolnshire. How long he stayed isn’t clear.

By his own account, Denman was “never really happy” in England. “How could I have been?” he wrote. Canada was another matter. “Childhood glimpses of the Canadian Rockies formed a lasting impression,” he wrote, “a first link in a chain of events leading from one mountain range to another.” Even as an adult, he still felt a nostalgia for his birthplace, “which distance and time cannot remove.” He grew up, in his own words, with “the far-away look of a dreamer.”

After five years as an apprentice electrical engineer, Denman departed for Africa and secured a job in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. “I had dreamed of mountains, but had to be content with a barren desert,” he wrote.

Denman hamming it up in the ‘barren desert.’

On his first leave, he rode fish lorries south to the Ruwenzori, the Mountains of the Moon, in the Belgian Congo. Camped alone below the snow line, he “first came to think about Everest,” and decided he wanted to be the first to climb all eight of the Virunga Mountains, a chain of volcanoes straddling the borders of today’s Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, and Uganda.

After serving “rather unspectacularly” in the Second World War, he set out from Bulawayo, in what was then Southern Rhodesia, for the Virungas, climbing them with local porters and guides and, often, no boots. Years later, he still claimed to be “the only one to have climbed all eight.”

Denman meant to climb Everest the same way, with a couple of local men and no army of porters. To him, the mountain was “essentially a mountaineering project pure and simple,” as he put it in his book, “wholly a matter of man pitting himself against the highest mountain in the world.”

Anything grander was out of reach, anyway. By his own count, he had “only £250 left over from my Virunga expedition” to cover his equipment, food, and the whole journey from Bulawayo to Darjeeling and back. His camera was “a cheap second-hand one, with punctured bellows,” and a watch was beyond his means. Nor did he have permission to enter Tibet.

Denman left Bulawayo in February 1947 and landed in Bombay on March 15. On the long train ride across India, the clickety-clack of the wheels “seemed to say, ‘You fool, turn back. You fool, turn back,'” he wrote.

In Darjeeling, a shop window full of mountain photographs caught his eye, and the name over the door, Paul, reminded him of someone from his reading on Everest: Karma Paul, the interpreter who had worked with the prewar British expeditions. A few questions inside the shop brought Karma Paul himself. He was no climber, but he listened to Denman’s mad plan. His response was one word: “Impossible!”

Karma Paul “took a lot of convincing,” Denman recalled, but told him to come back at 11 the next morning, when, Denman wrote, “he would introduce me to a capable Sherpa who might be willing to go with me.” In the meantime, Denman needed a permit to enter Sikkim, which meant signing a declaration that he would not go beyond Sikkim into Tibet. “I hated the duplicity that was involved,” he wrote, “but it was unavoidable.”

Two men were waiting in Karma Paul’s office the next morning. One was Ang Dawa. The other was Tenzing Norgay, a “Tiger” of the prewar Everest expeditions, who had already climbed to 27,000 feet on the mountain. Denman thought him wiry and vigorous. At first, he noted, Tenzing “remained unsmiling.”

Tenzing, Denman, and Ang Dawa. Photo: earldenman.com

Karma Paul, who called the plan “sheer suicide,” washed his hands of it, so Denman took the Sherpas back to his “bleak little apartment” and was frank about how little he could pay. Then he played his last card. With an official expedition, he told Tenzing, he would be just a porter, left in camp while the sahibs went for the top. With Denman, “If I succeed, you will succeed as well.” After a quiet word with Ang Dawa, Tenzing answered with a half-smile: “We will try.”

In Tiger of the Snows, the autobiography he told to author James Ramsey Ullman (Tenzing never learned to read or write), he admits he knew better. “Any man in his right mind would have said no,” he said. “But I couldn’t say no. For in my heart, I needed to go, and the pull of Everest was stronger for me than any force on earth.”

Because of that declaration, secrecy mattered. The three men left Darjeeling separately, met at an agreed spot outside town, and took the standard expedition route through Sikkim. At the Tibetan frontier, Tenzing steered them off the patrolled trade route and over a little-used pass.

On the trek to Everest. Photo: earldenman.com

By his account, hardly a day went by without trouble. Food ran short. At one point, the loaded yaks tumbled down a slope, very nearly taking the party’s supplies with them. When a patrol stopped them and ordered them back, they talked their way out of arrest, made a show of retreating, and then looped around. After that, they gave every town and village a wide berth until they reached the Rongbuk Monastery, at the foot of Everest’s North Side.

Tenzing hadn’t seen the mountain in nine years. “The old excitement returned, as strong as ever,” he said. “Here I was again where I was meant to be.”

From Rongbuk, they moved quickly, carrying everything themselves and pitching a new camp every day. Denman later calculated that the 1933 British expedition had needed 16 to 24 days to get as far as they got in four. Speed was their only advantage. Their clothes weren’t windproof, they had run out of tea, and their two tents, Tenzing recalled, “gave as much protection as a sheet of paper.”

Denman hardly slept. On his second night on the mountain, he wrote, sleep “would not come,” and he lay pummeling himself for warmth and wondering whether dawn would ever arrive. The Sherpas, meanwhile, hauled the loads without complaint. Reaching one camp after barely resting all the way up, they set them down, he wrote, “as though they were only slight encumbrances, like a load of children on a zoo elephant.”

That night, the weather turned. A “savage wind, like the breath from a Tibetan mastiff,” came up, and Tenzing shared his sleeping bag with him. Lying there, Denman wrote, “I realized properly, for the first time, how miserably poor we were and what little chance we stood.” By then, food had lost its taste, apart from cheese and slabs of milk chocolate studded with nuts and raisins. He kept the chocolate within reach at night, peeling off his gloves for every bite and sucking it slowly off the nuts to pass the hours. Outside, the ice pinnacles cracked “like pistol shots.”

At the foot of the North Col, they wrestled their single tent into the wind, piling rocks on the guy ropes where the pegs wouldn’t go into the frozen ground. The col itself looked less frightening than Denman had expected. Three men could climb it safely, he thought, but not in that wind. That night, he prayed, “Help me to do the right thing. Do not rob me of the chance to go forward, but give me strength to go back if I must.” He was frank about how little he cared what happened to him. “My whole life was Everest,” he wrote. “I did not want to live if we failed.”

The tent flapped all night, and two pegs tore loose. By morning, he admitted, his prayers had turned to “bitter oaths.” They drank hot cocoa at first light. Nobody discussed what to do next, but all three began taking down the tent, and they went up rather than down. “We would not give in so easily,” Denman wrote. On the slope below the col, the wind returned at full strength, and the sky turned to “an unrelieved dark mass, almost black.”

They turned around at about 23,500 feet by Denman’s reckoning. Jon Krakauer, in Into Thin Air, puts it closer to 22,000. Their hands were “on the verge of frostbite.” “We held our consultation, if it could be called a consultation,” Denman wrote. “We had played our hand.”

Denman, Tenzing said later, was “a determined, almost fanatic man with a fixed idea. But he was not crazy.” He agreed to turn back, and for that, Tenzing said, “I am as grateful as for anything that has happened in my life.” They came down almost at a run. Denman was in a hurry to put the mountain behind him, Tenzing remembered, “as if it were a thing he no longer loved but hated.”

His boots fell apart, and for a few days he walked barefoot. “My bitterness was like an open wound as we hastened down,” Denman wrote. He knew they had “attempted more than was humanly possible,” and that there was no disgrace in that. He felt humiliated all the same. The whole trip, from Darjeeling to Everest and back, took five weeks.

Denman returned in January 1948 with warmer boots and proper sleeping bags. What he didn’t have was a permit. Tenzing met him in Darjeeling, “all smiles,” assuming he had one, and when Denman said he didn’t, the smile faded. Tenzing told him it was too dangerous. Tibetan authorities were now looking for them, and neither Sherpa would risk another illegal crossing. So, a dejected Denman left all his gear with Tenzing, including a wool balaclava, in “the unwarranted hope” of a permit within a year or two. “It was the last time I was to see either of them,” he wrote.

Tenzing didn’t give up on his Canadian friend. That June, his wife wrote that Tenzing was in Lhasa, “trying his utmost to procure a pass for you.” Tenzing, who had his mail read to him and dictated his replies, kept writing. Of the gear Denman had left him, he wrote in a later letter, “Now and then I use them.” In January 1953 came another: “If you get permission, I rather prefer to accompany you than any other party.” Denman quoted it in an application to climb Everest in 1954 with a party of Sherpas led by Tenzing. Success, if it came, he wrote, “would be shared equally.”

Tenzing, right, and his wife. Photo: earldenman.com

It didn’t come to that. Tenzing joined John Hunt’s British expedition instead, his seventh trip to Everest, or “six times, including Denman,” by his own count. Looking back, he called Denman “a strange man” but “a brave one, a man with a dream,” and was sorry he had never come closer to realizing it. “In 1953, when I gained the top of Everest,” Tenzing said, “I was wearing a woolen balaclava helmet that he had left to me; so at least a little part of him has reached his goal.”

Denman, for his part, wrote that he was delighted a Sherpa had been given the first chance at the top, and especially this one, a man “for whom I have such a special affection and admiration.”

Denman did get to see the first film about Tenzing’s historic climb. At a private preview of Conquest of Everest, reported in the Johannesburg Sunday Express in January 1954, he said, in what the reporter called “his quiet, unassuming voice,” “I’d like to have another crack at her. Perhaps I will, too.” But with Tibet closed to him, he admitted the following year that he had “neither chance nor money” to go back.

Denman at work on a Volkswagen. Photo: earldenman.com

In South Africa, Denman wrote wildlife talks for SABC radio and newspaper columns against apartheid and, by 1961, worked at a Volkswagen assembly plant. That year, Tenzing got back in touch after a long silence. “Believe me, I often think about you and talk to my friends about our days in the mountains together,” he wrote. As for the factory job, “A man of the mountains cannot be happy with machines.”

Denman was eventually forced out of South Africa, which he blamed in part on those columns. His wife, Mary, stayed behind, and he later settled in New Zealand, where he received a letter from Tenzing in 1976, addressed to “My dear friend Denman.” Of their trip through Tibet, Tenzing wrote, “It was rather a tuf time, but I enjoyed it.” Denman kept writing and, in 1985, published The Fiercest Fight, an account of the struggle against apartheid.

Late in life, Denman was hit from behind by a car while cycling into town and never fully recovered. He died in December 1994, two days before his 80th birthday, from injuries his family chiefly blames on the accident.

Lisa Jones, a therapist in Bristol, England, learned about Earl Denman from her father, Graham, his nephew. She and her son, Frank, now look after his papers, which she keeps in a trunk in her living room. The family remembers a grumpy, solemn man, insular and quiet, with “no belly laughs.” Frank, who read more of the papers than anyone, called him privileged and arrogant. “I’m not sure he did it all through charm and good looks,” Jones says.

As a therapist, she sees a link to his childhood. For a boy of four sent away from his parents, she says, it would have felt like abandonment, which she believes left him wary of people and more at home in wild places. But she doesn’t think fame was the point. “It feels like he’s doing it for him.”

In 1984, Toronto filmmaker Vic Sarin wrote to Denman about making a documentary. His last question was the hardest: “Did you feel that you had failed or won in your attempt?” Denman had answered it, in a way, 30 years earlier in his book. Failure, he wrote, “though painful, is better than frustrated longing.”

Alone to Everest reads like something from the age of Burton and Livingstone, earnest and old-fashioned, and what stayed with me was its wistfulness. Every decade or so, around the anniversary of the climb, I pitched his story. Nobody seemed interested. Lisa Jones knows the feeling. The rest of the family, she says, showed little interest in the papers. “There’s a little pilot light here,” she says, “and I’m going to ignite it again.” Earl Denman may not be in Tenzing. But he is in that famous photograph of his old friend, if you know what you’re looking at: the wool helmet on Tenzing’s head, at 29,000 feet, where its owner never got to go.

Tenzing, directed by Jennifer Peedom, opens in select theaters on October 9 and streams on Apple TV from October 16.

Mark Sissons is a Vancouver-based travel and lifestyle journalist who contributes to the Globe and Mail, Vancouver Sun, Toronto Star, NUVO, Robb Report, and other major publications. More at marksissons.com.

#265. UK Man Completes Longest Unsupported Ocean Row

After 327 days, 17 hours and 30 minutes at sea, Dave “Dinger” Bell has completed one of the most ambitious ocean rowing expeditions ever attempted. The UK man rowed 28,700km solo and unsupported from the west coast of Peru to Kenya across both the Pacific and Indian Oceans without stopping.

He set off from Peru on November 9, 2025, armed with 350 days’ worth of food, and a plan for crossing two oceans that hinged on how he felt when he had finished his crossing of the Pacific Ocean and reached Australia. If in good shape, he would cross the notoriously tricky Torres Strait and cross into the Indian Ocean so that he could row to Mauritius, the original end point of the row.

One of the strangest problems came in the South Pacific. By April, he was making too much progress. If this kept up, he would reach the Coral Sea during cyclone season. For weeks, he had to reduce his rowing hours. For someone whose entire expedition depended on covering distance, weeks of forced inactivity became a major challenge.

“I was too quick, so I had to slow down,” Bell told the BBC. “To sit, mid-ocean, knowing you’ve still got seven, eight, nine months at sea but not be rowing was one of the hardest things, psychologically, that I’ve ever had to deal with.”

In May, he was finally able to row through the Coral Sea, although the wind almost constantly pushed him in the wrong direction. At one point, the waves were so large that he almost capsized. Water flooded into the boat, setting off his EPIRB, and he had to make some frantic InReach calls to assure everyone he was okay. By the end of the month, he could see Australia from his boat, a huge milestone in his journey. There was no question in his mind about continuing across the Indian Ocean, so he picked his way across the Great Barrier Reef and through the Torres Strait.

After making it through the Strait, he paused for a few days on para-anchor and gave himself some time to rest and sort out equipment and electrical issues. Bell then continued along Australia’s northern coast before striking out into the Indian Ocean.

The second ocean of his journey brought a whole different set of problems. In July and August, he seemed to switch back and forth between calm conditions and storms with large swells, heavy rain, and awful visibility. At the start of August, gale-force winds reached 30 knots, and a massive wave slammed into his boat. Water swamped the cabin through the air vents, soaking his sleeping cabin and triggering the emergency beacon. Bell contacted Coast Guard officials to alert them to a potential rescue. Luckily, the weather soon abated, and no intervention was required.

Bell spent several days, and once almost a week, riding out conditions on his para-anchor. “There is no prize for pushing your luck,” he later wrote on social media. “Sometimes the smartest thing you can do is stop, wait, and let the ocean have its moment.” When the weather finally eased, he discovered that the autopilot controls had stopped working. Still, he was able to continue.

All of this meant the planned finish location had to change. Bell had originally intended to end his row in Mauritius, but persistent southeasterly currents and weather made that impossible. Continuing to Kenya and mainland Africa added roughly 1,800km and three weeks to the expedition. As he was making such good time, he still had enough food and supplies for the additional few weeks the detour added to his journey. Even with the additional distance, he made it back to dry land well before his 350-day aim, and with 20 days’ worth of food left.

Bell managed to stay upbeat throughout the row, despite being completely isolated for almost a full year. He used podcasts, audiobooks, and voice notes to avoid constantly watching the clock, and relished any encounter with wildlife. At different points, he had birds hitch a ride with him and whitetip sharks following his boat for weeks, swimming on either side as he rowed.

The final approach was almost as strange for him as the beginning of the row. In the final few days of the row, he described his head as “all over the place.” After months of thinking purely about moving the boat forward and looking hours ahead, the prospect of getting back onto dry land was overwhelming. He described the prospect of stepping ashore, thinking about the practicalities of walking, sleeping in an actual bed, and dealing with people again as “bewildering.” Bell predicted “total sensory overload.” He said the last week on the ocean had been the calmest of his life.

When he finally arrived in Kilifi, he was joined by two small support boats, and a helicopter flew above him. On the beach, his family, friends, support team, and the local press greeted him.

“I’ve not stepped off that boat since the ninth of November. This is the first time I’ve touched land,” he told reporters in Kenya as he made his way onto land, slightly hunched over, but surprisingly stable for someone who hadn’t walked in months.

He has since updated followers that after a few days back “in the land of luxury of dry, clean clothes and a bed that doesn’t move,” he is doing well, can stand up straight, and walk without assistance.

#266. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

An Interview With Tenzing Norgay’s Son and Director of the New Biopic: Tenzing Norgay’s role in the first ascent of Everest has often been overshadowed by the fame and recognition given to Edmund Hillary. The new film Tenzing aims to readdress that and tell the story from Norgay’s perspective.

Drawing on decades of research, the film follows Norgay from his childhood in the Himalaya through to the 1953 summit. Director Jennifer Peedom and Norgay’s son, Norbu Tenzing, explain how the film grew out of their years-long friendship, why they feel Norgay’s story had been overlooked for so long, and the biopic’s emphasis on Norgay as a person rather than simply as the man who climbed Everest with Edmund Hillary.

A Lightning Strike Highlights Common Mountain Shelter Myth: A recent lightning strike on Utah’s Mount Timpanogos killed a 19-year-old hiker and injured nine others after the group sought refuge from a severe thunderstorm by crowding into the Tin Shack, a small metal lookout built in 1927.

When lightning struck the building, everyone inside was shocked, highlighting the dangerous misconceptions surrounding lightning safety. Unless shelters have proper electrical wiring or plumbing to safely ground the current, they can leave people vulnerable. Meteorologists and lightning researchers also pick apart myths such as getting into the “lightning position” — crouching low with your feet together.

Kayakers paddle the rescued sheep to safety. Photo: Sea Kayak Shetland/Facebook

The Sheep Rescuer of the Shetland Islands: Jason Fenn, a sea-kayak guide on the Shetland Islands, has developed an unusual side mission: rescuing sheep that become stranded on the steep coastal cliffs. Since taking over Sea Kayak Shetland last year, Fenn has rescued nine sheep, with one recent operation requiring a 60m rappel.

His latest rescue occurred during a kayaking trip with a group of American paddlers, who spotted a sheep stranded on a cliff and decided the planned tour could wait while they worked together to save the animal.

America’s First 5.15d: In 2025, Sean Bailey climbed America’s hardest sport route, its first and only 5.15d (9c). Duality of Man sits in Arizona’s Dry Canyon, and remained unclimbed in its entirety until Bailey spent three seasons working on it.

It combines the existing 5.14c Lee Majors with two brutally difficult boulder problems on a steep, smooth limestone headwall. An online grade calculator suggests the sequence could warrant a 5.16a rating, but that remains speculative until other climbers attempt and assess the route.

Bonbon Anglais Established in Madagascar: British climbers Matt Johnston, Bert Lam, Alvin Li, and Mike Turner have established Bonbon Anglais, a new seven-pitch route on the Chameleon Wall in Madagascar’s Tsaranoro massif.

The route was climbed ground-up and features difficulties up to 6b+/A0, or 7b+ if climbed entirely free. The team focused on making the route accessible to visitors and local climbers looking to develop their skills, so they fully bolted the route using 316L stainless-steel bolts, with larger 12mm bolts and stainless rings at the belays.

Donna Carpenter Narrates 50 Years of Snowboarding History: Donna Carpenter looks back on five decades of snowboarding in Sideways Revolution, Burton’s new documentary celebrating the company’s 50th anniversary.

Carpenter built Burton with her husband, Jake Burton Carpenter, and reflects on how dramatically the sport has changed since Jake began making boards in Vermont. For her, 1985 was a pivotal year: It was when Burton started making boards with the “DNA” of the modern snowboard. By 1986, their boards were being manufactured in a proper factory, and Jake took a team of riders he had assembled to make their first film, Winter Waves.

Almost a Quarter of My Graduating Class is Dead: Three guides discuss how different the fantasy of being a mountain guide can be from the reality. It is not just endless powder and jaw-dropping remote locations. Becoming a guide takes years of training, living out of vans, financial sacrifices, and, most importantly, understanding the responsibility of managing clients and knowing when to say no.

The risks are real: All have friends who have died or seriously injured themselves in the mountains. Guide Erin Smart talks about having lost her partner, also a mountain guide, in an accident earlier this year. The risks might seem relatively small to a person who is only skiing or climbing occasionally, but the odds shift drastically when you spend decades in that environment.

No Sound Was There But My Scream: Britain’s mountains are packed with stories of giants, ghosts, fairies, and mythical creatures. Their remote landscapes are the perfect backdrop for tales of magic and ancient folklore.

Hanna Lindon explores legends from around the country, from the giant behind the Old Man of Storr and Giant’s Causeway to the ghost stories of the Lake District’s corpse roads and remote bothies, including Ben Alder Cottage.

She also looks at the famous Grey Man of Ben Macdui, whose enormous footsteps have been reported by several climbers, as well as more unusual mysteries, such as alleged big-cat sightings in Cumbria. From kelpies and selkies to the Loch Ness Monster and the Wulver, centuries of storytelling continue to give Britain’s wild places an eerie sense of mystery.

Hiking in the mist on Ben Macdui. Photo: Jerry Kobalenko

#267. Almost Three Times More Crevasse Falls in the Austrian Alps This Summer

In a sign of the times, a relentless summer heatwave above 3,000m has caused crevasse falls in the Austrian Alps to nearly triple against the 10-year average.

Between May and September 2026, according to the alpine accident database of the Austrian Board for Alpine Safety, the country recorded 19 crevasse incidents compared to the long-term mean of seven. Weeks of above-freezing temperatures stripped away the protective snowpack, leaving behind fragile snow bridges, bare ice, and forced closures on several established glacier routes. Tragically, one of these falls proved fatal on the Wildspitze in Tyrol.

In a striking contrast, deaths during the summer actually fell to 62, down from 78 in 2025 and a long-term mean of about 80, even as the overall number of accidents rose, according to Bergsteigen. Half of the accidents and 33 of the 62 deaths occurred in Tyrol.

The number of people either rescued unhurt or non-fatally injured increased. Uninjured people in distress were about 70% more numerous than in 2017, and injuries were up by almost half. The seasonal death toll has stayed near 80 for years; 62 is low, close to the record 61 from 2014.

From May 1 to September 13, 2,742 people hiked, climbed, went on high-mountain tours, or used a via ferrata, compared with a 10-year average of 2,351. Hiking still accounts for most of the trouble, representing 65 percent of those rescued unhurt, 47 percent of the injured, and half of the deaths. Falls or slips caused 30 of those fatalities, while cardiovascular emergencies caused 18.

#268. Weekend Warm-Up: Cycling 54,000Km Around the World

In this film, Morgan Monchaud and friends Brian Mathe and Siphay Vera embark on a three-year cycling journey across the globe. Bertrand Dolci, the only team member with significant cycling experience, occasionally joins them. With no budget for accommodation, they sleep on couches, in barns, and by roadsides, across deserts, jungles, mountains, and cities.

Cycling across the salt flats of Patagonia. Photo: Screenshot

We find our cyclists in Patagonia, already eight months out of France. Proceeding northwards at a frenetic pace, they enter the Amazon. With so much ground to cover, the film doesn’t linger on any one location or incident. A dreamlike procession through shifting landscapes is interrupted by personal or practical asides, such as bike repairs and local TV appearances.

In the Amazon, they struggle to push their bikes along muddy roads in stifling heat, following a hand-drawn map. After 40 days in the so-called Green Inferno, a very Biblical number of days to struggle in such an environment, they emerge.

While the trio rents a boat to Panama, the film flashes back to their earlier detour. Following in the footprints of Monchaud’s father, who sailed to Antarctica with friends in 1980, they sail into the Drake Passage. Their storm-tossed boat survives the challenge, gliding swan-like among the white masses of the Antarctic coast.

Monchaud’s father tags along for this leg. Photo: Screenshot

Back in Colombia, they join the crew of a retired Frenchman headed to Panama. Monchaud feels these brief encounters are the beauty of travel, and why they conducted the trip on a shoestring budget.

Montage-ing up through Central America and Mexico, they cross the border into Arizona. They head to Phoenix instead of my hometown of Tucson, which is a huge mistake in my opinion, though it does allow them to pick up Etienne Houles, their missing fourth Musketeer. Tales of their adventures have finally inspired him to quit his job and, wisely, leave Phoenix.

Then it’s up the West Coast and into Canada. Recalling the stories of Jack London, they hit on a new side-quest: build a raft and paddle down the Yukon River.

A bad fall sends Houles back to France, saddened but undaunted. The remaining three build their raft. Photo: Screenshot

Joined by Dolci, their DIY, GPS-less raft floats down the river, looking for all the world like a Canadian remake of Aguirre, the Wrath of God. Nevertheless, they survive the journey to Alaska.

Oceans being generally unbikeable, they hop a flight to the Oceania stage and reunite with a recovered Houles.

“Seeking adventure is only a pretext to meet people,” Monchaud explains, as they help clear fallen trees for their hosts, an elderly New Zealand couple. Monchaud is always happy to talk to a friendly local, but is rarely moved by their safety advice. When an Australian cop advises them not to bike into the outback, where the next water station is 250km away, they do so anyway.

Their final leg takes them through Southeast Asia from Bangkok to Laos, where Vera’s family is from. They navigate blindly through the tropical forest, then up into the mountains to a family reunion.

Despite visa issues in China, they make it to Kazakhstan. After a final side-quest to learn foraging skills with a shepherd family, the trio re-enters Europe via Istanbul. Their return to France marks three years and 54,000km.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#269. Japanese Open New Route in the Karakoram

A month ago, a Japanese team went quietly into the Karakoram and opened a difficult new route.

Takaaki Nagato, Ryo Masumoto, and Hiroki Yamamoto climbed the south face of 6,677m Koz Sar in the Batura Muztagh range. They climbed for 14 days in capsule style to complete their new 1,400m line. The team needed six portaledge camps before summiting on August 29. It took them two further days to descend.

Team member Yamamoto was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after the first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hidesuke Taneishi. Taneishi is currently on his way to attempt the first ascent of Gangapurna West, also in Nepal.

#270. A Plan B First Ascent: Nepal Landslides Force Veteran Italians to Change Peaks

It’s become their custom: Nives Meroi and Romano Benet are back in Nepal to attempt a new route or a first ascent of a scarcely visited 6,000m peak. The recent landslides affecting the Manang region have forced them to change their destination, but not their ambitions.

Their original goal was a new route on the south face of 7,134m Tilicho, north of Annapurna. However, landslides caused by heavy rain last weekend have severely affected that region. The Italian couple, who always walk to their base camp, were unable to reach Tatopani, the starting point of the trek. Usually, the town is accessible by road, but now even footpaths are not possible.

“We were told there were 46 landslides along the route, and conditions of the path to base camp [beyond Tatopani] are unknown,” Meroi told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu.

Benet posted today that they have found an alternative goal, something they can reach on foot rather than by helicopter. Hiking in is part of the expedition for them, and they have no wish to change that.

“We’ve decided to explore the Jugal Himal area, recently opened to climbers,” Benet wrote. “Information is scarce, but we’ve decided to attempt unclimbed Jugal II (6,518m).”

The main peaks of the Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

Meroi and Benet, who have both summited all the 8000’ers without supplemental oxygen, have also pioneered several new routes and first ascents. Meroi earned a Piolet d’Or for her climb of Kabru South in the Kangchenjunga region. For Jugal II, Tine Cuder of Slovenia has joined them as a third.

The Jugal Himal is quite close to Kathmandu, just northeast of town on the border with Tibet. It’s reachable by bus with a few days’ trekking, as Paul Ramsden explained when he opened a new route on Jugal Spire with Tim Miller. This climb also earned them a Piolet d’Or.

These peaks have been so rarely visited because until 2023, they were closed to climbing. That spring, Nepal opened Jugal I (6,591m) and Jugal II (6,518m), together with five other peaks in the area.

In spring 2024, veteran Um Hong-gil of South Korea launched a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi, to unclimbed Jugal I and Jugal II. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II, which remains unclimbed, according to The Himalayan Database.

Climbers, circled, on the final ridge of Jugal I. Photo: Korean-Nepalese Friendship Expedition 2024

Several Nepal trails remain closed due to landslides. Because of contradictory information on social media, trekkers should verify with local outfitters or tourism boards. While the Manaslu Circuit is open, landslides have severely affected the Manang region in general and the Annapurna Circuit in particular. Meanwhile, an avalanche cut the Thorong La, the highest point of the Annapurna trail. Check yesterday’s images, below.

Nepal’s National Trust for Nature Conservation said today that trekking permits for Annapurna are available again, but area trekkers reported that several major landslides have seriously damaged even the Annapurna South Side Base Camp trek. There are power outages and no cell connection.

“As of now [October 1], above Manang, everything is closed,” trekker Krishna Acharya has just posted on Facebook’s Annapurna Circuit Trek group.

The change of plans of even this hardcore Italian team suggests that the area is not yet suitable for trekking.

#271. Unicycling Around the World

Shakhriyer Azizov of Tajikistan left Istanbul in November 2024, heading east and aiming to cycle around the world. Nearly two years later, he is crossing China. For most long-distance cyclists, this would be extremely slow going, but Azizov has a major disadvantage — he’s riding a 27.5-inch unicycle.

Bigger wheels mean faster speeds and longer distances, but Azizov prefers the small size. With the smaller 27.5-inch wheel, he can easily find replacement tires, rims, and spokes. “But I pay for it by covering less distance per wheel revolution. Given the same number of hours, a wheel with a larger radius will travel a third more distance,” he told a Tajik news outlet. On just the one small wheel, he can cover up to 60km per day, at an average speed of around 13km an hour.

From Istanbul, Türkiye, Azizov traveled through Georgia, Armenia, Iran, Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and then into China. Though he carries camping gear, he has found little need for it through most of Central Asia.

“How many times do you think I slept in a tent in 579 days? 12 times! Often people invite me into their homes, especially in Kazakhstan, but in general, in any country, I’ve been welcomed like a brother,” he told a Kazakh news site, Khabar.

His exact onward route is unclear, but he will eventually head south through Southeast Asia. He says he will cycle through Australia, the United States, and Europe before completing the journey in Istanbul. He has covered over 6,000km so far.

Born in Tajikistan but raised in Russia, Azizov does not have an expedition background. Before the trip, he worked as a trader.

As a child, Azizov remembers being fascinated by unicyclists at carnivals, but he wasn’t an experienced rider before this trip. In fact, almost unbelievably, Khabar claims he learned to ride in just three days before leaving Istanbul.

The choice of a unicycle is partly to increase the difficulty of his trip, and partly for attention: Azizov is documenting his journey on both YouTube and Instagram. “As a connoisseur of quality video games, I’ve never enjoyed playing on easy difficulty levels. To fully enjoy a game as it was intended, it’s important to me to play on the hardest difficulty,” he told Your.TJ. “[And] you must admit, far fewer people would have known about my round-the-world trip if I had traveled on a regular bicycle.”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#272. Kayaking Solo Around Great Britain

Only a dozen kayakers had successfully paddled alone around Great Britain when Ian Hayward launched from Lowestoft, northeast of London, on April 26. Paddling clockwise, he closed the circle on September 13, after 141 days.

A former outdoor educator, the 58-year-old Hayward had retired the year before. No newbie to water sports, he had decades of paddling experience, including slalom, surf, marathon, sprint, and open canoeing. He’d been sea kayaking since his teens. At the same time, this was his first multi-week expedition.

After a tiring day on the water. Photo: goosejuice_adventures/Instagram

Performance Sea Kayak, which maintains a record of such circumnavigations, sets the distance around Britain as 3,185km. A week after launching, Hayward passed his first major obstacle, the Thames Estuary, notable for its heavy marine traffic. Other critical sections included the English Channel (heavy traffic and headlands), the Welsh tidal areas, Scotland’s west coast, Cape Wrath, Pentland Firth, and the exposed North Sea.

Sometimes, calm, serene moments metamorphosed almost instantly into “brutally harsh” or “terrifying” conditions. Just days from the end of the expedition, Hayward was still describing the experience in terms of judgment, resilience, and decision-making rather than simply endurance.

Happy times: Following wind, following tide. Photo: goosejuice_adventures/Instagram

Sea kayaks can carry a month or so of food, but not four months, so Hayward frequently replenished his supplies en route. Although he camped occasionally, he was happy to accept offers of hospitality, especially from local sailing clubs.

The 1980 expedition by Paul Caffyn and Nigel Dennis is considered the first successful kayak circumnavigation of the British coastline. It took them 85 days, including 68 paddling days, two rest days, and 15 weatherbound days.

One of Hayward’s nights in a tent. Photo: goosejuice_adventures/Instagram

The first solo was by Chris Duff of the U.S. in 1986. The formidable Duff also circumnavigated Iceland, Ireland, and the South Island of New Zealand, which he covered in his well-written book, Southern Exposure.

John Willacy is the only person known to have soloed Great Britain twice: clockwise in 2012 (72 days) and counterclockwise in 2015 (83 days).

In the summer of 2025, Sebastian Szubski set a Fastest Known Time for the circumnavigation, finishing in under 37 days. Earlier, the former Brazilian Olympic canoeist set a 24-hour distance record, paddling an astonishing 251km.

Including Hayward, 23 other expeditions (totaling 36 paddlers) have completed the route. Hayward was the 13th soloist. At age 58, he says he might be the oldest to do so, though that has not been confirmed.

#273. There Were Survivors of the Himlung Avalanche

All previous reports suggested that the avalanche on Himlung last Sunday killed everyone in base camp. Fourteen kitchen staff and two guides did, in fact, perish beneath four meters of snow. However, Everest Chronicle now notes that 11 people whose tents were pitched away from the slide path survived. Witnesses explained that the avalanche didn’t sweep away tents or men, but buried them deeply in their tents.

Yesterday, the Nepal National Mountain Guides Association sent a new team to retrieve the remaining bodies. The recovery workers have had to dig tunnels to find them.

The first searchers, led by Mingma G, found four bodies. By then, it was obvious that they would find no survivors among the 16 missing. Mingma G called off the search, alleging the bodies were buried too deeply to be shoveled out. He opted to wait until the snow had melted enough to access the remains.

But the recovery effort resumed at the request of some relatives of the deceased staff and of Himalayan Holidays Trek & Expeditions, the outfitter for whom most of the victims worked.

Two of the previous rescuers, Pasang Kaji Sherpa and Bikram Karki, are leading the current team, which includes about 10 additional support personnel. This larger workforce has been able to dig tunnels under the snow and retrieve three more bodies yesterday and eight more today. With the four bodies that the first searchers uncovered, that’s 15 in all. As night fell on Nepal, only one person remains missing.

Himlung was expected to receive several climbing teams this season. After the tragedy, the list of permits issued by Nepal’s Department of Tourism shows one team still going to Himlung, with six foreign members.

#274. Freerider Dies in Patagonian Avalanche

French freerider Juliette Willmann of Chamonix has died in an avalanche in Patagonia.

The 29-year-old was ski touring on Cerro Creston, about 35km from El Chalten, with her husband, the mountain guide Pierre-Idris Mehdi. A snow slab broke loose under them around 12:30 pm on September 29, carrying both of them 400m down the mountain.

According to Alpine Mag, Willmann was found buried about 1.5m deep, with no vital signs. CPR failed to revive her. Her husband was injured but survived and was evacuated.

An established freerider, Willmann won the Freeride World Qualifier in 2018, then competed on the Freeride World Tour from 2019 to 2022. Her best season was 2021, with two second-place finishes and fourth overall, before she left the circuit for high-mountain skiing.

An investigation into the exact circumstances of her death is underway.

#275. Denis Urubko to Attempt Winter Broad Peak -- and a New Route on Everest

Denis Urubko has a busy few months ahead. He will attempt a new route on winter Broad Peak, then in the fall, he will go for an unclimbed line on Everest. Not bad for a guy who insisted in 2020 that he was done with the 8,000’ers.

Urubko revealed his plans during a mountaineering lecture in Ekaterinburg, Russia, on September 14, Russian Climb‘s Elena Laletina told ExplorersWeb.

Denis Urubko in Ekaterinburg. Photo: Marina Gevorkyan/Snob.ru

Urubko has summited Broad Peak twice in summer and attempted it in winter six years ago. He started that winter expedition with Don Bowie of Canada and continued on his own when Bowie retired. A close call with an avalanche forced him down.

Broad Peak has been climbed in winter once before, by Polish pioneers Krzysztof Wielicki, Maciej Berbeka, Adam Bielecki, Tomasz Kowalski, and Artur Malek in 2013. They reached the summit very late in the day, and Berbeka and Tomasz Kowalski perished during the descent.

Denis Urubko on winter Broad Peak, 2020. Photo: Denis Urubko

Interestingly, the Polish climbers summited on March 5, well within the calendar definition of winter — but Urubko has always followed a stricter definition, based on the Gregorian Calendar used in Russia. For him, winter begins on December 1 and ends on February 28. He will climb Broad Peak according to this interpretation of winter, in January and February.

Urubko will not be alone on Everest next fall. At least one commercial team (Furtenbach Adventures) will launch a guided expedition up the normal route.

He is also not the only Russian with a new line on Everest in mind. A four-member team led by Andrey Vasiliev is currently on its way to the mountain for an “off-the-normal-route” climb. Their original plan was to attempt a new, no-oxygen line on Everest in the spring of 2027. It remains to be seen what they will do this fall, on what was to have been just a shakedown trip to test themselves and their gear.

Everest’s Khumbu Icefall in the fall, during one of Andrzej Bargiel’s ski attempts. Photo: Pawlikowski Media

After a failed attempt to solo winter Broad Peak in February 2020, Denis Urubko claimed he was done with the 8,000’ers and would focus on sport climbing instead. Just months afterward, however, he returned to the Greater Ranges to try to break Juan Oiarzabal’s record number of 8,000m climbs without oxygen. He blamed the media for misunderstanding what he said about retiring.

Urubko and Cardell on the summit of Nanga Parbat. Photo: Denis Urubko/FEDME

Urubko opened a new winter route on Koshar Gang in February 2022, then returned to Pakistan in summer to make a first ascent of a 5,000m peak. He then did Broad Peak (normal route in less than 15 hours), and Gasherbrum II and K2 solo.

In 2023, he attempted a new route on Gasherbrum I with partner Maria Cardell. They climbed the normal route in preparation, but in the end, they failed to bag the new line. Urubko then returned to Gasherbrum I in winter with only a porter to help him cross the crevassed glacier. It was a near-disaster: Urubko fell into a crevasse and had to rescue himself and retreat on his own, frostbitten, down the valley to the hospital in Skardu.

After a long recovery, he returned to the high mountains last year, forging a new route on Nanga Parbat with Cardell, despite dangerous conditions. Several climbers died from falling rocks during that dry, hot year.

#276. Epic Kayak Journey: 4,000Km From Kamchatka to Chukotka

In the most ambitious sea kayak expedition in that area since Jon Turk paddled from Japan to Alaska in 1999-2000, Ivan Klochkov has covered 3,840km along the northeastern coast of Russia from Kamchatka to Chukotka.

Turk’s expedition actually inspired Klochkov’s quest. After a year and a half of preparation, the Russian kayak guide left Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, the capital of Kamchatka, on May 24. After 124 days on the water, he pulled into the tiny village of Uelen, Chukotka, on September 1. Uelen lies just past Cape Dezhnev, the easternmost point of Asia, which overlooks the Alaskan side of the Bering Strait.

A small sail nudged Klochkov along when the winds were right. Photos: Ivan Klochkov

Klochkov handled the rough and foggy conditions along the North Pacific coastline mostly alone. His father joined him for the first 627km in Kamchatka; the other 3,000+km he paddled on his own.

His isolated route often featured long cliff sections with nowhere to land. On one particularly wild stretch, between Ust-Kamchatka and Chukotka, he hurried 600km in 17 days.

Not every one of Klochkov’s camps was austere. Photo: Nataliya Grigoryeva

Although Meta is banned as an “extreme organization” in contemporary Russia, Klochkov has managed to have an Instagram account. Images and videos from the expedition show dark water, rocky coasts, and a lot of brown bears. Often, they investigated his camp. To rest easier, he rigged up an electric fence around his tent. Later in Chukotka, he also had to deal with polar bears.

Just two of the many too-curious bears Klochkov had to deal with. Photos: Ivan Klochkov

#277. Manaslu Definitely Over, But Everest, Dhaulagiri, and Makalu Remain in Play

The few climbers who had hoped to climb Manaslu after the storm have finally called it quits. Their Base Camp tents are buried in snow, and the mountain is in terrible shape. But while Manaslu is definitely over, Dhaulagiri climbers are still patiently waiting, encouraged by the upcoming arrival of Andrzej Bargiel’s team.

The 8K Expeditions crew is keeping fit by shoveling snow off their tents at the base of Dhaulagiri. Paul Clarke told ExplorersWeb that massive avalanches recently fell down the slopes. The one in the video above was well off the normal route. “We’re going to wait four to five days before venturing up to Camp 1 and checking the route above,” he said.

That route is not visible from Base Camp, so to get an early preview, Clarke flew a drone 1,000 vertical meters above them. “There’s still a huge amount of snow on the North Face, but you can see strong winds ripping across the summit, so hopefully between the wind and the avalanches, the mountain [will] continue to clear,” he wrote on social media.

The upper half of Dhaulagiri looked like this yesterday. Drone image by Paul Clarke/@outdoorpirate

Andrzej Bargiel, aiming to ski down Dhaulagiri, landed with his team in Kathmandu yesterday but has not shared his schedule.

The Russian team that confirmed a no-O2 attempt on Everest off the normal route is on its way to Namche Bazaar. Another three-member team also plans an alpine-style attempt on Makalu — likely Russians Denis Aleksander and Artem Tsensenivski, also from Russia. Earlier, they had hoped to acclimatize on Manaslu, but now they will need to find an alternative.

Remarkably, over the last few days, the number of Manaslu permits has continued to swell, reaching an all-time record of 500. As we previously wrote, it is unclear whether these guided climbers will recover any of their money because of the early cancellation.

A completely buried dome tent at Manaslu Base Camp. Photo: Summit Force

Summit Force clung to hope until yesterday. “If weather and mountain conditions allow, our team will make another attempt during the next suitable summit window,” Miles Sherpa had posted last weekend. On Monday, he confirmed his dome tents were still standing. Some of the gear had been damaged, but “their team [which stayed in Base Camp during the storm] is safe,” he wrote.

Instagram post by Miles Sherpa of Summit Force on Monday, September 28.

However, the company’s head, Nga Tenji Sherpa, said yesterday that they had finally called off their expedition. “At this stage, continuing…is no longer safe or practical,” he wrote. Like other outfitters, he cited safety reasons.

“All our team, climbers, guides, and staff are now safely back home,” Caroline Pemberton of Climbing the Seven Summits told ExplorersWeb. “The conditions that ensued with the storm made it unsafe to continue. Safety is always our first priority.”

Chhepal Sherpa, leading a small team and supported by Alex Txikon of Spain, has also left the mountain.

Madison Mountaineering called their Manaslu expedition off last Saturday. They are focusing instead on Ama Dablam in late October.

Trekkers are back on the trails. They are moving more slowly on the snowed-up paths but are enjoying a pristine white environment under bright sun:

The Manaslu Circuit, including the highest point at Larke Pass, is also open again, according to tourism associations. So are the trails in the Khumbu. The way to Everest Base Camp is doable, and a number of climbers are landing in Lukla this week and trekking to Namche Bazaar before tackling one of the region’s 6,000m peaks.

The Thorong La, the highest pass in the Annapurna Circuit, is still closed, according to The Tourism Times, as is the Tilicho Lake Trek in Manang.

#278. There Will Be An Everest Expedition This Fall, Off The Normal Route

While commercial climbers lay aside their summit hopes on the hyper-popular Manaslu, two small teams, both from Russia, are setting off toward a lonely Everest (8,848m) and Jannu (7,710m).

After some meetings in Kathmandu last weekend, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shipilov, and Natalya Belyankina obtained the funds they needed to climb Everest in the next few weeks.

“What a crazy start to the expedition,” Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb.

The four climbers want to test their gear and scout a new line on Everest that they will attempt in earnest next spring. Their original idea was to climb the usual South Col route, but Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb that they are applying for a permit to climb off the normal route.

For modestly financed crews like this one, there might be a monetary reason for this. A fall permit on Everest’s normal route costs $7,500 per climber but only $5,000 if they try a different way. “We will decide which route we climb once we get there,” said Vasiliev.

Climbing Everest as a solitary team, with the mountain overloaded with snow after the recent storm, is quite different from what commercial climbers experience during a typical spring. The four of them will be completely alone as they find their way across the Khumbu Glacier. If they head toward the Western Cwm before diverging to their new line, they will have to find their own way through the Khumbu Icefall.

The team does not intend to use supplemental oxygen. Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb that the whole idea is to test themselves on a “higher 8,000’er.” They did a new route on Manaslu last year and made two previous attempts on the South Face of Cho Oyu. Both peaks only slightly surpass the 8,000m mark.

At the same time, a second Russian team led by Sergey Romanenkov will attempt a new route on the formidable  Jannu (7,710m) in the Kangchenjunga region.

Anna Piunova of the Mountain Club reported that the team intends to link first ascents of Langchung Khang (6,786m) and neighboring Langpo Peak (6,965m). They will then attempt a new route up the southeast side of Jannu, attaining the ridge via a system of icefalls. They will then join Lionel Terray’s 1962 first ascent line. After summiting, they will descend the same way.

The team includes Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin. Together, they climbed Gasherbrum II in 2024. They have not shared more specific climbing plans, but Artemov says they will fly to Nepal next week and spend 40 days in the mountains.

Some of the best fall expeditions of the last few years have taken place on Jannu. Americans Alan Rousseau, Matt Cornell, and Jackson Marvell made an alpine-style ascent of the north face in 2023, while last year, France’s Benjamin Vedrines and Nico Jean reached the peak’s East summit (7,468m), also via the north face and in alpine style. Both climbs were awarded a Piolet d’Or.

#279. A Kazakh Man Is Cycling From Astana to Australia

Alikhan Ormakhanov of Kazakhstan is 100 days and 5,000km into a round-the-world bike journey that the young man hopes will transform him into a seasoned world traveler.

Ormakhanov left Astana, his country’s capital, on June 5 and has been pedaling ever since — through Kazakhstan, China, and Vietnam. Details are scarce, but we know that his first major destination is Australia. However, that is not the end of his ride. He told TV7, a Kazakh television station, that he plans to continue cycling through Europe and the Americas before eventually making it back to Astana.

Although he had no experience in long-distance cycling when he began, he prepared meticulously for a year before leaving, collecting touring gear and training. Of the three countries he has traversed as of late September, Ormakhanov says Kazakhstan was the easiest, because of the hospitality he experienced. Truckers and motorists often stopped to give him water and food — sometimes so much, he couldn’t fit it all on the bike.

Dealing with the heat and humidity of China was a different experience, but he made it through to Vietnam in good time and is ready to continue south. Every night, he sets up his tent by the roadside and camps.

Ormakhanov hasn’t said how he intends to cross the water sections to Australia. The distance from Astana to Australia is 10,000 to 12,000km, depending on the route.

#280. Why Were Local Crews Left in Base Camp During a Major Storm?

Mingma G, leader of the rescue team on Himlung, has given up any hope of finding survivors among the 12 base camp workers still missing. He suspended search efforts for the bodies until the snow melts. But a key question remains: Why keep crews at peril in base camp during storms while clients are told to leave?

“We recovered four bodies, making it clear that no one survived,” Mingma G wrote yesterday. He added that the 12 missing kitchen staff are buried under more than four meters of snow. With only shovels, the rescue team cannot dig that deep. “We will…retrieve the bodies as soon as the snow melts a bit more,” he said.

Several outfitters were planning expeditions on Himlung. Will they now cancel their climbs, or will they set up new tents and base camp kitchens while the corpses of the deceased lie below them? In a new update published yesterday, Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism says that no permits have been granted for Himlung yet. However, there are also no permits yet for Ama Dablam, Nepal’s most popular peak in October and November. On these peaks, permits are often issued at the last minute, so their absence does not in itself reveal anything.

The tragedy raises questions about safety protocols for local base camp teams. Several institutions in Nepal warned climbers, trekkers, and residents of the country’s mountain areas to stay in safe areas. There were no foreign climbers on Himlung at the time of the incident.

Obviously, the local operators never considered that a relatively safe base camp like Himlung’s would be buried completely. “The avalanche was enormous — no one had believed that Himlung Base Camp could experience something on that scale,” Mingma G wrote yesterday.

However, the weather front that hit Nepal last weekend had been forecast days in advance. Alerts were issued in plenty of time. Local outfitters always insist that “safety comes first” as the reason for canceling expeditions and bringing foreign climbers down to safer ground. However, this does not seem to apply to their base camp staff. Whatever safety protocol was in place, it was clearly inadequate after 14 people died in a supposedly safe camp.

Local staff also remained in camp on Manaslu during the storm, even after outfitters canceled their expeditions for the rest of the season. Foreign climbers were airlifted or guided down the valley, while high-altitude Sherpas reportedly dismantled the upper camps and brought down the materiel. However, dismantling Manaslu’s huge Base Camp, which can accommodate 1,000 people, is not easy. Most tents remained, together with an undetermined number of local workers.

Alexander Abramov, leader of the Seven Summits Club team, filmed a significant number of these workers as they finally retreated to Samagaon village over the weekend, while the gale raged. As seen in the video, they were poorly equipped, had no crampons, and tried to help each other as they dragged themselves down on frozen ground toward Samagaon.

Abramov also posted some photos of his base camp tents, totally buried under snow:

Meters of snow on Manaslu. Photo: Alex Abramov/7 Summits Club

#282. Revisiting Manaslu’s Two Worst Avalanches: 1972 and 2012

This year has been brutal in the high ranges. In July, an avalanche on Broad Peak killed 10. Weeks later, glacial floodwaters on the Nepal–Tibet border left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing. And just yesterday, an avalanche in Himlung’s Base Camp likely killed all 16 staff members.

Even before that, the fall season ended prematurely on Manaslu. Heavy snow, an avalanche in Camp 3 that killed two, and a big storm emptied Base Camp, despite a record number of permits.

Manaslu (8,163m) has always had a fierce reputation. Two of its worst days came exactly 40 years apart, in 1972 and 2012. In those years, avalanches hit the same weak point: mid-mountain camps under ice and loaded slopes. Today, we revisit those tragedies.

In 1972, only two expeditions were attempting Manaslu, both in the spring. A South Korean team was returning to the Northeast Face after a tragic first attempt the year before. The other expedition was Austrian, aiming at the more technical South Face.

The Koreans were led by Kim Jung-Sup, the eldest of three brothers on the mountain. He was a busy businessman who joined at the last minute for his family’s sake. His younger brother, Kim Ho-Sup, was the climbing leader. A third brother, Kim Yae-Sup, was also on the team. So was a brother-in-law. It was a family affair.

There were 12 members in all, plus 10 high-altitude Sherpas and additional porters. They left Kathmandu in late February 1972.

The mission that brought the family back to the Northeast Face was to recover another brother. Kim Ki-Sup had died the previous spring at about 7,600m. During a windy summit attempt, he fell into a crevasse and died, according to the American Alpine Journal. Kim Ho-Sup had vowed to summit this time and bring the body of his brother home.

Climbers retreat from Manaslu due to dangerous conditions, September 2026. Photo: Sanu Sherpa/Summit Force

The 1972 party carried a sled to lower Kim Ki-Sup’s body down the mountain. They planned to use the same climbing route as the year before. Kim Ho-Sup told Elizabeth Hawley that the east side was technically no trouble, but the previous year they had been “swimming in snow,” with high winds driving powder into their faces.

“Man’s power is nothing against terrible wind,” he said. At least, they already knew where the bad crevasses and icefalls were.

There were fixed ropes up to 7,600m from the earlier attempt. They intended five camps, with the highest pitched 100m or 200m higher than the year before so that the final summit attempt would be easier. They set up Base Camp by March 10, and a first summit party was planned for mid-April.

By early April, they had established Camp 3 at 6,500m. By the night of April 9-10, heavy snow loaded the mountain. Two Sherpas warned Kim Yae-Sup, the youngest of the three brothers, that there was too much snow. They worried about the slopes above.

Kim Yae-Sup woke around midnight to melt water for an early start. At around 3:15 am, he heard a roar. He woke the two men sharing his tent (Park Chang-Hee and Japanese photographer Kazunari Yasuhisa), and they tried to get out. The avalanche struck before they could exit. It carried the three of them 800m down the mountain in three shattering bounces before they stopped. Park told Kim his midsection was crushed and his spine broken. Yasuhisa said his left rib and right shoulder were broken. The ordeal had just begun.

Then a second avalanche swept Kim down another 300m and buried both his companions. Three more slides and gale-force winds followed. Somehow, Kim survived with badly frostbitten feet and fingers. Two Sherpas also survived the destruction of Camp 3.

In September 2026, a falling serac triggered an avalanche on Manaslu. Frame from a video. Photo: Phurba Sonam Sherpa

The rest of Camp 3 was gone. Among the dead was climbing leader Kim Ho-Sup. In all, 15 died: 4 Koreans, the Japanese photographer, 9 high-altitude Sherpas, and one Sherpa cook.

The names of the Sherpas, later provided by Pemba Tshering Sherpa and published in Rising Nepal, included sirdar Pemba Rinji of Jorsale (also known as Lama Ngawang Chultim), second sirdar Rinji Wangel of Phaplu, Solu, climbing Sherpa Ang Tendi of Thami, 28-year-old Ang Mingma, 37-year-old Angmingma, Andrita, Pasang Nima, Angtendi, Ang Dawa, Phurba Tenzing, Gyalze, and a Sherpa cook named Wangel.

Four surviving Koreans who had not been at Camp 3 remained on the mountain to collect what gear they could. The expedition was over. Kim Yae-Sup was flown out by helicopter with his eldest brother and team reporter Yun Byung-Hae.

The Himalayan Database records this as one of the deadliest single events on any 8,000m peak up to that time.

Reinhold Messner on the 1972 Manaslu expedition. Photo: Reinhold Messner/Instagram

While the Koreans were still reeling, the Austrian expedition was establishing itself on the opposite side of the mountain. Wolfgang Nairz led a strong team that included Reinhold Messner, Franz Jaeger, Andi Schlick, and Horst Fankhauser. They carried most of their own loads and had a few Sherpas.

On April 25, Messner and Jaeger left Camp 4 at 7,400m for the summit. Jaeger turned back after a few hours, saying that the long, difficult traverse without oxygen was beyond him that day. Messner continued alone, reached the top around 2 pm, and started down in a rapidly worsening storm. He spent hours searching for the tent in fog and wind, nearly lost, before finding it, but Jaeger was not there.

Fankhauser and Schlick, who had come up from Camp 3, went to look. The storm intensified. They dug a snow cave. Unfortunately, Schlick died of cold and exhaustion during the night. Jaeger was never found. Fankhauser survived the night in the cave. At dawn, he made his way back to the tent. With Messner, he searched the plateau in vain. The fresh snow had buried everything.

Avalanche danger and deep snow prevented others from coming up to help. Messner later described the South Face as combining the character of a classic ridge route with the scale of the great faces he had already climbed on Nanga Parbat and Annapurna I. After the deaths, the expedition abandoned the mountain. Messner suffered frostbitten fingers, and Fankhauser had frostbitten feet. Fortunately, both later recovered.

Manaslu Base Camp in the autumn of 2026. Photo: EliteExped/Instagram

In 2012, the scene on Manaslu had changed completely. A total of 67 teams attempted the mountain, 54 of them in the autumn. That year, 129 people reached the summit, 111 of them in the post-monsoon season. But the autumn also proved tragic.

Camp 3 was established in its usual location at 6,700–6,800m, directly below hanging ice on the North Ridge. After waiting out a storm, the teams moved back up. On the night of September 22–23, climbers from half a dozen expeditions were sleeping in their tents at Camp 3, while many Sherpas had been sent down to make room.

On September 23 at 4:30 am, a serac collapsed at about 7,500m. It triggered a large slab avalanche that swept through the camp. It buried or tore apart the tents, carrying them and their occupants hundreds of meters down the slope. The air blast flattened tents at Camp 2 but caused no deaths there. However, the teams at Camp 3 were not that lucky.

A German team had planned a higher Camp 3 but never reached it. Their tents at the normal Camp 3 site were buried. Leader Robert Hochreiter cut his way out of his tent unharmed, but another member, Christian Mittermeyer, was killed. Martin Neubauer suffered a knee injury from ice debris, and Andreas Reiter fractured a vertebra and was helicoptered to Kathmandu. Another member, Ralf Rieske, had frostbitten fingers and bruised ribs.

A French-led team lost five people. Ludovic Challeat and Thomas Grenier had gone up from Base Camp on September 22 and slept at Camp 3. Others had climbed more slowly. The avalanche killed expedition leader Fabrice Priez, Catherine Ricard, Philippe Bos, Dominique Ouimet, and Challeat. Survivors included Thomas Grenier, Claude Belmas, and Arnaud Manel, who were rescued from Camp 2. Several more climbers were evacuated from Base Camp.

A Spanish team lost Marti Gasull. He and Karma Sherpa were sleeping in a tent that was swept down toward 6,000m. Gasull died, while Karma Sherpa survived uninjured.

An Italian team established Camp 3 at 6,700m on September 22. Alberto Magliano and Dawa Dorje Sherpa shared a tent. Unfortunately, both were buried 1.5m deep and found dead after two hours of probing. Silvio Mondinelli and Christian Gobbi survived. All tents in Camp 2 were destroyed by the blast, but no one was hurt.

A French-American ski team had pitched Camp 3 at 6,800m. Greg Costa and Glen Plake shared one tent, while Remy Lecluse occupied another. Plake was swept 300–400m into a crevasse. He was badly bruised but conscious and finally crawled out. Costa and Lecluse vanished with their tents. Plake descended on oxygen and left the mountain as quickly as possible.

In total, 11 climbers died in the avalanche. Rescue helicopters flew multiple sorties that day. The season continued for some teams after the debris was cleared. The year 2012 produced both a high number of summits and, according to The Himalayan Database, the second-worst death toll in the mountain’s recorded history after 1972.

Looking down toward Camp 3 on Manaslu. Photo: Ben Darce/Instagram

The 1972 Korean camp was at 6,500m on the northeast side. The 2012 Camp 3 was at a similar elevation on what is now the standard route. In 2012, the trigger was ice falling from above onto snow-loaded slopes. In 1972, heavy new snow and repeated avalanches overwhelmed Camp 3, causing the tragedy. Manaslu’s climbing history shows avalanches accounting for nearly half of all deaths on the mountain.

Teams this autumn chose to leave, but the mountain had already made the decision for them.
