#283. Couple Nearly 6,000km Through Walk From Moscow to Vladivostok

Russian couple Tamara Pogosyan, 31, and Pavel Shabalin, 33, are over halfway through a unique honeymoon. They set out on foot from Moscow on January 19 toward Vladivostok, and have already walked more than 6,600km.

The pair had no previous expedition experience. Pogosyan says the idea came to them on January 7 after watching a YouTube video. Within 12 days, they had researched long-distance walking journeys, bought gear, and set off from their home in Moscow.

“We had no special physical training, just casual fitness, nothing more,” Pogosyan told Russian news site RBC Life. “The only thing we did before the start was walk a trial route around Moscow in one day. It was about 20km, and we walked with backpacks already filled with the things we planned to take on the trip. That was probably all our training.”

Pogosyan and Shabalin typically cover between 30 and 40km each day. They carry large backpacks but do not use any form of motorized transport.

The pair have gained a following on Russian social media and are often greeted by welcome parties in rural communities. Recently, in the village of Ablatuysky Bor, the village mayor turned out to welcome them and show them the local sights.

Tamara Pogosyan and Pavel Shabalin with the mayor of Ablatuysky Bor. Photo: Ablatuyskoye Provincial Government

Their route has been quite direct. Sticking to southern Russia, they moved from Moscow into the Volga/Ural regions, then on to Omsk. In June, after around 3,700km, they arrived in Novosibirsk, the capital of Siberia. By late August, they were in Irkutsk, breaking 5,500km. They have recently passed Lake Baikal and crossed into the Republic of Buryatia on September 2. Next up will be the province of Zabaykalsky Krai.

The couple estimates that their journey will cover 10,000km and had aimed to finish in late 2026, though at their current pace, it looks like they’ll reach Vladivostok early in the New Year.

A traditional bread-and-salt greeting in central Siberia. Photo: Pogosyan/Shabalin

#284. Himlung Avalanche: Four Bodies Found, No Survivors

The latest news from Himlung is devastating: The huge snowfall triggered an avalanche that buried Himlung Base Camp completely. So far, four bodies have been excavated, and hope is quickly fading to rescue any of the 16 people who were in Base Camp.

“There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides with different companies,” the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) reported. “The two guides have been found, but sadly, both were deceased.”

The victims were Chhebi Bhote and Pasang Bhote (found yesterday) and Birendra Gurung and Ghan Shyam Rai (found today).

Rescuers look for bodies at Himlung Base Camp today. Photo: NNMGA

The weather finally cleared yesterday, permitting a helicopter to reach the area in the evening. Today, more personnel have reinforced the rescue efforts. Mingma G of Imagine Nepal leads the eight-member team. Once again, as on Broad Peak in late July, he has lost at least two members of his staff. With him are other Sherpa guides with IFMGA accreditation: Pasang Kaji Sherpa, Pimba Tenzing Bhote, Ashish Gurung, Tsering Pemba Sherpa, Bikram Karki, Dandu Sherpa, and Pasang Rinzi Sherpa.

Rescuers dig deeply on Himlung today. Photo: NNMGA

Video footage shows that over two meters of snow cover the flat plateau where Base Camp is located:

The NNMGA notes that the area is not especially avalanche-prone, yet meters of snow buried it. Gorskie Mapie of Poland has created a map of the area showing a gentle slope above Base Camp. All suggests a slide avalanche, in which fresh snow slid over frozen ground.

Location and direction of the avalanche toward Himlung’s BC; with the steepness indicated on a NASA map by Gorskie Mapie.

While hopes to find survivors fade, the question remains: What happened, why, and how can it be avoided in the future?

#285. Fourteen Missing As Avalanche Hits Himlung Base Camp

An avalanche has buried the base camp at the foot of Himlung, a 7,000m peak that several outfitters are guiding this fall. Fourteen local workers are missing. Nepal’s mountains are receiving intense snowfall these days, and everyone was urged to stay in villages to remain safe.

“Two of those unaccounted for are from Imagine Nepal, and eight are from Himalayan Holidays Nepal, the Expedition Outfitters Association of Nepal originally told The Kathmandu Post. A later update increased the number of missing to 14. All are Nepalese. The authorities admit that the bad weather is hampering the rescue efforts. Helicopters are grounded, and volunteers on foot have also been unable to reach the camp.

There are no foreigners yet on Himlung, as the route is not fixed and Nepal’s Department of Tourism has not yet issued any permits. Last week, rope-fixing teams were assigned to prepare the routes on Himlung and Ama Dablam, but with the big storm approaching, it’s unlikely that they had a chance to start. However, local staff could have been setting up and supplying the base camp in advance of visitors.

Details remain sketchy, but an avalanche at base camp height is rare. Himlung (7,126m) lies in the Nar-Phu Valley, near the Tibetan border. The base camp is usually on flat ground, a respectable distance from the mountain flanks.  Last year, it lay on completely dry ground. (Check the feature image of this story and a complete ascent video by 8K Expeditions here).

Himlung Base Camp in a snowy fall. Photo: Climbing the Seven Summits/Mike Hamill

The storm dumped loads of snow on the mountains as expected, forcing climbers and trekkers to retreat. The Manaslu season has been called off, although a handful of climbers and their guides continue to wait in Samagaon or Pokhara for a possible summit chance when the weather settles down. Six climbers also remain at Base Camp on Dhaulagiri, shoveling snow but safe.

Still shocked by last month’s lethal floods, Nepal authorities have made an extra effort to disseminate warnings, information, and alerts about the storm, which originated in the Bay of Bengal last week. The Annapurna Conservation Area closed to visitors for the weekend, and other popular spots have issued warnings urging trekkers and climbers to stay well away from higher passes, avalanche-prone areas, and even rivers and low-lying mountain slopes that may be prone to floods or landslides from the rain at lower altitudes. Yet surprisingly, a significant number of staff evidently remained at Himlung’s base camp.

The new popularity of Himlung centers around a tourism law currently under debate in Nepal’s parliament. It would make climbing a 7,000m peak in Nepal a prerequisite for foreigners before attempting Everest.

Imagine Nepal markets Himlung as “an ideal peak for climbers who already have experience climbing at elevations of 6,000m and are looking to push their altitude experience to the next level.” The outfitter explained that this season, their team planned an expedition to Manaslu and later, Himlung.

The current accident recalls a death that occurred on Himlung during a major storm last year. Chin Tark Chan, 49, of Australia, fell ill shortly before reaching the summit of Himlung just as the weather worsened. The bad weather hampered rescue attempts, and issues with the insurance company, which alleged the climber was stranded at 6,800m, above the altitude limit of helicopters. Eventually, the climber was carried down to Camp 3, where he died.

The storm has created problems in several mountain areas. Trekkers and climbers in Samagaon, the village leading to Manaslu Base Camp, were jolted by strong tremors and a powerful roar at 3 am on Sunday.

“We rushed out of our rooms, looking for a safe place. We did not know where to go,” Nepalese IFMGA  guide Abiral Rai posted on social media. The cause was not an earthquake, but a landslide above a nearby village. There are no victims reported so far, but both locals and visitors ran outside for safety:

Rai, together with a client, is one of the few who still refuse to call off their Manaslu expedition. They have been waiting at Samagaon for the storm front to pass.

#286. A Bold New Route on Peru's Most Difficult Peak

On September 11, a three-person international team established a new route on 6,108m Chacraraju West in Peru’s Cordillera Blanca in the Peruvian Andes. Raymond Eckland, Jon Zerain, and Josue Sanchez graded their 850m new line on the south face as WI4+ M5 90°, ED VI. They named it Shumaq Warmi.

The new route on Chacraraju West. Photo: Josue Sanchez/Instagram

The climb took them six days. During the first two days, the weather kept them in their tents. On the third day, they climbed in near-winter conditions, with heavy snowfall at times. They broke trail in fresh snow, crossed precarious ice bridges, and large crevasses. Eight hours later, they set up their first bivy at the foot of the wall, beside a cave that gave them just enough space for the tent.

Opening the new route on the south face of Chacraraju West. Photo: Josue Sanchez/Instagram

They left at 4 am the next day. The trio climbed the 80° bergschrund of wet snow and entered a very exposed M5 of delicate moves leading to the couloir. They kept going until they passed — quickly! — through a zone where the rocks were falling like bullets to the crux of the route: a 70m wall of WI4+ ice.

Night fell, and it took two hours to find a “decent” place to sleep. They ate and slept as well as they could, sitting with wet boots inside soggy sleeping bags, with thermal blankets on top. It was one of the worst nights of their lives, according to the climbers.

Looking down. Photo: Josue Sanchez/Instagram

The climbers left for the summit, again at 4 am. They passed the last M5 crux and came out onto the summit shoulder at 10:15 am. An hour and a half later, Eckland, Zerain, and Sanchez topped out on the main summit of Chacraraju West. The climbing was sustained, with pitches of 60–70° and very exposed mixed sections. Two pitches of pure ice were especially remarkable, reaching 90°.

For the descent, they made 13 rappels from the summit and short sections of downclimbing, then left the glacier and descended a zone of poor rock to Laguna 69, where a friend was waiting. They ended the long day at midnight.

Below the summit, at dawn, Eckland saw a white patch of snow with a woman’s face, which inspired the route’s name. Shumaq Warmi means ‘beautiful woman’ in Quechua. Photo: Josue Sanchez

Chacraraju has two distinct summits: 6,108m Chacraraju West, and 6,001m Chacraraju East.

In the 1950s, Chacraraju was widely considered the most difficult unclimbed mountain in the Peruvian Andes. Rival international expeditions scouted its terrifyingly steep, fluted ice walls and giant, unstable summit cornices and declared it impossible to climb with the technology of the time.

American climber John C. Oberlin perfectly described the fearsome reputation of the mountain. In a 1955 scouting report published in The Alpine Journal, Oberlin wrote that conquering Chacraraju’s summit “will apparently require siege or suicide, or perhaps both, if its summit is ever to be reached.”

Those rival teams all chose to retreat rather than face what they saw as a suicidal endeavor.

Difficult and dangerous terrain. Photo: Josue Sanchez

The higher west peak was ultimately first climbed on July 31, 1956, by a French expedition led by the legendary Lionel Terray. The summit party consisted of Maurice Davaille, Claude Gaudin, Raymond Jenny, Robert Sennelier, Pierre Souriac, and Terray by the northeast face and northeast ridge. They needed 11 days of grueling, continuous siege tactics just to overcome the final 800 vertical meters.

According to Terray, the ascent of Chacraraju was one of the most arduous and difficult climbs of his entire life. He considered it the hardest and most dangerous peak in the Peruvian Andes.

Chacraraju East was later climbed on August 5, 1962, by Terray, Rene Dubost, Paul Gendre, Guido Magnone, and Jacques Soubis via the northeast ridge and east face. At the time, it marked the very last unclimbed 6,000m summit in the Cordillera Blanca.

Even today, the easiest routes on the mountain are graded ED or ED+ (ED stands for Extremely Difficult). Chacraraju is still widely regarded as the steepest and most difficult 6,000’er in the Andes, and many parties never risk the final cornices to step onto the true summits.
